That tactical choice does not convert the order into a constitutional one and should not be recorded in this project as a concession that the government was correct.

Likewise, this Field Guide does not depend on provoking an arrest or forcing a test case before it will make a supported legal classification.

docs.title: The project's job
docs.text:
The Field Guide is not merely a directory of government rules.

It is also an evidence-driven audit of whether government restrictions and enforcement practices stay within constitutional limits.

That means the project should actively:

  • identify protected activity;
  • locate claimed restrictions;
  • trace their legal source;
  • find the asserted justification;
  • obtain the evidentiary record behind them;
  • compare how they are enforced;
  • identify constitutional defects where supported;
  • distinguish facial from as-applied problems;
  • preserve contrary authority;
  • use CPRA or FOIA to obtain the government's own records; and
  • update the Registry when stronger evidence changes the conclusion.

See Restriction Audit, What Can I Actually Do in Each Forum?, Indoor Public Common Spaces, and the Facility Registry methodology.

docs.title: California 1A Auditor's Field Guide
docs.text:
Research baseline: September 30, 2026

This directory is the California handbook. The goal is to build a rigorous statewide legal spine first, then add facility-specific chapters and case studies.

California is Active as of September 30, 2026. CA-GATE-01 through CA-GATE-10 are met. The qualification record contains 69 Supported / 4 Researched-Unresolved / 0 Gap / 0 Not Applicable rows. Facility-research maturity is now Researching after post-activation reconciliation of the Contra Costa pilot set; the complete 58-county coverage inventory remains the statewide index. Formal qualification remains traceable through the California Jurisdiction Qualification Matrix and the CA-GATE-10 activation record.

docs.title: Federal-first reading order
docs.text:
This handbook is a California overlay on the nationwide federal baseline, not a substitute for it. For any field question, use this order:

  1. Start with Constitution First and the relevant National core doctrine.
  2. Identify the controlling federal constitutional rule and the facts that make that rule applicable.
  3. Add California constitutional provisions, statutes, regulations, and cases only where they validly supplement the federal baseline, provide additional protection, impose a lawful state-specific restriction, or otherwise change the practical analysis.
  4. Add county, city, agency, facility, or property-specific rules only after the superior federal and state layers are identified.

A state rule that appears more restrictive does not automatically control merely because it is state law. The handbook must distinguish a valid state-law overlay from a restriction that would conflict with controlling federal constitutional law, federal preemption, or another superior rule. Likewise, a California rule that provides greater protection should be identified as an additional state protection rather than mistaken for the source of the underlying federal right.

The working sequence is therefore: federal constitutional baseline → nationwide doctrine → California overlay → local/facility application.

docs.title: Standing scenario
docs.text:
The canonical factual baseline is now NC-STANDING-01 v1.

California's standing-scenario.md is the jurisdiction overlay/crosswalk. It maps the neutral facts to California Penal Code, Brown Act, Ninth Circuit, identification, trespass/removal, assembly, and recording doctrine.

Unless a scenario says otherwise, the person begins lawfully present at the specific vantage/area, peacefully gathers information, and has no silent fighting, threats, unreasonable noise, obstruction, intimidation, restricted-area entry, unlawful-assembly participation, assumed credential, or other invented misconduct.

Another person's objection or anger does not silently change those facts. Later orders, closures, detention, warnings, restrictions, or changed conduct create new branches that California law then analyzes.

The handbook does not depend on professional status or credentials. Identification demands remain a separate legal question rather than an assumed duty built into the baseline.

docs.title: Federal premises in California
docs.text:
Federal premises are maintained separately under docs/federal/.

For a federal facility located in California, the project does not assume that the California Penal Code, CPRA, or other California facility rules automatically govern merely because the building is physically in California. Federal-premises research begins with federal constitutional law, the applicable federal statute/regulation, agency/facility rules, and federal cases. California law is checked only when a specific jurisdictional or incorporation doctrine makes it relevant.

This separation prevents the California state/local handbook from being accidentally treated as the governing conduct or records code for USPS property, federal courthouses, GSA-controlled buildings, or other federal premises.

docs.title: Field-rule philosophy
docs.text:
A field rule should be short enough to remember but narrow enough to be defensible.

Bad field rule:

If the public can walk into the lobby, it is a public forum.

Better field rule:

Public access and public-forum status are different questions. Classify the specific area and activity. A public-facing government interior can be a nonpublic or limited forum, while an adjacent ordinary public sidewalk can have a different classification. See public-forum-doctrine.md.

Bad field rule:

There is a "No Recording" sign, so recording here is illegal.

Better field rule:

A sign is evidence that a restriction is being asserted; it is not proof of the restriction's legal validity or criminal enforceability. Identify the written policy, who adopted it, the authority supporting it, the specific area/activity it governs, and any independent removal or criminal statute. See facility-investigation-methodology.md.

Bad field rule:

The agency owns the building, so any employee can make rules for visitors.

Better field rule:

Identify who adopted the rule, the Constitution/statute/charter/enabling law that gives the entity power, the instrument used to adopt it, any delegation to the employee or security actor enforcing it, superior-law preemption, and the separate removal or criminal-enforcement bridge. See restriction-audit.md and Sweep 013.

Bad field rule:

Public property means they cannot trespass you.

Better field rule:

Identify the actual trespass provision. For a public agency open to the public, Penal Code § 602.1(b) requires intentional interference by obstruction or intimidation plus refusal after the qualifying request; § 602(o) instead concerns property not open to the general public; § 602(q) concerns a public building when it is regularly closed. Other law or a lawful facility restriction may independently matter.

Bad field rule:

They trespassed me once, so returning to any public part of the building is automatically criminal.

Better field rule:

Separate the administrative exclusion from the later criminal offense. Check the order's issuing authority, scope, duration, current access facts, and the Penal Code provision actually asserted on reentry. California's § 602(o) effect of an individualized prior ban on otherwise generally open property remains Researched-Unresolved. See trespass-removal.md and Sweep 014.

Bad field rule:

If police detain me in California, I always have to show physical ID.

Better field rule:

A request, verbal identity, carrying a document, producing a document, a search for ID, false identification, citation, and booking are different questions. Sweep 014 did not locate a general pedestrian carry-ID statute; Landeros bars refusal from manufacturing suspicion where none otherwise exists, while Vanegas leaves the broader otherwise-lawful-detention affirmative-ID issue unresolved.

Bad field rule:

Someone complained that I was loud, so that proves disturbing the peace.

Better field rule:

Identify the actual § 415 subsection and conduct. For communicative noise, In re Brown narrows § 415(2) to imminent-violence danger or use of purported communication as a guise to disrupt lawful endeavors; separate valid facility volume rules may still apply.

Bad field rule:

Swearing at or criticizing a police officer is automatically disorderly conduct or obstruction.

Better field rule:

Profanity, criticism, and verbal challenge to police receive substantial First Amendment protection. Fighting words, genuine threats, challenges to fight, or conduct that actually delays/obstructs a lawful police duty are separate changed-fact branches. See disorderly-conduct.md and Sweep 016.

Bad field rule:

Staff said I was harassing customers, so § 602.1 is established.

Better field rule:

Translate "harassing" into conduct. Public-agency § 602.1(b) requires intentional interference by obstruction or intimidation plus the qualifying leave request/refusal; refusal does not create a missing interference predicate.

Bad field rule:

Police declared an unlawful assembly, so everyone nearby became a participant.

Better field rule:

Separate § 408 participation from § 409 remaining. California's lawful-purpose unlawful-assembly branch is constitutionally narrowed to actual violence or imminent danger; participation requires knowing participation, while a lawful § 409 warning can reach nonparticipants who willfully remain once its predicates exist.

Bad field rule:

If there is police tape, crossing or remaining behind it is automatically § 409.5.

Better field rule:

Identify the actual closure authority and statutory predicates. A § 409.5 calamity/command-post closure has specific source, scope, notice, and criminal elements; specialized closure statutes can use different wording.

Bad field rule:

Only credentialed press have a First Amendment right to record a protest or police activity.

Better field rule:

Special California statutes can give qualifying news representatives additional access/protection, but ordinary constitutional recording and newsgathering analysis is separate. § 409.7's undefined media-qualification terms should not be converted into a universal credential requirement or automatic self-publisher exemption.

Bad field rule:

Riley means police can never take my phone.

Better field rule:

Separate physical seizure from digital search. Police may sometimes lawfully secure or seize a phone, but the initial seizure needs its own authority, continued retention must remain reasonable, and Riley generally requires a warrant or another recognized exception before searching digital contents. See police-encounters.md and Sweep 015.

Bad field rule:

If I offer to show police my video, they can browse the rest of my phone.

Better field rule:

Consent has a scope. Offering one identified recording does not automatically equal consent to inspect unrelated messages, photos, accounts, or files. State the limit clearly and preserve whether the device was later taken by order rather than consent.

Bad field rule:

Police reports and 911 records are exempt, so there is nothing I can get.

Better field rule:

Separate the underlying investigatory record from mandatory public information. If § 7923.600 applies, §§ 7923.610 and 7923.615 can still require specified arrest, complaint/request, response, and incident information; later statutes can also require particular recordings or officer records.

Bad field rule:

All bodycam footage becomes public after 45 days.

Better field rule:

Government Code § 7923.625's specialized timeline applies to recordings depicting a defined critical incident—officer firearm discharge at a person or force causing death/GBI. Other BWC footage follows other CPRA rules, and retention under Penal Code § 832.18 is a separate question.

Bad field rule:

Officer personnel records are confidential, period.

Better field rule:

Start with current Penal Code § 832.7. It preserves confidentiality generally but expressly makes enumerated incident and sustained-misconduct categories public, with its own redaction and delay rules. Older confidentiality cases cannot be applied as though those amendments never occurred.

Bad field rule:

The employee used a personal phone, so the recording is private.

Better field rule:

Under City of San Jose, a work-related writing does not lose potential public-record status merely because it is created or stored on a personal account/device. Analyze content, context, purpose, scope of employment, disclosure exemptions, and the agency's search duty separately.

Bad field rule:

I requested the video, so deleting it automatically violates the CPRA.

Better field rule:

City of Gilroy holds that the CPRA itself is not a general retention statute. Give a preservation notice, promptly request the record and applicable retention schedule, and distinguish lawful routine disposition from other retention law, litigation-preservation duties, or deliberate destruction.

Bad field rule:

Recording police is always legal.

Better field rule:

Penal Code § 148(g) expressly says recording a public/peace officer in public, or from a place the recorder has a right to be, does not by itself establish § 148 obstruction, reasonable suspicion, or probable cause.

Bad field rule:

If I am detained, police have to read me Miranda rights.

Better field rule:

A Terry detention is a Fourth Amendment seizure but is not automatically Miranda custody. Analyze the justification for the detention separately from whether custodial interrogation rules have attached.

Bad field rule:

Hiibel says I have to identify whenever police detain me.

Better field rule:

Hiibel upheld Nevada's specific stop-and-identify statute during a valid Terry stop. In California, identify the particular statute, context, and applicable case law before treating an ID request as compulsory, and never provide a false identity.

The guide should teach the actual elements, not magic phrases.

docs.title: Remaining specialized research families
docs.text:
The ordinary California qualification branches are covered by the matrix and Sweeps 011–018. The following work remains specialized, changed-fact, facility-specific, or remedies-oriented rather than an activation-blocking ordinary-branch Gap:

  • facility-specific government-building forum classifications and local rule sources;
  • Vehicle Code § 2806.5 edge questions beyond the ordinary pedestrian-stop notice branch;
  • force/arrest-conversion, collective-knowledge, mistake-of-law/fact, and full traffic-stop doctrine beyond the ordinary encounter tree;
  • the expressly Researched-Unresolved otherwise-lawful-detention affirmative-ID boundary;
  • the expressly Researched-Unresolved alphanumeric-passcode / foregone-conclusion edge;
  • specialized digital-warrant, cloud-provider, forensic-extraction, compelled-deletion, and CalECPA questions;
  • school/campus, K-12, courthouse, federal-premises, and other facility-specific access rules;
  • specialized CPRA exemption/retention families and local retention schedules;
  • independent California constitutional doctrines beyond the propositions necessary for the ordinary canonical branches;
  • §1983, Bane Act, qualified immunity, municipal liability, damages, suppression, discovery, and other remedies beyond the field-use escalation/preservation branch.

Earlier sweep notes that described caller reliability, fighting words/true threats, plain feel, ordinary recording-device seizure, public-agency interference, emergency scenes, or ordinary law-enforcement records as "pending" have been superseded by Sweeps 014–018 and the final qualification review.

docs.title: Completeness rule
docs.text: Qualification means the overlay can responsibly run the canonical ordinary scenarios; it does not mean the handbook contains every California statute, every facility rule, or every remedies doctrine. Remaining specialized entries must stay visibly labeled rather than being mistaken for either completed ordinary doctrine or activation-blocking Gaps.

docs.text:

docs.title: How to read this map
docs.text:
These are provisional qualification statuses based on the research already in the repository. They answer whether the present corpus is sufficient for the matrix row—not whether the law is favorable to an auditor.

  • Supported means the existing corpus contains enough authority/research to run the ordinary branch responsibly, subject to recorded local facts and limitations.
  • Researched-Unresolved means the project has meaningfully researched the issue but preserves a genuine unresolved boundary rather than inventing a categorical answer.
  • Gap means the present research record is not sufficient for an activation-grade branch.
  • Not Applicable would require a documented legal reason; none is assigned in this population pass.

A Gap count is not a project-completeness percentage. Multiple rows can point to the same missing doctrinal slice. The activation backlog therefore uses deduplicated work packages below.

docs.title: Re-evaluation rule
docs.text:
When a Gap package is researched, update the affected rows individually. Preserve Researched-Unresolved when a systematic search demonstrates that the controlling answer is genuinely unsettled; do not convert uncertainty to Supported merely to reduce the Gap count.

If new research exposes a missing national recurring scenario rather than a California-specific hole, update the national scaffold first and then re-run the affected California rows.

These numbers do not activate California and are not a completeness score. See QUALIFICATION-EVIDENCE-MAP.md for branch rationales and California Final Adversarial Qualification Review for the final substantive gate review.

docs.title: Activation transition: county inventory
docs.text:
California county research is downstream of state qualification, not a prerequisite to it.

At activation, the workflow created and validated the complete California county inventory as CountyCoverageUnit records. Every county began Unresearched; later promotion requires reconciliation against the qualified California framework and the applicable human review.

docs.title: Assemblies, Dispersal Orders, and Emergency Scenes
docs.text:
Research status: Core California Penal Code text and the ordinary controlling case layer are reviewed for unlawful assembly, dispersal warnings, observer-versus-participant distinctions, emergency closures, and protest/emergency recording. Sweep 017 preserves specialized/local closure law and the undefined § 409.7 media-qualification edge separately. Last verified: September 29, 2026.

This chapter covers California statutes that are commonly relevant when peaceful First Amendment activity occurs near protests, demonstrations, public meetings, emergency scenes, police lines, or disaster closures. It does not assume that a peaceful observer becomes part of an unlawful assembly merely by being present nearby.

docs.title: Short field rule
docs.text: Peaceful presence near a protest or emergency does not by itself answer whether a dispersal order or closure is lawful. Identify the exact authority being invoked, whether its statutory predicates exist, whether notice was actually given, whether the person is inside the area covered by the order, and whether a statutory exception applies.

docs.title: Penal Code § 403 — disturbing or breaking up a lawful meeting
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=403.

Section 403 makes it a misdemeanor, without authority of law, to willfully disturb or break up a lawful assembly or meeting, subject to the section's stated exceptions.

Field rule: Mere attendance, observation, recording, disagreement, or criticism is not the statutory text. The section requires willful disturbance or breaking up of the meeting.

Limit: What conduct legally amounts to disturbs or breaks up requires case-law analysis. Do not reduce the statute to a subjective complaint that someone was uncomfortable.

docs.title: Penal Code § 407 — unlawful assembly
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=407.

Section 407 defines an unlawful assembly as two or more persons assembled either:

  • to do an unlawful act; or
  • to do a lawful act in a violent, boisterous, or tumultuous manner.

Field rule: A gathering is not an unlawful assembly merely because it is a protest, contentious, unpopular, or being recorded. The statutory definition must be satisfied, together with controlling constitutional case law.

docs.title: Penal Code § 408 — participation in a rout or unlawful assembly
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=408.

Section 408 makes participation in a rout or unlawful assembly a misdemeanor.

Field rule: The statute targets participation in the prohibited assembly; it should not be treated as establishing that every observer, journalist, passerby, or person recording nearby is necessarily a participant. Case law is required to define the participation element and constitutional limits.

docs.title: Penal Code § 409 — remaining after lawful warning to disperse
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.

Section 409 applies to a person who remains at the place of a riot, rout, or unlawful assembly after it has been lawfully warned to disperse, subject to the statute's exceptions for public officers and persons assisting them.

Field rule: Failure to disperse under § 409 is not simply refusal to obey any request to leave. The statutory text ties the offense to a riot, rout, or unlawful assembly and a lawful warning to disperse.

Doctrine status: Sweep 017 now supplies the ordinary warning/audibility, opportunity-to-comply, participant/observer, and First Amendment limitation layer through In re Brown, Wagner, Dubner, Collins, Nelson, and related authority. Geographic/local closure details and specialized facility rules remain changed-fact dependencies.

docs.title: Penal Code § 409.5 — calamity and emergency command-post closures
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.5.

Section 409.5 authorizes specified public officers and employees to close an area when a calamity creates a menace to public health or safety and separately permits specified officers to close the immediate area surrounding an emergency field command post or other command post activated to abate a listed calamity, riot, or civil disturbance.

Subdivision (c) states that an unauthorized person who willfully and knowingly enters an area closed under subdivision (a) or (b) and willfully remains after receiving notice to evacuate or leave commits a misdemeanor.

Subdivision (d) provides a statutory access rule for duly authorized representatives of a news service, newspaper, or radio or television station or network, subject to the section's terms.

Field rule: Before treating ordinary police tape as a § 409.5 criminal closure, identify whether the statutory closure authority and factual predicates actually apply. Conversely, a qualifying calamity or command-post closure is a materially different situation from an ordinary public sidewalk or government lobby.

docs.title: Important § 409.5 / § 409.6 text difference
docs.text:
The misdemeanor language of § 409.5(c) is not worded the same way as the avalanche statute in § 409.6(c).

  • § 409.5(c) is written in terms of an unauthorized person who willfully and knowingly enters the closed area and then willfully remains after notice to leave.
  • § 409.6(c) separately reaches both an unauthorized person who enters and remains and an unauthorized person who willfully remains in the closed area after receiving notice to leave.

Why it matters: The Field Guide should preserve the elements the Legislature actually wrote rather than paraphrasing both statutes as though they were identical.

Limit: This textual distinction does not itself establish that a person who was already inside a § 409.5 closure may always remain. Other statutes, lawful orders, emergency authority, or constitutional doctrine may independently affect the situation. The case-law layer remains necessary.

docs.title: § 409.5 press limitation
docs.text:
Section 409.5(d) uses specific statutory language concerning duly authorized representatives of a news service, newspaper, or radio or television station or network.

The project should not rewrite that special statutory access rule into a universal citizen exemption. It also should not treat the statute's category as a universal definition of who possesses First Amendment newsgathering rights. Whether an independent journalist or self-publisher qualifies under this particular provision is a separate question requiring statutory and case-law analysis.

docs.title: Penal Code § 409.6 — avalanche-area closures
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.6.

Section 409.6 is a specialized avalanche-area closure statute. Its subdivision (c) expressly reaches an unauthorized person who willfully and knowingly enters and remains after notice or an unauthorized person who willfully remains within a closed area after receiving notice to leave.

Classification: Specialized. It is retained because it demonstrates that California's emergency-closure statutes are not textually interchangeable and may matter in a location/event-specific audit.

docs.title: Penal Code § 409.7 — special news-representative protections at demonstrations and related closures
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.7.

Section 409.7 applies when peace officers close specified command-post areas or establish police lines or rolling closures at demonstrations, marches, protests, or rallies involving activity protected by the First Amendment or Article I of the California Constitution.

For a duly authorized representative of a news service, online news service, newspaper, or radio or television station or network, the section provides specified access and protection from intentional assault, interference, or obstruction while gathering information, and specified protection from citation for failure to disperse, curfew, or Penal Code § 148(a)(1) when gathering, receiving, or processing information. The statute also provides a mechanism to contact a supervisory officer after detention, subject to circumstances, and states that other applicable laws may still be enforced against unlawful activity.

docs.title: Do not equate § 409.7 with the entire First Amendment right to gather news
docs.text:
Section 409.7 supplies a special California statutory protection package in the circumstances it describes. It is not the source of every constitutional right to observe or record public officials.

The statute does not, in its text, define duly authorized representative or online news service. Therefore the Field Guide should not categorically declare that an independent journalist, self-publisher, auditor, blogger, or citizen journalist either qualifies or does not qualify without supporting authority.

Similarly, a person who does not qualify for § 409.7's special statutory protections may still possess independent First Amendment protections for lawful recording, observation, speech, or newsgathering. Those constitutional questions require their own doctrine and cannot be answered solely by § 409.7.

Field rule: Treat § 409.7 as an additional statutory protection for people who fall within its terms—not as a licensing system for constitutional journalism and not as a declaration that everyone carrying a camera receives the same special access.

docs.title: Penal Code § 415 — disturbing the peace
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=415.

Section 415 covers three distinct categories:

  1. unlawfully fighting in public or challenging another person in public to fight;
  2. maliciously and willfully disturbing another person by loud and unreasonable noise; and
  3. using offensive words in public that are inherently likely to provoke an immediate violent reaction.

A fuller treatment belongs in disorderly-conduct.md.

Field rule for this chapter: Do not use disturbing the peace as a generic label for peaceful recording, criticism, or mere public discomfort. Analyze the actual statutory category being asserted.

docs.title: Penal Code § 415.5 — school and campus variant
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=415.5.

Section 415.5 contains a school/community-college/university variant of fighting, loud-and-unreasonable-noise, and provocative-offensive-words offenses and includes its own scope and exceptions.

Classification: Specialized. Handle the details in the future school/campus chapter rather than applying § 415.5 as a general public-property rule.

docs.title: Penal Code § 416 — assembly for disturbing the peace or committing an unlawful act
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=416.

Section 416(a) applies when two or more persons assemble for the purpose of disturbing the public peace or committing an unlawful act and do not disperse after being directed or commanded to do so by a public officer.

Field rule: Purpose is written into the statute. Peaceful people gathered for lawful observation, recording, criticism, or petitioning should not be analytically collapsed into § 416 merely because an officer says disperse; the actual statutory predicates and constitutional limits still matter.

docs.title: In re Brown / Collins — not every protest is an unlawful assembly
docs.text:
In re Brown, 9 Cal.3d 612 (1973) constitutionally narrows §§ 407–408 when a group assembled for a lawful purpose. The assembly must actually be violent or pose a clear and present danger of imminent violence; boisterous or tumultuous is not an independent catch-all basis.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/9/612.html

Collins v. Jordan, 110 F.3d 1363 (9th Cir. 1997) holds that limited violence at earlier demonstrations does not justify a blanket ban on later peaceful demonstrations. The present assembly must be analyzed on its present facts.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/110/1363/527029/

Current CALCRIM 2685–2686 preserve the violence/imminence and warning structure:

https://www.justia.com/criminal/docs/calcrim/2600/2685/

https://www.justia.com/criminal/docs/calcrim/2600/2686/

docs.title: § 408 participation versus § 409 remaining
docs.text:
In re Wagner, 119 Cal.App.3d 90 (1981) requires knowing participation for § 408. A person who joined a lawful assembly can acquire a duty to disassociate after learning that it has become unlawful.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/119/90.html

Section 409 is different. Once an actual riot, rout, or constitutionally valid unlawful assembly exists and a lawful dispersal warning is given, § 409 can reach a person who willfully remains at the place even if that person was not a participant in the underlying violence.

Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001) supplies the critical ordinary-observer limit. On facts lacking the violence/imminence needed for a valid unlawful-assembly predicate, police could not simply collapse a photographer/legal observer into participants; the court said police must at least differentiate participants from innocent bystanders absent those compelling circumstances.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/266/959/582256/

Field rule: observer status is not absolute immunity, but presence near unlawful actors is not itself proof of § 408 participation or a substitute for § 409's predicates.

docs.title: Warning, audibility, and opportunity to comply
docs.text:
Penal Code § 726 supplies the traditional dispersal-command authority. Current CALCRIM 2686 states that no magic wording is required, but the words must tell a reasonable person that an official order to leave is being given and must be communicated in a reasonable manner that ensures the order is heard.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=726.

Published People v. Cipriani, 18 Cal.App.3d 299 (1971) and Wagner recognize amplified/public-address warnings rather than requiring an officer literally to stand inside a dangerous crowd.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/18/299.html

The reviewed authorities do not create a universal fixed countdown after a warning.

docs.title: Nelson — egress and force during dispersal
docs.text:
In Nelson v. City of Davis, 685 F.3d 867 (9th Cir. 2012), officers used pepperball force against unarmed people where warnings were not adequately audible, the primary exit was blocked, and members of the group were attempting to comply or waiting for directions. The Ninth Circuit held the force unreasonable on the plaintiff-favorable facts.

Official source: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2012/07/11/10-16256.pdf

Field rule: preserve whether the warning could actually be heard, what area had to be left, whether a usable exit was available, whether the person was trying to comply, the threat posed by that person, and what force followed.

docs.title: Emergency perimeters and statutory media access
§ 409.5 is not a generic police-tape offense
docs.text:
For a calamity closure under § 409.5(a), identify the actual calamity, the menace to public health/safety, the authorized closing official, the area, and whether the menace continues.

For a command-post closure under subdivision (b), identify the activated command post and the immediate area actually closed.

Subdivision (c)'s misdemeanor text is conjunctive: it addresses an unauthorized person who willfully and knowingly enters the closed area and then willfully remains after notice to leave. Section 409.6 uses materially different wording for its specialized avalanche closure.

A barricade, marker, police line, or tape can evidence a closure; it does not itself identify the statute or establish every criminal element.

docs.title: Leiserson v. City of San Diego
docs.text:
Leiserson v. City of San Diego, 184 Cal.App.3d 41 (1986) is the published California authority for § 409.5(d)'s qualifying media-access provision.

The court held that danger inherent in a disaster site does not itself nullify the statutory press-access rule. Police may nevertheless restrict access when they reasonably determine unrestricted access would interfere with emergency operations, and restrictions should extend only as far and as long as necessary to prevent that interference.

The judgment for the City was sustained because substantial evidence also supported treating the crash site as a possible crime scene, a separate basis not governed by § 409.5(d)'s disaster-access guarantee.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/184/41.html

Field rule: qualifying statutory media access is substantial but not unlimited, and it is not a general license to enter an independently valid crime scene.

docs.title: § 409.7 — demonstration/protest media protection
docs.text:
Section 409.7 supplies special protections for a duly authorized representative of a news service, online news service, newspaper, or radio/television station or network in the covered demonstration/police-line/rolling-closure setting.

Within its terms, the statute provides specified access and protection against intentional assault/interference/obstruction while gathering information, and specified protection against citation for failure to disperse, curfew, or § 148(a)(1). It preserves enforcement of other laws for independent unlawful conduct.

The statute does not define duly authorized representative or online news service. Sweep 017 did not locate controlling published California appellate authority creating a universal credential or self-publisher test.

Project status: qualification for the statute's special media package can therefore be a RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED changed-fact edge. The ordinary member-of-public constitutional branch does not depend on claiming § 409.7 status.

docs.title: Constitutional recording/newsgathering is separate from statutory press access
docs.text:
Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995) and Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018) supply the ordinary Ninth Circuit recording framework. Lawful recording of matters of public interest receives First Amendment protection, subject to location, restriction, and independent-law analysis.

Leigh v. Salazar, 677 F.3d 892 (9th Cir. 2012) recognizes a qualified First Amendment access inquiry for the press and public to observe government activities under the experience/logic framework. It remanded for that analysis rather than creating an unrestricted right to every government scene.

Sources:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/55/436/578292/

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/16-55719/16-55719-2018-08-14.html

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/11-16088/11-16088-2012-04-16.html

docs.title: Index Newspapers — important preliminary-injunction posture
docs.text:
Index Newspapers LLC v. U.S. Marshals Service, 977 F.3d 817 (9th Cir. 2020) is a published order denying a stay of preliminary injunctive relief in the Portland protest litigation. It strongly protects newsgathering/retaliation interests on its unusual record, but should not be rewritten as a universal rule that anyone identifying as press or legal observer may ignore every otherwise lawful dispersal order.

Source: https://openjurist.org/977/f3d/817/index-newspapers-llc-v-united-states-marshals-service-4795058

docs.title: Los Angeles Press Club v. Noem — current retaliation authority
docs.text:
In Los Angeles Press Club v. Noem, No. 25-5975 (9th Cir. Apr. 1, 2026), the Ninth Circuit affirmed the likelihood of success on First Amendment retaliation claims based on evidence of force directed at journalists, legal observers, and peaceful protesters—including people standing apart from unlawful actors or attempting to comply.

The panel did not reach the plaintiffs' separate right-of-access merits theory because the retaliation theory was enough, and it vacated/remanded portions of the injunction as overbroad.

Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-9th-circuit/118261014.html

Project rule: this is strong current anti-retaliation authority, not a new universal press-access or dispersal-exemption holding.

docs.title: What this chapter does not establish
docs.text:
These statutes do not, by themselves, establish:

  • that every police line or piece of tape is a criminal exclusion zone;
  • that every gathering ordered to disperse was legally an unlawful assembly;
  • that an observer automatically becomes a participant in unlawful conduct committed by others;
  • that every dispersal order is constitutionally sufficient;
  • that press status under §§ 409.5 or 409.7 is identical to the constitutional freedom of the press;
  • that a person outside a special statutory press category therefore lacks constitutional recording/newsgathering protection;
  • that an independent journalist necessarily qualifies or necessarily fails to qualify under § 409.7;
  • that a person may ignore a legally valid emergency closure or dispersal order.

docs.title: Remaining specialized/local work
docs.text:
The ordinary statewide assembly/dispersal/emergency-observer branch is now doctrine-reviewed. Remaining work is changed-fact or specialized:

  • municipal emergency and curfew ordinances;
  • wildfire/evacuation-specific statutes and local orders;
  • federal or military closures;
  • court-specific press access;
  • credential-program challenges;
  • the undefined § 409.7 duly authorized representative / online news service edge;
  • specialized crowd-control/use-of-force questions beyond the ordinary warning/compliance branch; and
  • law-enforcement-record disclosure after an incident, which remains GAP-08.

For § 415 noise/fighting-words and § 148 obstruction, use Disturbing the Peace and Disorderly Conduct / Sweep 016 rather than duplicating those doctrines here.

Detailed research record: Sweep 017.

docs.title: Constitutional Foundations
docs.text:
Research status: Core constitutional architecture needed by the ordinary qualification branches is reviewed across this chapter and the substantive forum, recording, police, meeting, and records chapters. Broader independent California constitutional/shield/remedies questions remain specialized. Last verified: September 29, 2026.

This chapter is the California constitutional overlay for the Field Guide. It begins from the controlling federal constitutional baseline and then identifies California provisions that may add protection, supply an independent state-law rule, or otherwise affect the analysis. It does not by itself answer every facility-access or recording question. Forum doctrine, statutes, regulations, court rules, and facility-specific law can materially change the analysis.

docs.title: Federal baseline first
docs.text:
Before applying California law, identify the controlling federal rule. For this project, the recurring federal baseline includes the First Amendment's speech, press, petition, assembly, and newsgathering interests; Fourth Amendment limits on detention, seizure, and search; Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment protections where applicable; and federal public-forum and retaliation doctrine.

Use Constitution First for the nationwide framework and the National core chapters for recurring factual branches. California law enters after that baseline is identified.

California may provide additional rights or independent state-law protections, and it may impose state-specific rules in areas where federal law permits them. But a California restriction cannot be treated as controlling merely because it is more restrictive: it still must be compatible with the federal constitutional floor and any applicable federal supremacy or preemption rule.

Field sequence: federal constitutional baseline → nationwide doctrine → California overlay → local/facility application.

docs.title: Short field rule
docs.text: A California audit may implicate several distinct constitutional interests at once: speech/press, petition/assembly, access to government information, privacy, due process, freedom from unreasonable searches/seizures, and protection against compelled self-incrimination. Do not collapse those into a single slogan such as First Amendment means I can record anywhere.

docs.title: California Constitution
docs.text: Primary source for Article I: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&article=I

docs.title: Article I, § 1 — privacy
docs.text:
California expressly identifies privacy as an inalienable right.

Why it matters: Government transparency and recording questions can intersect with privacy interests. Article I, § 3(b) itself expressly preserves the privacy right in § 1, so the access-to-information provision is not a command to disregard privacy law.

Limit: The existence of a privacy interest does not automatically establish that a particular restriction on observation or recording is lawful. The actual statute, regulation, case law, forum, and facts still matter.

docs.title: Article I, § 2(a) — speech and press
docs.text:
California provides that every person may freely speak, write, and publish sentiments on all subjects, subject to responsibility for abuse of the right, and that law may not restrain or abridge liberty of speech or press.

Why it matters: This is an independent state constitutional speech/press foundation in addition to the federal First Amendment.

Research note: The extent to which California's speech clause provides broader protection in a particular government-property setting is a case-law question and should not be assumed from the text alone.

docs.title: Article I, § 2(b) — source and unpublished-material shield text
docs.text:
Section 2(b) contains California's constitutional shield language for specified publishers, editors, reporters, and other persons connected with or employed by newspapers, magazines, periodicals, press associations, wire services, radio stations, or television stations. Within the terms of the provision, it protects against contempt for refusing to disclose certain sources or unpublished newsgathering information.

The text defines unpublished information broadly enough to include material such as notes, outtakes, photographs, tapes, and other data not itself disseminated to the public.

Why it matters: Auditors and independent journalists may preserve unpublished recordings, notes, and source material. This provision therefore belongs in the Field Guide's research universe even though its application is specialized and doctrine-heavy.

Important limit: Do not use § 2(b) as a universal definition of who counts as press, journalist, or news media for every other California or federal law. Different statutes use different language. Penal Code § 409.7, for example, expressly refers to a duly authorized representative of a news service, online news service, newspaper, or radio or television station or network, which is not identical to the language of § 2(b).

The project should not assume that an independent journalist or self-publisher either qualifies or fails to qualify under a separate statute merely by comparing labels. That requires analysis of the particular statutory text and relevant case law.

docs.title: Article I, § 3(a) — petition and assembly
docs.text:
California protects the rights to instruct representatives, petition government for redress, and assemble freely to consult for the common good.

Why it matters: Public comment, demonstrations, petitioning, and other direct engagement with government can implicate this provision as well as the federal First Amendment.

docs.title: Article I, § 3(b) — access to government information
docs.text:
California expressly gives the people a right of access to information concerning the conduct of the people's business and states that meetings of public bodies and writings of public officials and agencies shall be open to public scrutiny.

Section 3(b)(2) directs that authorities furthering access be broadly construed and authorities limiting access be narrowly construed. Section 3(b) also preserves existing privacy and confidentiality protections and expressly references public-records/open-meeting law.

Field rule: This is a powerful transparency provision, but it is not a standalone rule that every government room, record, computer screen, conversation, or physical area must be open to observation or recording.

docs.title: Article I, § 7 — due process and equal protection
docs.text:
California prohibits deprivation of life, liberty, or property without due process and denial of equal protection.

Why it matters: Removal, exclusion, government-imposed restrictions, and selective enforcement can raise due-process or equal-protection questions depending on the facts and governing law.

docs.title: Article I, § 13 — searches and seizures
docs.text:
California protects persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures and imposes warrant requirements.

Why it matters: A detention is a seizure for Fourth Amendment purposes under federal doctrine, and searches/seizures of phones, cameras, bags, recordings, or other property may raise both federal and California constitutional issues.

Important California construction rule: Article I, § 24 states that specified California criminal-procedure rights—including the right to be free from unreasonable searches and seizures—are construed consistently with the U.S. Constitution in criminal cases.

docs.title: Article I, § 15 — self-incrimination and due process in criminal causes
docs.text:
Section 15 provides, among other protections, that a person may not be compelled in a criminal cause to be a witness against themselves and may not be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process.

Why it matters: This is the California constitutional counterpart relevant to compelled self-incrimination. It should be analyzed separately from whether a person must identify themselves or comply with a lawful detention/order under a specific statute or case.

docs.title: Article I, § 24 — relationship to federal constitutional rights
docs.text:
Section 24 first states that rights guaranteed by the California Constitution are not dependent on rights guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution. It then imposes an important criminal-case construction rule for specified rights, including equal protection, due process, search/seizure, privacy, self-incrimination, double jeopardy, and others.

Field rule: Do not assume every California constitutional provision necessarily tracks federal law in every context; also do not ignore § 24's express consistency rule for the criminal-procedure rights it lists.

docs.title: First Amendment
docs.text:
Official text: https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-1/

Protects freedom of speech and press and the rights of peaceable assembly and petition.

Why it matters: This is the principal federal constitutional foundation for recording/observing government activity, speaking, petitioning, public comment, and forum doctrine. The actual scope depends heavily on place, government purpose, forum classification, and applicable restrictions.

Press/newsgathering note: The existence of a special statutory protection for certain news representatives does not mean everyone outside that statutory category lacks First Amendment protection. Constitutional recording/newsgathering analysis and a statute such as Penal Code § 409.7 are separate layers and must not be collapsed into each other.

docs.title: Fourth Amendment
docs.text:
Official Constitution Annotated resource: https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/amendment-4/

Protects against unreasonable searches and seizures and governs warrants.

Why it matters: Police encounters can move from consensual contact to detention or arrest; searches and seizures of devices/property require separate Fourth Amendment analysis.

docs.title: Fifth Amendment
docs.text:
Official text/resource: https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/amendment-5/

Protects against compelled self-incrimination and includes federal due-process protections.

Jurisdiction note: The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause restrains the federal government. State and local government due-process analysis ordinarily runs through the Fourteenth Amendment and applicable state constitutional provisions.

docs.title: Fourteenth Amendment, § 1
docs.text:
Official Constitution Annotated resource: https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-14/

Prohibits states from depriving persons of life, liberty, or property without due process and from denying equal protection.

Why it matters: Most California state/local First Amendment and Fourth Amendment claims operate against state/local actors through federal constitutional doctrine applied to the states, together with any independent California constitutional protections.

docs.title: What these provisions do not establish by themselves
docs.text:
None of these provisions, standing alone, establishes all of the following:

  • that every government-owned property is a public forum;
  • that every area open to the public may be recorded without restriction;
  • that a person may enter staff-only, secured, closed, or otherwise restricted areas;
  • that privacy/confidentiality statutes cease to apply in government buildings;
  • that an order from an official is necessarily lawful or necessarily unlawful;
  • that a detention, search, seizure, exclusion, or arrest is valid merely because an official asserts authority;
  • that a person must be institutionally credentialed media before constitutional newsgathering protections can exist.

Those questions require the next layers of the Field Guide: forum doctrine, facility-specific law, statutory elements, and controlling cases.

docs.title: Doctrine location and remaining specialized questions
docs.text:
This page is the constitutional architecture/crosswalk, not the sole repository of case doctrine.

The ordinary qualification propositions are developed in:

  • public-forum-doctrine.md — federal and California speech/forum architecture;
  • recording-public-officials.md and lawful-vantage-privacy.md — recording/newsgathering/privacy;
  • police-encounters.md — incorporation bridge, detention/search/seizure, self-incrimination, and device issues;
  • public-meetings.md — meeting speech/comment/removal;
  • assembly-emergency-scenes.md — assembly/newsgathering/emergency scenes; and
  • public-records-evidence-preservation.md — California access-to-information implementation.

Remaining specialized questions include the full independent reach of some California constitutional provisions beyond the ordinary canonical facts, Article I § 2(b)'s application to modern/independent newsgatherers, and remedies/suppression doctrines not required for the current operational branch.

Do not infer from those specialized questions that the already-mapped ordinary qualification branches lack constitutional authority.

docs.title: Disturbing the Peace and Disorderly Conduct
docs.text: California does not have one generic offense that means "someone was uncomfortable with your behavior." Two provisions especially worth separating are Penal Code §§ 415 and 647.

docs.title: Penal Code § 415 — disturbing the peace
docs.text:
Section 415 criminalizes three categories of conduct:

  1. unlawfully fighting in public or challenging another person in public to fight;
  2. maliciously and willfully disturbing another person by loud and unreasonable noise; or
  3. using offensive words in public that are inherently likely to provoke an immediate violent reaction.

Primary source: California Penal Code § 415

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Under the project's standing scenario, the assumed auditor is not fighting, challenging anyone to fight, creating § 415(2) unlawful noise, or using words that satisfy § 415(3).

A government employee, contractor, visitor, security guard, or private individual becoming angry, offended, uncomfortable, or confrontational does not by itself supply one of § 415's statutory categories. Another person's reaction can be relevant context, but it does not substitute for the auditor's own conduct or the offense elements.

Therefore, if § 415 is asserted, identify which subsection and which conduct allegedly satisfy it rather than accepting "you are causing a disturbance" as though that were statutory text.

When a patron, employee, or officer uses a conclusion such as "harassment," "disruption," "interference," "hostile," or "disturbance," apply the Standing Scenario's Allegation-to-Elements Check.

Detailed authority: Sweep 016 — Disorder, Unreasonable Noise, Fighting Words, Threats, and Obstruction.

docs.title: In re Brown, 9 Cal.3d 612 (1973)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court rejected a construction that would make all loud public speech criminal merely because it disturbs another person.

For communicative shouting/cheering, the generic § 415 noise offense is narrowed to two circumstances:

  1. a clear and present danger of imminent violence; or
  2. purported communication used as a guise to disrupt lawful endeavors rather than a genuine effort to communicate.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/9/612.html

The current Judicial Council instruction, CALCRIM 2689, uses the same alternatives:

https://www.justia.com/criminal/docs/calcrim/2600/2689/

Field rule: "loud" and "unreasonable" are not satisfied merely by a raised voice plus a complaint. Preserve purpose, context, actual interference, location, time, and whether the volume is communication or disruptive conduct.

This does not invalidate properly drawn content-neutral volume/time/place/manner rules for particular facilities. Those must be analyzed under their own authority.

docs.title: Changed-fact comparator — People v. Superior Court (Commons)
docs.text:
In People v. Superior Court (Commons), 135 Cal.App.3d 812 (1982), probable cause existed on materially different facts involving very loud laughter/shouting in a hotel hallway around 1 a.m., where occupants were disturbed and the volume could be treated as disruptive rather than genuine communication.

Source:

https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-court-of-appeal/1839130.html

The project therefore does not turn Brown into a universal right to shout anywhere.

docs.title: Jefferson v. Superior Court, 51 Cal.App.3d 721 (1975)
docs.text:
Profanity alone does not establish § 415(3). The court requires context, provocative manner, and a clear/present danger that violence will immediately erupt.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/51/721.html

docs.title: In re John V., 167 Cal.App.3d 761 (1985)
docs.text:
Whether words are fighting words depends on the surrounding circumstances rather than a word list.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/167/761.html

docs.title: In re Alejandro G., 37 Cal.App.4th 44 (1995)
docs.text:
Words directed at police are not categorically immune from § 415(3), but officer status matters because trained officers are expected to exercise greater restraint. The court distinguished mere vulgar/annoying criticism from an express challenge to fight and threats of actual violence.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/37/44.html

docs.title: Federal/Ninth Circuit police-criticism layer
docs.text:
• City of Houston v. Hill, 482 U.S. 451 (1987) — substantial verbal criticism/challenge of police is protected.
  • Duran v. City of Douglas, 904 F.2d 1372 (9th Cir. 1990) — obscene gestures/expletives toward an officer did not supply lawful detention/arrest grounds on those facts.
  • United States v. Poocha, 259 F.3d 1077 (9th Cir. 2001) — profanity and aggressive posture did not convert the speech into fighting words on the facts there.

Sources:

https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/482/451/

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/904/1372/388209/

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/259/1077/575656/

Field rule: criticism, profanity, and verbal challenge directed at police are not themselves crimes. Actual fighting words, challenges to fight, threats, or independent obstructive conduct are different branches.

docs.title: Listener hostility / heckler-veto caution
docs.text:
Published Ninth Circuit Center for Bio-Ethical Reform, Inc. v. Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, 533 F.3d 780 (9th Cir. 2008) treats restrictions based on the audience's reaction to the content of speech as content based.

Source:

https://openjurist.org/533/f3d/780/center-for-bio-ethical-reform-inc-v-los-angeles-county-sheriff-department

That does not prevent officials from addressing actual threats, obstruction, unlawful noise, or valid neutral facility rules. It does prevent "people are upset by what you're saying/showing" from silently becoming the missing offense element.

docs.title: Obstruction / interference labels
docs.text: "You're obstructing" requires an identified law and an actual duty/business/function that was obstructed.

docs.title: Penal Code § 148(a)(1)
docs.text:
Protected verbal challenge must be separated from actual resistance/delay/obstruction.

  • People v. Quiroga, 16 Cal.App.4th 961 (1993) — § 148 does not criminalize mere failure to comply "with alacrity"; verbal dispute of police authority is protected.
  • Mackinney v. Nielsen, 69 F.3d 1002 (9th Cir. 1995) — seconds of delayed compliance and verbal protest did not supply § 148 probable cause.
  • In re Muhammed C., 95 Cal.App.4th 1325 (2002) — repeated refusal to move away from a patrol car that caused officers to interrupt/delay their lawful work supported § 148.
  • In re N.S., G065591 (Cal. Ct. App. Sept. 8, 2026) — current published comparator; physically leaving the location, repeated refusals, pursuit, and approximately ten minutes of actual delay distinguished Quiroga. Its underlying search holding is school-specific.

Sources:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/16/961.html

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/69/1002/609814/

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/95/1325.html

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2026/g065591.html

Field rule: the line is not "speech versus physical contact." The line is whether the person actually willfully resisted, delayed, or obstructed an officer's lawful performance. Mere argument, criticism, or momentary slow compliance is not automatically enough.

docs.title: Penal Code § 602.1(b) — public agency
docs.text:
For a public agency open to the public, § 602.1(b) separately requires intentional interference by obstruction or intimidation, a qualifying leave request, and refusal. Section 602.1(d)(2) excludes constitutionally protected activity.

Published Ninth Circuit Dubner rejects inferring the missing interference element merely from refusal. Published California People v. Turner applies the same distinction under related § 602.1(a); its changed facts included repeated employee interruptions over hours. Unpublished Ninth Circuit Mackey v. Meyer is the direct DMV comparator where a dispatch label of "harassing customers" was contradicted by video showing no obstruction/intimidation.

See Trespass and Removal and Sweep 012.

Field rule: "harassing customers" is not an element. Identify the obstructive/intimidating conduct.

docs.title: Threats are not the same as fighting words
docs.text:
A § 415(3) fighting-words theory asks whether speech is inherently likely in context to provoke an immediate violent response.

A true-threat theory asks whether the communication threatens unlawful violence and satisfies the constitutionally required speaker mental state.

docs.title: Counterman v. Colorado, 600 U.S. 66 (2023)
docs.text:
The Supreme Court requires at least subjective recklessness as to the threatening nature of a communication in true-threat prosecutions.

Source:

https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/600/22-138/

docs.title: Penal Code § 422 / In re George T.
docs.text:
California § 422 has its own demanding elements, including specific intent that the statement be taken as a threat, objective/contextual gravity/immediacy requirements, and actual reasonable sustained fear.

Current statute:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=422

In In re George T., 33 Cal.4th 620 (2004), the California Supreme Court independently reviewed a student's ambiguous "dark poetry" and held the circumstances insufficient to establish a § 422 criminal threat.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2004/s111780.html

Because § 422 requires specific intent that the statement be taken as a threat, its statutory mens rea is more demanding than Counterman's recklessness floor on that issue.

Field rule: preserve the exact words and context. A threat to sue, complain, publish, request records, or otherwise invoke lawful consequences is not a threat of unlawful violence merely because an official experiences it as hostile.

docs.title: Penal Code § 647 — disorderly conduct
docs.text:
Section 647 is a list of specifically defined offenses. It is not a free-floating power to arrest a person merely for behaving unusually or making another person uncomfortable.

Primary source: California Penal Code § 647

docs.title: Loitering provisions relevant to common audit claims
docs.text:
Section 647(d) concerns loitering in or around a public toilet for the purpose of engaging in or soliciting a lewd, lascivious, or unlawful act.

Section 647(h) concerns a person who loiters, prowls, or wanders on the private property of another without visible or lawful business with the owner/occupant. The statute defines "loiter" there as delaying or lingering without a lawful purpose on the property and for the purpose of committing a crime as opportunity may be discovered.

Under the standing scenario, § 647(h) will ordinarily fall outside scope because the auditor is not silently assumed to be on another's private property without lawful purpose and for the purpose of committing a crime as opportunity may be discovered. Do not rely on public ownership alone: a government office can occupy leased or privately owned property, so analyze the actual property/access facts when they matter.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
"Loitering" should never be treated as a generic synonym for "standing around longer than an employee wants."

When a public employee or officer uses the word, identify the exact statute, ordinance, regulation, or facility rule being invoked and compare its actual elements with the conduct observed.

docs.title: Useful factual questions
docs.text:
• Which statute are you referring to?
  • Which subsection?
  • What specific conduct are you saying satisfies that subsection?
  • Are you saying the issue is noise, fighting, threatening words, obstruction, or something else?

docs.title: Remaining facility/specialized work
docs.text:
The statewide ordinary branch is now doctrine-reviewed for § 415 noise, fighting words, police-directed criticism, true threats, § 148 obstruction, and § 602.1(b) interference.

Remaining changed-fact/local work includes:

  • particular local noise/disorder ordinances;
  • facility-specific conduct rules and authority/delegation;
  • school/campus § 415.5 and related specialized rules;
  • stalking/harassment statutes when the actual facts satisfy their specialized predicates;
  • meeting disruption and assembly/dispersal doctrine, which remain in GAP-07; and
  • threat statutes other than the ordinary § 422 branch when specifically invoked.

docs.text:

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Research the facility before testing the policy.

The project-methodology status describes this page's workflow function. Legal propositions referenced here remain subject to the verification status in the substantive chapters, authority index, and sweep ledgers.

A strong facility investigation should establish what the law says, what the agency says its policy is, how the policy was adopted, how employees and police have applied it, and what actually happens during a peaceful field visit.

The goal is not to manufacture a confrontation. It is to document and test a defined legal or policy question under the project's standing scenario.

docs.title: 1. Start with a research question
docs.text:
Do not begin with "let's see whether they kick us out." Begin with a proposition that can be tested.

Examples:

  • Does this facility actually have a written no-recording policy?
  • What area does the policy cover?
  • What statute, regulation, order, or other authority does the agency claim supports it?
  • Is a visitor sign-in or identification rule written down?
  • Has the agency previously instructed staff to call police when a person records from a place they may lawfully be?
  • What offense have officers previously relied on when enforcing the policy?
  • Are favorable and unfavorable expressive reactions treated differently at a public meeting?
  • Has a policy changed after a complaint, claim, lawsuit, or earlier audit?

The research question belongs in the facility file before the visit.

docs.title: 2. Build the authority chain
docs.text:
A sign or employee instruction is not the end of the analysis. Trace the claimed authority through each layer.

Layer Research question Constitution / controlling cases What federal and California constitutional rules govern the specific area and activity? Statute / regulation / court rule / ordinance What enacted law actually authorizes or limits the conduct? Agency policy What does the agency's written rule say, who issued it, and when was it adopted or revised? Facility implementation What signs, screening procedures, visitor instructions, or employee practices implement the policy? Enforcement practice What have security staff, supervisors, or police actually done when the rule was invoked? Exclusion / removal authority Who is authorized to restrict access or order departure from this specific area, and what law, policy, property-management authority, or other rule supports that action? Police / criminal authority If police intervention occurs, what particular offense or detention/arrest basis is asserted, and what facts support that basis or satisfy the offense elements? Remedy / follow-up What administrative, records, complaint, civil, or judicial process applies if the policy or enforcement appears unlawful?

The project should never collapse these into one proposition such as "there is a sign, therefore it is illegal to record" or "the employee wants the person gone, therefore police have arrest authority."

docs.title: 2A. Verify the authority and delegation chain
docs.text:
When a material facility rule is located, do not stop at its text. Build the authority record far enough to answer who could adopt it and who may enforce it.

For each material restriction, record when available:

Authority field Research target Rule-maker Exact governing body, agency, department, official, or other actor that adopted the rule Entity type State agency, general-law city, charter city, county, charter county, special district, board/commission, joint-powers entity, court, or other entity Enabling authority Constitution, statute, charter, enabling act, ordinance, regulation, resolution, agreement, or necessarily implied power Adoption instrument Regulation, ordinance, resolution, order, board policy, department policy, or other identified form Adoption date/version Current effective version and any material superseded versions Required procedure State APA where applicable, or the local/statutory/charter adoption procedure governing the entity Internal delegation Governing body/entity → department → manager/official/employee/security actor State-law conflict Any duplication, contradiction, occupied-field, charter-home-rule, or specialized-preemption question Federal conflict Any express, field, or conflict-preemption issue under the relevant federal scheme Enforcement bridge Separate authority for removal, exclusion, citation, detention, arrest, or criminal prosecution Confidence VERIFIED, PARTIALLY-VERIFIED, or UNRESOLVED

A missing local delegation document is not proof that no authority exists. Mark the chain unresolved and use targeted public-source research or CPRA to obtain the ordinance, resolution, charter provision, enabling law, delegation, contract, or other source needed to resolve it.

The statewide framework is in Sweep 013 — Delegated Authority and Preemption.

docs.title: 3. Build a pre-visit facility research packet
docs.text: Before field verification, gather what is reasonably available.

docs.title: Facility and access facts
docs.text:
Record:

  • agency and facility name;
  • ownership or controlling agency where relevant;
  • exact areas open to the public;
  • public hours;
  • entrances and security checkpoints;
  • appointment, badge, sign-in, or identification conditions;
  • public counters, waiting rooms, meeting rooms, hallways, secured doors, employee workspaces, and exterior areas;
  • posted signs and their exact wording;
  • available floor plans, public maps, meeting-room diagrams, or visitor instructions.

Do not assign one forum label to the entire address merely because the building has a public lobby.

docs.title: Property and boundary evidence — standard facility pass
docs.text:
Property research is now a standard part of the facility SOP wherever practical, not something reserved only for locations that already look complicated.

Every facility should receive a baseline property pass. A deeper boundary pass is required whenever ownership, control, right-of-way, easements, shared parking, plazas, approaches, or other boundary facts could materially affect access, forum, removal, or trespass analysis.

This is especially important for sidewalks, plazas, forecourts, parking lots, shared civic campuses, leased facilities, joint-use buildings, transit property, large corporate/government campuses, and approaches that may cross from public right-of-way onto differently controlled property.

docs.title: Baseline property pass
docs.text:
Where official sources are reasonably available:

  1. Search the facility address in county assessor, parcel, or official GIS sources.
  2. Record the parcel/APN or equivalent identifier.
  3. Record the current record owner if an official source supports it.
  4. Identify the operational agency/controller if different from the owner.
  5. Capture the official parcel/GIS source, layer name, and retrieval date.
  6. Identify immediately adjacent parcels when they affect entrances, sidewalks, plazas, parking, campus circulation, or likely field positions.
  7. Note any obvious public-right-of-way, easement, shared-control, or lease question.
  8. Assign a boundary confidence of VERIFIED, PARTIALLY-VERIFIED, or UNRESOLVED.

A facility does not need a boundary dispute before this baseline pass is useful. The result may simply establish that no material property ambiguity has been identified.

docs.title: Deeper boundary pass when material
docs.text:
When boundaries could change the legal analysis, continue the chain:

  1. Address → parcel/APN. Use assessor, county parcel, or official city/county GIS sources.
  2. APN → assessor parcel map / parcel-book reference. Record the map-book/page or equivalent reference where available.
  3. Parcel map → recorded maps and surveys. Look for subdivision maps, parcel maps, records of survey, corner records, deeds, or other recorded instruments needed to understand the geometry.
  4. Identify adjacent parcels. A parking lot, plaza, walkway, or campus may occupy a different parcel from the facility building.
  5. Resolve public right-of-way separately. Use official engineering, public-works, street, dedication, right-of-way, or survey records for sidewalks, street margins, medians, alleys, and approaches where relevant.
  6. Check easements and access rights. Look for public-access easements, dedications, reciprocal-access agreements, or other recorded interests when the activity depends on them. Do not assume that the absence of an easement from one map proves none exists.
  7. Resolve operational control separately from ownership. Review leases, licenses, MOUs, joint-use agreements, operating agreements, parking agreements, maintenance agreements, or similar records when another agency or entity may control the space.
  8. Overlay legal evidence with the physical site. Match verified lines and control facts to the actual entrance, sidewalk, forecourt, parking stalls, benches, landscaping, driveways, or other specific areas being analyzed.
  9. Preserve and grade the evidence. Record what each source proves, what it does not prove, and the remaining confidence level.
  10. Use public-records requests when necessary. If the public source record cannot resolve a material ownership/control/right-of-way question, request the deed, map, agreement, easement, dedication, or other underlying record rather than guessing.

Useful official sources can include:

  • deeds and recorded parcel or subdivision maps;
  • county assessor or parcel records;
  • city/county GIS parcel layers;
  • official right-of-way, engineering, survey, or public-works maps;
  • city-owned or county-owned property layers;
  • recorded easements and dedication records;
  • leases, licenses, easements, joint-use agreements, MOUs, or operating agreements;
  • parking or maintenance agreements where they identify control of a specific area.

Keep four questions separate:

  1. Who owns the land?
  2. Who controls or operates the particular area?
  3. What access rights, easements, or public-right-of-way interests apply?
  4. What constitutional forum classification follows for the particular activity?

The answer to one does not automatically answer the others. A parcel may be government-owned but leased or operationally controlled by another entity; a sidewalk may lie within or next to a government parcel yet function as public right-of-way; a privately owned parcel may carry a public-access easement; and a publicly accessible parking lot does not become a traditional public forum merely because the public may park there.

For each material boundary source, record the source URL, source type, parcel/APN or other identifier, layer or map name, date retrieved, what proposition the source supports, and any limitation. Use a boundary-confidence field such as VERIFIED, PARTIALLY-VERIFIED, or UNRESOLVED.

When an interactive GIS viewer materially supports the facility analysis, preserve an export, PDF, or screenshot when practical in addition to the live link. Dynamic viewers can later change layers, symbology, parcel selection, or URLs. A preserved view should be treated as evidence of what the project reviewed on that date, not as a substitute for a deed, survey, recorded map, or other source needed to resolve a disputed legal boundary.

For facilities where boundary evidence is material, keep a small facility-specific evidence manifest linking the live source and identifying any preserved copy. A practical project layout is docs/research/evidence/<facility-slug>/README.md, with preserved exports or screenshots stored alongside it when repository/file tooling permits. The manifest should say what each item proves and, just as importantly, what it does not prove.

Consumer map imagery may help explain physical layout, but it should not be the sole source for a legal property-line conclusion.

docs.title: Policy and authority records
docs.text:
Look for or request:

  • photography, video, audio, media, visitor-conduct, security, and public-access policies;
  • administrative regulations, general orders, manuals, directives, bulletins, FAQs, and staff instructions;
  • the ordinance, statute, regulation, resolution, order, or other authority cited for the policy;
  • adoption records, revision history, effective dates, and superseded versions;
  • training materials addressing cameras, auditors, media, disruptive visitors, removal, trespass, public comment, or records requests;
  • signage specifications or records showing who authorized a posted restriction;
  • security contracts and post orders where public and disclosable;
  • retention policies for surveillance, body-camera, dispatch, or incident records.
