The fact that a record is requested does not guarantee disclosure. Exemptions, privileges, privacy rules, and specialized statutes must still be analyzed.

docs.title: Prior-incident records
docs.text:
Where relevant and lawfully obtainable, collect:

  • prior complaints about the same policy;
  • incident reports;
  • calls for service and CAD/dispatch records;
  • body-camera or other official recordings;
  • written trespass notices or exclusion orders;
  • citations or arrest records identifying the offense relied upon;
  • claims, lawsuits, settlements, published judicial decisions, or administrative rulings;
  • correspondence showing how the agency interpreted the policy;
  • later policy revisions following an incident.

Preserve chronology. A policy adopted after an incident cannot be silently treated as the policy that governed the earlier event.

docs.title: Historical enforcement and chilling review
docs.text:
Every mature pilot-facility sweep should ask not only what the rule says now, but whether government has previously warned, removed, excluded, cited, arrested, prosecuted, or otherwise burdened people for the same or materially similar activity.

This review is documentary first. It is not a request to recreate an old confrontation.

Potential sources include:

  • prior warnings, cease orders, removal directives, suspensions, bans, and trespass notices;
  • police calls for service, CAD/dispatch entries, incident reports, citations, arrests, and charging records;
  • criminal prosecutions and dispositions;
  • administrative complaints, internal reviews, claims, civil-rights suits, settlements, injunctions, and published opinions;
  • board, council, commission, or library minutes discussing expressive activity or enforcement;
  • superseded policies, training, directives, and signage;
  • records showing why a policy was revised or withdrawn; and
  • evidence that a person stopped otherwise protected or potentially protected activity because an official threatened enforcement.

Useful search terms should be tailored to the facility but can include:

leafleting, handbill, petition, solicitation, filming, photography, recording, First Amendment, free speech, trespass, removal, suspension, patron conduct, disturbance, harassment, protest, and demonstration.

docs.title: Chilling / compliance event
docs.text:
An arrest or prosecution is not required before an enforcement event matters.

A chilling / compliance event occurs when reliable evidence shows that a government warning, threat, rule, or enforcement posture caused a person to stop, relocate, refrain from, or materially alter protected or potentially protected activity.

The project should record the event without automatically declaring it unconstitutional. The legal question remains whether the restriction was valid under the law controlling at that time.

Prigmore v. City of Redding, 211 Cal.App.4th 1322 (2012), is a useful California library example: the record included warnings under the City's challenged leafleting policy and evidence that some people stopped leafleting because they feared arrest. The Court of Appeal later sustained preliminary injunctive relief against most of the challenged restrictions while treating the parking-lot vehicle-leafleting restriction differently. The lesson for this methodology is that chilling can be constitutionally material even when the event never becomes a completed prosecution.

docs.title: Date-sensitive historical assessment
docs.text:
Historical enforcement must be assessed against the law, policy, area, and known facts that existed when the event occurred. Do not apply a later case or policy retroactively without analyzing whether it merely clarified existing law or actually changed the governing rule.

For each historical event, use one of these working assessments:

  • ADJUDICATED_UNLAWFUL — a court or competent tribunal actually held the relevant challenged policy or enforcement unlawful on the issue being recorded;
  • APPARENTLY_INCONSISTENT_WITH_THEN_CONTROLLING_LAW — the governing authority already existed and the documented facts appear inconsistent with it, but no adjudication of this event is claimed;
  • CONSTITUTIONALLY_SUSPECT_NEEDS_RECORDS — available facts raise a concrete constitutional question, but records or factual development are still needed;
  • LATER_LAW_CHANGED_OR_CLARIFIED — later authority materially changed or clarified the analysis and the project should not silently project the modern rule backward;
  • LAWFUL_OR_DISTINGUISHABLE — the documented conduct, area, restriction, or legal posture materially differs from the protected scenario or is supported by identified authority; or
  • UNRESOLVED — the evidence or law does not support a more specific assessment.

These are project research classifications. Except for ADJUDICATED_UNLAWFUL, they are not judicial findings.

docs.title: 4. Use CPRA as a research tool, not as a slogan
docs.text:
California Constitution article I, section 3(b) recognizes a right of access to information concerning the conduct of the people's business and provides that the writings of public officials and agencies shall be open to public scrutiny, subject to lawful limitations.

Government Code § 7922.525 states that public records are open to inspection during agency office hours and that every person has a right to inspect public records except as otherwise provided. The existing CPRA chapter contains the project's detailed rules on requests, searches, exemptions, personal devices, retention, and preservation.

Useful pre-visit requests can seek the actual policy and its provenance, not merely ask the agency whether recording is "allowed."

See Public Records and Evidence Preservation.

Primary sources:

  • California Constitution art. I, § 3(b): https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&article=I&sectionNum=SEC.+3.
  • Government Code § 7922.525: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.525

docs.title: 5. Classify policy questions before the visit
docs.text:
Facility files should use research flags rather than prematurely declaring an agency unlawful.

Suggested flags:

  • SUPPORTED-BY-IDENTIFIED-AUTHORITY — a current source has been identified that appears to support the rule;
  • AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED — the policy exists, but the project has not yet identified adequate authority for or against it;
  • POTENTIAL-FACIAL-CONFLICT — the written rule itself appears to conflict with controlling law and requires final legal review;
  • POTENTIAL-AS-APPLIED-CONFLICT — the rule may be lawful in some applications but prior enforcement raises a constitutional/statutory issue;
  • POTENTIAL-VIEWPOINT-COMPARATOR — comparable favorable and unfavorable expression appears to have been treated differently;
  • POLICY-TO-CRIMINAL-AUTHORITY-GAP — a policy violation appears to have been treated as sufficient basis for detention, citation, arrest, or criminal trespass without the required offense elements or legal bridge being identified;
  • SUPERSEDED-OR-REVISED — the policy has changed and historical versions must not be treated as current.

These are research flags, not court holdings.

docs.title: 6. Plan a peaceful field verification
docs.text:
The visit should test the defined question while preserving the standing scenario.

Before entering, decide:

  • what specific area is being observed;
  • what activity is being tested;
  • what policy is expected to be invoked;
  • what conduct is deliberately being avoided;
  • what factual questions would distinguish a lawful restriction from an unsupported one;
  • whether the visit will include a records request, observation only, consensual conversation, public comment, or some combination;
  • what evidence should be preserved if police are called.

A useful investigation is reproducible. Another researcher should be able to understand what was tested and why.

docs.title: 7. Consensual conversation can state the investigative purpose
docs.text:
This methodology applies to an ordinary member of the public. It does not depend on profession, organizational affiliation, or carrying any project or role credential.

If an official voluntarily asks what the person is doing, a truthful response can be as simple as:

I am gathering information about this facility's recording and public-access policies and how they are enforced.

Where prior research has identified a concrete issue:

I am investigating whether this facility's policy or enforcement practice conflicts with California or federal law.

Those statements explain the purpose of the activity. They do not claim special access or create a new legal privilege.

docs.title: 8. Document policy enforcement as evidence
docs.text:
During the visit, preserve:

  • the exact area and time;
  • normal public hours;
  • signs and where they are posted;
  • the identity/role of the official when reasonably available;
  • the exact rule or policy cited;
  • whether a written copy is offered or refused;
  • the legal authority the official says supports the rule;
  • the specific conduct the official says is prohibited;
  • whether similarly situated people are treated differently;
  • warnings and opportunities to comply;
  • whether the government describes the issue as policy, trespass, obstruction, disturbance, safety, privacy, security, or something else;
  • whether the reason changes after police arrive.

Statements are evidence of what an official said. They are not, by themselves, proof that the official's legal interpretation is correct.

docs.title: 9. If police arrive, document the policy-to-law transition
docs.text:
A central research question is whether law enforcement identifies an independent legal basis for intervention or simply treats the employee's preference as sufficient.

Useful factual questions include:

  • Am I free to leave?
  • Am I being detained?
  • What is the reason for the stop?
  • What specific offense do you reasonably suspect?
  • Which statute, ordinance, regulation, or other legal authority are you relying on?
  • What conduct are you saying satisfies its elements?
  • Is the issue a facility policy violation, or are you saying the policy violation itself constitutes a crime?
  • Who has authority to order removal from this particular area?
  • Is the order limited to this area or the entire property?

The guide does not assume that every policy is invalid or that officers may never assist with a lawful facility restriction. It requires the authority chain to be identified.

California has a separate stop-notice rule relevant to pedestrian detentions at facilities. Vehicle Code § 2806.5 requires a peace officer making a traffic or pedestrian stop, before questioning related to a criminal investigation or traffic violation, to state the reason for the stop, unless the officer reasonably believes withholding the reason is necessary to protect life or property from an imminent threat. The Field Guide retains the pedestrian-stop application here; traffic-stop doctrine is outside the current facility-audit focus. The statutory notice requirement is not the same as a requirement to disclose every fact underlying reasonable suspicion.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=2806.5

docs.title: 10. Post-visit investigation
docs.text:
The field visit usually creates a second records phase.

Depending on the event, request or preserve:

  • CAD/dispatch logs;
  • body-camera and other official recordings;
  • incident reports;
  • employee emails or messages concerning the encounter where potentially public and disclosable;
  • supervisor instructions;
  • the policy/version actually relied upon;
  • records showing policy changes after the encounter;
  • retention schedules;
  • complaints, use-of-force records, citations, or exclusion records where applicable and lawfully available.

Compare the contemporaneous records with what officials said on scene. Preserve contradictions without overstating what they prove.

docs.title: 11. Member-of-public baseline
docs.text:
The Field Guide does not depend on professional status or credentials.

A person using this methodology is analyzed as a member of the public unless a genuinely role-specific law applies. The baseline is intended to work for a person carrying only a phone. The legal analysis starts with the rights, duties, and restrictions that apply to the person in the specific place and activity.

No project ID or other self-created credential is required by this methodology. Likewise, the existence or absence of such a credential does not determine whether the person's activity is protected.

Identification demands during police encounters are analyzed separately in police-encounters.md. The project does not treat an officer's desire to investigate, the fact that someone "called the police," or a request for identification as interchangeable with an actual legal duty or authority concerning identification.

docs.title: 12. Facility-registry integration
docs.text:
Every mature facility entry should eventually contain both legal classification and evidence history.

Minimum fields:

  • facility and controlling agency;
  • specific area;
  • access status and public hours;
  • federal forum classification;
  • California Speech Clause classification;
  • activity analyzed;
  • current written policy;
  • policy source/provenance;
  • claimed legal authority;
  • signage/implementation;
  • prior incidents;
  • prior police/security enforcement;
  • exclusion/removal authority previously invoked;
  • offense/detention/arrest authority previously invoked;
  • comparator evidence;
  • current research flag(s);
  • field-verification date/result;
  • post-visit records obtained;
  • unresolved questions;
  • last verified.

The resulting record should let a reader trace:

controlling law → enacted authority → written policy → implementation → prior enforcement → field verification → post-incident records.

That chain is the core investigative product.

docs.title: Quality rule
docs.text:
The project should seek facilities with documented legal or policy questions, not invent misconduct to create a test.

A strong investigation is one where the standing scenario remains intact and the disputed government action can therefore be evaluated without guessing whether unrelated obstruction, threats, noise, restricted-area entry, or other misconduct occurred.

docs.title: What Can I Actually Do in Each Forum?
docs.text:
This page translates forum classification into a practical question:

What kinds of First Amendment activity may I engage in here, and what changes when the place is a TPF, LPF, or NPF?

The answer is activity-specific. A forum label does not create one universal yes/no rule for speech, signs, leaflets, recording, public comment, tabling, or other expression.

The shorthand is:

TPF: general expressive activity is presumptively within the forum's historic function, subject to valid restrictions. LPF: ask whether the speaker, subject, and activity fit the channel the government actually opened. NPF: government may reserve the property for its intended use, but restrictions must still satisfy the applicable reasonableness and viewpoint-neutrality rules. Recording: always run a separate recording analysis; forum status alone does not answer it.

A designated public forum, while intentionally kept open for general public expression, ordinarily receives the same federal forum standard as a traditional public forum.

docs.title: How to read the matrix
docs.text:
The table uses these practical baselines:

  • STRONG BASELINE — the activity is ordinarily within the expressive use associated with the forum, although valid time/place/manner, safety, permit, privacy, or other rules may still apply.
  • PURPOSE-DEPENDENT — the activity is protected when it fits the speakers, subjects, uses, or procedures for which the limited forum was opened.
  • NO GENERAL FORUM ENTITLEMENT — the forum category itself does not give a general right to use the property for that activity. An actual restriction still must be lawful, and another constitutional/statutory doctrine may independently protect the activity.
  • SEPARATE DOCTRINE — forum status is not enough to answer the question. Recording, public meetings, confidential communications, press access, and similar activities can have additional rules.

These are not substitutes for the actual rule at the facility.

docs.title: At-a-glance activity matrix
docs.text: Activity Traditional / designated public forum Limited public forum Nonpublic forum Speech / conversation STRONG BASELINE. Peaceful speaking, discussion, criticism, advocacy, and conversation are core uses of streets, sidewalks, parks, and similarly opened public fora. Content-neutral time/place/manner rules may regulate noise, congestion, location, duration, and similar effects. PURPOSE-DEPENDENT. Protected when the speech fits the subjects, speakers, or use for which the channel was opened. Government may keep the forum within those limits if the limits are reasonable and viewpoint neutral. NO GENERAL FORUM ENTITLEMENT. Ordinary conversation and criticism do not disappear, but government may reasonably preserve the property for its intended governmental function. Viewpoint discrimination remains a serious problem. Signs / display STRONG BASELINE. Handheld signs and visual advocacy are classic expression, subject to valid size, placement, attachment, safety, traffic, duration, and similar content-neutral rules. PURPOSE-DEPENDENT. A sign fitting the opened event/channel may be protected; unrelated displays may fall outside the forum's purpose. NO GENERAL FORUM ENTITLEMENT. Expressive display can be more readily restricted to protect the function of the space, but the restriction still needs the applicable reasonableness/viewpoint-neutrality support. Leaflets / literature STRONG BASELINE. Peaceful distribution of literature is a classic First Amendment activity in ordinary streets, sidewalks, and parks, subject to legitimate obstruction, litter, crowd-flow, and similar rules. PURPOSE-DEPENDENT. Distribution may be allowed if it fits the opened channel; a government may keep a meeting room, library program, or other limited channel from becoming a general distribution venue. NO GENERAL FORUM ENTITLEMENT. The government may often prohibit or confine literature distribution where it would interfere with the property's intended function, so long as the governing restriction is lawful. Petitioning STRONG BASELINE. Seeking signatures, advocating a cause, and petition-related conversation are strongly associated with public-forum activity, subject to nonobstruction and valid location/time rules. PURPOSE-DEPENDENT. Petitioning must fit the opened purpose unless another rule creates a broader right. NO GENERAL FORUM ENTITLEMENT. A nonpublic property need not be converted into a petition-signature venue merely because the public enters for government business. Assembly / demonstration STRONG BASELINE. Peaceful assembly and demonstration are core public-forum uses. Large events may be subject to valid permit, route, sound, crowd-control, safety, and scheduling rules. PURPOSE-DEPENDENT. Assembly is protected to the extent the government opened the channel for meetings, gatherings, public comment, or similar participation. NO GENERAL FORUM ENTITLEMENT. Government generally may prevent the area from being turned into an unrelated demonstration venue when doing so is reasonably connected to the property's function and viewpoint neutral. Solicitation PROTECTED BUT MORE REGULABLE. Solicitation has expressive components, but requests for money, immediate exchanges of funds, commercial solicitation, and aggressive solicitation can receive different treatment from pure leafletting or advocacy. Check the exact ordinance/rule. PURPOSE-DEPENDENT. Government may often exclude fundraising or commercial solicitation if it falls outside the channel it opened. NO GENERAL FORUM ENTITLEMENT. Solicitation can usually be restricted more readily when inconsistent with the facility's service, security, traffic, or operational purpose. Photography / video / audio recording SEPARATE DOCTRINE; OFTEN STRONGEST HERE. A lawful public vantage and public-interest subject strengthen the First Amendment analysis, but forum status does not override privacy law, restricted-area rules, court rules, safety perimeters, or actual interference. See the detailed recording section below. SEPARATE DOCTRINE. Ask whether recording fits the opened channel and whether an independent statute or First Amendment rule protects it. Public-meeting recording is a major example. SEPARATE DOCTRINE. NPF does not mean "no cameras." The government may have greater authority to impose a reasonable, viewpoint-neutral recording restriction tied to the facility's function, but the restriction must actually exist and activity-specific protections can still control. Public comment NOT CREATED BY THE PHYSICAL FORUM ALONE. Standing on a public sidewalk does not create a right to address a government body as part of its official meeting. STRONG WITHIN THE OPENED COMMENT CHANNEL. Public-comment periods are classic limited-forum examples; reasonable time/topic/procedure rules may apply, but viewpoint discrimination and removal based merely on criticism are constitutionally suspect. California open-meeting statutes add separate rights. NO GENERAL RIGHT FROM NPF STATUS. A service lobby or office does not become an official public-comment forum merely because someone wants to make a speech there. Tabling / physical setup EXPRESSIVE BUT PHYSICALLY REGULABLE. A table, booth, easel, tripod array, canopy, chairs, or other setup can combine speech with occupation of public space. Valid permit, size, placement, duration, fire/safety, pedestrian-flow, and property-use rules may apply even when the message is protected. PURPOSE-DEPENDENT. A setup may be allowed if the opened channel permits it; government can often limit furniture/equipment to what the program or room rules allow. NO GENERAL FORUM ENTITLEMENT. A right to speak or record does not automatically create a right to install equipment or occupy floor/counter space. Expressive clothing STRONG BASELINE. Clothing, buttons, symbols, and messages are expressive activity, although specialized settings can have valid narrowly supported rules. PURPOSE-DEPENDENT BUT VIEWPOINT SENSITIVE. Reasonable rules tied to the channel's function may apply; selective treatment of viewpoints remains suspect. PROTECTED EXPRESSION CAN STILL EXIST. Sammartano and Mansky illustrate that a nonpublic-forum label does not let government suppress expressive apparel without a sufficiently reasonable, workable, viewpoint-neutral rule. Press / information gathering STRONG LAWFUL-VANTAGE BASELINE; NO SPECIAL ACCESS STATUS. Reporting, observing, interviewing willing persons, taking notes, and lawful recording can receive strong protection, but being "press" does not create a superior right to enter restricted government property. PURPOSE-DEPENDENT / SEPARATE DOCTRINE. Press activity may fit an opened channel or may be governed by separate meeting, court, credential, security, or access rules. NO SPECIAL PRESS RIGHT OF ENTRY. The press generally does not acquire access to government-controlled areas unavailable to the public merely because the purpose is newsgathering. Lawful information gathering from places otherwise open remains a separate First Amendment question.

docs.title: Photography, video, and audio recording
docs.text: Recording deserves its own analysis because it does not fit neatly into the forum categories.

docs.title: 1. Start with the lawful vantage point
docs.text:
Ask:

  1. Where exactly is the recorder standing?
  2. Does the recorder have the right to be there?
  3. What subject is being recorded?
  4. What actual rule is claimed to restrict the recording?
  5. Is the claimed problem the recording itself or independent conduct such as obstruction, unsafe proximity, noise, or entry into a restricted area?

This matters even in an NPF. A nonpublic-forum label establishes the forum standard; it does not manufacture a camera prohibition.

For the California privacy overlay—public versus limited-audience visibility, windows/glass, device-assisted constructive intrusion, visible screens/documents, computer access, voyeurism, and confidential audio—see Lawful Vantage, Public View, and California Privacy Boundaries.

docs.title: 2. Public officials and police
docs.text:
The Ninth Circuit has recognized First Amendment protection associated with filming matters of public interest, including police activity. Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995), is the project's core police-recording authority. Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018), reinforces that photography restrictions require attention to the particular location, forum, rule, and governmental justification.

California Penal Code § 148(g) adds a particularly useful statutory rule. The fact that a person photographs or makes an audio/video recording of a public officer or peace officer, while the officer is in a public place or the recorder is in a place the recorder has the right to be, does not by itself constitute § 148(a) obstruction and does not by itself create reasonable suspicion or probable cause.

That does not create a right to enter a place the person otherwise may not be, cross a lawful safety perimeter, physically interfere, or ignore an independently valid restriction.

docs.title: 3. Still photography
docs.text:
Still photography normally avoids the separate audio-consent problem, but location and subject still matter.

A camera pointed at a publicly visible officer, building exterior, public meeting, sign, or other matter of public interest from a lawful vantage presents a different problem from photographing:

  • confidential records visible only because the recorder moved into a restricted position;
  • protected computer screens;
  • secure access-control details subject to a valid specialized rule;
  • private medical/client information;
  • a courtroom governed by a court-specific rule; or
  • a subject for which another law creates a specific restriction.

The project therefore never reduces the question to "photography is legal in public."

docs.title: 4. Video recording
docs.text:
Video recording has the same location/subject questions as still photography and can additionally capture audio.

A rule that lawfully regulates a tripod, lighting rig, obstruction, noise, or physical setup is not automatically a lawful rule against the act of handheld recording itself. Analyze the camera activity and the equipment/space use separately.

docs.title: 5. Audio recording and California Penal Code § 632
docs.text:
Audio requires an additional California privacy analysis.

Penal Code § 632 applies to intentionally recording a confidential communication without the consent of all parties. The statute defines a confidential communication by the circumstances and excludes communications made in a public gathering, in legislative/judicial/executive/administrative proceedings open to the public, and other circumstances where the parties may reasonably expect the communication may be overheard or recorded.

Accordingly:

California is not accurately summarized as "two-party consent everywhere."

The correct question is whether the particular communication is confidential under § 632 and whether another statutory exception or rule applies.

A conversation occurring in a government lobby is not automatically confidential merely because it happens indoors, and it is not automatically nonconfidential merely because the lobby is open to the public. Acoustic conditions, the participants' conduct, the nature of the interaction, separation from other patrons, and the objective circumstances can matter.

docs.title: 6. Open public meetings
docs.text:
For a Brown Act local-agency meeting, Government Code § 54953.5 supplies a right independent of ordinary forum doctrine: a person attending an open and public meeting has the right to record the proceedings unless the legislative body reasonably finds the recording cannot continue without noise, illumination, or obstruction of view that constitutes or would constitute a persistent disruption.

Government Code § 54954.3 separately requires public-comment opportunities within its scope and prohibits a local legislative body from prohibiting public criticism of agency policies, programs, services, or the acts or omissions of the legislative body, while permitting reasonable regulations such as time limits.

This is a good example of why the Field Guide always asks:

Is there an activity-specific statute that gives a clearer answer than the forum label alone?

docs.title: 7. Recording in an LPF
docs.text:
An LPF often requires two simultaneous questions:

  • Does the underlying activity fit the forum's opened purpose?
  • Does a separate law protect recording that activity?

Examples:

  • A city-council comment period is limited to the meeting's lawful comment structure, but recording the open meeting also receives statutory protection.
  • A library meeting room may be an LPF for eligible community meetings; that does not automatically make the entire library interior an unrestricted filming location.
  • A study room can be opened for study/collaboration without being opened as a general media-production studio.

docs.title: 8. Recording in an NPF
docs.text:
An NPF gives government more room to preserve the facility for its intended use, but the correct sequence is:

  1. identify the exact public-access subarea;
  2. identify the subject being recorded;
  3. identify an actual recording restriction, if one exists;
  4. identify the governmental interest and connection between that interest and the restriction;
  5. test reasonableness and viewpoint neutrality;
  6. apply any independent recording statute/case/policy;
  7. separate recording from additional conduct;
  8. only then analyze removal/trespass/enforcement authority.

This is why the Registry can say Concord Police lobby: NPF / HIGH federally while separately saying that noninterfering recording of a public-facing officer from a lawful vantage has strong activity-specific support.

docs.title: Activity-specific field questions
docs.text:
When the forum classification is known but an expressive activity is challenged, useful factual questions include:

  • What specific activity are you saying is prohibited: speaking, signs, leaflets, recording, solicitation, tabling, or something else?
  • What specific area does the restriction cover?
  • What written rule, ordinance, regulation, contract term, or policy are you enforcing?
  • Does the rule regulate the message, the activity, or only how/where the activity is conducted?
  • What part of this activity is inconsistent with the purpose of this forum?
  • Does the same rule apply to comparable speakers and viewpoints?
  • If recording is the issue, what subject or information are you saying creates the privacy, security, safety, or operational concern?
  • If physical equipment is the issue, would handheld activity without the setup be permitted?
  • If removal is being ordered, what independent authority supports exclusion from this particular area?

These questions preserve the issue. They are not magic words and do not require an employee or officer to conduct constitutional litigation on scene.

docs.title: TPF / designated public forum
docs.text:
General expression is the baseline; regulation needs the appropriate constitutional justification.

Ask: What valid rule controls the time, place, manner, safety, equipment, or conduct?

docs.title: LPF
docs.text:
The government opened a channel, not necessarily the whole property for every expressive purpose.

Ask: Does my speaker status, subject, and activity fit what the government opened?

docs.title: NPF
docs.text:
The government may preserve the property for its intended function, but "nonpublic" is not "First Amendment free."

Ask: What actual restriction exists, how does it reasonably relate to the property's purpose, and is it viewpoint neutral?

docs.title: Recording in any forum
docs.text:
Forum status is only one layer.

Ask: Where am I, what am I recording, what actual restriction applies, and is there an independent recording right or privacy rule?

docs.title: Challenging a restriction
docs.text:
This matrix states the baseline for the activity. If an agency rule burdens that activity, do not stop at "a rule exists."

Run the Restriction Audit:

protected activity → forum/location → actual restriction → authority → constitutional test → enforcement authority

The project does not treat an agency mandate as lawful merely because it has been posted or adopted.

docs.title: Key authorities
docs.text:
• Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators' Association, 460 U.S. 37 (1983).
  • Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense & Educational Fund, Inc., 473 U.S. 788 (1985).
  • United States v. Grace, 461 U.S. 171 (1983).
  • Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 491 U.S. 781 (1989).
  • Christian Legal Society Chapter v. Martinez, 561 U.S. 661 (2010).
  • Norse v. City of Santa Cruz, 629 F.3d 966 (9th Cir. 2010) (en banc).
  • Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002).
  • Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky, 585 U.S. 1 (2018).
  • Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995).
  • Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018).
  • Houchins v. KQED, Inc., 438 U.S. 1 (1978).
  • California Penal Code §§ 148(g), 632.
  • California Government Code §§ 54953.5, 54954.3.

Primary statutory sources:

  • Penal Code § 148: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148
  • Penal Code § 632: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632.
  • Government Code § 54953.5: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54953.5
  • Government Code § 54954.3: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54954.3

docs.title: Indoor Public Common Spaces
docs.text:
This chapter applies the Field Guide's Constitution First method to indoor public common areas such as:

  • public lobbies;
  • foyers;
  • waiting areas;
  • shared public corridors;
  • public-facing vestibules;
  • general customer-service common space; and
  • other interior areas that members of the public may lawfully enter without individualized permission.

It does not automatically include:

  • employee-only or secure areas;
  • treatment/exam rooms;
  • evidence rooms;
  • records workspaces;
  • controlled interview rooms;
  • courtrooms governed by separate court rules;
  • classrooms governed by separate rules;
  • dedicated meeting rooms opened for a distinct expressive purpose; or
  • any space whose access is conditioned on individualized permission.

The exact area still controls.

docs.title: Short rule
docs.text:
Public access indoors does not automatically create a traditional public forum. But a nonpublic-forum label does not erase the First Amendment.

For ordinary government lobbies and similar service/common areas, the federal baseline is often nonpublic forum unless the government has intentionally opened the area as an expressive channel.

That classification answers only the forum question.

It does not answer:

  • whether photography or recording is protected;
  • whether a particular privacy rule is valid;
  • whether criticism may be prohibited;
  • whether expressive clothing may be banned;
  • whether casual conversation may be suppressed;
  • whether removal is lawful;
  • whether a policy violation creates criminal trespass; or
  • whether the California Speech Clause produces a broader result.

docs.title: 1. Start with access, not with the word "lobby"
docs.text:
Ask:

  1. Is this area ordinarily open to the public?
  2. Why is the public allowed in?
  3. Is access limited to transacting government business?
  4. Has the government invited private expressive activity there?
  5. Is the area physically and operationally distinct from nearby restricted space?
  6. Is the challenged activity passive, conversational, documentary, distributive, demonstrative, or physically occupative?

A public lobby used for transactions can be a nonpublic forum even though anyone may enter during business hours.

A meeting room inside the same building can be a limited public forum.

A municipal sidewalk immediately outside can be a traditional public forum.

Do not transfer one classification across those boundaries.

docs.title: 2. Federal baseline for ordinary government interiors
docs.text:
Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002), is the project's principal published Ninth Circuit government-building anchor.

The Ninth Circuit treated a judicial/municipal complex as a nonpublic forum because the building existed to conduct governmental and court business rather than to serve as a place for assembly and debate.

That does not mean "government interior = NPF" as a categorical rule.

It means that ordinary publicly accessible government interiors should be analyzed from:

  • the purpose of the space;
  • government intent;
  • access policy;
  • actual practice;
  • physical characteristics; and
  • the expressive channel, if any, the government intentionally opened.

A common waiting area whose purpose is moving members of the public through a government service is usually a stronger NPF candidate than a room the agency advertises for public meetings, civic discussion, public comment, or community use.

docs.title: 3. Nonpublic forum does not mean expression-free zone
docs.text:
Sammartano is especially important because the government lost on the restriction issue even after the court accepted the NPF classification.

The restriction on expressive clothing still had to be:

  1. reasonable in light of the purpose served by the forum; and
  2. viewpoint neutral.

The Ninth Circuit emphasized that reasonableness in a nonpublic forum requires more than ordinary rational-basis-style assertion. The record must contain evidence supporting the claimed connection between the restriction and the legitimate need.

That creates a useful indoor-common-space rule:

The government cannot use "this is a nonpublic forum" as the entire justification for suppressing expression.

The next questions are always:

  • What expression is being restricted?
  • What legitimate operational need is asserted?
  • What evidence supports the connection?
  • Is the rule broader than the demonstrated problem?
  • Is the rule viewpoint neutral?
  • Are simpler alternatives relevant to whether the restriction is reasonable?

The government does not have to choose the least restrictive imaginable rule in an NPF, but weak fit and obvious alternatives can matter to reasonableness.

docs.title: 4. Indoor common-space activity categories
docs.text: Different conduct creates different constitutional questions.

docs.title: Speech / conversation
docs.text:
Ordinary quiet conversation, criticism of government, asking questions, and verbal interaction do not disappear merely because the lobby is an NPF.

The government may regulate conduct that materially interferes with service delivery, noise limits, safety, queues, or employee access.

A rule suppressing criticism because staff dislike the viewpoint is a different constitutional problem.

docs.title: Expressive clothing
docs.text:
Sammartano is a direct warning against treating an NPF as a blank check to ban messages, symbols, affiliations, or criticism.

Expressive clothing is low-footprint expression. A restriction needs a real connection to the function of the space and must be viewpoint neutral.

docs.title: Leafleting, petitioning, demonstrations, and tabling
docs.text:
These activities use the physical space more intensively.

In an ordinary service lobby or waiting area, government generally has greater authority to reserve circulation, seating, counters, and queue space for official business.

That does not allow viewpoint discrimination.

A public lobby does not become a general demonstration or tabling venue merely because members of the public may enter it.

docs.title: Photography, video, and audio recording
docs.text:
Recording must be analyzed separately.

A nonpublic-forum label does not create a camera ban.

The sequence is:

lawful vantage → subject being recorded → protected recording interest → actual restriction → asserted government interest → constitutional test → privacy/confidentiality law → enforcement authority

The Ninth Circuit recognizes First Amendment protection for at least some acts of recording and information gathering, including recording matters of public interest. The constitutional strength of that protection can depend on the subject, location, and actual restriction.

See Recording Public Officials and What Can I Actually Do in Each Forum?.

docs.title: 5. Privacy is a justification to test, not a magic word
docs.text:
Indoor government common spaces can contain legitimate privacy concerns:

  • benefits applications;
  • medical information;
  • financial information;
  • addresses and telephone numbers;
  • victim/witness information;
  • computer screens;
  • private interviews;
  • intake forms;
  • personally identifying information.

Those concerns can support narrower rules.

But "privacy" is not self-proving.

A Constitution First restriction audit should identify:

  1. What information is actually exposed?
  2. Who is legally responsible for protecting it?
  3. What law makes it confidential?
  4. Is the information visible/audible from ordinary lawful public space?
  5. What safeguard has the facility implemented?
  6. What expressive activity is being restricted?
  7. Is the restriction tied to the actual privacy risk?
  8. Is the rule viewpoint neutral?
  9. Is a blanket ban justified, or is the problem limited to a narrower area, subject, screen, counter, or conversation?

docs.title: 6. HIPAA does not turn an ordinary visitor into the facility's compliance officer
docs.text:
HIPAA is frequently invoked too loosely in camera disputes.

The HIPAA Privacy Rule applies to covered entities and, in relevant respects, business associates.

An ordinary member of the public does not become a HIPAA covered entity or business associate merely by entering a public waiting area, lobby, or foyer.

Accordingly:

A facility cannot simply say "HIPAA" and thereby transfer its own HIPAA compliance obligations onto an unrelated visitor.

If a government health provider is a HIPAA covered entity, the covered entity is responsible for implementing the safeguards required by the Privacy Rule.

HHS expressly describes the obligation as one of reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards. The Privacy Rule does not require elimination of every possibility of incidental exposure.

Examples recognized by HHS include:

  • speaking quietly in public or semi-public areas;
  • limiting the amount of information exposed;
  • controlling screen access;
  • limiting unnecessary access;
  • positioning records appropriately;
  • protecting files and systems.

The fact that a visitor can incidentally see or overhear information does not automatically mean the visitor has violated HIPAA.

docs.title: 7. HIPAA also does not mean everything visible is fair game
docs.text:
The opposite overstatement is also wrong.

The fact that a person is lawfully standing in a public-access area does not automatically establish a right to deliberately record or publish every piece of information visible or audible from that location.

Other law may matter, including:

  • California Penal Code § 632 and confidential communications;
  • specialized confidentiality statutes;
  • court rules;
  • victim/witness protections;
  • privacy tort law;
  • harassment/stalking law;
  • valid narrowly supported facility restrictions; and
  • rules protecting secure or restricted areas.

The Field Guide therefore separates:

Who bears the HIPAA compliance duty? from Whether another law independently restricts the recorder's conduct.

Those are different questions.

For the broader California visual-privacy analysis—including limited-audience privacy, windows/glass, Civil Code § 1708.8, Penal Code § 647(j), exposed screens/documents, and the visual/audio distinction—see Lawful Vantage, Public View, and California Privacy Boundaries.

docs.title: 8. Public waiting areas and HIPAA
docs.text:
HHS guidance is particularly useful here.

HHS states that covered health care providers may not invite or allow media into treatment or other areas where PHI will be accessible without patient authorization.

But HHS also states that the HIPAA Privacy Rule does not require providers to prevent media from entering areas otherwise generally accessible to the public, which may include public waiting areas and entrance/exit areas.

That is an important allocation rule.

It means HIPAA itself does not transform every public waiting room into a legally closed camera-free zone.

If the facility wants to impose a recording restriction there, the restriction still needs its own legal and constitutional analysis.

docs.title: 9. Incidental disclosure is primarily a safeguard question for the covered entity
docs.text:
HHS recognizes that some incidental exposure can occur even when a covered entity is complying with HIPAA.

A visitor may overhear a conversation, see a patient name, or glimpse information in a public-facing environment.

HIPAA generally asks whether the covered entity used reasonable safeguards and complied with the minimum-necessary standard where applicable.

Therefore the Field Guide should not use either of these shortcuts:

"A visitor saw PHI, therefore the visitor violated HIPAA."

or

"A visitor saw PHI, therefore the facility necessarily violated HIPAA."

The correct question is whether the covered entity used reasonable safeguards under the circumstances and whether the visitor's own conduct implicates some independent law.

docs.title: 10. "HIPAA says you cannot record" — field analysis
docs.text:
If a government employee invokes HIPAA to prohibit recording in a public-access common area, preserve the statement and separate the questions.

Useful follow-up questions include:

  • Are you saying HIPAA directly regulates me as a member of the public?
  • What specific recording policy are you enforcing?
  • Where is that policy published?
  • What area does it cover?
  • What specific privacy interest is exposed here?
  • Is the concern a computer screen, a conversation, a patient, a form, or the entire room?
  • What statute, regulation, or policy gives the agency authority to impose that restriction?
  • Is the restriction against recording itself, or against capturing identified confidential information?
  • Does the same rule apply to agency photography, security cameras, contractors, or authorized media?
  • What authority supports removal if I do not comply?

These are evidence-preservation questions, not magic words.

docs.title: 11. Facility design matters
docs.text:
A facility cannot necessarily justify a broad recording ban merely because it has designed a public lobby in a way that unnecessarily exposes confidential information.

The project should investigate whether:

  • monitors face the public;
  • intake conversations occur at audibly open counters;
  • records are left visible;
  • sign-in sheets disclose more information than necessary;
  • private conversations are conducted in circulation areas;
  • staff rely on visitors averting their eyes rather than implementing safeguards;
  • narrower privacy zones or screens already exist;
  • the agency itself records the area continuously.

These facts can matter to whether the government's asserted privacy justification is reasonable and whether a blanket restriction actually fits the demonstrated need.

This does not mean the Constitution requires every agency to rebuild its lobby, nor does it mean a recorder may intentionally defeat legitimate safeguards.

It means the government should not be allowed to make its own poor information-security design invisible by automatically shifting the burden to protected expression.

docs.title: 12. Indoor common-space classification workflow
docs.text:
For every lobby, foyer, waiting area, or general shared interior space:

  1. Map the exact publicly accessible area.
  2. Document the purpose of public access.
  3. Determine whether an expressive channel was intentionally opened.
  4. Assign the federal forum classification.
  5. Analyze California separately.
  6. Identify the protected activity actually at issue.
  7. Locate the claimed restriction.
  8. Identify its legal source.
  9. Identify the asserted operational/privacy/security interest.
  10. Demand evidentiary fit under the governing constitutional standard.
  11. Separate HIPAA/entity duties from visitor duties.
  12. Identify any independent law governing the recorder.
  13. Analyze removal/trespass only after the restriction itself is tested.

docs.title: 13. Working presumptions for the Registry
docs.text: These are research presumptions, not categorical legal rules.

docs.title: Ordinary government lobby / foyer / waiting area
docs.text:
Federal: usually NPF candidate, often HIGH or MEDIUM confidence once purpose/access facts are established.

Why: public access is generally provided to transact government business, not for unrestricted expressive activity.

Do not infer: no speech rights, no recording rights, automatic camera ban, automatic removal authority.

docs.title: Intentionally opened meeting/comment/community space
docs.text: Federal: often LPF when government intentionally opens the channel to defined speakers, topics, groups, or civic uses.

docs.title: Ordinary public sidewalk immediately outside
docs.text: Federal: ordinarily TPF if it is a genuine municipal sidewalk rather than a purpose-built facility access route.

docs.title: Restricted employee/secure interior
docs.text: Access: NOT PUBLICLY ACCESSIBLE unless facts establish otherwise.

docs.title: 14. Core authorities
docs.text:
• Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators' Association, 460 U.S. 37 (1983).
  • Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense & Educational Fund, Inc., 473 U.S. 788 (1985).
  • Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002).
  • Freedom Foundation v. Washington Department of Ecology, No. 20-35007 (9th Cir. Dec. 21, 2020) (unpublished; administrative-lobby comparator).
  • Make the Road by Walking, Inc. v. Turner, 378 F.3d 133 (2d Cir. 2004) (persuasive waiting-room comparator).
  • Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995).
  • Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018).
  • Project Veritas v. Schmidt, 125 F.4th 929 (9th Cir. 2025) (en banc).
  • California Penal Code § 632.
  • 45 C.F.R. §§ 160.103, 164.502, 164.530.
  • HHS Office for Civil Rights, HIPAA guidance on covered entities, incidental disclosures, reasonable safeguards, and media access.

docs.title: 15. Project rule
docs.text:
Indoor public access is not permission from government to exercise a right, and it is not surrender of the right either.

The job is to identify the precise indoor forum, identify the protected activity, identify the actual restriction, and make the government carry the constitutional burden that belongs to it.

And where the government invokes privacy:

Protecting legally confidential information is primarily the duty of the entity that possesses and discloses it. A member of the public does not become the government's HIPAA compliance agent merely by standing lawfully in public common space.

That principle does not erase independent privacy laws that may apply directly to the recorder.

docs.title: Lawful Vantage, Public View, and California Privacy Boundaries
docs.text:
This chapter is the California overlay for national-core scenario NC-VANTAGE-01 — Lawful-Vantage Observation and Recording / Matters Exposed to Public View.

It answers a recurring question:

A person is somewhere they may lawfully be and can see a person, vehicle, building interior, document, screen, or other subject from there. What changes when the person looks, photographs, records video, captures audio, uses zoom or another device, crosses a boundary, or manipulates/accesses something?

docs.title: Short field rule
docs.text:
Start with the exact vantage and the exact method. Ordinary visual observation, photography, or video of something genuinely exposed to ordinary public view from a place the observer may lawfully occupy is materially different from entering private/restricted property, defeating a barrier, using a device to obtain private activity that ordinary lawful viewing could not obtain, secretly viewing a legally protected private zone, recording a confidential communication, or accessing a computer/system.

Two shortcuts are rejected:

Visible does not mean "all privacy is gone."

and

Objection does not mean "recording is automatically unlawful."

California law is context-specific. Ask who could ordinarily see or hear the subject, from where, through what shielding, by what technology, and under what independent privacy/property/audio rule.

docs.title: 1. Establish the vantage before analyzing the camera
docs.text:
Document:

  1. exact observer location;
  2. ownership/control/access status of that location;
  3. public hours or other right-to-remain conditions;
  4. whether the observer crossed a line, gate, doorway, fence, landscaping boundary, secured area, or other limit;
  5. whether the observer touched, opened, moved, reached through, repositioned, or defeated anything;
  6. whether the subject is public, private, or mixed;
  7. whether the view was ordinarily available to the general public or only to a limited audience;
  8. whether optical/electronic equipment materially changed what could be perceived; and
  9. whether audio was captured.

A subject does not acquire control over adjacent property merely because the subject can be seen from there. Conversely, a person does not acquire a right to remain on private property merely because the property is open to some visitors.

docs.title: 2. Public place observation versus intrusion
docs.text:
California's intrusion tort supplies an important baseline.

In Shulman v. Group W Productions, Inc., 18 Cal.4th 200 (1998), the California Supreme Court explained that intrusion requires an intentional intrusion into a private place, conversation, or matter in a manner highly offensive to a reasonable person. Ordinary observation, photography, or recording in a public place generally does not supply the private-place element merely because the subject would rather not be observed.

That principle is useful, but it is not an all-purpose permission slip. The same case recognizes privacy in genuinely secluded places/conversations and rejects the idea that newsgathering creates a blanket privilege to violate generally applicable privacy law.

Source: https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/shulman-v-group-w-productions-inc-31911/

Field rule:

If the subject is genuinely exposed to ordinary public observation from the observer's lawful location, that fact materially weakens an intrusion claim. If the observer penetrates a zone of seclusion or uses a different method to obtain otherwise private matter, run the privacy branches below.

docs.title: 3. Visibility is not binary: general-public exposure versus limited audience
docs.text:
Sanders v. American Broadcasting Companies, Inc., 20 Cal.4th 907 (1999) is critical because it rejects a simplistic rule that being visible or audible to someone eliminates all privacy.

The California Supreme Court held that a worker in an office not generally open to unfettered public access could have a limited expectation against covert television recording even though coworkers could see or hear the same interactions.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/20/907.html

Hernandez v. Hillsides, Inc., 47 Cal.4th 272 (2009) likewise recognized a reasonable visual-privacy expectation against hidden video monitoring in an enclosed shared office. The court separately concluded that the intrusion was not sufficiently offensive on the particular facts, illustrating that privacy expectation and ultimate liability are separate questions.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2009/s147552/

docs.title: Field distinction
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Is this subject visible to anyone walking down an ordinary public sidewalk?
  • Or only to coworkers, tenants, invited customers, patients, staff, or another bounded group?
  • Is the observer using the same ordinary vantage those people use?
  • Did the subject employ doors, blinds, tint, partitions, walls, access controls, or positioning to limit the audience?
  • Is the recording persistent/covert in a way materially different from ordinary human observation?

Do not replace those questions with:

"Someone could see it, therefore everyone may record it."

docs.title: 4. California constitutional privacy is a separate layer
docs.text:
California Constitution article I, section 1 expressly protects privacy.

Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn., 7 Cal.4th 1 (1994) identifies the core state constitutional framework: a legally protected privacy interest, a reasonable expectation of privacy in the circumstances, and a serious invasion. Countervailing interests may affect the ultimate result.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/7/1.html

This is another reason the Field Guide does not use visibility as a binary switch.

Important limitation: the existence of a privacy interest does not by itself establish that a particular camera restriction, exclusion, arrest, or government policy is lawful. Government restrictions must still be tested under the relevant First Amendment/forum and other authority.

California Constitution: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&article=I

docs.title: 5. Windows, windshields, glass doors, and transparent barriers
docs.text:
A transparent barrier is a fact, not a magic legal category.

Record:

  • where the observer is standing;
  • whether that vantage is ordinarily available to the public;
  • whether the observer moved onto private/restricted property;
  • whether curtains, blinds, tint, privacy film, covers, fencing, orientation, or other shielding exists;
  • whether the observer opened, touched, moved, reached through, pressed against, or otherwise manipulated anything;
  • whether the observer used ordinary eyesight/camera capture or a device that materially revealed something ordinary lawful viewing could not;
  • the type of room/space being viewed; and
  • whether the observer had an intent made relevant by a particular statute.

docs.title: Penal Code § 647(i)
docs.text:
Section 647(i) addresses peeking through a door/window while loitering, prowling, or wandering upon the private property of another without visible or lawful business with the owner or occupant.

That private-property predicate matters. Do not paraphrase § 647(i) as though it criminalizes every look through every window from a public sidewalk.

Source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=647

docs.title: Penal Code § 647(j)(1)
docs.text:
Section 647(j)(1) separately reaches viewing by specified instrumentalities—including cameras, mobile phones, binoculars, and similar devices—into:

  • a bedroom;
  • bathroom;
  • changing/fitting/dressing room;
  • tanning booth; or
  • another area in which the occupant has a reasonable expectation of privacy,

when done with the statutory intent to invade privacy.

This means:

Glass does not create a universal "window exception" to a privacy-zone statute.

Apply the actual statutory elements.

docs.title: 6. Fourth Amendment window cases are analogy only
docs.text: California search cases can help identify relevant vantage facts, but they regulate government searches and are not a civilian photography license.

docs.title: People v. Berutko, 71 Cal.2d 84 (1969)
docs.text:
Police were lawfully present in a common area and observed through an aperture in the resident's window coverings. The court treated the lawful/common vantage and what was exposed from that vantage as important to the Fourth Amendment analysis.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2d/71/84.html

docs.title: Lorenzana v. Superior Court, 9 Cal.3d 626 (1973)
docs.text:
The converse matters too: police use of a private side-yard vantage not open/common to the public changes the constitutional analysis.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/9/626.html

docs.title: People v. Camacho, 23 Cal.4th 824 (2000)
docs.text:
The officers' presence in an area of private property where the public was not invited mattered even though they could see through an uncovered window.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/23/824.html

Field Guide rule:

These cases may support the factual question "Was this an ordinary lawful vantage?" They do not establish "anything police could constitutionally see may be photographed by any private person."

docs.title: 7. Physical intrusion and device-assisted constructive intrusion
Civil Code § 1708.8(a) — physical invasion
docs.text: Section 1708.8(a) creates civil liability when a person knowingly enters another's land/airspace without permission or otherwise trespasses in order to capture a visual image, sound recording, or other physical impression of the plaintiff engaged in private, personal, or familial activity, when the statutory offensiveness requirement is met.

docs.title: Civil Code § 1708.8(b) — constructive invasion
docs.text:
Subdivision (b) does not require physical trespass. It addresses use of a device to offensively attempt to capture private/personal/familial activity where the image/sound/impression could not have been achieved without trespass unless the device were used.

Source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1708.8

This gives the Field Guide a concrete California test for some technology-enhanced observation.

Do not translate that statute into:

"Using zoom is illegal."

Instead ask the statutory question:

Did the device permit capture of private activity that could not otherwise have been achieved without trespass?

The answer is fact-specific.

docs.title: 8. Ordinary camera capture versus persistent/covert surveillance
docs.text:
California privacy cases recognize that recording technology can sometimes be more intrusive than ordinary human observation.

In Hernandez, the court discussed the privacy significance of persistent hidden video monitoring while still requiring the separate offensiveness/seriousness analysis.

Accordingly, preserve:

  • camera placement;
  • duration;
  • concealment;
  • proximity;
  • focus;
  • repeated targeting;
  • optical enhancement;
  • whether the view was general-public or limited; and
  • whether a specific statute adds an intent requirement.

The project does not label normal handheld recording in a public place "surveillance" merely because it is continuous. The point is to preserve legally relevant facts rather than assume the answer.

docs.title: 9. Documents, computer screens, identifiers, and other exposed information
docs.text: A visible screen/document problem should be broken into separate propositions.

docs.title: A. The custodian displayed or failed to shield the information
docs.text: Document what was visible from the ordinary lawful vantage and whether shielding/access controls existed.

docs.title: B. The observer looked at or photographed what was ordinarily visible
docs.text:
Analyze the applicable privacy/confidentiality law. Ask whom that law regulates and what acquisition/use conduct it restricts.

A label such as:

"confidential"

does not itself establish the observer's liability.

But visibility also does not automatically establish that all privacy/confidentiality interests disappeared.

docs.title: C. The observer accesses the device/system/data
docs.text:
That is a different factual event.

Penal Code § 502 regulates specified unauthorized access to computers, systems, networks, programs, services, and data.

Source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=502

Field rule:

Seeing a display left visible from your lawful position is analytically different from touching the computer, navigating it, logging in, opening files, accessing an account/network, defeating access controls, or otherwise obtaining stored data through the system.

This chapter does not state that photographing a screen visible from a lawful position is itself § 502 "access."

docs.title: 10. HIPAA and other custodian-side duties do not answer the observer question by themselves
docs.text:
Existing Indoor Public Common Spaces research shows why proposition separation matters.

HIPAA may impose safeguard duties on a covered entity. That does not automatically mean an unrelated visitor becomes the covered entity's compliance agent. Conversely, the custodian's obligation to safeguard information does not establish that the observer is free from every independently applicable privacy law.

Use:

custodian duty → observer conduct → independent observer law

as three separate propositions.

For medical, student, victim/witness, court, financial, or other specially protected data, identify the particular statute/regulation before drawing a conclusion.

docs.title: 11. Audio is a separate branch
docs.text: Visual recording and audio recording are not interchangeable in California.

docs.title: Penal Code § 632
docs.text:
Section 632 regulates intentional nonconsensual electronic amplification/recording of a confidential communication.

The statute's definition excludes communications made:

  • in public gatherings;
  • in open legislative, judicial, executive, or administrative proceedings open to the public; or
  • in circumstances where the parties may reasonably expect the communication may be overheard or recorded.

Source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632

docs.title: Flanagan v. Flanagan, 27 Cal.4th 766 (2002)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court held that § 632 confidentiality turns on an objectively reasonable expectation that the conversation is not being overheard or recorded, rather than merely an expectation that its contents will not later be repeated.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/27/766.html

Field rule:

A visually unobjectionable camera angle can still create a separate California audio question.

Penal Code § 632.7 and other communications provisions may apply to specialized telephone/electronic contexts and should be checked separately when those facts are supplied.

docs.title: 12. Public-interest recording remains a separate First Amendment layer
docs.text:
This privacy chapter does not replace the existing recording doctrine.

The Ninth Circuit's published authorities include:

  • Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995), involving filming matters of public interest/police activity; and
  • Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018), emphasizing exact location, forum, restriction, and government justification in a photography dispute.

California Penal Code § 148(g) also provides that, within its statutory location conditions, photographing or making audio/video recordings of a public/peace officer does not by itself establish Penal Code § 148(a), reasonable suspicion, or probable cause.

See Recording Public Officials and Police.

Those authorities do not erase California privacy law. Privacy law likewise does not erase First Amendment scrutiny of a government camera restriction.

docs.title: 13. Private property does not use one statewide slogan
docs.text: Two California Supreme Court decisions illustrate why the observer's right to remain must be established rather than assumed.

docs.title: Robins v. Pruneyard Shopping Center, 23 Cal.3d 899 (1979)
docs.text:
California recognized state-constitutional speech/petition protection on the facts of a large privately owned shopping center open to the public.

Source: https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/robins-v-pruneyard-shopping-center-30510/

docs.title: Golden Gateway Center v. Golden Gateway Tenants Assn., 26 Cal.4th 1013 (2001)
docs.text:
The judgment rejected the claimed state-constitutional leafleting right in a private residential portion of a complex not freely/openly accessible to the public. The three-justice lead opinion would have adopted a broad state-action limitation for article I, section 2(a); Chief Justice George concurred in the judgment on a narrower ground and expressly did not join that broad state-action discussion. The Field Guide therefore uses the case for its narrower private-property/access boundary, not as a majority holding establishing a universal state-action rule.

Source: https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/golden-gateway-center-v-golden-gateway-tenants-assn-32146/

Field rule:

Do not infer either that every private business may remove every speaker for any reason or that a business open to customers has become public property. Identify the actual property/access right, any California private-property speech doctrine, the observer's location, and the conduct at issue.

The existing trespass/property chapter supplies the separate statutory layer.

docs.title: 14. "Stop filming," "move away," or "leave"
docs.text:
An objection does not finish the analysis.

Record:

  1. who made the demand;
  2. what property that person/entity actually controls;
  3. the observer's exact location;
  4. the activity the demand targets;
  5. the specific privacy/property/policy authority cited;
  6. whether the observer has crossed or manipulated anything;
  7. whether any independent misconduct occurred; and
  8. whether police/security later translated the objection into "trespass" or "illegal recording."

If government conditions continued access on ending recording/speech/observation, also run NC-COMPLAINT-01.M — conditional access / derivative trespass.

That California exclusion issue is maintained separately in GAP-02; closing GAP-01 does not prejudge whether a particular "stop recording or leave" order is lawful.

docs.title: 15. Operational decision tree
docs.text:
For ordinary California lawful-vantage disputes:

Where exactly am I?
        ↓
Do I have a present right to remain at this vantage?
        ↓
Is the subject exposed to general public view,
or only to a limited/controlled audience?
        ↓
Did I cross, touch, open, move, reach through,
manipulate, defeat shielding, or access a system?
        ↓
Could ordinary lawful viewing perceive the matter,
or did a device materially obtain otherwise inaccessible private activity?
        ↓
Is this a §647(j)-type protected private zone / privacy intent issue?
        ↓
Is audio being captured?
        ↓
Does §632 or another communication rule apply?
        ↓
Is sensitive data involved?
        ↓
Which law regulates the custodian, the observer,
acquisition, use, or publication?
        ↓
Has someone demanded stop / move / leave?
        ↓
What independent authority supports that demand?

docs.title: 16. Changed-fact and specialized checks
docs.text:
This ordinary branch does not claim completeness for every specialized privacy regime.

Open a dedicated check when material facts involve:

  • courtrooms or court-specific rules;
  • K-12/school or child-specific rules;
  • sexual/intimate-image recording or distribution;
  • medical/mental-health records or treatment spaces;
  • victim/witness protection;
  • trade secrets/proprietary data;
  • biometric/facial-recognition collection;
  • special surveillance equipment;
  • contractual confidentiality duties;
  • publication/private-facts liability distinct from acquisition;
  • federal property; or
  • another statute specifically regulating the subject/data/location.

Those specialized facts do not keep the ordinary lawful-vantage branch in perpetual Gap status. They are changed-fact triggers.

docs.title: 17. Project rule
docs.text:
The California overlay uses this shorthand:

Lawful vantage is the starting question, not the final answer. Visibility is evidence, not a universal waiver of privacy. Objection is evidence, not a universal camera ban.

Then identify the actual California privacy/property/audio/access rule.

docs.title: Core authorities
docs.text:
• Cal. Const. art. I, §§ 1, 2(a), 3(b)
  • Civil Code § 1708.8
  • Penal Code §§ 502, 632, 647(i)-(j)
  • Hill v. NCAA, 7 Cal.4th 1 (1994)
  • Shulman v. Group W Productions, Inc., 18 Cal.4th 200 (1998)
  • Sanders v. American Broadcasting Companies, Inc., 20 Cal.4th 907 (1999)
  • Hernandez v. Hillsides, Inc., 47 Cal.4th 272 (2009)
  • Flanagan v. Flanagan, 27 Cal.4th 766 (2002)
  • Robins v. Pruneyard Shopping Center, 23 Cal.3d 899 (1979)
  • Golden Gateway Center v. Golden Gateway Tenants Assn., 26 Cal.4th 1013 (2001)

For detailed research trail and authority classification, see Sweep 011.

docs.title: Police Encounters — Detention, Identification, Questioning, Arrest, and Devices
docs.text:
Research status: This chapter reviews the core federal constitutional and California authorities governing the recurring transition from peaceful First Amendment activity to police contact. The principal encounter sequence is covered at the doctrine level: consensual contact, Fourth Amendment seizure/detention, reasonable suspicion, identification demands, protective frisks, probable-cause arrest, Fifth Amendment/Miranda questioning, and recording-device seizure/search. Sweep 014 reconciles California identification authority; Sweep 015 now separates physical device seizure, retention/diligence, frisk/plain-feel/container rules, consent scope, Riley digital-search limits, news-material statutes, and compelled biometric access. The ordinary device branch is supported; the general lawful-detention affirmative-ID issue and the specialized compelled alphanumeric-passcode/foregone-conclusion edge remain expressly RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED rather than converted into categorical rules.

A First Amendment audit can quickly implicate several constitutional layers:

  • First Amendment: what expressive/recording activity is protected and what restrictions may government impose?
  • Fourth Amendment: when may government seize the person, frisk, arrest, seize property, or search it?
  • Fifth Amendment: when may government compel testimonial self-incrimination and what rules govern custodial interrogation?
  • Fourteenth Amendment: the incorporation bridge through which relevant federal Fourth/Fifth Amendment protections apply to California state and local actors, plus its own due-process/equal-protection protections.

California Constitution article I, sections 13 and 15 supply parallel state search/seizure and self-incrimination protections. Their complete independent state-doctrine layer remains separately queued.

docs.title: Encounter map
docs.text:
Analyze each stage separately:

  1. Consensual contact — may the person decline questions or terminate the encounter?
  2. Seizure/detention — has police conduct restrained liberty under the Fourth Amendment?
  3. Reason for stop / reasonable suspicion — for a California pedestrian stop within this project's current scope, what reason was stated before covered questioning, and what specific, articulable facts actually justified the detention when it began?
  4. Scope/duration — is the investigation reasonably related to its basis and pursued diligently?
  5. Identification — is identification merely requested, or does a specific law require it here?
  6. Frisk — is there a separate reasonable basis to believe the person is armed and dangerous?
  7. Arrest — did facts known to police establish probable cause?
  8. Questioning/self-incrimination — is the person merely detained, or in Miranda custody and being interrogated?
  9. Phone/camera — is police asking for consent, physically seizing the device, or searching digital contents?
  10. Afterward — release, property return, records preservation, and remedies are distinct questions.

The legal threshold can change during the encounter. Do not collapse the entire interaction into one label.

For crowd-control, dispersal, police-line, and emergency-perimeter encounters, see Assemblies, Dispersal Orders, and Emergency Scenes and Sweep 017. That branch separately preserves warning audibility, observer/participant status, egress/opportunity to comply, force, and statutory-media protections.

docs.title: 1. Consensual encounter versus Fourth Amendment seizure
docs.text:
Police do not need reasonable suspicion merely to approach a person in a public place, identify themselves, ask questions, or request identification so long as the circumstances would communicate to a reasonable person that the person may decline the requests or otherwise terminate the encounter.

A Fourth Amendment seizure occurs when physical force or a show of authority restrains liberty under the governing doctrine. A show-of-authority seizure generally requires submission to that authority.

A useful field question is:

Am I free to leave?

This helps clarify the officer's asserted posture. It is not a magic constitutional test; courts examine the totality of circumstances.

docs.title: People v. Tacardon, 14 Cal.5th 235 (2022)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court rejected a bright-line rule that use of a spotlight necessarily detains a person. On the facts before it, the deputy approached a parked vehicle with a spotlight but without emergency lights, blocking the vehicle, drawing a weapon, or initially issuing a command. The court required a totality-of-circumstances analysis.

Official sources:

  • https://supreme.courts.ca.gov/case/s264219-people-v-tacardon
  • https://www.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/S264219.PDF

Field rule: police attention is not automatically a detention. Commands, physical restraint, blocking movement, threatening displays, emergency lights, weapons, multiple officers, tone, and other circumstances can matter.

docs.title: 2. Terry detention — reasonable suspicion
docs.text:
Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968) recognizes a limited investigative seizure short of arrest. Police may briefly detain a person when reasonable suspicion is supported by specific and articulable facts that criminal activity is afoot. Reasonable suspicion is less than probable cause, but more than a hunch.

Official source:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/pdfs/USReports/USREPORTS-392_PDFA.pdf

docs.title: People v. Flores, 15 Cal.5th 1032 (2024)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court held the facts there insufficient for reasonable suspicion.
