docs.title: Records Requests and Retaliation
docs.text:
Public-records activity can reveal the evidentiary basis for a government restriction. It can also become part of a later retaliation dispute.

The Field Guide does not presume that an unfavorable response after a CPRA or FOIA request is retaliation. It documents the chronology and tests the legal elements.

docs.title: First distinction: statutory access is not the same as a freestanding constitutional right of access
docs.text:
FOIA and the California Public Records Act create statutory rights of access to covered government records.

The Supreme Court has not recognized a general First Amendment right to obtain all government records. The records statute therefore supplies the disclosure right in the first instance.

That does not mean government is free to punish constitutionally protected speech, criticism, petitioning, recording, or other protected activity merely because a records request is also involved.

docs.title: Ninth Circuit retaliation framework
docs.text:
A typical First Amendment retaliation claim against a government official asks whether:

  1. the plaintiff engaged in constitutionally protected activity;
  2. the government took an adverse action that would chill a person of ordinary firmness from continuing that activity; and
  3. there was a sufficient causal relationship between the protected activity and the adverse action.

The precise nature of the retaliatory act is not always dispositive. Threats, coercive measures, investigations, discipline, exclusion, or other exercises of government power can matter when they are used because of protected activity.

Key Ninth Circuit authorities include Capp v. County of San Diego, 940 F.3d 1046 (9th Cir. 2019), and O'Brien v. Welty, 818 F.3d 920 (9th Cir. 2016).

docs.title: Public-records requests themselves: do not oversimplify
docs.text:
O'Brien involved a student who had publicly criticized university officials, posted political views, and made several public-records requests. The Ninth Circuit held that the complaint adequately alleged protected First Amendment activity and allowed a retaliation claim to proceed.

Some later district-court decisions have read O'Brien as support for treating a public-records request as protected speech in a retaliation analysis. Other district courts have stated more narrowly that there is no general constitutional right to request or receive government records.

Project rule: do not rest a retaliation claim on the slogan "every records request is independently protected by the First Amendment." Identify the complete protected activity: criticism, petitioning, journalism/information gathering, recording, public advocacy, publication, or another protected act, and then analyze how the records request fits the chronology.

The statutory right to make the request remains important even where the constitutional theory is disputed.

docs.title: Retaliatory arrest has additional doctrine
docs.text:
If the alleged retaliation is an arrest, ordinary retaliation doctrine is not the whole analysis.

Nieves v. Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391 (2019), generally makes probable cause important to a retaliatory-arrest claim, subject to the Court's recognized exception involving objective evidence that otherwise similarly situated people not engaged in the same protected speech were not arrested.

In Gonzalez v. Trevino, 602 U.S. 653 (2024), the Supreme Court rejected an overly cramped approach to that exception. The objective evidence need not take the form of a nearly identical comparator case; the relevant question remains whether objective evidence supports the claim that otherwise similarly situated people not engaged in the protected speech ordinarily were not arrested for the conduct at issue.

Official opinion:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/23pdf/22-1025_1a72.pdf

Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach, 585 U.S. 87 (2018), addressed a distinct retaliatory-arrest theory involving an alleged official municipal policy of retaliation.

For facility encounters, keep the Fourth Amendment and First Amendment questions separate. Evidence that reasonable suspicion or probable cause never existed—or later dissipated—belongs in the seizure analysis. Evidence that an otherwise available enforcement power was used because of protected recording, criticism, petitioning, or information gathering belongs in the retaliation analysis. See Police Encounters.

Do not convert ordinary retaliation cases into a claim that probable cause is irrelevant to every arrest.

docs.title: What to preserve when retaliation is suspected
docs.text:
Preserve contemporaneously:

  • the exact request and timestamp;
  • acknowledgment/tracking number;
  • every response and amendment;
  • agency statements about the requester;
  • new restrictions imposed after the request;
  • orders to leave or cease recording;
  • calls to law enforcement;
  • trespass/exclusion notices;
  • unusual identification demands;
  • threats of criminal or administrative consequences;
  • evidence of materially similar requesters or speakers treated differently;
  • policy changes or newly created signage;
  • emails or public statements showing motive;
  • timing between protected activity and adverse action;
  • subsequent records requests for the incident generated by the response.

Temporal proximity can be evidence, but timing alone does not automatically prove retaliatory motive.

docs.title: Retaliation follow-up request package
docs.text:
When an adverse government action follows a records request, consider a second, tightly scoped request for:

  • communications mentioning the requester, email address, request number, organization, channel name, or known alias;
  • internal routing notes for the request;
  • records of meetings/calls discussing the requester;
  • records directing staff how to respond to the requester;
  • security or law-enforcement contacts concerning the requester;
  • incident reports/CAD/bodycam related to the interaction;
  • exclusion/trespass documentation;
  • policy/signage changes made after the request;
  • complaints about the requester's conduct;
  • training or guidance cited as the reason for the response;
  • logs showing who accessed or changed the request record;
  • retention schedules for those records.

Do not assume every requested item is disclosable; privacy, privilege, security, law-enforcement, and other exemptions may apply. Request segregable nonexempt material and the legal basis for any withholding.

docs.title: A denial is not automatically retaliation
docs.text:
A lawful exemption, fee dispute, reasonable clarification request, ordinary queue delay, or good-faith disagreement over scope does not become unconstitutional retaliation merely because the requester is critical of the agency.

The analysis becomes stronger when the record shows an adverse governmental action beyond ordinary records administration and a concrete connection to protected activity.

docs.title: Field Guide posture
docs.text:
The records chapter and restriction-audit chapter should be used together:

Request the rule → request the evidence behind the rule → compare enforcement → preserve any adverse response → test retaliation separately.

That is more useful than assuming either good faith or bad faith in advance.

docs.title: Restriction Audit — Testing Government Rules Against the Constitution
docs.text:
This chapter implements the Field Guide's governing Constitution First principle.

The Field Guide does not treat a government sign, policy, employee instruction, ordinance, regulation, or statute as constitutionally valid merely because it exists.

The research sequence is:

Right → forum/location → actual restriction → legal authority → constitutional test → enforcement authority

A government rule is evidence of what government proposes to enforce. It is not the final answer to what government may lawfully enforce.

docs.title: Project rule
docs.text:
When a restriction burdens protected expression, the project must do more than inventory the rule.

For each material restriction, ask:

  1. What activity is burdened?
  2. speech / conversation;
  3. signs / display;
  4. literature;
  5. petitioning;
  6. assembly / demonstration;
  7. solicitation;
  8. photography / video / audio;
  9. public comment;
  10. tabling / physical setup;
  11. expressive clothing;

  12. press / information gathering.

  13. Where exactly does the rule apply?

  14. ordinary sidewalk;
  15. plaza;
  16. parking lot;
  17. public lobby;
  18. service counter;
  19. meeting room;
  20. secure or restricted area;

  21. online or other nonphysical channel.

  22. What is the rule's legal source?

  23. statute;
  24. regulation;
  25. ordinance;
  26. court rule/order;
  27. formally adopted agency policy;
  28. contract/use agreement;
  29. posted condition;
  30. unpublished directive;

  31. employee instruction.

  32. Does the government actor actually have authority to impose it?

  33. What constitutional standard applies?

  34. strict scrutiny or another content-based rule;
  35. time/place/manner scrutiny;
  36. limited-forum reasonableness + viewpoint neutrality;
  37. nonpublic-forum reasonableness + viewpoint neutrality;
  38. activity-specific recording, meeting, press, privacy, or petition doctrine;

  39. California Speech Clause analysis where broader or independently relevant.

  40. What governmental interest is asserted?

  41. safety;
  42. privacy/confidentiality;
  43. traffic/pedestrian flow;
  44. disruption;
  45. testing integrity;
  46. security;
  47. protection of records/screens;
  48. operational efficiency;

  49. another identified interest.

  50. What evidence connects the restriction to that interest?

  51. Is the restriction broader than the justification?

  52. Is it content based or viewpoint discriminatory?

  53. Is it vague, standardless, or selectively enforced?

  54. What independent authority supports removal, citation, detention, arrest, or exclusion if the person does not comply?

A rule should not be promoted from "government says so" to "lawful restriction" without that analysis.

docs.title: Conditional-access / derivative-trespass check
docs.text:
When government says:

stop recording / stop speaking / stop observing or leave

do not treat the resulting leave order as a substitute for the restriction analysis above.

Run four separate propositions:

  1. Underlying restriction — is the activity restriction valid under the applicable forum/activity/privacy/security doctrine?
  2. Exclusion authority — what statute, regulation, order, policy authority, or property rule authorizes removal for violating that valid restriction?
  3. Enforcement elements — what independent elements must be satisfied before detention, citation, or arrest? For California Penal Code § 602.1(b), refusal alone does not supply intentional interference by obstruction/intimidation.
  4. Changed facts — did closing time, restricted-area entry, actual obstruction, a valid security condition, reentry, or another later fact independently change the result?

The project records the complete chronology because a downstream trespass label does not retroactively validate the upstream restriction.

Conversely, a valid prospective restriction in a limited/nonpublic forum can sometimes be enforced before actual disruption; the absence of disruption is not a categorical answer.

California doctrine and source trail: Trespass and Removal from Public Agencies and Sweep 012.

docs.title: Delegated-authority / preemption check
docs.text:
A restriction can be constitutionally permissible in the abstract and still lack a valid authority chain. When a facility relies on a policy, sign, directive, visitor condition, or employee order, run these propositions separately:

  1. Rule-maker — is this a state agency, general-law city, charter city, general-law county, charter county, special district, board/commission, joint-powers entity, court, department, or individual employee?
  2. Enabling authority — what Constitution, statute, charter, enabling act, ordinance, regulation, resolution, order, agreement, or necessarily implied power authorizes the rule?
  3. Required adoption form — was the restriction adopted through the legally required process? For a California state executive agency, a generally applicable rule that implements, interprets, or makes specific administered law may implicate the APA and underground-regulation doctrine. Do not automatically apply that state-APA rule to local governments.
  4. Delegation to the actor — even if the entity possesses the power, who may create, interpret, post, waive, or enforce the rule; order departure; or request police action?
  5. Superior-law conflict — does California state/local preemption, charter-city home rule, another specialized state-law rule, or federal express/field/conflict preemption displace or limit the rule?
  6. Constitutional validity — authorization and nonpreemption do not end the First Amendment, California Speech Clause, due-process, or other constitutional analysis.
  7. Enforcement bridge — identify the separate authority for removal, exclusion, citation, detention, arrest, or criminal prosecution. A policy violation does not become a crime merely because the rule is otherwise valid.

California source trail: Sweep 013 — Delegated Authority and Preemption.

docs.title: Restriction-status labels
docs.text:
The project should distinguish these statuses:

RULE LOCATED The rule exists. No constitutional conclusion yet.

AUTHORIZED / CONSTITUTIONAL SUPPORT STRONG The rule has a clear legal source and strong authority supporting its application to the defined activity/location.

CONSTITUTIONALITY UNRESOLVED The rule exists, but controlling authority or outcome-determinative facts are insufficient to classify its validity confidently.

FACIALLY SUSPECT The text itself raises a substantial constitutional problem such as viewpoint discrimination, unbounded discretion, or a categorical burden broader than the governing forum/activity doctrine appears to permit.

AS-APPLIED SUSPECT The text may be valid in some applications, but the documented enforcement against the activity/person/location appears inconsistent with the rule's purpose, forum standard, comparators, or governing authority.

LIKELY INVALID / STRONGLY CONTRADICTED BY CONTROLLING AUTHORITY Use only when the project's authority chain is strong enough to support that conclusion. State the exact conflict and do not substitute rhetoric for analysis.

UPHELD / BINDING SUPPORT A controlling court has upheld the materially same restriction/application, or binding authority otherwise strongly resolves the issue.

The Registry should never collapse RULE LOCATED into PROHIBITED.

docs.title: Constitutional supremacy is not a permission-seeking model
docs.text:
The project does not ask:

"Did the agency publish a rule allowing me to exercise the right?"

It asks:

"Is this protected activity, and if government restricts it, can government justify the restriction under the governing constitutional/statutory standard?"

That distinction is especially important for photography and recording. An agency's failure to publish a camera policy does not create the right; conversely, publishing a camera ban does not prove the ban is constitutional.

docs.title: Facility Restriction Corpus
docs.text:
For facility research, this chapter is operationalized through the Restriction Corpus SOP.

The corpus collects every reasonably applicable rule capable of affecting public access, expression, recording, privacy, removal, or enforcement, then keeps rule existence separate from constitutional validity.

The project uses public sources first and CPRA second. CPRA is reserved for material unpublished gaps such as internal directives, training, signage authorization, enforcement instructions, and actual incident history.

docs.title: Stress-testing a restriction before field work
docs.text:
A documentary restriction audit should try to locate:

  • current rule text and all incorporated documents;
  • adoption authority and effective date;
  • revision history;
  • stated purpose/justification;
  • training bulletins and employee guidance;
  • FAQs, signage templates, and enforcement instructions;
  • complaints about the rule;
  • prior incidents, exclusions, citations, arrests, or removals invoking it;
  • internal/external correspondence discussing interpretation;
  • litigation, claims, settlements, or corrective actions involving the rule;
  • comparable activity the agency permits;
  • public statements by officials about why the rule exists;
  • retention and evidence policies relevant to enforcement records.

Privileged attorney-client material or other exempt records may be withheld. The existence of a privilege claim does not eliminate the value of requesting the surrounding nonprivileged records.

docs.title: Selective enforcement / viewpoint evidence
docs.text:
Preserve evidence when materially similar conduct receives different treatment.

Examples:

  • favorable signs permitted while critical signs are prohibited;
  • agency-created filming allowed while public filming is banned without a distinct justification;
  • supporters allowed to remain while critics are removed for the same conduct;
  • one group permitted to leaflet/use a meeting room while an opposing viewpoint is denied;
  • a restriction first appears only after criticism, recording, or a records request.

Different treatment is not automatically unconstitutional; materially different conduct can justify different treatment. The point is to preserve comparator facts so viewpoint and retaliation questions can actually be tested.

docs.title: Records requests are part of the restriction audit
docs.text:
Use CPRA for California state/local agencies and FOIA for federal agencies to obtain the evidentiary record behind a restriction.

High-value targets include:

  • the policy and all superseded versions;
  • implementing memoranda;
  • employee training;
  • signage orders/templates;
  • incident reports;
  • dispatch/CAD records;
  • body-worn-camera footage;
  • complaints and commendations;
  • exclusion/trespass notices;
  • enforcement statistics;
  • emails discussing the rule;
  • records discussing specific incidents;
  • after-action reviews;
  • risk/security assessments, subject to valid exemptions;
  • retention schedules for the resulting evidence.

See: - California Public Records and Evidence Preservation - Records Requests and Retaliation - Federal Freedom of Information Act

docs.title: Exposure means evidentiary rigor
docs.text:
The project should identify unconstitutional or unsupported mandates when the evidence supports that conclusion.

It should also preserve the difference between:

  • a rule we dislike;
  • a rule that is burdensome;
  • a rule that might be unconstitutional;
  • a rule strongly contradicted by controlling authority; and
  • a rule actually held invalid.

That distinction makes the criticism more credible, not less forceful.

docs.title: California Standing Scenario Overlay
docs.text:
California inherits the jurisdiction-neutral factual baseline in:

NC-STANDING-01 — Canonical Standing Scenario

This page no longer defines the national facts. It maps those facts to California-specific statutes, Ninth Circuit authority, and California public-meeting/encounter branches.

The governing rule is:

National core supplies the facts. California supplies the law.

If this page appears to conflict with the national factual baseline, the national scenario controls the baseline and this page must be corrected as an overlay rather than silently changing the shared facts.

docs.title: 1. California baseline crosswalk
docs.text:
The national scenario assumes initial lawful presence, peaceful information gathering, no invented obstruction/threat/noise, no restricted-area entry, no assumed ID credential, no targeted private-person conduct, and no hidden additional misconduct.

California maps those facts as follows.

National standing fact / issue California overlay consequence Initial lawful presence in the specific area Do not begin by presuming Penal Code trespass. Later removal/exclusion is a new fact analyzed under forum/access law, Penal Code §§ 602/602.1 where applicable, and the authority supporting the order. Peaceful observation/recording/questioning/criticism Analyze under the applicable First Amendment/Ninth Circuit branch, California Constitution where material, recording statutes, forum doctrine, and facility restrictions. No blocking/physical interference Do not silently supply Penal Code § 148(a)(1), § 602.1 obstruction/intimidation, or another interference predicate. No threats/fighting/challenge to fight Do not silently supply Penal Code § 415(1)/(3), § 422, stalking/threat statutes, or analogous changed-fact offenses. No loud and unreasonable noise Do not silently supply Penal Code § 415(2); communicative-noise doctrine is analyzed under In re Brown and the current California layer. No intentional obstruction/intimidation of public-agency business Do not silently supply Penal Code § 602.1(b). A later refusal to leave does not itself manufacture a missing obstruction/intimidation predicate. No independent willful resistance/delay/obstruction of police Do not silently supply Penal Code § 148(a)(1). Recording alone is separately addressed by § 148(g). No unlawful-assembly participation/remain facts Do not silently supply Penal Code §§ 407–409 or 416. A later lawful dispersal order is a changed fact. No assumed physical ID/credential Do not infer a California identification duty from possession. The lawful-detention affirmative-ID boundary remains Researched-Unresolved; citation, arrest, booking, driver, false-ID, and specialized-access rules are separate. No physical manipulation beyond lawful vantage Use the California lawful-vantage/privacy/audio/technology overlay rather than converting visibility into intrusion. No targeted uninvolved private-person conduct If a private person voluntarily engages or becomes directly relevant to government conduct, document the interaction without silently adding harassment/following/stalking facts.

docs.title: 2. California allegation-to-elements mapping
docs.text:
The national core's Allegation-to-Elements Check applies directly in California.

When an employee, visitor, security worker, caller, or officer uses a conclusion such as:

  • trespassing;
  • harassing;
  • disruptive;
  • hostile;
  • aggressive;
  • interfering;
  • intimidating;
  • disturbing the peace; or
  • threatening;

strip the conclusion back to observable conduct and then test the actual California rule.

Common California branches include:

  • Penal Code § 415 — fighting, loud/unreasonable noise, fighting words;
  • Penal Code § 148 — resistance/delay/obstruction;
  • Penal Code §§ 602 / 602.1 — trespass/public-agency interference;
  • Penal Code § 422 — criminal threats;
  • Penal Code §§ 407–409 / 416 — assembly/dispersal;
  • Penal Code § 646.9 — stalking, when its specialized predicates are actually present;
  • meeting-specific Government Code / Penal Code rules; and
  • a valid ordinance, regulation, or facility rule whose authority and constitutional validity must still be tested.

See:

  • Disturbing the Peace and Disorderly Conduct
  • Trespass and Removal
  • Police Encounters
  • Assemblies, Dispersal Orders, and Emergency Scenes
  • Restriction Audit

docs.title: 3. Recording public officials and police
docs.text:
The national baseline does not itself decide that recording is lawful everywhere.

In California, apply:

  • Penal Code § 148(g) for the rule that recording a public or peace officer in the stated circumstances does not, by itself, constitute § 148(a), reasonable suspicion, or probable cause;
  • Ninth Circuit recording authority;
  • location/forum/access rules;
  • privacy/audio rules; and
  • valid safety, operational, or facility restrictions.

See Recording Public Officials and Police Encounters.

Primary source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148.

docs.title: 4. Identification overlay
docs.text:
The national baseline assumes no ID card or credential is silently present. California does not turn that factual assumption into a categorical rule that identification can never be required.

Current California project status:

  • no general pedestrian carry-ID statute equivalent to Nevada's Hiibel statute has been identified;
  • a consensual request for ID is not itself a legal duty;
  • refusal cannot manufacture reasonable suspicion where individualized suspicion is otherwise absent;
  • a lawful Terry detention does not by itself authorize a patdown search for identification;
  • false identification can independently implicate Penal Code § 148.9;
  • citation/release, arrest, booking, driver, and specialized-facility rules can create separate consequences; and
  • whether refusal to identify during every otherwise lawful California Terry detention independently supplies § 148 probable cause remains Researched-Unresolved after Vanegas and the older California cases.

See Police Encounters and Sweep 014.

docs.title: 5. Complaint-driven police-response overlay
docs.text:
Use:

NC-COMPLAINT-01 — Complaint-Driven Police Encounter

The national scenario supplies the factual postures. California supplies:

  • Penal Code trespass/interference elements;
  • Ninth Circuit detention/caller-reliability/exculpatory-evidence law;
  • California identification law;
  • California false-report/emergency-call statutes;
  • exclusion/removal authority;
  • evidence preservation/CPRA procedure; and
  • constitutional/forum analysis for conditional access such as stop recording or leave.

The California baseline does not silently adopt a caller's accusation.

docs.title: California-specific unresolved branches
docs.text:
The qualification matrix currently preserves:

  • the individualized prior-ban / Penal Code § 602(o) effect on otherwise generally open property; and
  • the general otherwise-lawful-detention affirmative-ID issue

as Researched-Unresolved where they affect NC-COMPLAINT-01.D / CA-F4.5 / CA-F5.8.

Immediately available video and continuing detention remain separately analyzed under NC-COMPLAINT-01.G–I.

docs.title: 6. Lawful-vantage overlay
docs.text:
Use:

NC-VANTAGE-01 — Lawful-Vantage Observation and Recording

California adds:

  • state privacy/confidential-communication statutes;
  • California and Ninth Circuit lawful-vantage/recording authority;
  • forum/property/exclusion doctrine;
  • Penal Code changed-fact offenses if physical intrusion or other conduct is actually supplied; and
  • California rules governing audio capture, technological enhancement, or specialized privacy interests.

The neutral fact that something is visible from a lawful vantage does not itself resolve every California privacy, audio, publication, or exclusion question.

See:

  • Recording Public Officials
  • Public Forum Doctrine
  • Trespass and Removal
  • Sweep 011.

docs.title: 7. California public-meeting variant
docs.text:
For a California Brown Act meeting, inherit the national meeting facts and add the California legal layer.

Unless changed by the scenario:

  • the speaker follows otherwise lawful time limits and procedural rules governing their own comment period;
  • a brief expression such as applause, laughter, a gesture, or short verbal reaction is not assumed to actually disrupt, disturb, impede, or render infeasible the orderly conduct of the meeting;
  • the person does not threaten force; and
  • favorable and unfavorable audience reactions are documented separately for viewpoint-neutrality analysis.

Government Code § 54957.95 currently defines disrupting in terms of behavior that actually disrupts, disturbs, impedes, or renders infeasible the orderly conduct of the meeting and ordinarily requires the statutory warning sequence before removal.

Government Code § 54954.3 separately protects public criticism of agency policies, programs, services, acts, and omissions subject to lawful meeting rules.

Sources:

  • https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54957.95
  • https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54954.3

Ninth Circuit overlay:

  • Norse v. City of Santa Cruz, 629 F.3d 966 (9th Cir. 2010) (en banc): https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2010/12/15/07-15814.pdf

See Public Meetings.

docs.title: 8. California assembly/emergency variant
docs.text:
For protests, demonstrations, dispersal orders, emergency scenes, or police perimeters, inherit the national facts and apply the California overlay.

Do not silently assume:

  • Penal Code § 408 participation merely because someone is present;
  • Penal Code § 409 liability without a valid unlawful-assembly predicate and lawful warning;
  • that the warning was audible;
  • that a usable exit route existed;
  • that ordinary police tape by itself establishes Penal Code § 409.5 criminal liability;
  • that an ordinary recorder possesses § 409.7 special media status; or
  • that special statutory press protections define the entire First Amendment right to observe/record.

See Assemblies, Dispersal Orders, and Emergency Scenes and Sweep 017.

docs.title: 9. Changed facts restart California analysis
docs.text:
The national changed-fact rule applies without modification.

Examples especially important in California include:

  • an employee/supervisor orders departure;
  • a public-facing area becomes closed;
  • a facility invokes screening, appointment, or restricted-area rules;
  • an officer establishes a lawful perimeter;
  • an officer announces detention;
  • a dispersal warning is given;
  • a public-meeting chair invokes a meeting rule;
  • the person changes conduct or location;
  • an agency identifies a local ordinance/regulation/policy;
  • actual noise, obstruction, intimidation, threat, interference, or other misconduct appears.

A later removal order does not retroactively make the original lawful presence a trespass. It creates a new branch:

underlying restriction/exclusion authority → validity → notice/order → later remain/reentry conduct → actual California offense elements

See Sweeps 012–014.

docs.title: 10. California statutory crosswalk
docs.text:
These statutes are overlay authorities, not national assumptions.

  • Penal Code § 148: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148.
  • Penal Code § 148.9: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148.9
  • Penal Code § 403: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=403.
  • Penal Code §§ 407–409: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?division=&chapter=1.&part=1.&lawCode=PEN&title=11.
  • Penal Code § 415: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=415.
  • Penal Code § 422: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=422.
  • Penal Code §§ 602 / 602.1: see Trespass and Removal.
  • Penal Code § 647: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=647.
  • Government Code §§ 54954.3 / 54957.95: see Public Meetings.

docs.title: 11. Qualification consequence
docs.text:
With NC-STANDING-01 v1 as the canonical factual source:

  • California no longer supplies the national standing facts;
  • NC-COMPLAINT-01 and NC-VANTAGE-01 can inherit a jurisdiction-neutral baseline;
  • California statutes and Ninth Circuit rules remain in this overlay and substantive chapters; and
  • the California qualification matrix can be rerun without importing California-specific law into the national baseline.

This closes the substantive work for CA-GATE-08 subject to final qualification review. It does not activate California and does not satisfy CA-GATE-09 or CA-GATE-10.

docs.title: Trespass and Removal from Public Agencies
docs.text:
Research status: Penal Code §§ 601-603 and the complete current § 602 / § 602.x family have been reviewed at the primary-text level. Controlling/published doctrine is reviewed for § 602(m), § 602(q), the common intentional-interference structure of § 602.1, the ordinary conditional-access / derivative-trespass sequence, and the statewide prospective-exclusion framework. Sweep 014 also researches later reentry and identification. One important California statutory edge remains genuinely unresolved: whether an individualized prior ban, without another access change, makes otherwise generally open property not open to the general public for § 602(o).

This chapter addresses the recurring audit problem in which a government employee or peace officer treats you were asked to leave as though it were a complete criminal-trespass rule. California's trespass statutes are more specific than that.

Under the project's standing scenario, the auditor begins lawfully present in the specific public area and is not assumed to be obstructing, intimidating, threatening, or otherwise committing an independent offense. A later order to leave is therefore treated as a new fact: the guide analyzes the authority for the order and the consequences of remaining rather than retroactively assuming the auditor was already trespassing.

docs.title: Short field rule
docs.text:
Within the California trespass statutes reviewed here, there is no general formula that reduces criminal trespass in an ordinary public-agency interior to:

A government employee asked you to leave, therefore remaining is automatically criminal trespass.

Identify the actual statute or other legal authority, then test its elements against the facts. Different provisions turn on materially different predicates: whether property is open to the general public, whether a public building is closed, whether someone is intentionally obstructing agency business, whether a person entered and occupied property without consent, whether a secured area is posted, or whether screening was intentionally avoided.

A lawful policy or facility restriction can still matter even when a particular trespass subsection does not fit. Conversely, the existence or violation of a policy does not by itself establish every element of a criminal-trespass offense.

Important separate question: open to the public is an access description, not a forum classification. A public-facing lobby may be open for agency business while still being a nonpublic or limited forum for expressive activity. Forum status must be analyzed separately, often area by area within the same facility. See public-forum-doctrine.md.

docs.title: Penal Code § 602 — complete subsection matrix
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.

Section 602 lists numerous distinct ways to commit trespass. For peaceful public-facility auditing, only a subset is ordinarily central, but the entire current subsection range is accounted for below so that 602 is not treated as an undifferentiated label.

Subdivision Primary-text rule Field Guide classification § 602(a) Cutting/destroying/injuring timber on another's land N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(b) Carrying away timber from another's land N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(c) Maliciously injuring/severing attached property or produce N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(d) Taking earth/soil/stone from a city lot without license N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(e) Taking earth/soil/stone from land recognized as a street/alley/avenue/park without authority N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(f) Damaging specified signs/notices or placing advertisements/signage on property without permission N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(g) Shellfish-bed entry/injury/removal and boundary damage N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(h) Posted animal-raising land/building entry and related conduct SPECIALIZED § 602(i) Opening/damaging fences/gates or damaging specified no-shooting signs N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(j) Building fires on posted land without written permission N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(k) Entering land for purpose of injuring property/property rights or intentionally interfering with, obstructing, or injuring a lawful business/occupation carried on by the possessor REVIEW-LATER; specific-intent provision § 602(l) Entry onto cultivated/fenced or qualifying posted land plus specified additional conduct, including refusal to leave SPECIALIZED; primarily land/property context § 602(m) Entering and occupying real property or structures without consent DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART; occupying requires nontransient, continuous possession § 602(n) Driving a vehicle on property known not to be open to the general public without consent SPECIALIZED § 602(o) Refusing/failing to leave property not open to the general public after the specified request DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART; ordinary access distinction reviewed, individualized-prior-ban effect RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED § 602(p) Entering land declared closed under Public Resources Code § 4256 after required posting SPECIALIZED § 602(q) Refusing/failing to leave a public building during hours when it is regularly closed to the public, after a qualifying request, where circumstances indicate no apparent lawful business DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART § 602(r) Knowingly skiing in a posted closed area/trail N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(s) Hotel/motel nonpayment/removal provision N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(t) Reentry/refusal on specified private property after qualifying prior conviction and notice N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(u) Unauthorized entry into posted airport operations areas, passenger-vessel terminals, or restricted public-transit areas SPECIALIZED secured-area rule § 602(v) Intentionally avoiding access screening for sterile airport/passenger-vessel/public-transit areas SPECIALIZED secured-area rule § 602(w) Refusal to leave domestic-violence shelter-based program after request SPECIALIZED § 602(x) Entry/remain in posted neonatal/maternity/birthing areas without lawful business; enhanced consequence after refusal SPECIALIZED § 602(y) Intentionally avoiding posted screening when entering/reentering a courthouse or city/county/state building RETAINED for courthouse/government-building screening chapter

docs.title: § 602(m) — entering and occupying means more than transient presence
docs.text:
The statutory text uses the conjunctive phrase entering and occupying real property or a structure without consent.

This is no longer merely a textual inference. In In re Catalano, 29 Cal.3d 1 (1981), the California Supreme Court explained that the predecessor subdivision requires occupation of the property, a nontransient, continuous type of possession; the subdivision was later renumbered to current § 602(m) without substantive change to this language.

The published Ninth Circuit decision Edgerly v. City & County of San Francisco, 599 F.3d 946 (9th Cir. 2010) applied that rule to probable cause. Officers knew that Edgerly had been on fenced property for only a matter of minutes. The Ninth Circuit held those facts did not give a reasonable officer probable cause under the entering-and-occupying subdivision. The court nevertheless found probable cause under a different trespass statute, § 602.8(a), because the property was fenced and posted. That second holding is an important warning not to turn the § 602(m) limitation into a blanket no trespass rule.

Current Judicial Council CALCRIM No. 2931 likewise instructs that the prosecution must prove that, after entering without consent, the defendant occupied some part of the property continuously until removed.

Doctrine-reviewed field rule: Mere momentary or transient presence is not enough for § 602(m)'s occupying element. Another trespass provision can independently fit the same facts.

Case sources:

  • In re Catalano, 29 Cal.3d 1 (Cal. 1981): https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/29/1.html
  • Edgerly v. City & County of San Francisco, 599 F.3d 946 (9th Cir. 2010): https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2004/03/17/9917319.pdf
  • Judicial Council CALCRIM materials: https://courts.ca.gov/advisory-body/criminal-jury-instructions-advisory-committee

docs.title: § 602(o) — property not open to the general public
docs.text:
Section 602(o) expressly concerns land, real property, or structures not open to the general public. Its refusal-to-leave language should not be quoted as though it were a universal rule for an ordinary public counter, lobby, library floor, or other place currently open to the public.

Areas within a generally public-facing property can still be separately restricted or not open to the general public. The exact area and current access conditions matter. James v. City of Long Beach is a persuasive public-property example: the city-owned baseball facility was treated as not open to the general public during a game because entry was limited to ticket-holders. That does not convert every publicly owned facility into § 602(o) property.

Sweep 014 also reviewed the harder individualized prior-ban question. Blankenhorn v. City of Orange said in a private-shopping-center probable-cause posture that a prior notice arguably rendered generally open property not open as to the particular person. Later federal district courts applying California law have disagreed over how far that reasoning extends. No published California appellate decision located in the sweep squarely resolves whether an individualized ban alone changes otherwise generally open public-facing property into § 602(o) property.

Field Guide status: ordinary area/access classification is reviewed; the individualized-prior-ban effect is RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED. Do not pick a preferred side and present it as settled California law.

docs.title: Caution: do not overstate § 602(o)'s constitutional-savings language
docs.text:
The text broadly contains a labor-activity exception. It also contains constitutional-activity language in the sentence addressing housing-authority property. Courts have not spoken with one clear published voice about whether that constitutional language operates as a general exception to all of subdivision (o) or specifically as part of the housing-authority rule.

A federal district court in Cuviello v. Cal Expo read the constitutional phrase as linked to the housing-authority clause rather than as a subdivision-wide exemption. By contrast, the 2026 Court of Appeal opinion People v. Hsiung read the phrase broadly while rejecting a First Amendment challenge—but that discussion appears in Part III, which the Court of Appeal expressly excluded from publication. It is therefore not precedential California authority.

Field Guide rule: Do not presently claim that § 602(o) contains a settled subdivision-wide constitutional exemption. Analyze the actual constitutional right independently and continue the case-law research.

docs.title: § 602(q) — public buildings after closing
docs.text:
Section 602(q) expressly addresses a public building of a public agency, but its text is limited to hours when the building is regularly closed to the public. It also requires a request from a regularly employed guard, watchperson, or custodian and circumstances that would indicate to a reasonable person that the person has no apparent lawful business to pursue.

Published California authority confirms that those limitations matter. In Parrish v. Municipal Court, 258 Cal.App.2d 497 (1968), the Court of Appeal considered the predecessor-lettered version of this same public-building closing-hours rule. A welfare-rights advocate remained in a county welfare building hours after its regular closing. The court treated regular closing, a qualifying request, and the apparent lawful business inquiry as substantive predicates and held that the latter uses an objective reasonable-person standard. The opinion also relied on In re Bacon for the proposition that expressive/grievance activity that may be lawful during open hours does not itself require a public building to remain open after its regular closing.

Doctrine-reviewed field rule: § 602(q) is a closing-hours statute, not a general daytime removal provision. The apparent lawful business component is objective rather than whatever the person personally believes.

Case source:

  • Parrish v. Municipal Court, 258 Cal.App.2d 497 (Cal. Ct. App. 1968): https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2d/258/497.html

docs.title: § 602(y) — security screening is its own rule
docs.text: Section 602(y) concerns intentionally avoiding submission to the screening and inspection of one's person and accessible property when entering or reentering a courthouse or city/county/state building, where the entrances carry the required notice. It is not a generic prohibition on recording or peaceful presence after successfully passing security.

docs.title: Screening is not the same thing as a visitor sign-in or ID requirement
docs.text:
A visitor log, badge procedure, appointment check, request to state a destination, or demand to show identification is a separate access-policy question. Section 602(y)'s text does not itself say that refusal to write one's name in a binder, state a purpose, or produce identification is criminal trespass.

A government office may still be able to impose reasonable, viewpoint-neutral visitor conditions under other lawful authority, especially in a nonpublic or limited-purpose forum. The legal analysis therefore has two steps:

  1. Is the visitor condition itself lawful for this particular area and purpose?
  2. If a person refuses it, what statute or other authority actually supports exclusion, detention, or arrest?

Do not collapse the facility has a sign-in policy into § 602(y) makes refusal a crime.

docs.title: Prospective exclusions and later reentry
docs.text:
An immediate order to leave and a prospective order not to return are different government acts.

For a prospective exclusion, preserve:

  • who issued it and under what delegated authority;
  • the exact property and areas covered;
  • duration and expiration;
  • the actual conduct relied on;
  • evidence of future risk;
  • whether unrelated public business remains possible;
  • notice and opportunity to respond;
  • appeal/review procedure;
  • whether the order remains effective during review; and
  • the California statute claimed to criminalize later reentry.

docs.title: Reza v. Pearce — binding Ninth Circuit breadth/duration limit
docs.text:
In Reza v. Pearce, 806 F.3d 497 (9th Cir. 2015), the Ninth Circuit reviewed an exclusion from an Arizona Senate building treated as a limited public forum. Material disputes existed over whether Reza had actually disrupted proceedings and whether he presented a legitimate future-disruption risk. On the plaintiff-favorable facts, a complete building-wide and initially indefinite exclusion was unreasonable, especially where it prevented unrelated future access to legislative proceedings and an elected representative.

Official Ninth Circuit opinion:

https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2015/11/19/13-15154.pdf

Narrow field rule: a prior incident does not automatically justify a broad future exclusion. The actual misconduct, supported future risk, scope, duration, alternative access, and viewpoint neutrality matter.

Reza does not hold that every public-facility suspension is unconstitutional. It is forum- and facts-specific.

docs.title: Officer reliance is a separate question
docs.text: Reza separately granted qualified immunity to officers who enforced the facially valid exclusion under Arizona trespass law. That does not import Arizona's statute into California. It does reinforce the project rule that the validity of the underlying exclusion, the later officer's knowledge/reliance, the actual California offense, and civil qualified immunity are separate questions.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
When an exclusion materially deprives a protected liberty/property interest, Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) supplies the general procedural-due-process balancing framework: the private interest, risk of erroneous deprivation/value of additional safeguards, and government interest/burden.

Do not infer that every same-day removal requires a formal predeprivation hearing. For longer or broader suspensions, record notice, opportunity to respond, review/appeal, duration, geographic scope, emergency justification, and access to necessary government services.

Detailed authority and the unresolved later-reentry branch: Sweep 014.

docs.title: Penal Code § 602.1 — interference with business/public-agency operations
docs.text:
For broader treatment of labels such as disruptive, harassing, hostile, and interfering, including § 148 obstruction and § 415 noise/fighting-words theories, see Disturbing the Peace and Disorderly Conduct and Sweep 016.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.1

docs.title: § 602.1(b) — public agency open to the public
docs.text:
For a public agency open to the public, § 602.1(b) requires:

  1. intentional interference with lawful public-agency business;
  2. accomplished by obstructing or intimidating employees carrying on the business or people there to transact business; and
  3. refusal to leave after a qualifying request from the office manager/supervisor or a peace officer acting at that person's request.

The statute does not say employee asks + refusal = offense.

Under this project's standing scenario, the auditor is not blocking access, physically interfering, threatening, creating unreasonable noise, or invading personal space. That makes the statute's actual intentional interference / obstruction / intimidation language especially important.

docs.title: Published appellate guideposts — policy violation is not automatically the crime
docs.text:
In Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001), a photographer/legal observer was arrested near the Moscone Center under § 602.1. The Ninth Circuit described § 602.1 as requiring both intentional interference and refusal to leave and expressly rejected the argument that the intent-to-interfere element could simply be inferred from refusal. The record showed no deliberate obstruction or intimidation: Dubner was photographing, conversing, and positioned away from the doors.

The precise statutory wording quoted in Dubner concerned the business-establishment version of § 602.1 rather than today's public-agency subdivision (b), so the case should not be overstated as a published construction of every detail of current § 602.1(b). But the same intentional-interference/obstruction-or-intimidation structure appears in current subdivision (b), and Dubner is binding Ninth Circuit authority on the Fourth Amendment probable-cause consequences of treating refusal alone as sufficient under § 602.1.

California's published Hamburg v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 116 Cal.App.4th 497 (2004) reaches a closely related point under § 602.1(a): violating or refusing to accept otherwise enforceable time/place/manner rules does not necessarily constitute the misdemeanor. The criminal § 602.1 question remains whether the statutory obstruction/intimidation/interference elements occurred. Hamburg involved private retail property, not a public-agency interior, so it does not decide the forum or policy authority of a government facility. It does strongly support keeping was the rule enforceable? separate from were the elements of § 602.1 committed?

A later unpublished Ninth Circuit decision, Mackey v. Meyer, 675 F. App'x 705 (9th Cir. 2017), applied Dubner specifically to § 602.1(b) at a California DMV and found no probable cause where video contradicted assertions of obstruction/intimidation. Because that disposition is unpublished, this guide retains it only as a research cross-check, not binding precedent.

Field rule: Do not concede that I refused to leave or I violated policy supplies the missing obstruction/intimidation facts. Ask what conduct is alleged to constitute intentional interference and separately identify the authority for the underlying policy/exclusion.

Case sources:

  • Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001): https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/266/959/582256/
  • Hamburg v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 116 Cal.App.4th 497 (Cal. Ct. App. 2004): https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2004/a101829.html

docs.title: § 602.1(d)(2) — constitutionally protected activity is expressly excluded
docs.text:
Current § 602.1 contains an additional limitation that is especially important in public-facility recording disputes. Subdivision (d)(2) states that the section shall not apply to a person on the premises who is engaging in activities protected by the California Constitution or the United States Constitution.

This means § 602.1 cannot be used by simply assuming that the expressive activity being challenged is criminal interference. The analysis should identify the activity first and ask whether it is constitutionally protected on the actual facts.

The Ninth Circuit expressly noticed this statutory structure in Center for Bio-Ethical Reform, Inc. v. Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, 533 F.3d 780 (9th Cir. 2008), contrasting statutes such as § 602.1 that use shall not apply language for constitutionally protected activity with a broader school-statute savings clause. The court's discussion does not itself decide whether a particular activity is protected, but it confirms that the carveout is substantive statutory text rather than surplusage.

A useful public-agency sequence is therefore:

identify the activity → determine whether it is constitutionally protected on these facts → apply § 602.1(d)(2) if protected → identify any additional conduct → test obstruction/intimidation and refusal elements → consider any independently applicable law

The carveout is not immunity for independently unprotected conduct. A person who is speaking, petitioning, observing, or recording can still engage in separate obstruction, intimidation, threats, unreasonable disruption, or other unlawful acts. Section 602.1(e) also expressly preserves the application of other law.

A nonbinding federal habeas case, Sherman v. Yolo County Sheriff (E.D. Cal. 2010), illustrates that distinction. The record supporting the library § 602.1(b) conviction included evidence of rule violations, verbally abusive conduct, frightened patrons leaving, and repeated refusal to leave. The court did not treat simultaneous assertions of constitutional rights as immunizing independently disruptive conduct. That case is retained only as a factual cross-check, not controlling construction of subdivision (d)(2).

docs.title: Local police-lobby comparator — Wilson v. County of Contra Costa
docs.text:
Wilson v. County of Contra Costa, No. 14-cv-03491-SI (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2015) is a particularly close California facility comparator. At the motion-to-dismiss stage, the court allowed a First Amendment retaliation claim to proceed where the plaintiff alleged that he was recording officers performing their duties in the public lobby of the Contra Costa County Sheriff's Office and was arrested after an officer noticed the recording.

The same order rejected § 602.1(b) as an established probable-cause basis on the pleaded facts, which included allegations that officers physically blocked the plaintiff from leaving and that he had difficulty standing and walking. The court did not hold that § 602.1(b) can never apply in a sheriff/police lobby, and it expressly recognized that later evidence might show intentional interference and refusal.

Wilson is a federal district-court pleading-stage decision, not binding Ninth Circuit precedent, and the case did not reach a final merits adjudication of the surviving recording claim. Its proper use is narrow but valuable:

  • recording officers in a public law-enforcement lobby is not automatically equivalent to § 602.1 interference;
  • refusal/remaining must still be separated from the statute's obstruction/intimidation predicate;
  • the protected-activity question and any additional unprotected conduct must be analyzed separately.

Updated field rule: For § 602.1 at a public agency, do not stop at policy violation or refusal to leave. Identify the alleged obstruction/intimidation, test the current subdivision (d)(2) constitutional-activity carveout, then identify any independent law that might still apply.

Sources:

  • Penal Code § 602.1: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.1
  • Center for Bio-Ethical Reform, Inc. v. Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, 533 F.3d 780 (9th Cir. 2008): https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/05-55294/0555294-2011-02-25.html
  • Wilson v. County of Contra Costa, No. 14-cv-03491-SI, Dkt. 103 (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2015): https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/california/candce/3%3A2014cv03491/279647/103/

docs.title: § 602.1(c) — knowingly material misrepresentation of law
docs.text:
This separate public-agency provision is easy to overlook. It applies where a person intentionally interferes with public-agency business by knowingly making a material misrepresentation of the law to people there to transact business with the agency, followed by refusal to leave after the qualifying request.

The 2017 legislative materials describe the amendment as aimed at a then-perceived gap involving illegitimate solicitors who made material misrepresentations of law to people transacting business with public agencies. The statute still must be applied according to its enacted elements.

Field implication: The project should be meticulous about stating law accurately. A good-faith disagreement over legal interpretation is not textually identical to knowingly making a material misrepresentation, but controlling judicial construction of subdivision (c) remains to be researched.

docs.title: § 602.1(e) — other law still matters
docs.text:
Section 602.1 does not supersede other law. Therefore:

I do not satisfy § 602.1(b) is not the same proposition as no other lawful authority can require me to leave.

That distinction is central to the Field Guide.

docs.title: Conditional access and derivative trespass
docs.text:
This section addresses the recurring sequence:

lawful presence → recording/speech/observation → "stop the activity or leave" → refusal/continued activity → removal → claimed trespass

The project treats that as a chain, not as a single event.

docs.title: 1. Test the upstream activity restriction first
docs.text:
A public-facing government interior can be a limited or nonpublic forum. That does not make every restriction lawful.

For federal First Amendment analysis, a nonpublic-forum restriction still must be reasonable in light of the forum's purpose and viewpoint neutral. Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002) is the project's key Ninth Circuit government-building anchor. It treated the judicial/municipal complex before it as nonpublic while still rejecting restrictions that lacked sufficient support and, in part, were viewpoint discriminatory.

A valid restriction also does not always require waiting for actual disruption. Simpson v. Municipal Court, 14 Cal.App.3d 591 (1971) upheld a narrow ban on picketing inside the State Capitol even though the conduct was peaceful and nonobstructive because the restriction addressed a particular expressive method and was tied to the building's deliberative function.

People v. Fogelson, 21 Cal.3d 158 (1978) likewise recognizes that protected activity can be regulated to prevent legitimate interference, harassment, or fraud, but requires precision and narrow standards related to permissible interests.

Field rule:

Absence of prior disruption is relevant, but it is not a universal defense to every valid prospective restriction. The restriction itself still has to survive the applicable forum/activity test.

docs.title: 2. Then identify the independent exclusion/removal authority
docs.text:
Do not treat the sentence leave as the legal authority.

Ask whether government is relying on:

  • Penal Code § 602.1(b);
  • a particular § 602 subdivision;
  • another statute/regulation/order;
  • a lawful facility access rule;
  • local delegated authority; or
  • a specialized court/school/security rule.

For ordinary public-agency property, § 602.1(b) requires intentional interference by obstruction or intimidation plus refusal after the qualifying request. Current § 602.1(d)(2) expressly excludes constitutionally protected activity, while § 602.1(e) preserves other independently applicable law.

docs.title: 3. Refusal does not manufacture missing § 602.1 elements
docs.text:
Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001) is binding Ninth Circuit authority on § 602.1's common interference/refusal structure. Even assuming refusal to leave, the court found no probable cause where the evidence did not establish intentional interference; it rejected inferring that missing element merely from refusal.

Mackey v. Meyer, No. 15-55186 (9th Cir. Jan. 11, 2017) is an unpublished, nonprecedential but unusually close public-agency comparator. A preacher outside a California DMV had been asked to leave and refused. The panel held there was no probable cause for § 602.1(b) where the officer observed no obstruction or intimidation despite a dispatch description that the man was "harassing" customers.

Field rule:

They asked you to leave, you refused, and they want you trespassed do not substitute for an offense's independent elements.

docs.title: 4. An unsupported exclusion cannot bootstrap itself
docs.text:
California's In re Hoffman, 67 Cal.2d 845 (1967) involved peaceful leafleting at Union Station after participants were told to stop the activity or leave. The court relied on Brown v. Louisiana, 383 U.S. 131 (1966) and rejected the theory that protected, noninterfering activity could be turned into punishable presence merely through an unsupported order to leave.

The narrow project proposition is:

A downstream refusal does not, by itself, answer whether the upstream exclusion was lawful.

That is not a universal right to remain after any order. It prevents circular reasoning.

docs.title: 5. Later changed facts can independently alter the result
docs.text:
An initially questionable exclusion dispute can become a different case if later facts arise.

Examples:

  • regular public hours end;
  • the person enters a restricted subarea;
  • actual obstruction/intimidation begins;
  • unreasonable noise or another independent offense arises;
  • a valid neutral security rule becomes applicable;
  • the person later reenters after a separately valid exclusion; or
  • another statute's specific elements are satisfied.

Parrish v. Municipal Court, 258 Cal.App.2d 497 (1968) illustrates the neutral-closing-hours point: lawful presence earlier in the day did not create an indefinite right to remain after a county building regularly closed.

Do not erase a later independent offense merely because the encounter began with protected activity.

docs.title: 6. Recording-specific conditional demands
docs.text:
When an official says:

stop recording or leave

the Field Guide treats that as two government acts:

  1. a recording restriction; and
  2. a conditional exclusion.

Run:

exact area/forum → recording/activity protection → restriction/justification → content/viewpoint → exclusion authority → offense elements → later changed facts

Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018) confirms that photographing/recording matters of public interest receives First Amendment protection while emphasizing that the nature of the location matters. It does not create unlimited camera access to government interiors.

For lawful-vantage privacy boundaries, see Lawful Vantage, Public View, and California Privacy Boundaries.

docs.title: 7. Retaliation remains a separate proposition
docs.text:
Even where government possesses lawful authority to regulate conduct, the reason an official actually uses that authority can matter under First Amendment retaliation doctrine.

The project therefore keeps separate:

  • whether the restriction was legally available;
  • whether the exclusion satisfied that restriction;
  • whether the officer had probable cause for a later offense; and
  • whether the adverse action was substantially motivated by protected activity.

See Records Requests and Retaliation for the existing O'Brien, Nieves, and Gonzalez layer.

docs.title: Operational rule
docs.text:
For the standing peaceful scenario:

Do not begin the analysis with "he refused to leave." Begin with why the duty to leave allegedly arose. Test the activity restriction, then the exclusion authority, then the actual trespass/offense elements, then any later changed facts.

The converse is equally important:

A valid, viewpoint-neutral, adequately supported restriction tied to the function of the particular forum can sometimes be enforced before actual disruption occurs.

Detailed research trail: Sweep 012 — Conditional Access, Removal, and Derivative Trespass.

docs.title: Adjacent trespass/property provisions reviewed
docs.text:
The complete currently numbered § 602.x family and immediate surrounding trespass provisions were reviewed so that specialized statutes are not mistaken for general rules.

Authority Subject Classification § 601 Trespass following a credible threat with intent to execute the threat N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.2 Limits certain county written-permission ordinances for vacant/unimproved private land N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.3 Remaining lodger in specified owner-occupied dwelling after termination N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.4 Unauthorized selling/peddling on specified airport property SPECIALIZED § 602.5 Unauthorized entry/remain in noncommercial dwelling/residential place N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.6 Closed state/county/district/citrus-fair buildings or grounds; qualifying order plus failure to identify/account for presence SPECIALIZED; important ID-demand contrast § 602.7 Unauthorized selling/peddling on specified transit property SPECIALIZED § 602.8 Entry onto cultivated/fenced/posted land; includes express constitutional-activity exception SPECIALIZED; can independently matter even when § 602(m) does not § 602.9 Taking/claiming residential dwelling for unauthorized rental N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.10 Physical-force obstruction of students/teachers at UC/CSU/community-college facilities SPECIALIZED school/campus rule § 602.11 Physical detention/obstruction preventing entry/exit of health-care facility, place of worship, or school; statute expressly says physically does not include speech SPECIALIZED § 602.12 Entry onto residential property of academic researcher for purpose of chilling/interfering with academic freedom N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.13 Unauthorized entry into posted animal enclosure at zoo/circus/traveling exhibit SPECIALIZED § 603 Forcible entry into occupied/occupiable building plus property damage N/A-STANDING-SCOPE

docs.title: § 602.6 — why it matters even though it is specialized
docs.text:
Section 602.6 is a useful antidote to vague claims that California always requires a person in a government facility to identify themselves. It is a specific statute for specified fair buildings/grounds when they are not open to the general public, after a qualifying direction to leave and determination that the person lacks apparent lawful business or another legitimate reason for remaining; the statute then expressly includes failure to identify and account for one's presence.

That specialized text should not be generalized into a statewide public employee asks for ID → ID is mandatory rule.

docs.title: Live removal / trespass decision tree
docs.text:
This is a factual and legal sorting tool, not a set of magic words.

For complaint-driven police responses, also run the national-core Complaint-Driven Police Encounter. That scenario prevents the word trespassed from collapsing four materially different questions:

  1. the person never entered the disputed property;
  2. the person entered but left when requested;
  3. the person currently remains after a request to leave; or
  4. the person is outside the property and has only been given prospective no-entry notice.

California Penal Code analysis must identify which posture actually occurred. A prospective warning does not prove a completed past trespass, and an accusation that someone crossed a property line remains a factual allegation that can be tested against property evidence and contemporaneous video.

docs.title: 1. Establish the status of the specific area
docs.text:
Do not classify the entire building with one label if the encounter occurs in only part of it. Ask/document:

  • Is this government property?
  • What specific area am I in: exterior sidewalk/plaza, vestibule, public lobby, service counter area, meeting room, secured hallway, staff-only area, courtroom, records room, etc.?
  • Is this particular area presently open to the general public?
  • Is the building within normal public hours?
  • Is this area restricted/secured/staff-only even though another part of the building is public-facing?
  • Is there a posted closure, screening requirement, visitor sign-in rule, badge rule, appointment rule, or other access condition?

This immediately separates provisions such as § 602(o), § 602(q), and § 602(y).

Do not equate public access with public-forum status. A lobby can be open for agency business while remaining a nonpublic or limited-purpose forum. Forum classification is a separate constitutional inquiry and may differ from one area of the same facility to another.

docs.title: 2. Identify the rule being invoked
docs.text:
If an employee says policy says no filming, you must sign in, or you must show ID, distinguish:

  • the written facility policy;
  • whether the rule is a screening rule, visitor-management condition, or identification demand;
  • any statute/regulation/order authorizing the restriction;
  • the forum/access classification of the specific area;
  • any applicable constitutional limitation; and
  • the criminal statute, if police are threatening arrest.

A policy can be legally valid without itself being the criminal offense. Conversely, calling something policy does not immunize it from constitutional review. Hamburg is a useful statutory reminder that enforceability of a rule and commission of a § 602.1 crime are separate questions.

For planned facility investigations, Facility Research and Field Verification provides the project workflow for tracing the authority chain from controlling law to written policy, signage, prior enforcement, exclusion/removal authority, and any separate detention/citation/arrest authority invoked.

docs.title: 3. Identify the alleged conduct
docs.text:
Useful questions include:

  • What specific conduct are you saying violates the rule?
  • Is the asserted violation simply that I am recording?
  • Is the asserted violation that I declined to sign a visitor log or show identification?
  • Is this a security-screening requirement, or a separate visitor-access policy?
  • Who am I allegedly obstructing or intimidating?
  • What agency business am I intentionally interfering with?
  • Are you saying this particular area is not open to the general public?
  • Are you saying the building is currently closed?

If § 602.1 is asserted, Dubner makes the distinction between refusal and intentional interference especially important.

docs.title: 4. If police arrive, separate removal authority from detention authority
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Am I being detained?
  • What offense do you reasonably suspect?
  • Which Penal Code section/subdivision are you relying on?
  • What facts satisfy its elements?

A facility employee's desire that someone leave and a peace officer's authority to detain/arrest are analytically distinct questions.

Edgerly is also a useful reminder that probable cause must ultimately connect to a particular statutory offense. An officer can rely on a different offense from the one first announced if the known facts objectively establish it, so the correct field question is not merely Did you cite the wrong subsection? but What actual offense do the known facts establish?

docs.title: 5. Treat ID as a separate legal question
docs.text:
Do not provide false identifying information. Penal Code § 148.9 separately criminalizes specified false/fictitious identification conduct during a lawful detention or arrest.

If an officer or employee asserts that identification is mandatory, identify the legal basis rather than assuming a universal California stop-and-identify or government-building sign-in rule. Sweep 014 confirms no general pedestrian carry-ID statute was located, while preserving as RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED the California § 148 consequence of refusing to identify during every otherwise lawful Terry detention. Citation, arrest, booking, driver, and specialized-facility rules can differ. See police-encounters.md.

docs.title: 6. If the encounter reaches a final arrest threat
docs.text:
A useful evidentiary question is:

Are you ordering me to leave under threat of arrest, and what law are you relying on?

If the person chooses to comply, they can make clear that compliance is under protest and not consent to the asserted legal basis. If the person chooses to remain, the risk changes substantially because an officer may arrest first and the legal merits may be litigated later.

The Field Guide's purpose is to help a person understand that choice and preserve the factual/legal record, not to pretend a correct legal argument guarantees that an arrest will not occur.

docs.title: What remains unresolved or facility-specific
docs.text:
This chapter now distinguishes completed research from genuinely unsettled boundaries.

Researched-Unresolved statewide edges:

  • whether an individualized prior exclusion, without another access change, makes otherwise generally open property not open to the general public under § 602(o); and
  • the separate detention-stage identification question described in police-encounters.md.

Facility/fact dependencies rather than statewide research gaps:

  • forum classification of a particular lobby, counter, library area, DMV, courthouse, or similar space;
  • visitor sign-in, badge, appointment, and ID conditions tied to a particular facility;
  • exact local/agency authority and delegation for a suspension;
  • specialized secured-area statutes/regulations;
  • exact protected interest and procedural safeguards for a particular exclusion; and
  • § 602.1(c)'s material-misrepresentation provision when that subsection is actually invoked.

Do not convert either a facility dependency or a Researched-Unresolved boundary into a categorical favorable answer.
