Canonical scenario ID: NC-COMPLAINT-01

Standing baseline: NC-STANDING-01 v1. Unless this scenario expressly changes a fact, the canonical standing facts remain in force. Complaint labels do not silently override those facts.

This national-core scenario addresses a recurring encounter that is structurally similar across jurisdictions even though the underlying trespass, disorderly-conduct, obstruction, false-report, and exclusion statutes vary by state.

The recurring pattern is:

A person is peacefully recording or observing from a place they believe they may lawfully be. A private citizen, employee, security worker, or government employee objects. The recorder may never have entered the disputed property, may have entered and already left when requested, may still be present after a request to leave, or may only have received prospective notice not to enter. The complainant calls police and characterizes the recorder as trespassing, hostile, escalating, disruptive, threatening, suspicious, or otherwise criminal. Police arrive while some or all of the encounter has been continuously recorded.

The national core supplies the Fourth Amendment, First Amendment, evidence-handling, and caller-reliability framework. Each jurisdiction overlay supplies the actual elements of trespass, disorderly conduct, obstruction/interference, false reporting, misuse of emergency services, and any local exclusion authority.

This scenario does not presume that the complainant lied, that the recorder is correct about the property boundary, or that police lack reasonable suspicion when they arrive. It requires those propositions to be tested rather than assumed.

docs.title: Core principle
docs.text:
A complaint is information to evaluate, not a legal conclusion.

The encounter must be reduced to:

exact location → alleged facts → source/reliability → actual offense elements → initial RS/PC → contradictory evidence → continuing RS/PC → disposition

Labels such as trespasser, hostile, escalating, disruptive, suspicious, or threatening should be translated into observable conduct before they are treated as evidence of an offense.

The question is not:

Did somebody use a crime-like word?

It is:

What did the caller say actually happened, how does the caller claim to know it, what offense could those facts satisfy, and what information did police possess when they acted?

docs.title: 1. Fix the physical location first
docs.text:
Property location can be outcome-determinative.

Document separately:

  • where the recorder was when the disputed conduct allegedly occurred;
  • whether the recorder ever crossed the relevant property boundary;
  • whether the place that visually resembles a public sidewalk is actually public right-of-way or privately owned frontage;
  • whether the recorder was inside an area open to the public;
  • whether the recorder had already left before police arrival;
  • where the recorder was standing when the complainant called;
  • where the recorder was standing when police made contact.

Do not silently convert:

person standing on public right-of-way adjacent to property

into:

person presently trespassing on that property.

Likewise, do not assume that an area is public property merely because members of the public commonly walk through it. Property ownership, public access, and public-forum status are separate questions.

docs.title: 2. “Trespassed” must be decomposed into four different factual postures
docs.text:
The phrase you have been trespassed is too ambiguous for legal analysis.

Every jurisdiction overlay must separately analyze at least these four postures.

docs.title: NC-COMPLAINT-01.A — Never entered the disputed property
docs.text:
The recorder remained outside the relevant property boundary.

Questions:

  • Does the state's asserted trespass offense require entry, occupation, presence, or remaining?
  • What facts support an inference that entry occurred?
  • Is the complainant describing actual location or merely using the label trespassing?
  • Is immediately available video or other objective evidence capable of resolving the boundary/location question?

A prospective warning not to enter does not retroactively establish that a prior trespass occurred.

docs.title: NC-COMPLAINT-01.B — Entered, then left when requested
docs.text:
The recorder entered an area but departed after a qualifying request to leave.

Questions:

  • Was the initial entry lawful or privileged?
  • Does the jurisdiction's offense require refusal/failure to leave after notice?
  • Did any completed offense occur before the request?
  • Was the request made by a person legally authorized to give it?
  • Does later prospective exclusion have separate legal requirements?

Leaving when asked does not establish a universal nationwide defense to every trespass offense. It means the jurisdiction must identify what offense, if any, was complete under its own law.

docs.title: NC-COMPLAINT-01.C — Currently remains after a request to leave
docs.text:
The recorder is presently on the disputed property after someone has requested departure.

Questions:

  • Is the location actually the complainant's/government's property?
  • Is the area open to the public?
  • Was the requester authorized?
  • What statutory/regulatory provision governs remaining?
  • Are additional elements required, such as intent, interference, notice, restricted-area status, or lack of lawful business?
  • If government property is involved, what constitutional/forum restrictions apply to the exclusion?

This posture creates materially different immediate risk from a person who is already off the property.

docs.title: NC-COMPLAINT-01.D — Prospective no-entry notice only
docs.text:
The recorder is outside the property and is told not to enter or return in the future.

Questions:

  • Who has authority to issue the notice?
  • What property/areas and duration does it cover?
  • Does state law make prior notice independently relevant to a later offense?
  • Does government property require process, cause, tailoring, or constitutional review before a prospective exclusion?
  • Is police merely conveying a private owner's instruction, or invoking an enforceable statutory exclusion process?
  • Does communicating or documenting the notice require the recorder's identity at all?
  • If police request or demand identification, what separate statute, detention rule, citation/arrest procedure, booking rule, or other authority creates any legal duty to identify?
  • Can the notice be communicated to an unidentified person even if later enforcement would require proof that the same person received it?

A prospective notice is not proof of a completed past trespass. The existence of a notice also does not by itself answer whether the recipient has a legal duty to identify; the jurisdiction must identify independent authority for any compulsory identification requirement.

docs.title: NC-COMPLAINT-01.M — Conditional access / derivative trespass
docs.text:
This branch applies when an otherwise lawful or arguably lawful presence becomes the subject of a removal/trespass sequence because continued access is conditioned on ceasing expressive or information-gathering activity.

Recurring pattern:

record/speak/observe → "stop the activity or leave" → activity continues → exclusion/removal order → remaining or reentry → trespass enforcement

The branch does not presume that the underlying activity is protected everywhere or that every removal order is invalid. It prevents the later trespass label from erasing the legal question that generated the duty to leave.

Questions:

  • What exact activity triggered the conditional-access demand?
  • Was the demand expressly conditional, such as stop recording or leave, or does the chronology otherwise connect the restriction to the activity?
  • What rule, policy, statute, regulation, property authority, forum doctrine, or other law allegedly authorized the underlying restriction?
  • Was any independent misconduct identified before the exclusion order, such as obstruction, actual disruption, restricted-area entry, threat, safety interference, or another supplied fact?
  • If government property is involved, what forum/access and First Amendment rules govern conditioning continued access on ceasing the activity?
  • If private property is involved, what actual property/exclusion authority applies, and where was the observer physically located?
  • Was the removal/exclusion order itself lawful under the applicable authority?
  • If the person remained or later reentered, what distinct trespass elements then apply?
  • Did police or later decisionmakers analyze only the downstream refusal-to-leave fact while ignoring the upstream restriction/exclusion that created it?
  • What evidence preserves the chronology: video, policy text, body camera, incident report, written exclusion notice, or witness account?

National-core rule: preserve and analyze the entire causal chain. A downstream trespass allegation does not make the legality of the upstream recording/speech restriction or exclusion analytically irrelevant.

docs.title: 3. Convert characterization into alleged facts
docs.text:
When a caller says the recorder is:

  • trespassing;
  • hostile;
  • escalating;
  • disruptive;
  • threatening;
  • suspicious;
  • harassing;
  • refusing to cooperate;

the research/field record should ask what observable conduct supports the characterization.

Examples:

hostile may mean:

  • spoke critically;
  • raised voice;
  • used profanity;
  • approached someone;
  • made a threat;
  • made no threat but refused to stop recording.

Those are legally different facts.

disruptive may mean:

  • interrupted a government proceeding;
  • blocked a service line;
  • interfered with staff work;
  • caused other people to complain;
  • merely continued recording despite objections.

Again, those are different facts.

The national rule is allegation-to-elements analysis. The state overlay determines which facts satisfy the actual offense.

docs.title: 4. Caller and 911 reliability are part of the Fourth Amendment analysis
docs.text: A call to police can contribute to reasonable suspicion or probable cause, but the fact that information traveled through 911 does not make every allegation automatically reliable.

docs.title: Florida v. J.L., 529 U.S. 266 (2000)
docs.text:
The Supreme Court held that a bare anonymous tip that a person possessed a gun lacked sufficient indicia of reliability to justify a stop and frisk. The tip accurately identified a person at a location, but reliability as to identity did not establish reliability as to the alleged illegality.

Source:

https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/529/266

docs.title: Navarette v. California, 572 U.S. 393 (2014)
docs.text:
The Court found reasonable suspicion where the 911 report had materially stronger reliability indicators, including a claimed eyewitness account, close temporal connection, and features of the 911 system that reduced anonymity/accountability concerns.

Source:

https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/12-9490

National-core rule: assess the totality of circumstances supporting the caller's basis of knowledge and reliability. Do not use either slogan:

  • 911 call = reasonable suspicion; or
  • caller allegation can never justify a stop.

For an identifiable employee, citizen, or security worker who personally claims to have observed conduct, the reliability analysis may be stronger than for an unknown anonymous caller. The underlying factual allegation still must matter to an actual offense.

docs.title: 5. Trespass probable cause remains an offense-elements inquiry
District of Columbia v. Wesby, 583 U.S. 48 (2018)
docs.text:
The Supreme Court's unlawful-entry analysis illustrates that probable cause turns on the totality of circumstances, including facts bearing on whether suspects knew or should have known they lacked permission. Officers need not accept a suspect's innocent explanation at face value when other circumstances support a contrary inference.

Source:

https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/15-1485

National-core use: Wesby does not create one nationwide substantive trespass offense. It demonstrates the Fourth Amendment method: identify the actual offense, consider the totality of facts relevant to its elements, and evaluate what a prudent officer could reasonably infer.

Each state must therefore map NC-COMPLAINT-01 to its own trespass elements.

docs.title: 6. Police do not have to become “Dick Tracy”
docs.text: The national core must preserve the limiting principle.

docs.title: Baker v. McCollan, 443 U.S. 137 (1979)
docs.text:
In the context of custody under a facially valid warrant, the Supreme Court rejected a constitutional requirement that officials independently investigate every claim of innocence or perform an error-free investigation.

Sources:

https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/443/137

https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-443/pdf/USREPORTS-443-137.pdf

This prevents the Field Guide from claiming:

Police must exhaust every possible lead, prove guilt on scene, or investigate every defense before acting.

But Baker does not answer every warrantless-arrest or immediately-available-evidence problem. Federal circuits have expressly distinguished an obligation not to disregard material exculpatory information from a duty to conduct an exhaustive investigation.

docs.title: 7. Immediately available exculpatory evidence
docs.text:
For this scenario, immediately available exculpatory evidence means objective evidence that:

  1. directly bears on a material factual predicate of the suspected offense;
  2. is known to the officer or affirmatively identified to the officer;
  3. can be accessed with little or no additional investigative burden;
  4. is sufficiently specific that the officer can understand what allegation it allegedly contradicts; and
  5. could materially undermine reasonable suspicion or probable cause if it shows what the person claims.

The strongest recurring example is continuous contemporaneous video.

This term does not mean every video is necessarily exculpatory, complete, authentic, dispositive, or required to be viewed in every circumstance.

docs.title: 8. Multi-circuit federal authority: “no exhaustive investigation” is not “ignore what is in front of you”
docs.text: These circuit cases are not universally binding nationwide. They are preserved in the national core because they illuminate a recurring federal Fourth Amendment question and become binding/persuasive according to the applicable circuit.

docs.title: Eighth Circuit — Kuehl v. Burtis, 173 F.3d 646 (8th Cir. 1999)
docs.text:
Kuehl states that an officer contemplating arrest is not free to disregard plainly exculpatory evidence even when incriminating evidence, standing alone, could suggest probable cause. The Eighth Circuit emphasized the totality of all information and distinguished a reasonably thorough investigation from requiring a mini-trial.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/173/646/548042/

Field significance: this is one of the clearest formulations that “probable cause existed if I look only at the incriminating side” is not the complete inquiry.

docs.title: Eleventh Circuit — Kingsland v. City of Miami, 382 F.3d 1220 (11th Cir. 2004)
docs.text:
Kingsland explicitly distinguished the rule that officers need not independently investigate every asserted claim of innocence from the narrower problem of turning a blind eye to immediately available exculpatory information. It also rejected selective investigation as a permissible way to manufacture or preserve probable cause.

Sources:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/382/1220/570494/

Eleventh Circuit opinion archive entry: https://media.ca11.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/

Field significance: this is a particularly useful response to the overbroad slogan police don't have to investigate your innocence.

docs.title: Tenth Circuit — Baptiste v. J.C. Penney Co., 147 F.3d 1252 (10th Cir. 1998)
docs.text:
Police responded to a shoplifting allegation, viewed surveillance footage recording the very conduct the security guards characterized as theft, and nevertheless relied on the guards' interpretation. The Tenth Circuit held the video had to be considered independently in the totality of circumstances and concluded probable cause was lacking.

In footnote 8, the court stated that, absent exceptional circumstances, when a videotape of the conduct at issue is known and readily accessible to an officer investigating the alleged crime, the officer must view it rather than delegate the probable-cause determination to the accuser.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/147/1252/634968/

docs.title: Later Tenth Circuit treatment — Craft v. White, No. 19-2213 (10th Cir. Jan. 14, 2021) (unpublished)
docs.text:
In an unpublished Order and Judgment, the Tenth Circuit characterized the categorical video language in Baptiste footnote 8 as dictum and declined to find a clearly established duty where the officer was not at the scene, did not possess the video, and sought a warrant rather than making the same kind of immediate warrantless arrest.

Official source:

https://www.ca10.uscourts.gov/opinion/19-2213

Field significance: Craft is useful later Tenth Circuit treatment but is not a published precedential limitation on Baptiste. It reinforces why the national core should not misstate Baptiste footnote 8 as a Supreme Court rule or universal categorical duty.

docs.title: Ninth Circuit — Yousefian v. City of Glendale, 779 F.3d 1010 (9th Cir. 2015)
docs.text:
The Ninth Circuit states that an officer may not ignore exculpatory evidence that would negate probable cause. On the particular facts, however, the suspect's self-defense account did not negate probable cause because victim/witness evidence still supported the assault allegation.

Official source:

https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2015/03/05/12-57269.pdf

Field significance: contradictory evidence is not automatically dispositive. The question is whether the evidence actually negates or materially dissipates the basis for probable cause.

docs.title: Ninth Circuit — United States v. Holcomb, No. 23-469 (9th Cir. July 17, 2026)
docs.text:
In a search context, the Ninth Circuit held that probable cause dissipated after officers discovered and viewed video showing that the alleged crime described in the warrant almost certainly had not occurred. The opinion reiterates that officers may not disregard facts tending to dissipate probable cause.

Official source:

https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2026/07/17/23-469.pdf

Field significance: when officers actually view objective video that undermines the alleged offense, probable cause is not frozen at the moment it was first established.

docs.title: 9. What the national core can and cannot presently say
Supported national propositions
docs.text:
The national core may safely state:

  • reasonable suspicion and probable cause depend on the totality of facts known to police, not merely a complainant's legal label;
  • caller/tip reliability is relevant to whether an accusation supports a seizure;
  • police need not perform an exhaustive investigation or eliminate every possible innocent explanation before acting;
  • federal appellate courts in multiple circuits hold that plainly or immediately available exculpatory information can be material to probable cause and may not simply be disregarded under the circumstances addressed by those cases;
  • probable cause is capable of dissipating when later information materially undermines its basis;
  • objective video can be especially important when it records the same conduct the complainant is characterizing as criminal.

docs.title: Researched-Unresolved national proposition
docs.text:
The national core should not presently state:

Every officer in every jurisdiction has a categorical constitutional duty to watch every exculpatory video a suspect offers before detention or arrest.

No Supreme Court case located in this review states that rule, and the circuit authorities differ in facts and formulation. An unpublished Tenth Circuit order, Craft v. White, later described Baptiste's broad video-viewing footnote as dictum in a materially different warrant case.

For qualification purposes, the universal categorical-duty proposition is Researched-Unresolved, while each circuit overlay must determine what binding rule applies there.

docs.title: 10. Field articulation: identify the proposition, not merely “I have video”
docs.text:
The useful field move is not to demand a generalized investigation.

A person can identify:

  1. the allegation;
  2. the exact fact the evidence addresses;
  3. the continuity/time span of the evidence;
  4. its immediate availability; and
  5. the limited scope of the offer.

docs.title: General field formulation
docs.text:
When the recording actually covers the relevant period and supports the statement, use the disputed factual predicate as X rather than merely repeating a legal label:

The allegation is X. I have continuous video from before the call through your arrival showing that X did not occur. It is queued and I am offering to play that specific recording for you. I do not consent to any broader search of my device.

Replace X with the concrete alleged fact whenever possible. For example, prefer:

The allegation is that I entered the property.

over:

The allegation is that I trespassed.

The first identifies the factual predicate the recording can objectively confirm or contradict; the second may merely repeat somebody else's legal conclusion.

A disruption variant could be:

The allegation is that I was yelling and disrupting operations. I have continuous video from before the call through your arrival showing the entire interaction, including the volume and content of the conversation. It is queued and I am offering to play that specific recording for you. I do not consent to any broader search of my device.

If the officer declines:

For the record, I offered you continuous video that directly addresses the allegation and you declined to review it. What facts are you relying on now, and am I free to leave?

These are evidence-preservation formulations, not magic words and not guarantees against detention or arrest.

Avoid unnecessarily converting the encounter into a case-law recital. Naming Kuehl, Kingsland, Baptiste, Yousefian, or Holcomb may be useful when appropriate, but identifying exactly what the objective evidence proves is usually more important than reciting a citation.

docs.title: 11. Evidence-offered checkpoint
docs.text:
Every jurisdiction's encounter tree must preserve this event.

material allegation
        |
objective contradictory evidence exists?
        |
        +-- no --> continue ordinary RS/PC analysis
        |
        +-- yes
             |
      officer informed of:
      - exact evidence
      - exact allegation addressed
      - immediate availability
             |
        +----+----+
        |         |
   reviewed     declined/not reviewed
        |         |
 what did it    why declined?
 actually show? what other facts support RS/PC?
        |         |
        +----+----+
             |
     does RS/PC remain?

The research record should capture:

  • what evidence was offered;
  • when it was offered;
  • what proposition the person said it established;
  • whether the officer viewed it;
  • whether the officer declined;
  • any reason given for declining;
  • what other inculpatory facts the officer identified;
  • whether the asserted offense changed;
  • whether detention continued;
  • whether arrest occurred.

docs.title: 12. Showing a phone does not imply consent to search the phone
docs.text:
When the evidence is on a phone or camera, the Fourth Amendment/device-search question remains separate.

A field user may clarify:

I am offering only this identified recording. I do not consent to any broader search of my device.

The national scenario does not prescribe whether a person should physically hand over an unlocked device. That choice can create practical and legal risks and should be analyzed separately under the applicable device-search doctrine.

The key evidence checkpoint is that the relevant recording was identified and made reasonably available, not that the person surrendered unrestricted access to the device.

docs.title: Edge case — officer threatens or seeks a warrant for the recording device
docs.text:
A less common variation may occur when a person identifies exculpatory video and the officer responds by threatening to seek, or stating an intent to seek, a warrant for the phone/camera instead of reviewing the specifically offered recording.

Do not infer from the warrant reference alone that the officer acted unlawfully, retaliated, or intimidated the person. A lawful warrant can be sought when the governing requirements are satisfied.

Preserve the event because it raises separate questions:

  • what completed or suspected offense supposedly supplies probable cause;
  • what facts support that probable cause after considering information tending to dispel it;
  • what nexus allegedly connects evidence of that offense to the device;
  • what data/device scope the officer proposes to search or seize;
  • whether the person was offering only a particular recording;
  • whether the warrant statement was made in response to that limited offer;
  • whether the statement was used to seek consent, device surrender, identification, or other compliance;
  • whether the officer reviewed or declined the specifically identified exculpatory recording before escalating to broader device process.

The existence of a recording can help establish that relevant evidence may be stored on a device. It does not by itself establish that the underlying suspected crime occurred.

That distinction should remain explicit:

Crime probable cause asks whether there is adequate reason to believe the offense occurred. Evidence nexus asks why evidence of that offense is likely to be found in the place or device to be searched. A nexus cannot substitute for crime probable cause.

In Warden v. Hayden, 387 U.S. 294 (1967), the Supreme Court explained that evidentiary material must have a nexus to criminal behavior and that probable cause for evidence concerns reason to believe the evidence sought will aid a particular apprehension or conviction.

Source:

https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/387/294

For phones, Riley v. California, 573 U.S. 373 (2014), holds that police generally must obtain a warrant before searching digital information on a seized cell phone, subject to recognized case-specific exceptions such as exigent circumstances.

Source:

https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/13-132

A statement such as I recorded the entire incident may therefore support a nexus between a particular recording and the incident while the recording itself may simultaneously be exculpatory and undermine the factual basis for the suspected offense. Those are separate Fourth Amendment questions.

This remains an edge-case evidence checkpoint rather than a required standalone qualification branch unless later research shows it is sufficiently recurring or doctrinally distinct to warrant promotion.

docs.title: 13. First Amendment retaliation overlay
docs.text: If police action is allegedly motivated by recording, criticism, refusal to answer consensual questions, or other protected expression, a First Amendment retaliation issue may arise.

docs.title: Nieves v. Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391 (2019)
docs.text:
The Supreme Court generally made the existence of probable cause a barrier to a retaliatory-arrest claim, subject to a narrow exception involving objective evidence that similarly situated people not engaged in the same protected speech were not arrested.

Source:

https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/17-1174

Field significance: the probable-cause analysis is not merely a Fourth Amendment side issue. Whether the alleged trespass/disorderly conduct actually supplied probable cause can materially affect a later retaliation claim.

The national scenario must therefore preserve:

  • protected activity;
  • statements suggesting retaliatory motive;
  • alleged offense;
  • actual probable-cause facts;
  • immediately available contradictory evidence;
  • comparator/differential-enforcement evidence where it exists.

docs.title: 14. False accusations and false reports remain primarily a state overlay
docs.text:
The national scenario records whether a caller made factual statements that objective evidence appears to contradict.

It does not automatically label the caller a criminal or state that a false 911 call is a felony.

Each jurisdiction must research:

  • knowingly false crime reports;
  • knowingly false emergency reports;
  • misuse of 911/emergency systems;
  • obstruction or interference statutes;
  • enhanced penalties tied to injury, emergency response, bias, or other aggravating facts;
  • required mental state;
  • who qualifies as the recipient of the false report;
  • whether the statement is a factual assertion or merely a mistaken legal conclusion.

Distinguish:

“He is trespassing.”

which may be an incorrect legal characterization,

from:

“I personally watched him enter our lobby, ordered him out five times, and he is still inside.”

when contemporaneous video may show that those factual assertions never happened.

A state false-report analysis should focus on knowingly false material facts, statutory elements, and proof of the required mental state—not merely the fact that the complainant disliked recording or reached the wrong legal conclusion.

docs.title: 15. Canonical branch matrix
docs.text:
Every jurisdiction qualification matrix must map these branches.

Branch ID Required question NC-COMPLAINT-01.A Was the recorder ever on the disputed property, and what law applies if not? NC-COMPLAINT-01.B What is the legal effect of entering but leaving when requested? NC-COMPLAINT-01.C What law governs currently remaining after a request to leave? NC-COMPLAINT-01.D What is the effect and permissible scope of prospective no-entry notice, and what separate authority governs any claimed duty to identify for that notice? NC-COMPLAINT-01.E What factual allegations and actual offense elements support initial detention? NC-COMPLAINT-01.F What caller/tip reliability rule applies? NC-COMPLAINT-01.G What binding circuit rule governs offered/known exculpatory evidence? NC-COMPLAINT-01.H When can reasonable suspicion or probable cause dissipate? NC-COMPLAINT-01.I How does immediately available video affect the continuing detention/arrest analysis? NC-COMPLAINT-01.J What First Amendment retaliation rule applies? NC-COMPLAINT-01.K What state/local false-report or emergency-call laws apply to knowingly false factual allegations? NC-COMPLAINT-01.L What records should be preserved/requested after the encounter: 911 audio, CAD/dispatch, body camera, CCTV, incident reports, exclusion notices, complaints, and related evidence? NC-COMPLAINT-01.M When access is conditioned on stopping recording/speech/observation, was the underlying restriction and resulting exclusion lawful before downstream trespass enforcement is analyzed?

A jurisdiction cannot mark this encounter complete by researching only its basic trespass statute.

docs.title: 16. Records and post-incident evidence
docs.text:
This scenario should automatically queue preservation/retrieval of evidence likely to establish what information existed at each stage:

  • 911 audio and transcript where available;
  • CAD/dispatch entries;
  • caller identity where lawfully disclosable;
  • body-worn camera;
  • dash camera;
  • facility CCTV;
  • private/security CCTV if obtainable;
  • officer notes/reports;
  • security/incident reports;
  • written trespass or exclusion notices;
  • property maps, assessor records, easements/right-of-way records where boundary is disputed;
  • employee/security policy;
  • radio traffic;
  • citations/arrest paperwork;
  • complaint/investigation records where applicable.

The analytical purpose is to reconstruct:

what was alleged → what police were told → what police observed → what contradictory evidence was offered → what police reviewed → what police relied upon → what action followed

docs.title: 17. Scenario safeguards
docs.text:
This scenario assumes the ordinary standing facts unless a specific variant says otherwise:

  • no threats;
  • no assault;
  • no intentional obstruction;
  • no fighting;
  • no deliberate interference with emergency activity;
  • no intentional targeting of uninvolved private persons;
  • no entry into clearly restricted areas;
  • no intentional entry/remain/filming into child-designated areas;
  • normal conversational conduct unless the evidence establishes otherwise.

New facts can change the legal analysis.

The scenario also does not presume that remaining on property after a disputed removal order is tactically advisable. Legal validity, arrest risk, and field strategy remain separate questions.

docs.title: 18. Authority classification for qualification
docs.text:
For any jurisdiction:

  • U.S. Supreme Court authority is controlling on federal constitutional propositions.
  • The jurisdiction's own federal circuit authority is binding on federal district courts in that circuit and must be identified separately.
  • Other-circuit cases such as Kuehl, Kingsland, or Baptiste are persuasive unless they are from the applicable circuit.
  • State appellate authority controls/persuades according to that state's hierarchy on state-law offense elements.
  • Facility policy or a complainant's characterization is evidence of what was asserted, not self-validating law.

Do not flatten this research into a single nationwide slogan.

docs.title: 19. Field Guide shorthand
docs.text:
The project may use this shorthand internally and in field-oriented summaries:

No duty to become a detective does not mean permission to ignore plainly material evidence already in front of the officer.

That sentence is an explanatory synthesis, not a quotation from one controlling nationwide case. The underlying authority must still be cited by circuit.

A second useful shorthand is:

“Trespassed” is not one legal event. Ask whether the allegation concerns prior entry, refusal to leave, current presence, or future notice.

Again, the state overlay supplies the actual offense.

docs.title: Lawful-Vantage Observation and Recording — Matters Exposed to Public View
docs.text:
Canonical scenario ID: NC-VANTAGE-01

Standing baseline: NC-STANDING-01 v1. Unless this scenario expressly changes a fact, the canonical standing facts remain in force. The lawful-vantage scenario adds vantage/method facts; it does not import jurisdiction-specific privacy, property, audio, or exclusion law.

This national-core scenario addresses a recurring problem that is broader than police recording:

A person is lawfully present at a particular vantage point and observes or records people, property, activity, vehicles, documents, displays, or interiors that are visible from that location. The subject may be government or private. Someone objects to the observation or recording, claims the material is private/confidential/sensitive, demands that recording stop, demands that the observer move or leave, or calls police/security.

The scenario supplies a common decision tree. It does not create a categorical rule that everything visible may always be recorded, and it does not convert private property into public property merely because it can be seen from a public place.

Each jurisdiction overlay must identify the authority governing the actual observation/recording method, location, privacy interest, audio capture, exclusion authority, and any enforcement action.

docs.title: Core principle
docs.text:
Start with the observer's lawful vantage and method, then identify any independently applicable restriction.

Do not begin with either slogan:

  • I can see it, therefore I can always record it; or
  • the subject objects, therefore observation/recording is unlawful.

The analytical spine is:

observer's location/right to remain → subject/activity exposed to view → observation/recording method → claimed privacy/confidentiality/restriction → governing authority → enforcement/exclusion consequence

Government confidentiality duties, private confidentiality duties, property rights, privacy rights, and the observer's conduct are separate propositions. One does not silently establish another.

docs.title: 1. Canonical branch matrix
docs.text:
Every jurisdiction qualification matrix must map these branches.

Branch ID Required question NC-VANTAGE-01.A Is the observer lawfully present at the vantage point, and what authority governs the right to remain there? NC-VANTAGE-01.B What rules govern ordinary visual observation, photography, or video of people, property, activity, vehicles, or interiors exposed to ordinary view from that lawful vantage? NC-VANTAGE-01.C How do transparent windows, windshields, doors, or other transparent barriers affect the analysis when the observer does not cross, open, touch, manipulate, or defeat the barrier? NC-VANTAGE-01.D What law applies when documents, screens, records, identifiers, or other potentially sensitive/confidential information are left visible from the lawful vantage? NC-VANTAGE-01.E What changes when the observer physically enters, reaches into, touches, moves, opens, manipulates, defeats a barrier/covering, or otherwise intrudes beyond ordinary observation? NC-VANTAGE-01.F What separate rules apply to technological enhancement, audio capture/confidential communications, voyeuristic/privacy offenses, or other methods that may implicate interests not presented by ordinary unaided visual observation? NC-VANTAGE-01.G If an owner, employee, official, security worker, or officer demands that observation/recording stop, that the observer move, or that the observer leave, what independent authority supports that restriction or exclusion and what property/forum facts control?

A jurisdiction cannot mark this scenario complete by answering only whether the observer possessed a camera.

docs.title: 2. Fix the vantage point before analyzing the subject
docs.text:
Document separately:

  • the exact location from which observation/recording occurred;
  • ownership and access status of that location;
  • whether the observer had a right to remain there at that time;
  • whether a boundary, barrier, restricted area, or access condition was crossed;
  • whether the observer touched or manipulated property;
  • whether the observer changed vantage after an instruction or restriction; and
  • whether the subject was government, private, mixed, or uncertain.

Do not infer that a subject controls the observer's location merely because the subject can be seen from there.

Likewise, do not infer that lawful presence at the vantage point resolves every separate privacy, audio, technology, or conduct restriction.

docs.title: 3. Public/private subject neutrality
docs.text:
The same decision tree applies when the subject is:

  • police or other public officials;
  • government vehicles;
  • government offices or facilities;
  • private businesses;
  • private vehicles;
  • storefronts or office windows;
  • documents/screens visible from outside;
  • mixed public/private operations; or
  • another category supplied by the facts.

The subject's public or private status can change the applicable authority, but it does not change the need to identify:

  1. the observer's location;
  2. the method of observation/recording;
  3. the specific claimed restriction; and
  4. the authority supporting that restriction.

docs.title: 4. Transparent barriers are facts, not magic words
docs.text:
A window, windshield, glass door, or similar transparent barrier creates facts that must be preserved:

  • what was actually visible without crossing the barrier;
  • whether curtains, tint, privacy film, blinds, covers, positioning, or other shielding existed;
  • whether the observer remained on the lawful side of the barrier;
  • whether the observer opened, moved, touched, pressed against, reached through, or otherwise manipulated anything;
  • whether zoom, magnification, directional equipment, or another enhanced method was used; and
  • whether audio was also captured.

The jurisdiction overlay determines the legal consequence of those facts.

docs.title: 5. Visible sensitive/confidential information requires proposition separation
docs.text:
When a government employee, business, or other person leaves potentially sensitive information visible, preserve at least these distinct questions:

  1. Was the observer lawfully present?
  2. Was the information ordinarily visible from that vantage?
  3. Did the observer use ordinary observation/recording or an enhanced/intrusive method?
  4. What confidentiality/privacy duty, if any, binds the person or entity displaying the information?
  5. What law, if any, independently restricts the observer's acquisition, recording, retention, use, or publication?
  6. Does an asserted confidentiality rule regulate the custodian/employee, the observer, or both?
  7. Did anyone attempt to convert the custodian's failure to shield information into an offense or removal basis for the observer without identifying independent authority?

Do not assume that a confidentiality duty imposed on a custodian automatically transfers to every observer. Do not assume the opposite either; the overlay must identify the actual law.

docs.title: 6. Ordinary observation versus intrusion/manipulation
docs.text:
This scenario deliberately distinguishes passive observation from conduct that changes the physical or technological facts.

Examples requiring a fresh branch analysis include:

  • entering private or restricted property;
  • opening a door, compartment, drawer, gate, cover, or vehicle;
  • touching, moving, repositioning, or manipulating property;
  • reaching through an opening or into a vehicle/building;
  • bypassing or defeating a privacy/security barrier;
  • accessing a computer, device, network, account, or stored data;
  • using technology that materially changes what could otherwise be perceived from the lawful vantage;
  • intercepting communications; or
  • engaging in conduct covered by a specific privacy/voyeurism law.

The standing scenario does not silently add any of those facts.

docs.title: 7. Objection does not finish the legal analysis
docs.text:
When someone says:

  • stop filming;
  • you cannot look in our windows;
  • that information is confidential;
  • you cannot film this vehicle;
  • move away;
  • leave; or
  • we are calling police;

record the statement, but identify the actual authority separately.

For a government actor or government-controlled location, the analysis may require forum/access doctrine, recording protections, content/viewpoint analysis, time/place/manner or forum-specific tests, privacy/security interests, and exclusion/removal authority.

For a private owner or business, property/exclusion authority and the observer's actual location remain distinct. A demand concerning private property does not silently establish control over neighboring public property.

Police/security response must preserve the exact claimed location, conduct, restriction, and legal basis rather than translating objection into the conclusion trespass or illegal recording.

docs.title: 8. Relationship to conditional access and derivative trespass
docs.text:
If the sequence becomes:

record/observe → "stop recording or leave" → continued recording → removal/exclusion → trespass enforcement

use NC-COMPLAINT-01.M in addition to this scenario.

The later trespass question does not erase the need to test the underlying restriction/exclusion that created the alleged duty to leave.

docs.title: 9. Qualification rule
docs.text:
A jurisdiction overlay qualifies this scenario only when it can responsibly distinguish:

  • lawful vantage from unlawful presence;
  • ordinary visual observation/recording from physical intrusion or manipulation;
  • transparent-barrier observation from barrier defeat;
  • visible sensitive information from unlawfully accessed information;
  • visual recording from separately regulated audio/interception;
  • ordinary observation from technology-enhanced privacy intrusion where material;
  • private exclusion authority from government/forum restrictions; and
  • objection to observation from an independently lawful enforcement basis.

A genuinely unsettled proposition may be Researched-Unresolved. An unresearched material branch is a Gap.

docs.title: 10. Change triggers
docs.text:
Re-run the affected branch when facts change, including:

  • the observer moves onto different property;
  • access hours end;
  • the observer crosses or manipulates a barrier;
  • the method changes from ordinary viewing to enhanced technology;
  • audio capture becomes material;
  • a privacy/confidentiality statute is identified;
  • a government restriction or facility rule is invoked;
  • a private owner revokes permission on property the observer actually occupies;
  • police detain or arrest the observer; or
  • publication/use of captured information creates a separate legal question.

The scenario is an analytical scaffold, not a guarantee of outcome.

docs.title: Canonical Standing Scenario
docs.text:
Canonical scenario ID: NC-STANDING-01 Version: 1

The Field Guide uses one jurisdiction-neutral factual baseline so legal analysis tests the government's asserted authority without inventing unrelated misconduct.

This page contains facts and methodology only. It does not import any state's statutes, any circuit-specific doctrine, or any jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion into the national core.

Each jurisdiction overlay must map these facts to its own constitutional, statutory, regulatory, and case-law rules.

docs.title: 1. Baseline facts
docs.text:
Unless a chapter or scenario expressly changes a fact, assume the person being analyzed:

  1. begins in a place and specific area they may lawfully be, during a time when that area is open or otherwise available to them;
  2. has not entered an employee-only, secured, closed, screened, or otherwise restricted area unless the scenario expressly supplies that fact;
  3. is peacefully observing, photographing, filming, recording, asking questions, requesting records, criticizing government, or otherwise gathering information;
  4. is not blocking doors, counters, queues, sidewalks, roadways, traffic, or another person's movement;
  5. is not physically interfering with employees, officers, emergency personnel, visitors, or members of the public;
  6. is not touching, crowding, closely following, or entering another person's personal space;
  7. is not threatening anyone, fighting, or challenging anyone to fight;
  8. is not creating unreasonable noise or intentionally shouting over government business;
  9. is not intentionally obstructing or intimidating employees or people transacting business with a public agency;
  10. is not willfully resisting, delaying, or obstructing an officer through conduct independent of the activity being analyzed;
  11. is not participating in a riot, violent unlawful assembly, or other group misconduct unless a scenario expressly supplies that fact;
  12. has no additional misconduct silently added to the scenario; if a legal conclusion depends on another act, omission, intent, location, status, or circumstance, that fact must be expressly supplied;
  13. is not intentionally targeting uninvolved private individuals or their personal information;
  14. is not assumed to possess or carry an identification card, press credential, license, membership card, or other credential merely because they are present in public;
  15. does not initiate confrontational interaction with employees, officers, visitors, or private individuals; if another person voluntarily approaches, questions, criticizes, follows, or argues with the person, that choice to engage is not silently converted into misconduct by the person being analyzed; and
  16. when observing or recording through a window, windshield, door, opening, or other boundary, does not cross, open, touch, move, manipulate, reach through, defeat a covering or barrier, access a device/system, or otherwise physically alter the vantage unless the scenario expressly supplies that fact.

These are starting facts, not immunity rules.

For example, lawful initial presence does not decide whether a later restriction or order to leave is lawful. A later change in location, behavior, access status, emergency conditions, or government authority restarts the relevant branch.

docs.title: 2. Protected or disputed activity is not silently converted into misconduct
docs.text:
The person may:

  • criticize government;
  • ask officials to identify legal authority;
  • decline consensual conversation;
  • decline consent to a search;
  • request public records;
  • continue recording while remaining in the same physical location; or
  • disagree with an employee or officer.

Those facts are not silently converted into obstruction, intimidation, disturbance, trespass, interference, threat, or disorderly conduct.

Whether the activity is legally protected in the particular place and circumstances remains a legal question for the applicable jurisdiction, not a baseline fact.

docs.title: 3. Another person's reaction is not silently attributed to the person being analyzed
docs.text:
A government employee, contractor, security worker, visitor, or private individual may become:

  • uncomfortable;
  • angry;
  • offended;
  • argumentative;
  • confrontational; or
  • fearful.

That reaction is evidence of the encounter. It does not by itself establish what the person being analyzed did.

The guide therefore must not reason backward from:

someone became upset

to:

the person must have been obstructing, threatening, trespassing, harassing, intimidating, disturbing the peace, or disrupting government business.

The applicable law must still be matched to observable conduct.

docs.title: 4. Allegation-to-Elements Check
docs.text:
A recurring enforcement failure occurs when another person's reaction is converted into an objective-sounding accusation:

peaceful activity → objection or anger → "harassment," "disruption," "interference," "intimidation," "hostility," "suspicious behavior," or "disturbance" → government enforcement

Those labels are claims to test, not facts to inherit.

When a conclusion-like label is asserted, record the underlying observable facts:

  • who approached whom;
  • who followed whom, if anyone;
  • exact location and property boundary;
  • distance and physical positioning;
  • exact words and volume;
  • whether anyone blocked movement, access, or government business;
  • whether the person attempted to disengage;
  • what rule or offense was identified;
  • what element each alleged fact is supposed to satisfy;
  • what the caller, employee, witness, officer, or video actually establishes; and
  • what contemporaneous evidence bears on the claim.

This project calls that workflow the Allegation-to-Elements Check.

The phrase is project methodology, not a freestanding legal doctrine.

docs.title: 5. Identification baseline is factual, not a nationwide legal rule
docs.text:
The standing scenario does not assume that the person carries physical identification or a special credential.

That does not establish a nationwide rule that identification can never be required.

A jurisdiction overlay must separately analyze:

  • consensual requests for identification;
  • detention-stage duties, if any;
  • driver or licensed-activity duties;
  • citation/release procedures;
  • arrest and booking;
  • specialized facilities;
  • false identification;
  • physical production of a document;
  • searches for identification; and
  • administrative access conditions.

docs.title: 6. Lawful-vantage baseline
docs.text:
When the issue is observation or recording from a lawful vantage, assume unless expressly changed:

  • the person remains on the lawful side of any boundary;
  • ordinary visual observation does not involve touching or manipulating property;
  • a transparent barrier is not opened, moved, defeated, or crossed;
  • no device/system is accessed;
  • no hidden area is physically exposed by the observer; and
  • technological enhancement, audio capture, and publication are separate facts rather than silently included.

Use NC-VANTAGE-01 — Lawful-Vantage Observation and Recording / Matters Exposed to Public View for the detailed branch structure.

This baseline does not create the legal rule that everything visible may always be recorded.

docs.title: 7. Complaint-driven police-response variant
docs.text:
Use NC-COMPLAINT-01 — Complaint-Driven Police Encounter / Disputed Trespass and Immediately Available Exculpatory Evidence when a private citizen, employee, security worker, or government employee calls police and characterizes the person as trespassing, hostile, escalating, disruptive, threatening, suspicious, or otherwise unlawful.

The standing baseline does not silently adopt the caller's characterization.

The complaint-driven scenario separately preserves whether the person:

  1. never entered the disputed property;
  2. entered but left when requested;
  3. currently remains after a request to leave; or
  4. received only prospective no-entry notice.

It also preserves whether contemporaneous video or other objective evidence directly addresses a disputed factual predicate and whether police reviewed or declined it.

Each jurisdiction supplies its own trespass, disorder, obstruction, false-report, identification, and exclusion law.

docs.title: 8. Public-meeting variant
docs.text:
For a public-meeting scenario, assume unless expressly changed:

  • the person follows otherwise lawful procedural rules governing their own comment period;
  • a brief expression such as applause, laughter, a gesture, or a short verbal reaction is not assumed to actually prevent, break up, or materially impede the meeting;
  • the person does not threaten force;
  • favorable and unfavorable audience reactions are documented separately so viewpoint-neutrality questions can be tested against comparable conduct; and
  • any chair warning, removal order, decorum rule, or meeting-specific restriction is a new fact requiring analysis under the applicable jurisdiction's law.

The national baseline does not import any particular state's open-meeting statute or disruption definition.

docs.title: 9. Assembly and emergency-scene variant
docs.text:
Unless expressly changed, do not assume that peaceful presence near a protest, emergency, or police scene means the person:

  • participated in unlawful group conduct;
  • heard a dispersal order;
  • had a usable route to comply;
  • crossed a valid perimeter;
  • interfered with emergency personnel; or
  • possessed special media status.

A jurisdiction overlay must separately analyze:

  • assembly/dispersal authority;
  • warning and knowledge requirements;
  • observer-versus-participant rules;
  • emergency/perimeter authority;
  • opportunity to comply;
  • independent obstruction/interference;
  • recording from lawful locations; and
  • any special statutory media access.

docs.title: 10. New facts restart the analysis
docs.text:
The standing scenario is a starting point, not a prediction of the outcome.

Examples of facts that require a fresh branch analysis include:

  • an employee or authorized official orders the person to leave;
  • a facility claims an area is restricted;
  • normal public hours end;
  • a security-screening or appointment condition is invoked;
  • an officer establishes an emergency or crime-scene perimeter;
  • an officer states that the person is detained;
  • a statute, ordinance, regulation, court rule, or facility policy is identified;
  • the person changes position or conduct;
  • a public-meeting chair gives a warning;
  • a dispersal order is issued;
  • the government identifies conduct independent of recording, criticism, observation, or presence that it claims is unlawful; or
  • facts initially assumed absent actually occur.

A later removal command does not retroactively change the person's earlier location or conduct. Whether the person must obey that later command is a separate legal question.

docs.title: 11. Why this baseline exists
docs.text:
Without a fixed factual baseline:

  • a camera hypothetical can quietly become a shouting hypothetical;
  • a records request can quietly become an obstruction hypothetical;
  • an initially lawful presence can quietly become assumed trespass;
  • another person's anger can quietly become attributed misconduct;
  • an ordinary observer can quietly become treated as a protest participant; and
  • a request for identification can quietly become an assumed legal duty.

The canonical standing scenario prevents that drift.

If a legal conclusion depends on additional misconduct, authority, intent, status, location, warning, or changed conditions, the scenario must actually supply that fact.

docs.title: 12. Jurisdiction-overlay rule
docs.text:
A jurisdiction overlay may:

  • map these facts to its own statutes and cases;
  • add state-specific changed-fact branches;
  • add local-dependency questions;
  • identify genuine unresolved law; and
  • provide jurisdiction-specific operational language.

It may not silently alter the national baseline to make qualification easier.

If a jurisdiction needs a different factual assumption for a particular branch, that changed fact must be explicit and versioned in the relevant scenario or encounter record.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text: title: Public records: start here status: jurisdiction-routing-guide

docs.title: Public records: start here
docs.text: Public-records law depends first on which government holds the records. The Field Guide does not treat one state's records law as the nationwide default.

docs.title: Federal agency records
docs.text:
Use the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), 5 U.S.C. § 552, for records held by federal executive-branch agencies and components.

Open the Federal FOIA guide →

docs.title: State or local agency records
docs.text:
State and local agencies are generally governed by the applicable state's public-records law, not federal FOIA. Start with the jurisdiction where the agency sits and confirm the current statute, exemptions, deadlines, and appeal or enforcement process.

Browse jurisdiction coverage →

docs.title: California state and local agency records
docs.text:
For California state and local agencies, use the California Public Records Act (CPRA) guidance.

Open California public records and evidence preservation →

docs.title: 2. Keep the legal layers separate
docs.text:
A public-records request is usually a statutory access tool. It can support First Amendment research, public-forum analysis, policy verification, evidence preservation, and retaliation documentation, but the records statute itself is not a substitute for the constitutional analysis that governs recording, speech, access, or police encounters.

For those questions, start with the Field Guide's nationwide constitutional framework and then add the relevant jurisdiction-specific rules.

Start with Constitution First →

docs.title: 3. For Field Guide research
docs.text:
Records requests are especially useful for verifying whether a restriction or claimed rule is actually written, authorized, current, trained, enforced, or supported by an identified legal basis. Useful targets can include policies, directives, training materials, signage instructions, incident reports, complaints, enforcement statistics, and policy-change records.

Always route the request to the correct legal regime before relying on deadlines, exemptions, or appeal rights.

docs.title: Facility Registry
docs.text:
Data-driven working Registry. One compact row per facility. Forum classification, confidence, recording posture, and field verification are separate fields so a pending site visit does not make an otherwise answerable legal question look unresolved.

Forum labels below are project classifications, not claims that a court has adjudicated that exact address.

Constitution First: a government rule is recorded as a claimed restriction until its legal and constitutional support is analyzed. RULE LOCATED never means lawful prohibition by itself.

TPF traditional public forum LPF limited public forum NPF nonpublic forum UNRESOLVED a real gap could change the answer HIGH strong classification confidence MEDIUM defensible but more fact-sensitive FIELD PENDING verification only unless stated otherwise

Constitution First · How Registry classifications work · What can I actually do in each forum? · Registry data model · Machine-readable Registry JSON · Flat subarea CSV

docs.title: Registry data model
docs.text: The Facility Registry is designed around structured data rather than hand-authored facility pages.

docs.title: Source of truth
docs.text:
Each facility has one JSON record under:

registry/data/facilities/<slug>.json

The immutable facility_id is the durable machine identity. A human-readable slug, facility name, or address may change later without changing that ID.

For the current Contra Costa pilots the ID pattern is:

CA-013-F####

where 013 is the county namespace and the final number is a stable facility serial.

docs.title: Facility-level fields
docs.text:
A facility record stores identity and location, agency and facility type, property summary, last verification date, field-verification status, concise legal and recording summaries, field-check items, unresolved legal items, research/evidence links, authority references, index highlights, and subareas.

When historical research supports them, a facility record can also store:

  • rights_risk_signals — scoped evidence signals for a defined area/activity/policy and review period; and
  • enforcement_history — sourced warnings, removals, exclusions, police actions, prosecutions, chilling/compliance events, litigation, injunctions, policy changes, and related historical events.

These fields are optional. An unresearched facility is not assigned NONE merely because no history has been entered.

docs.title: Rights-Risk Signals
docs.text:
Current signal values are:

NONE · POSSIBLE · DOCUMENTED · ADJUDICATED

The signal is separate from forum classification, restriction-audit status, and field verification.

  • DOCUMENTED means reliable evidence documents a relevant adverse enforcement or chilling event; it is not a judicial finding that the action was unlawful.
  • ADJUDICATED is reserved for an actual court or competent-tribunal holding on the represented issue.

Signals must be scoped and include the period actually reviewed. Each signal has a stable signal_id, canonical activity, optional exact subarea_ids, a current_legal_assessment, and linked event_ids. A DOCUMENTED or ADJUDICATED signal cannot float free of the evidence history: it must point to at least one historical event.

docs.title: Enforcement-history assessments
docs.text:
Each historical event has a stable event_id, canonical activity, optional exact subarea_ids, one or more public/auditable source references, and a date-sensitive project assessment:

ADJUDICATED_UNLAWFUL · APPARENTLY_INCONSISTENT_WITH_THEN_CONTROLLING_LAW · CONSTITUTIONALLY_SUSPECT_NEEDS_RECORDS · LATER_LAW_CHANGED_OR_CLARIFIED · LAWFUL_OR_DISTINGUISHABLE · UNRESOLVED

This keeps historical evidence separate from modern law and prevents a later policy change from erasing what happened.

docs.title: Subareas are the legal unit
docs.text:
The building is not assigned one blanket forum label. Each subarea stores:

  • stable subarea_id;
  • public-access status;
  • federal forum classification and confidence;
  • California forum classification and confidence;
  • recording posture;
  • one or more Constitution First restriction audits identifying the activity, claimed restriction posture, and constitutional status;
  • optional indoor common-space analysis for public lobbies, foyers, waiting areas, service counters, shared corridors, and similar interior areas;
  • concise practical note;
  • unresolved reason when one exists; and
  • authority IDs supporting the result.

Current forum values are:

TPF · LPF · NPF · NOT_PUBLIC · UNRESOLVED

Current confidence values are:

HIGH · MEDIUM · LOW · NONE

NONE is reserved for an unresolved classification; a classified forum must carry an actual confidence level.

docs.title: Constitution First restriction audits
docs.text:
Each subarea must contain at least one restriction_audits entry. This prevents the Registry from treating a government rule as the legal conclusion.

Each audit stores:

  • the expressive activity being analyzed;
  • the current restriction status;
  • a concise constitutional posture;
  • the rule source when a rule has actually been located;
  • the governing constitutional test where useful;
  • supporting authority IDs for stronger conclusions; and
  • an explicit unresolved reason when constitutionality is unresolved.

A located rule is never automatically serialized as PROHIBITED. The data model distinguishes rule existence from constitutional validity.

See Constitution First and Restriction Audit.

docs.title: Indoor common-space / privacy fields
docs.text:
When an indoor public/common subarea has been hardened, indoor_common_space stores:

  • the type of shared interior space;
  • the privacy/confidentiality context actually identified;
  • whether HIPAA is indicated, potentially applicable, established as a covered-entity context, or unknown;
  • the facility's own safeguard responsibility;
  • any duty that actually applies to the visitor;
  • the effect of the privacy facts on recording analysis; and
  • supporting authority IDs.

This structure is intentionally separate from recording and restriction_audits.

A privacy interest does not automatically become a recording prohibition, and a facility's confidentiality duty does not automatically become a visitor duty.

The four pilot facilities currently use HIPAA_POSTURE = NOT_INDICATED; none has been established as a HIPAA covered-entity context in the Registry. Future health-related facilities must be researched before that status is promoted.

See Indoor Public Common Spaces.

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text: tools/registry/build_registry.py validates every record before generating public outputs. Among other checks, it rejects duplicate facility/subarea IDs, unknown classifications, invalid confidence combinations, unknown authority references, broken index-highlight references, and an unresolved result without an explicit unresolved_reason.

docs.title: Generated outputs
docs.text:
The site build generates:

  • the county-scale Registry index;
  • one detail page per facility;
  • registry.json for future client-side search/filtering; and
  • registry.csv, flattened to one row per facility subarea.

This is the base for later pagination, search, filter views, maps, XLSX workbooks, PDF field sheets, county packets, and statewide exports without rewriting the legal record in multiple formats.

docs.title: Export direction
docs.text: The next export layer can consume these same records instead of scraping the website. A single-facility workbook/PDF, a county packet, and a filtered statewide view can therefore all be generated from the same validated source fields.

docs.title: Facility Forum Map standard
docs.text: A facility is not field-ready merely because the Registry contains a general forum label. The Field Guide must identify the meaningful physical zones a lawful visitor can encounter and provide a supported First Amendment forum determination for each zone.

docs.title: Constitution-first rule
docs.text:
Government ownership, a posted rule, or an agency's own forum label does not by itself control the constitutional result. The project applies controlling federal doctrine to the best documented public facts, then records state-law overlays separately where they provide additional protection or a materially different analysis.

The project distinguishes three different forms of authority:

  1. Judicial determination — a court has classified the actual space or a materially identical forum.
  2. Agency position — the government has formally described the space, its purpose, or the expressive uses it permits or restricts.
  3. Field Guide determination — the project's legal assessment from controlling/analogous authority plus documented site facts.

An agency position is evidence. It is not a substitute for constitutional analysis.

docs.title: Required zone record
docs.text:
Every meaningful public-access zone should carry:

  • stable facility ID and zone ID;
  • zone name and physical description;
  • public-access status;
  • federal forum classification: TPF, DPF, LPF, or NPF;
  • federal legal confidence;
  • state-law forum classification where materially distinct;
  • geometric/boundary confidence;
  • factual basis for classification;
  • judicial authorities and whether each is exact or analogous;
  • agency position, if one is located;
  • ownership/control/ROW/easement evidence;
  • restriction audits by activity;
  • current signs/rules observed or sourced;
  • unresolved factual question, if any;
  • a concrete research task for every unresolved factual question.

docs.title: Two confidences, not one
docs.text:
Legal confidence measures how strongly doctrine and established facts support the forum classification.

Boundary confidence measures how precisely the project can place that classified zone on the ground.

These must not be collapsed. A municipal sidewalk may be a high-confidence TPF even while the exact transition between sidewalk and an adjoining forecourt remains medium-confidence geometry.

docs.title: No unexplained UNRESOLVED
docs.text:
UNRESOLVED is permitted only when a specific missing fact could materially change the classification. Every unresolved zone must state:

  • the missing fact;
  • why it matters;
  • the public record, field observation, or other source expected to resolve it;
  • the associated research task.

"No court has ruled on this exact square foot" is not by itself a valid unresolved reason. The project applies existing doctrine to the documented facts.

docs.title: Map geometry
docs.text:
Forum-map geometry should progress through three levels:

  1. Schematic — top-down research diagram sufficient to visualize zones, explicitly not a survey.
  2. Evidence-aligned — geometry traced from official site plans, parcel/ROW records, easements, or comparable authoritative mapping.
  3. Field-hardened — evidence-aligned geometry checked against current physical conditions/signage where boundary-dependent enforcement is plausible.

The UI must always disclose the current geometry level and must not imply survey precision that the evidence does not support.

docs.title: Judicial-source sweep
docs.text:
Before finalizing a facility map, research must search for decisions involving:

  • the exact facility;
  • the agency/library system;
  • the same facility type in the controlling federal circuit;
  • materially analogous physical spaces under Supreme Court precedent;
  • state constitutional cases where the state-law overlay is relevant.

Exact-site holdings outrank analogies. Analogies remain usable when their factual similarities and differences are documented.

docs.title: Member research workflow
docs.text:
A forum map is a research surface, not merely a finished illustration. Members should be able to select a zone and see:

  • current Field Guide determination;
  • confidence and evidence basis;
  • authorities;
  • restriction posture;
  • agency position;
  • missing evidence;
  • open map-hardening tasks.

Submitted records follow the ordinary immutable research/review workflow. Approval of a source does not automatically alter a forum classification; an Administrator-approved classification change should cite the approved evidence and preserve the prior determination in history.
