docs.title: Final controlling-case review incorporated before merge
docs.text:
The final PR #6 review promoted narrow propositions—not entire statutes—to doctrine-reviewed status:

  • In re Catalano, 29 Cal.3d 1 (1981) and Edgerly v. City & County of San Francisco, 599 F.3d 946 (9th Cir. 2010) — § 602(m) occupation requires nontransient, continuous possession; transient/minutes-long presence did not establish that element in Edgerly.
  • Parrish v. Municipal Court, 258 Cal.App.2d 497 (1968) — predecessor of § 602(q) is a public-building closing-hours rule; apparent-lawful-business inquiry is objective.
  • Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001) — refusal alone does not supply § 602.1 intentional interference/obstruction facts.
  • Hamburg v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 116 Cal.App.4th 497 (2004) — rule/policy enforcement and satisfaction of § 602.1 criminal elements remain separate; private-property facts limit its government-facility use.
  • People v. Hsiung (2026) — § 602(o) First Amendment discussion is in an expressly unpublished portion and is not relied on as precedent.

The final refinement also distinguishes specific-area public access, forum classification, security screening, visitor sign-in/ID policy, and criminal trespass authority. Section 602(y) is not treated as a generic visitor-log/ID statute.

Housekeeping correction recorded in Sweep 003: an earlier umbrella-ledger sentence saying no Sweep 002 proposition had reached doctrine review was stale after the final PR #6 case-law review. The detailed Sweep 002 ledger and merged chapter control; this umbrella ledger now matches them.

docs.title: Sweep 003 — California Public Records Act / evidence preservation
docs.text:
Review date: September 17, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-003-CPRA-EVIDENCE-PRESERVATION.md Handbook chapter: docs/california/public-records-evidence-preservation.md

Scope: targeted operational/preservation review. This is not yet a complete exemption-by-exemption sweep of all Government Code Division 10.

docs.title: Core statutory layer reviewed
docs.text:
• Gov. Code §§ 7920.530 and 7920.545 — public-record and writing definitions;
  • §§ 7921.000, 7921.010, 7921.300 — access, anti-evasion/lawful-destruction context, and purpose-neutral access;
  • § 7922.000 — justification for withholding;
  • §§ 7922.500-7922.605 — core request, inspection, copying, determination, denial, electronic-record, and duty-to-assist provisions;
  • §§ 7922.630-7922.640 — agency regulations/guidelines context;
  • §§ 7922.680, 7922.700-7922.725 — internet/enterprise-system provisions identified as contextual and queued for deeper relevance review;
  • § 7923.000 — enforcement/declaratory relief;
  • representative retention/destruction frameworks: Gov. Code §§ 12270-12279, 12275, 34090, 34090.6, 26202, 6200-6201.

docs.title: City of San Jose v. Superior Court, 2 Cal.5th 608 (2017)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • public-business writings do not cease being CPRA records merely because they are sent, received, or stored using personal accounts/devices;
  • public-record status depends on substantive relationship to public business, with content/context/purpose/audience/scope-of-employment factors;
  • primarily personal material with only incidental public-business references generally is not transformed into a public record;
  • agencies must make reasonable efforts to locate responsive material;
  • for likely personal-account/device records, agencies should communicate the request to employees and may reasonably rely on them to search their personal files/accounts/devices for responsive public-business records.

Auditor consequence: a personal-phone recording deliberately made on duty to document an official encounter is a strong public-record candidate, but the guide does not use the word always without the substantive-public-business analysis.

docs.title: City of Gilroy v. Superior Court, 19 Cal.5th 38 (2026)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • the CPRA itself does not impose a three-year preservation duty on all responsive records withheld as exempt;
  • the CPRA is not a general retention statute;
  • other retention/preservation law can independently apply;
  • declaratory relief can remain available for an ongoing rights/obligations dispute likely to affect future requests/conduct;
  • footnote 20 limits the no-CPRA-preservation holding to normal implementation/operation of routine retention practices and expressly leaves intentional destruction reflecting possible deliberate misconduct unresolved.

Auditor consequence: a preservation notice is useful evidence, but a pending CPRA request or statement of intent to request a record is not represented as an automatic CPRA litigation hold.

docs.title: Key Sweep 003 field distinctions
docs.text:
1. Public record ≠ automatically disclosable. Exemptions/redactions remain separate.
  2. Personal device ≠ private-record safe harbor. City of San Jose controls the categorical question.
  3. Search ≠ disclosure. An agency may need to search a personal device/account for qualifying records even if some responsive material is ultimately withheld.
  4. Disclosure ≠ retention. Gilroy separates CPRA access from retention law.
  5. Preservation notice ≠ magic legal hold. It still documents existence, knowledge, notice, and potentially intent.
  6. Routine lawful disposition ≠ deliberate destruction. The latter is expressly outside Gilroy footnote 20's resolved scenario.
  7. No universal retention period. State executive agencies, cities, counties, special districts, law enforcement, courts, and other bodies can have different statutes/schedules.
  8. Request the schedule. If evidence disappears, the governing retention/destruction policy becomes part of the factual/legal record.
  9. Do not declare a felony on scene. Government Code §§ 6200-6201 have their own record/custody/willfulness scope and must not be equated automatically with the CPRA definition.

docs.title: Practical output
docs.text:
The new chapter includes an auditor workflow for employee records me back:

  • establish on camera that a recording exists and its work-related context;
  • give a narrow preservation notice;
  • promptly submit a CPRA request including qualifying personal-device/account records;
  • invoke the City of San Jose search principle without demanding access to unrelated private content;
  • if withheld, demand the statutory withholding basis and segregable portions;
  • if missing/deleted, request retention schedules/policies, disposition/deletion records, metadata/audit logs if maintained, and communications about preservation/deletion;
  • analyze any destruction under the actual retention, litigation-preservation, and destruction law rather than asserting an automatic CPRA violation.

docs.title: Sweep 004 — Police Encounters: Fourth Amendment + Self-Incrimination
docs.text:
Review date: September 21, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-004-POLICE-ENCOUNTERS.md Handbook chapter: docs/california/police-encounters.md

Scope: targeted operational/doctrinal review of the encounter sequence that commonly follows protected recording or other First Amendment activity. This is not a complete Fourth Amendment, Fifth Amendment, criminal-procedure, or remedies sweep.

docs.title: Core encounter layer reviewed
docs.text:
• consensual police contact versus Fourth Amendment seizure;
  • Terry investigative detention and reasonable suspicion;
  • the requirement that the stop be justified at inception;
  • detention scope/duration baseline under Sharpe and traffic-specific Rodriguez;
  • protective frisk as a separate armed-and-dangerous inquiry;
  • probable-cause arrest and Devenpeck's objective-offense rule;
  • California identification distinctions: carry-ID versus request versus statutory/case-law duty versus false identification;
  • California Vehicle Code § 2806.5 pedestrian-stop notice relevant to facility audits, distinct from full reasonable-suspicion disclosure; the statute's traffic-stop branch is not developed in the current project scope;
  • Fourth Amendment detention versus Fifth Amendment/Miranda custody;
  • clear invocation of the privilege/right to remain silent under Berghuis and the plurality-limited Salinas discussion;
  • physical device seizure versus digital-content search; Riley warrant baseline;
  • explicit unresolved treatment of compelled unlocking/passcodes/biometrics.

docs.title: Principal authorities incorporated
docs.text:
Federal controlling authorities include Terry v. Ohio, Berkemer v. McCarty, United States v. Sharpe, Hiibel v. Sixth Judicial District Court, Devenpeck v. Alford, Berghuis v. Thompkins, Salinas v. Texas (plurality-limited proposition), Riley v. California, and traffic-specific Rodriguez v. United States.

California/Ninth Circuit anchors include:

  • People v. Tacardon, 14 Cal.5th 235 (2022) — totality-of-circumstances consensual-contact/seizure analysis; directed police attention does not itself establish a detention;
  • People v. Flores, 15 Cal.5th 1032 (2024) — particularized/objective reasonable suspicion required; high-crime-area context and the conduct there were insufficient in totality;
  • United States v. Landeros, 913 F.3d 862 (9th Cir. 2019) — passenger refusal to identify, without reasonable suspicion of an offense, did not supply reasonable suspicion and did not justify prolonging the traffic stop;
  • People v. Valle, A169080 (Cal. Ct. App. Sept. 18, 2024) — published California authority recognizing Vehicle Code § 2806.5's stop-reason notice requirement while keeping the federal objective Fourth Amendment justification inquiry separate.

docs.title: California identification findings
docs.text:
Primary text reviewed:

  • Penal Code § 148.9 — false/fictitious identity during qualifying lawful detention/arrest;
  • Penal Code § 853.5 — identity/thumbprint procedures in specified infraction-arrest citation context;
  • Vehicle Code § 2806.5 — for current project purposes, a pedestrian stop requires the reason to be stated before covered questioning, subject to the statute's imminent-threat exception;
  • Vehicle Code § 12951 — driver-specific license possession/presentation rule;
  • Vehicle Code § 40302 — specified custody/magistrate rules following nonfelony Vehicle Code arrest.

Bounded research conclusion: this targeted sweep has not identified a current general California pedestrian carry-ID statute or general statutory stop-and-identify law equivalent to the Nevada statute upheld in Hiibel. That does not mean identification or production of possessed identification can never be required. Older published California identification-production/search cases, including People v. Long, People v. Loudermilk, and People v. Garcia, still require a dedicated reconciliation, and specialized statutory contexts remain independently controlling.

Historical context: Kolender v. Lawson, 461 U.S. 352 (1983), invalidated California's former requirement that a detained person provide credible and reliable identification because the scheme was unconstitutionally vague. The history is useful, but the guide does not turn Kolender into a blanket rule against all modern California identification requirements.

docs.title: Key Sweep 004 field distinctions
docs.text:
1. Police contact ≠ detention. A consensual encounter requires no reasonable suspicion.
  2. Detention ≠ arrest. Terry permits a limited seizure based on reasonable suspicion.
  3. Detention ≠ frisk. A frisk requires its own armed-and-dangerous safety justification.
  4. Detention ≠ Miranda custody. A person can be seized for Fourth Amendment purposes without yet being in Miranda custody.
  5. Reasonable suspicion ≠ probable cause. Arrest ordinarily requires the higher threshold.
  6. Recording alone ≠ obstruction/RS/PC. Penal Code § 148(g) expressly supplies this bridge within its scope.
  7. Asking for ID ≠ proof of a general carry-ID or stop-and-identify law. Identify the actual California statute, context, and applicable case law before treating the request as compulsory.
  8. No general duty found ≠ permission to lie. Penal Code § 148.9 separately prohibits qualifying false/fictitious identification.
  9. Hiibel ≠ national stop-and-ID mandate. It upheld Nevada's statute during a valid Terry stop.
  10. Reason for stop ≠ full RAS recital. For pedestrian stops within this project's current scope, Vehicle Code § 2806.5 requires the reason for the stop before covered questioning, subject to its exception; reasonable suspicion itself must still exist when the seizure begins.
  11. Officer's announced offense ≠ entire arrest analysis. Devenpeck makes probable cause objective.
  12. Phone seizure ≠ digital search. Riley protects digital contents beyond ordinary search-incident-to-arrest authority.
  13. No Miranda warning ≠ illegal arrest. Arrest/seizure legality and custodial-interrogation safeguards are separate questions.
  14. Silence is not the safest invocation method. The guide recommends clear invocation rather than relying on an inference from silence.

docs.title: Remaining Sweep 004 research
docs.text:
Important unresolved areas include:

  • handcuffs, drawn weapons, prone positioning, transport, and when a Terry stop becomes an arrest;
  • anonymous/911/security/employee reports and informant reliability;
  • collective knowledge and mistakes of law/fact;
  • older California identification-production/search cases, including Long, Loudermilk, Garcia, and later applications;
  • plain-feel/container doctrine and consent searches;
  • full Miranda custody/interrogation/public-safety/waiver/reinitiation doctrine;
  • physical seizure/retention of phones and cameras;
  • warrant scope/particularity for devices;
  • compelled unlocking/passcodes/biometrics;
  • independent California Constitution article I §§ 13 and 15 doctrine;
  • excessive force, suppression, § 1983, qualified immunity, Bane Act, and municipal liability.

Those issues remain explicitly queued rather than converted into field slogans.

docs.title: Sweep 005 — Public-forum doctrine
docs.text:
Review date: September 17, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-005-PUBLIC-FORUM-DOCTRINE.md Handbook chapter: docs/california/public-forum-doctrine.md

Scope: core federal forum architecture, Ninth Circuit government-building/application doctrine, California Speech Clause overlay, and an area-level registry methodology. This is not a facility-by-facility classification sweep.

docs.title: Core federal layer reviewed
docs.text:
• Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators' Association — traditional/designated/nonpublic architecture;
  • Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense & Educational Fund — define the forum by the access sought; intentional opening; nonpublic reasonableness/viewpoint neutrality;
  • United States v. Grace and United States v. Kokinda — ordinary perimeter sidewalk versus special-purpose walkway distinctions;
  • Ward v. Rock Against Racism — public-forum content-neutral time/place/manner test;
  • International Society for Krishna Consciousness v. Lee — airport-terminal/separated-area context;
  • Rosenberger — viewpoint-discrimination principle;
  • Christian Legal Society / Wright / Hopper — limited-forum doctrine and terminology;
  • Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky — a nonpublic forum still requires a reasonable, workable speech rule.

docs.title: Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • the judicial/municipal complex before the court was a nonpublic forum even though people entered it to conduct public business;
  • location, purpose, and governmental intent matter;
  • nonpublic-forum restrictions still must be reasonable in light of forum purpose and viewpoint neutral;
  • the government did not obtain a free pass merely from the nonpublic classification: the evidentiary connection between the restriction and asserted safety/order needs still mattered.

docs.title: Norse v. City of Santa Cruz, 629 F.3d 966 (9th Cir. 2010) (en banc)
docs.text:
Retained propositions for the meeting crossover:

  • a city-council meeting opened to public participation is a limited public forum;
  • reasonable content/topic and time rules may apply, but viewpoint discrimination is not permitted;
  • the Ninth Circuit rejected a theory that First Amendment protection disappears after the public-comment period;
  • meeting removal doctrine remains tied to actual disruption rather than merely disfavored expression.

The Brown Act statutory layer remains separately governed by public-meetings.md.

docs.title: Camenzind v. California Exposition & State Fair, 84 F.4th 1102 (9th Cir. 2023)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • analyze physically/policy-distinct areas separately;
  • the enclosed/ticketed private-event portion was nonpublic on the facts;
  • the exterior area was a public forum under the California Speech Clause;
  • California's forum analysis differs from the federal one;
  • the panel acknowledged it was predicting unresolved California law for the precise state-constitutional issue, and a partial dissent disagreed with the majority's state-law analysis for the interior.

docs.title: California Speech Clause
docs.text:
• California Constitution art. I, § 2(a) is separately analyzed.
  • San Leandro Teachers Association v. Governing Board, 46 Cal.4th 822 (2009), classified internal school mailboxes as nonpublic under federal doctrine and separately rejected a broader California Speech Clause claim on the narrow facts. It also supplies an important warning against treating the older basic incompatibility formulation as the current California forum-classification rule.
  • International Society for Krishna Consciousness of California, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles, 48 Cal.4th 446 (2010), expressly declined to decide whether LAX was a public forum under the California Speech Clause; the challenged immediate-funds solicitation rule was valid even on an assumed-public-forum analysis.
  • Pruneyard, Ralphs Grocery, and Park Management are retained as context showing that California's Speech Clause can extend beyond federal public-forum doctrine and that location/access analysis is fact-sensitive. They are not converted into a universal rule that every public-facing property is a public forum.
  • Camenzind confirms that the old basic incompatibility classification approach used by some older Ninth Circuit cases rests on a doubtful foundation after San Leandro; the guide therefore does not use it as the current state-law classification test.

docs.title: Key Sweep 005 field distinctions
docs.text:
1. Public ownership ≠ public forum.
  2. Open to the public ≠ public forum.
  3. Classify the specific area/channel, not merely the building.
  4. Traditional/designated public forum ≠ limited/nonpublic forum. The governing restriction standard changes.
  5. Nonpublic ≠ no First Amendment rights. Reasonableness and viewpoint neutrality remain.
  6. Limited forum ≠ unrestricted forum. Government can confine speech to the forum's lawful purpose but cannot use the limit as a pretext for viewpoint discrimination.
  7. Federal classification ≠ automatic California classification.
  8. Forum status ≠ recording permission/prohibition. Separate recording, privacy, security, statutory, and facility rules may matter.
  9. Forum status ≠ criminal trespass. Constitutional restriction, exclusion authority, detention, and Penal Code elements remain separate questions.
  10. Unresolved is a legitimate registry result. Do not infer forum status from ownership, a public counter, or a sign.

docs.title: Registry consequence
docs.text:
Future facility records should contain, at minimum: facility, specific area, access status, federal forum classification, California Speech Clause classification, expressive activity analyzed, governing rule/policy, authority, confidence, and last-verified date.

The registry should use UNRESOLVED whenever authority is inadequate.

docs.title: Remaining facility work
docs.text: Still separately queued: police/sheriff lobbies, administrative-service facilities beyond the Concord DMV pilot, federal post-office/federal-premises facility work, public-library branches and systems beyond the initial Contra Costa pilot sites, courthouses and courtrooms, colleges/universities, K-12, transit property, public health facilities, digital forums, employee workspaces, and long-term exclusion orders.

docs.title: Sweep 006 — Contra Costa County Public Libraries
docs.text:
Review date: September 21, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-006-CONTRA-COSTA-LIBRARIES.md Handbook chapter: docs/california/public-libraries.md

Scope: targeted system-level facility-category sweep of the Contra Costa County Library. This is not a statewide survey of every California library system and does not assign a Registry status to the system or any branch.

docs.title: Prigmore v. City of Redding, 211 Cal.App.4th 1322 (2012)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • published California Court of Appeal authority involving the outdoor grounds of a municipal public library;
  • forum defined by the access sought rather than the whole library campus;
  • on the record, the public open space at the entry, entry/exit-door area, and adjacent parking lot were a traditional public forum;
  • classification depended on actual use, unrestricted access, physical/congregation characteristics, surrounding public spaces, and library function;
  • interior and exterior were expressly distinguished;
  • the older California "basic incompatibility" formulation was not used as the forum-classification test;
  • most challenged outdoor speech-zone/reservation restrictions were likely invalid at the preliminary-injunction stage, while the parking-lot vehicle-leafleting ban was upheld on its safety rationale.

Scope limit: do not convert the Redding property-specific holding into a universal rule that every library plaza, approach, or parking lot is automatically a traditional public forum. Footnote 11's broad interior observation is not treated as a categorical interior holding because the cited Faith Center forum was specifically the Antioch meeting room.

docs.title: Faith Center Church Evangelistic Ministries v. Glover, 480 F.3d 891 (9th Cir. 2007)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • the forum before the Ninth Circuit was the Antioch Library meeting room, not the entire library system or building;
  • the Antioch meeting room was a limited public forum on the policy/practice record before the court;
  • restrictions in a limited public forum are analyzed for reasonableness in light of forum purpose and viewpoint neutrality;
  • the decision strongly reinforces the project's rule that forum analysis follows the specific access sought.

The current Contra Costa meeting-room policy shows the historical religious-services restriction involved in that litigation struck through effective July 6, 2009. The old restriction is not treated as current County policy.

The 2009 district-court Establishment Clause ruling on remand is retained only as historical litigation context because it relied on the then-prevailing Lemon framework. Modern Establishment Clause doctrine, including Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, must be used for current analysis.

docs.title: Current Contra Costa policy layer reviewed
docs.text:
Official sources reviewed include:

  • Board-approved 2026 Patron Conduct Policy;
  • Board-approved 2026 Suspension Policy;
  • Children/Teen Areas policy;
  • meeting-room policy/rules and branch room directory;
  • rules for displays/distribution of non-library materials;
  • privacy materials;
  • special Self-Service Sundays access information.

The February 10, 2026 Board record confirms formal approval of the amended Patron Conduct and Suspension policies.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
1. Library building ≠ one forum. Main floors, children/teen areas, study rooms, meeting rooms, display channels, staff areas, restrooms, and exterior areas must be separately analyzed.
  2. System rule ≠ branch implementation. Some community rooms associated with branches are booked or controlled by cities/towns rather than solely by the County Library.
  3. Current library-activity predicate. The Patron Conduct Policy requires patrons to be engaged in activities associated with public-library use. Whether peaceful government observation/recording qualifies or can be excluded under that rule is unresolved.
  4. No dedicated public-facing camera rule located. The reviewed current policy portal and core policies did not reveal a dedicated ordinary-patron photography/videography policy. This is a research finding, not proof that no branch/internal/newer rule exists.
  5. Children/teen areas have purpose/age access conditions. This supplies a concrete example of lawful-presence analysis being area-specific.
  6. Patron-record privacy ≠ visitor-camera prohibition. Government Code § 7927.105 concerns qualifying library-maintained patron records; it is not treated as a categorical camera statute.
  7. Suspension and removal are separate from criminal trespass. The Suspension Policy cites Penal Code § 602 generically for return/refusal after suspension, but does not identify a subdivision or statutory element chain.
  8. Policy-to-criminal bridge was open at Sweep 006. The generic § 602 statement was originally flagged POLICY-TO-CRIMINAL-AUTHORITY-GAP; later Sweep 014 researches the statewide bridge and preserves the individualized-prior-ban/§ 602(o) question as RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED.
  9. Due process is duration/context sensitive. Sweep 006 did not locate controlling library-specific procedure for every suspension length; later Sweep 014 adds binding Ninth Circuit prospective-exclusion limits from Reza and the general Mathews procedural framework while leaving facility-specific protected-interest/process facts local.
  10. Display/distribution channels require separate review. Current subject restrictions, including political/candidate and religious-use rules, are recorded as AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED pending channel-specific forum analysis.

docs.title: Persuasive library cases retained with limits
docs.text:
• Kreimer v. Bureau of Police, 958 F.2d 1242 (3d Cir. 1992) — persuasive library-purpose/compatible-use analysis and close analogue to a library-activity requirement.
  • Neinast v. Board of Trustees, 346 F.3d 585 (6th Cir. 2003) — persuasive short-eviction due-process analysis on its facts.
  • Doe v. City of Albuquerque, 667 F.3d 1111 (10th Cir. 2012) — persuasive right-to-receive-information/access analysis; different forum terminology cautions against importing categorical labels.
  • Spiehs v. Morgan, No. 25-3174 (10th Cir. Sept. 8, 2026) — persuasive sign-restriction/library-purpose analysis; not a filming case and not controlling in California.
  • Van Den Heuvel v. Dorothy, No. 2:21-cv-02176 (E.D. Cal. 2022) — nonbinding screening-stage context for longer countywide library exclusions.

docs.title: Practical output
docs.text:
Sweep 006 establishes a system → branch → area/activity research model.

A branch file should separately establish property/control, exterior boundaries, ordinary/special hours, entrance conditions, main-floor use, designated children/teen/computer areas, study/meeting rooms, display channels, restrooms, restricted areas, recording signs/rules, removal authority, and any criminal-law bridge.

docs.title: Remaining library work
docs.text:
Still queued:

  • controlling law for peaceful photography/videography in ordinary California public-library interiors;
  • treatment of peaceful government observation/information gathering under library-purpose rules;
  • California Speech Clause application to library interiors/opened channels;
  • retaliation doctrine in library-recording disputes;
  • exact process required for different suspension lengths/scopes;
  • exact California trespass subsection after a valid or disputed suspension;
  • constitutional review of Contra Costa display/distribution restrictions;
  • branch-specific property and room-control research;
  • privacy/minor/program-specific restrictions;
  • physical seizure/search of cameras or phones if an encounter escalates.

docs.title: Sweep 007 — Concord Library Branch
docs.text:
Research dates: September 21–22, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-007-CONCORD-LIBRARY.md Status: branch documentary research in progress; no field observation; no branch-wide forum conclusion.

Sweep 007 is the first branch-level application of the Sweep 006 system → branch → area/activity method and the first full Facility Prep property/boundary prototype.

Current official-source findings:

  • Concord Library is at 2900 Salvio Street and operates ordinary staffed hours Monday through Saturday.
  • CCCL identifies two free public parking areas: a smaller front lot off Salvio Street and a larger rear lot off Parkside Drive adjacent to the Concord Civic Center.
  • Current City GIS resolves the Library as APN 111-240-006, owner field CONCORD CITY OF, 0.84 acres, with a positive City-Owned-Parcels match. The adjoining Civic Center candidate parcel is APN 111-240-014, owner field CONCORD CITY OF, 3.68 acres.
  • Assessor Book 111 Page 24 labels parcel 06 LIBRARY, parcel 14 CITY OF CONCORD, shows their relationship to Salvio/Parkside, and supplies Official Records references 3356 OR 502 and 636 OR 390.
  • City Road Centerline evidence identifies the closest Salvio and Parkside segments as Concord-owned/jurisdictional and reports sidewalks on both sides; exact surveyed ROW edges remain unresolved.
  • The assessor annotation 7 LSM 51 was resolved to County Public Works Record of Survey 7LSM51 (entry 126622, recorded 1940), whose public scan was retrieved and reviewed as historical-chain evidence rather than a modern boundary.
  • Public Works Recorded Maps searches by APN metadata 111 24 returned only 7LSM51. Broader Salvio/Parkside road-vicinity hits carried mismatched APN metadata and were not promoted as facility evidence. Broad anonymous map-index discovery is therefore substantially exhausted for this location.
  • RecorderWorks resolves 3356 OR 502 to document ID 16109166, 636 OR 390 to 12566187, and historical 454 OR 154 to 12286714, but the public viewer does not expose the images online. Manual copies are required if their contents become necessary.
  • A targeted City Engineering/current-ROW records request is prepared for the present Salvio/Parkside ROW edges, dedication/easement records, and exterior control/maintenance records adjacent to APNs 111-240-006 and 111-240-014.
  • Concord's current written meeting-room policies strongly support limited public forum classification under Faith Center, while actual-practice verification remains pending.
  • Concord has Self-Service Sunday access from 12–5 p.m. for approved patrons using card/PIN entry. The current agreement does not itself state a general patron photography/videography prohibition.
  • No dedicated public-facing Concord-specific ordinary-patron photography/videography rule has been located in the online sources reviewed.

Current branch posture: Gray / unresolved overall, but the property research has advanced from a generic ownership question to a narrow targeted-record stage. Highest-value next work is City Engineering/current-ROW acquisition, any necessary manual copies of the two current assessor-linked instruments, exterior control/parking agreement research, branch/security recording guidance, and physical/signage verification.

docs.title: Sweep 008 — Walnut Creek Library Branch
docs.text:
Research date: September 22, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-008-WALNUT-CREEK-LIBRARY.md Status: documentary branch sweep substantially developed; no field observation; no branch-wide forum conclusion.

Sweep 008 is the second branch-level Contra Costa library investigation and the same-category validation test for Facility Prep.

Key retained results:

  • official parcel evidence resolves Walnut Creek Library at APN 178-300-039, owner field WALNUT CREEK CITY OF, with adjoining civic APN 178-300-040 materially tied to the Civic Park setting;
  • the test demonstrated that the countywide parcel core generalized while Concord-specific address and ROW enrichments did not automatically generalize;
  • assessor and recorded-map handling exposed and corrected the MB / Subdivision Map source-enumeration issue;
  • the Broadway–Lincoln civic plaza, formal exterior approach, Civic Park connection, Civic Park proper, and surface lot have strong documentary support for public-forum treatment under area-specific doctrine, while exact physical verification remains pending where material;
  • the enclosed underground garage remains forum-unresolved and is not treated as equivalent to the open surface lot;
  • Oak View and Las Trampas are analyzed as separately opened room channels; group study rooms remain purpose-limited and do not inherit those room classifications;
  • no dedicated public-facing Walnut Creek-specific ordinary-patron photography/videography rule was located in the online sources reviewed as of September 22, 2026;
  • the branch remains Gray/unresolved overall because ordinary-interior recording/forum doctrine, the underground garage, certain control questions, and current signage/physical facts remain open.

Facility Prep consequence: the same-category prototype gate was satisfied. Reusable behavior was promoted into FACILITY-PREP-SOP.md, while municipality-specific enrichments remained modular.

docs.title: Sweep 009 — Concord DMV Field Office
docs.text:
Research date: September 22, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-009-CONCORD-DMV.md Status: documentary cross-category sweep substantially developed; field/current-access verification pending.

Sweep 009 is the first deliberate cross-category Facility Prep validation against a State administrative-service facility.

Key retained results:

  • official GIS resolves APN 126-490-004, owner field CALIFORNIA STATE OF, second owner/name field DEPT MOTOR VEHICLES, with current DMV sources independently supporting State ownership and DMV operation;
  • assessor and recorded-map evidence show the State/DMV parcel directly related to Meridian Park Boulevard while an intervening parcel lies between it and Diamond Boulevard, producing ADDRESS/FRONTAGE-MISMATCH and leaving the modern Diamond access right unresolved;
  • the project therefore now treats public facility address, parcel frontage, physical ingress route, legal access right, ownership, and operational control as separate facts;
  • ordinary municipal sidewalks can be analyzed separately once their location is established; exact ROW edges remain pending only where outcome-determinative;
  • federal nonpublic-forum treatment is strongly supported for the defined ordinary DMV lobby/waiting channel under the administrative-interior authorities, while California Speech Clause treatment remains unresolved because no sufficiently close California administrative-lobby authority was located;
  • knowledge-testing is treated as a purpose-limited activity, and DMV's cell-phone/testing-aid rule is not generalized into a branch-wide phone or camera ban;
  • no dedicated public-facing California DMV field-office ordinary-patron photography/videography rule was located in the online sources reviewed as of September 22, 2026;
  • customer parking, exterior queueing, entrance/approach geometry, and several California state-law exterior classifications remain area-specific and partially unresolved.

Facility Prep consequence: the cross-category validation succeeded, but the reusable result is the method, not a universal source adapter or inherited legal conclusion. The SOP now requires frontage/access-path validation and a facility-purpose doctrinal reset when moving to a new facility category.

docs.title: Sweep 010 — Concord Police Headquarters Public Lobby
docs.text:
Research date: September 22, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-010-CONCORD-POLICE.md Status: documentary cross-category sweep substantially developed; physical/current signage verification pending.

Sweep 010 tests the Facility Prep and forum methodology against a municipal law-enforcement headquarters while keeping the Concord GIS/jurisdiction environment constant.

Key retained results:

  • official parcel evidence resolves Police Headquarters at APN 126-124-036, owner CONCORD CITY OF, approximately 5.06 acres; assessor and road evidence strongly support direct Galindo Street frontage with no DMV-like address/frontage mismatch;
  • the public Community Service Desk/lobby and Records counter are verified public-facing service channels during stated weekday business hours, while restricted operational areas remain separate;
  • CPD Policy 423 affirmatively recognizes lawful public recording of department members performing official duties and distinguishes recording alone from interference;
  • Penal Code § 148(g) separately provides that recording an officer does not by itself constitute § 148(a), reasonable suspicion, or probable cause when the statute's location conditions are met;
  • no separate published Concord Police Headquarters lobby-wide ordinary-patron camera prohibition was located in the online sources reviewed;
  • the ordinary police lobby is strongly supported as a purpose-limited federal interior using the limited/nonpublic-forum restriction standard, while no published Ninth Circuit police-lobby filming holding was located and California Speech Clause treatment remains unresolved;
  • Wilson v. County of Contra Costa, No. 14-cv-03491-SI (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2015), supplies an unusually close local but nonbinding pleading-stage comparator: a First Amendment retaliation claim based on recording officers in the public Contra Costa Sheriff's lobby survived dismissal; the case did not reach final merits adjudication;
  • Penal Code § 632 audio privacy remains fact-specific under Flanagan's objectively reasonable confidentiality test; Wilson rejected a § 632 theory at the pleading stage where the alleged lobby conversations were audible to various members of the public;
  • current § 602.1(d)(2) expressly excludes constitutionally protected activity from § 602.1, while independent obstruction/intimidation and other law remain separately applicable;
  • the Police Department Community Meeting Room is a separate opened discussion channel; the public page references a Community Room Contract, but the contract itself was not located online;
  • narrow CPD records/protected-information/confidentiality policies support protection of actual sensitive information but are not converted into a public lobby-wide visitor camera ban.

Methodology consequence: Sweep 010 adds a dual-anchor model—forum/access authority and activity-specific authority may be different—and requires recording analyses to preserve both the recorder's location and the subject being recorded. It also formalizes the rule that forum classification establishes the standard for a restriction rather than proving that a restriction exists.

Current highest-value remaining facts are physical/current: entrance/lobby signage, counter/privacy configuration, controlled doors, restroom/public-area boundaries, and the parking/pedestrian approach.

docs.title: Sweep 011 — Lawful Vantage, Visual Privacy, and Exposed Information
docs.text:
Research date: September 28, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-011-LAWFUL-VANTAGE-PRIVACY.md Qualification package: GAP-01 Status: defined activation slice completed; row promotion subject to package review.

Key retained results:

  • California privacy doctrine does not use a binary visible/not-visible rule. Shulman supplies the ordinary public-place observation baseline, while Sanders and Hernandez preserve limited-audience and visual-surveillance privacy in appropriate circumstances;
  • Civil Code § 1708.8 separately addresses physical trespass undertaken to capture private activity and device-assisted constructive invasion where the capture could not otherwise have been achieved without trespass;
  • Penal Code § 647(i) retains a private-property loiter/prowl/wander predicate for its window-peeking branch, while § 647(j) separately protects specified interiors and other areas with a reasonable privacy expectation when its viewing/intent predicates are met;
  • Penal Code § 632 and Flanagan keep confidential audio analytically separate from visual recording;
  • Penal Code § 502 keeps actual computer/system/data access separate from merely seeing an exposed display;
  • Robins/Pruneyard and Golden Gateway prevent both private-property extremes: California recognizes a special private-shopping-center speech doctrine, but private property open to some visitors is not categorically public property or a universal expressive forum;
  • Fourth Amendment window/vantage cases (Berutko, Lorenzana, Camacho) are retained only as factual analogies about lawful/common versus private/off-limits vantage and are expressly not treated as civilian recording authority;
  • transparent barriers are analyzed through exact vantage, general-public versus limited visibility, shielding, manipulation, method/technology, subject/space, and specialized law rather than a categorical "window rule";
  • exposed documents/screens are analyzed by separating passive visibility from physical manipulation, system/data access, and independent confidentiality/privacy duties.

Qualification consequence: Sweep 011 supplies an ordinary California analytical test for CA-F2.1, CA-F2.3, and NC-VANTAGE-01.A–F. Specialized court, child, intimate-image, medical, biometric, trade-secret, federal-premises, and publication-only issues remain changed-fact checks rather than hidden assumptions in the ordinary scenario.

docs.title: Sweep 012 — Conditional Access, Removal, and Derivative Trespass
docs.text:
Research date: September 28, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-012-CONDITIONAL-EXCLUSION-DERIVATIVE-TRESPASS.md Qualification package: GAP-02 Status: defined activation slice completed; row promotion subject to package review.

Key retained results:

  • current Penal Code § 602.1(b) requires intentional interference with public-agency business by obstruction/intimidation plus refusal after a qualifying request; current subdivision (d)(2) expressly excludes constitutionally protected activity and subdivision (e) preserves other law;
  • § 602(o) remains textually limited to property not open to the general public, while § 602(q) separately covers regularly closed public buildings; a generic asked to leave theory must identify the actual statutory branch;
  • published Ninth Circuit Dubner rejects inferring § 602.1's missing interference element from refusal alone;
  • unpublished/nonprecedential Mackey v. Meyer supplies a direct California DMV comparator: refusal plus a generalized “harassing customers” report did not establish § 602.1(b) probable cause where the officer observed no obstruction/intimidation;
  • Brown v. Louisiana and California Supreme Court In re Hoffman support the narrow anti-bootstrap proposition that an unsupported activity-based exclusion does not become constitutionally sufficient merely because the person refuses to leave;
  • the opposite proposition is also preserved: Sammartano, Simpson, and Fogelson show that valid, sufficiently precise/viewpoint-neutral restrictions tied to the function of the particular forum may regulate activity prospectively without waiting for actual disruption;
  • Parrish preserves neutral changed-access facts such as regular closing time;
  • Askins supplies the recording-specific federal layer without creating unlimited government-interior camera access;
  • Wilson v. County of Contra Costa is retained only as a persuasive pleading-stage local comparator involving public sheriff-lobby recording and § 602.1 allegations;
  • the operational sequence is now: trigger → validity of activity restriction → exclusion authority → offense elements → later changed facts.

Qualification consequence at Sweep 012: the sweep supplied the ordinary California analytical test for CA-F3.4, CA-F4.1, CA-F4.6, NC-COMPLAINT-01.M, and NC-VANTAGE-01.G. Prospective/long-term exclusions, identification, delegated local authority, and specialized premises were intentionally left to separate packages; later Sweeps 013–014 address the first three of those layers while preserving their stated unresolved boundaries.

docs.title: Sweep 013 — Delegated Authority and Preemption
docs.text:
Research date: September 29, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-013-DELEGATED-AUTHORITY-PREEMPTION.md Qualification package: GAP-03 Status: defined activation slice completed; row promotion subject to package review.

Key retained results:

  • California state-agency rulemaking begins with delegated authority outside the APA itself: Government Code §§ 11342.1–11342.2 require regulations to remain within authority conferred by other law, consistent with the governing statute, and reasonably necessary to effectuate its purpose;
  • § 11340.5, OAL guidance, and Tidewater supply the underground-regulation branch for generally applicable state-agency rules that implement, interpret, or make specific administered law, while statutory exemptions and rule-specific facts remain material;
  • article XI § 7 supplies the baseline city/county local police-power rule subject to conflict with general laws;
  • Sherwin-Williams supplies the California local-preemption framework: duplication, contradiction, or express/implied field occupation;
  • article XI § 5 and City of Vista preserve the separate charter-city municipal-affairs/statewide-concern branch;
  • Dibb preserves the distinct charter-county structure rather than treating charter counties as charter cities;
  • county statutes §§ 23003–23004 supply express/necessarily implied and property-management powers, while § 25132 illustrates the important distinction between an ordinance violation and an informal policy violation;
  • Association of California Insurance Companies and American Federation of Labor reinforce the express/necessarily implied limits on state administrative power;
  • Robings supplies a published enabling-law/implied-power and joint-powers comparator for special public entities;
  • Arizona v. United States supplies the general federal express/field/conflict-preemption screen, with subject-specific federal law still required before reaching a preemption conclusion;
  • the operational sequence is now: rule-maker → enabling authority → required adoption form → actor delegation → superior-law preemption → constitutional test → enforcement bridge.

Qualification consequence: Sweep 013 supplies the ordinary statewide framework for CA-F3.5. Actual facility charters, ordinances, regulations, enabling acts, resolutions, employee delegations, and subject-specific preemption rules remain local/fact dependencies rather than a statewide analytical gap.

docs.title: Sweep 014 — Public-Agency Exclusion, Prospective Trespass, and Identification
docs.text:
Research date: September 29, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-014-PUBLIC-EXCLUSION-PROSPECTIVE-TRESPASS-ID.md Qualification package: GAP-04 Status: defined activation slice completed; affected rows re-evaluated individually.

Key retained results:

  • California's public-agency trespass analysis must distinguish public ownership from the current access status of the exact area: §602(o) applies to property not open to the general public, §602(q) separately addresses regularly closed public buildings, and §602.1(b) separately addresses intentional interference at a public agency open to the public;
  • allegation labels such as disruptive, harassing, or interfering do not substitute for the underlying conduct, policy predicates, or offense elements;
  • Reza v. Pearce supplies binding Ninth Circuit limits on broad prospective exclusion from a government forum: actual misconduct/future-risk evidence, scope, duration, unrelated future access, and narrower alternatives can matter;
  • Mathews v. Eldridge supplies the general procedural-due-process framework where a protected interest is being deprived, without creating one mandatory hearing procedure for every same-day removal or facility suspension;
  • later reentry must be analyzed anew against the order's current scope/duration and the California offense actually asserted;
  • the effect of an individualized prior ban on otherwise generally open property under §602(o) remains RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED: Blankenhorn used conditional language in a private-property probable-cause posture, while California federal district courts have applied that reasoning differently and no published California appellate decision located in the sweep squarely resolves the ordinary public-facing government-property question;
  • no current general California pedestrian carry-ID statute equivalent to Nevada's Hiibel statute was located;
  • Landeros confirms that refusal to identify cannot manufacture reasonable suspicion where individualized suspicion is otherwise absent;
  • Long and Loudermilk are fact-specific older identification-production cases; Garcia rejects turning a Terry patdown into a search for identification;
  • Quiroga, Chase C., §148.9, §853.5, and McKay preserve separate silence/refusal, false-ID, citation, arrest, and booking stages;
  • Vanegas does not decide that refusal to identify during every otherwise lawful California Terry detention supplies §148 probable cause, and the panel's qualified-immunity treatment leaves that substantive state-law boundary RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED;
  • an exclusion notice does not itself create a new criminal identification statute.

Operational sequence:

exact access status → actual conduct/rule → immediate-removal authority → prospective-exclusion authority → scope/duration/process → later-reentry offense → officer knowledge/reliance → identification stage/source of duty.

Qualification consequence:

  • CA-F4.3 → Supported;
  • CA-F4.5 → Researched-Unresolved;
  • CA-F4.7 → Supported;
  • CA-F5.8 → Researched-Unresolved;
  • NC-COMPLAINT-01.D → Researched-Unresolved.

After Sweep 014, the provisional California totals are 60 Supported / 4 Researched-Unresolved / 9 Gap, leaving GAP-05 through GAP-08 as the four open research packages.

docs.title: Sweep 015 — Recording-Device Seizure, Retention, Search, and Compelled Access
docs.text:
Research date: September 29, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-015-DEVICE-SEIZURE-RETENTION-SEARCH.md Qualification package: GAP-05 Status: defined activation slice completed; affected row re-evaluated.

Key retained results:

  • physical custody of a phone/camera and digital-content search are distinct Fourth Amendment acts;
  • Riley generally requires a warrant for digital contents even after arrest, while expressly preserving physical securing of a phone during lawful warrant pursuit;
  • Place supplies a narrow reasonable-suspicion temporary-property-detention framework rather than a generic authority to retain phones containing possible evidence;
  • Hicks requires probable cause for evidentiary seizure under plain view;
  • Dickerson confines plain-feel seizure to immediately apparent incriminating character without exploratory manipulation; merely feeling/recognizing a common phone does not create digital-search authority;
  • Camou rejects generalized digital volatility/remote wiping as a categorical exigency; any warrantless phone search must rest on a genuine case-specific need and be limited to that need;
  • Song Ja Cha, Dass, and Sullivan establish that retention duration is a totality/diligence inquiry rather than a fixed number of hours or days;
  • 2026 Carlson v. Chavez and 2025 Langham v. Noyd provide very current direct phone-retention comparators but are expressly unpublished/nonprecedential and are not used as binding doctrine;
  • Jimeno supplies the consent-scope rule, supporting the operational distinction between offering one identified video and consenting to browse an entire device;
  • the federal Privacy Protection Act can independently limit government seizure/search of qualifying work-product/documentary materials held for public dissemination, subject to statutory exceptions; its text does not make press credentials the trigger;
  • California Penal Code §1524(g) separately bars warrants for items described in Evidence Code §1070, but §1070 uses qualifying newsperson/media categories and is not assumed to cover every citizen recorder;
  • published Ninth Circuit Payne supplies a narrow Fifth Amendment biometric rule: compelled officer-selected thumb use on an already identified phone was non-testimonial because no cognitive exertion was required; its Fourth Amendment phone-search authority arose from parole conditions and does not transfer to an ordinary citizen;
  • published California People v. Ramirez reaches a similar fingerprint result on warrant-based facts;
  • published Ninth Circuit act-of-production authority supplies a foregone-conclusion framework, but the project does not claim a categorical circuit rule for compelled alphanumeric phone passcodes.

Operational sequence:

encounter stage → government act → initial seizure authority → duration/diligence → digital-search authority → frisk/plain-view/plain-feel/consent limits → news-material overlay → compelled-access method.

Qualification consequence:

  • CA-F5.9 → Supported.

The specialized alphanumeric-passcode/foregone-conclusion application remains a labeled RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED edge rather than an activation-blocking research Gap.

After Sweep 015, provisional California totals are 61 Supported / 4 Researched-Unresolved / 8 Gap, leaving GAP-06 through GAP-08 as the three open research packages.

docs.title: Sweep 016 — Disorder, Unreasonable Noise, Fighting Words, Threats, and Obstruction
docs.text:
Research date: September 29, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-016-DISORDER-NOISE-THREATS-OBSTRUCTION.md Qualification package: GAP-06 Status: defined activation slice completed; affected rows re-evaluated.

Key retained results:

  • California Penal Code §415 is three distinct offenses rather than a generic "disturbance" label;
  • In re Brown constitutionally narrows communicative loud-noise prosecution under §415(2): the ordinary criminal branch requires either imminent-violence danger or purported communication used as a guise to disrupt lawful endeavors;
  • current CALCRIM 2689 preserves that narrowing rule, while People v. Superior Court (Commons) supplies a changed-fact example where late-night very loud conduct could fall within the disruption branch;
  • Jefferson, In re John V., and In re Alejandro G. make §415(3) fighting-words analysis contextual; profanity alone is insufficient, police addressees are expected to exercise greater restraint, and an actual challenge to fight/violent threat can change the result;
  • City of Houston v. Hill, Duran, Mackinney, and Poocha preserve substantial First Amendment protection for criticism, profanity, and verbal challenge directed at police;
  • Center for Bio-Ethical Reform reinforces that audience hostility to message content does not silently become a content-neutral justification or missing offense element;
  • §148 requires actual willful resistance/delay/obstruction of a lawful official duty: Quiroga and Mackinney protect verbal dispute/momentary slow compliance, while Muhammed C. and current published In re N.S. illustrate changed facts involving repeated conduct and actual operational delay;
  • for public-agency §602.1(b), obstruction/intimidation and refusal remain separate predicates; Dubner rejects refusal as a substitute for interference, published Turner supplies a changed-fact related-subsection comparator, and unpublished Mackey remains only a direct DMV factual cross-check;
  • "harassment," "aggressive," "hostile," "interfering," and "causing a disturbance" remain characterizations to translate into observable conduct and an identified offense/rule;
  • fighting words and true threats are distinct: Counterman supplies the constitutional subjective-mens-rea floor for true threats, while California §422 and In re George T. impose their own specific-intent, gravity/immediacy, and sustained-fear elements.

Operational sequence:

actual conduct → exact offense/subsection → speech/conduct distinction → constitutional narrowing rule → actual interference/danger/effect → changed facts.

Qualification consequence:

  • CA-F6.1 → Supported;
  • CA-F6.2 → Supported;
  • CA-F6.3 → Supported.

After Sweep 016, provisional California totals are 64 Supported / 4 Researched-Unresolved / 5 Gap, leaving GAP-07 and GAP-08 as the two open research packages.

Assembly/dispersal warnings, emergency perimeters, observer-versus-participant questions, statutory news-representative protections, and protest/emergency recording remain GAP-07 rather than being smuggled into this package.

docs.title: Sweep 017 — Assembly, Dispersal, Emergency Perimeters, and Observer Recording
docs.text:
Research date: September 29, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-017-ASSEMBLY-DISPERSAL-EMERGENCY-RECORDING.md Qualification package: GAP-07 Status: defined activation slice completed; affected rows re-evaluated.

Key retained results:

  • In re Brown constitutionally narrows the lawful-purpose branch of California unlawful-assembly law to actual violence or a clear and present danger of imminent violence; boisterous or tumultuous is not independently enough;
  • Collins v. Jordan prevents prior limited violence from becoming a blanket prospective ban on later peaceful demonstrations;
  • §408 and §409 remain distinct: Wagner requires knowing participation for §408, while §409 can reach nonparticipants who willfully remain once an actual riot/rout/unlawful assembly and lawful warning exist;
  • Dubner supplies the ordinary observer/bystander limit: without the qualifying violence/imminence predicate, police cannot simply collapse a photographer/legal observer into participants;
  • §726 and current CALCRIM 2686 require an official dispersal order communicated in a reasonable way that ensures it is heard; no universal fixed countdown is invented;
  • Nelson makes audibility, exit route, blocked egress, attempted compliance, individual threat, and warning-before-force material to dispersal-force reasonableness;
  • §409.5 requires its actual calamity/command-post predicates; police tape or a line is evidence of a closure, not the legal source by itself;
  • §409.5(c)'s current misdemeanor text is conjunctive as to entry and later remaining, while specialized §409.6 uses materially different wording;
  • Leiserson protects qualifying §409.5(d) media access while allowing restrictions genuinely necessary to prevent interference with emergency operations and preserving a separate crime-scene basis;
  • §409.7 supplies a special statutory protection package for qualifying news/online-news representatives at covered demonstrations/police lines/rolling closures, but the statute does not define duly authorized representative or online news service;
  • no controlling published California appellate authority located in this sweep supplies a universal §409.7 credential/self-publisher test, so that special qualification remains a Researched-Unresolved changed-fact edge;
  • Fordyce/Askins/Leigh preserve ordinary constitutional recording/access analysis independently of special statutory media status;
  • published Index Newspapers is retained with its emergency-stay/preliminary-injunction posture and does not become a universal press dispersal exemption;
  • current published Los Angeles Press Club v. Noem strongly supports the retaliation branch for peaceful journalists/legal observers/protesters, but expressly did not reach the alternative right-of-access merits theory and narrowed the injunction.

Operational sequence:

exact event/area → actual statutory predicate → participant/observer status → lawful warning and audibility → route/opportunity to comply → remaining/reentry conduct → independent interference/unlawful conduct → recording/newsgathering overlay → force/arrest authority.

Qualification consequence:

  • CA-F7.3 → Supported;
  • CA-F8.1 → Supported;
  • CA-F8.2 → Supported;
  • CA-F8.3 → Supported.

After Sweep 017, provisional California totals are 68 Supported / 4 Researched-Unresolved / 1 Gap, leaving only GAP-08 as an activation-blocking research package.

docs.title: Sweep 018 — Law-Enforcement Records and Specialized Evidence Disclosure
docs.text:
Research date: September 29, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-018-LAW-ENFORCEMENT-RECORDS-DISCLOSURE.md Qualification package: GAP-08 Status: defined activation slice completed; affected row re-evaluated.

Key retained results:

  • current Government Code §7923.600 is the recodified law-enforcement investigatory-record exemption; §7923.630 preserves the construction/relationship of former §6254(f);
  • Williams preserves a broad investigatory-file exemption that does not automatically expire when an investigation ends, while mandatory statutory information still must be disclosed;
  • Haynie limits "investigation" to inquiries directed at whether a law violation may occur/has occurred and related investigation rather than everything law enforcement does;
  • ACLU Foundation and Castañares preserve the distinction between targeted suspected-law-violation investigation and bulk/routine/noncriminal-assistance collection;
  • routine facility CCTV is therefore not automatically a police investigatory record; a police-held investigative copy and host-agency original can present different custody/purpose facts;
  • §§7923.610 and 7923.615 require specified arrestee and complaint/request/response information even where the complete underlying investigatory record remains exempt;
  • §7923.625 specifically governs audio/video depicting defined critical incidents (officer firearm discharge at a person or officer force causing death/GBI), with its own active-investigation delay, reassessment, privacy/redaction, and subject-access structure;
  • Sacramento Television Stations treats §7923.625 as a specific legislative limit on the older investigatory-record regime for qualifying recordings and requires the actual statutory delay showing;
  • not every BWC recording is a critical-incident recording; ordinary detention/trespass footage can remain under other CPRA rules;
  • current Penal Code §832.7(b), as amended effective 2026, expressly makes enumerated officer records public notwithstanding ordinary personnel confidentiality and Government Code §7923.600, subject to its current redaction/delay rules;
  • current public §832.7 categories include firearm discharge, death/GBI force, specified sustained excessive-force/failure-to-intervene, sexual-assault, dishonesty, prejudice/discrimination, unlawful-arrest/search findings, and the statutory prohibited-agreement category;
  • §832.8's definition of a sustained finding matters where the public category depends on a sustained finding;
  • Copley Press remains historical confidentiality context, but later SB1421/SB16/current §832.7 create explicit public categories;
  • Becerra and First Amendment Coalition confirm the later §832.7 disclosure command and the need to harmonize rather than blindly apply older secrecy rules;
  • Long Beach preserves the ordinary officer-name disclosure rule on its on-duty-shooting facts, and current §832.7 expressly preserves that access;
  • Penal Code §832.18 principally addresses BWC policy/retention rather than public disclosure;
  • National Lawyers Guild v. City of Hayward prevents shifting ordinary BWC redaction labor to requesters as electronic "data extraction";
  • disclosure remains distinct from retention under City of Gilroy and record-specific retention statutes/schedules.

Operational sequence:

record/custodian → investigatory-record status → mandatory information carveout → critical-incident audio/video override → peace-officer-record override → privacy/safety/redaction → electronic format/cost → retention/preservation separately.

Qualification consequence:

  • CA-F9.4 → Supported.

After Sweep 018, provisional California totals are 69 Supported / 4 Researched-Unresolved / 0 Gap.
