docs.title: Forum perimeter
docs.text:
Cornelius is the principal framing rule: identify the forum with reference to the access sought. A speaker seeking access to a particular channel or subset of property does not automatically place the entire government property at issue.

Camenzind applies this operationally by separately analyzing exterior and enclosed portions of the same fairgrounds because a physical boundary and different policies separated them.

Retained project rule: registry and handbook classifications must be area/channel-specific.

docs.title: Traditional public forum
docs.text:
Perry identifies streets and parks as paradigmatic traditional public forums. Grace applies traditional-forum protection to the perimeter public sidewalks at the Supreme Court grounds, while Kokinda shows that a government-owned sidewalk constructed for a special purpose is not automatically equivalent to an ordinary municipal sidewalk.

Retained project rule: do not classify by visual appearance alone.

docs.title: Designated public forum
docs.text:
Under Perry and Cornelius, government may intentionally open nontraditional property for public discourse. Intent is central; selective permission or ordinary public access is insufficient by itself.

Retained project rule: require evidence of intentional opening before labeling a nontraditional government interior a designated public forum.

docs.title: Limited public forum
docs.text:
The Ninth Circuit uses limited public forum for a forum intentionally opened only to certain speakers or subjects. Wright states the operative standard as reasonableness plus viewpoint neutrality.

Because courts have used the designated/limited/nonpublic labels somewhat inconsistently over time, the guide records the actual standard rather than relying on terminology alone.

docs.title: Public-meeting crossover
docs.text: Norse v. City of Santa Cruz confirms in this circuit that a city-council meeting opened to public participation is a limited public forum. The court rejected the theory that attendees lose all First Amendment protection after the formal public-comment period and reiterated the actual-disruption requirement in the meeting-removal cases. The Brown Act's statutory rules remain a separate layer.

docs.title: Nonpublic forum
docs.text:
Perry and Cornelius permit subject/speaker distinctions tied to forum purpose so long as they are reasonable and viewpoint neutral. Mansky confirms reasonableness requires a sensible standard capable of consistent application.

Sammartano is the core Ninth Circuit California-facing government-building case for this sweep. It agreed that the judicial/municipal complex was a nonpublic forum because the complex was built and operated to conduct governmental/court business rather than assembly/debate. The court nevertheless found the record inadequate to justify several expressive-clothing restrictions and found viewpoint problems.

Retained project rule: nonpublic does not mean constitution-free.

docs.title: Public access versus forum status
docs.text:
Sweep 002 already established the statutory importance of whether property is open to the general public for certain trespass provisions. Sweep 005 establishes that this is not the same inquiry as federal forum classification.

A public-facing lobby can be open for transactions yet still fail the tradition/designation tests for a public forum. Conversely, an exterior sidewalk can be a traditional public forum even when the adjacent interior is not.

The guide must therefore keep separate:

  1. ownership;
  2. whether the specific area is open to the public;
  3. forum classification;
  4. visitor/security conditions;
  5. expressive/recording rule;
  6. removal authority;
  7. criminal-trespass elements.

docs.title: Viewpoint discrimination
docs.text:
Cornelius, Rosenberger, and Sammartano support the project rule that viewpoint neutrality remains independently important even where government can impose subject-matter limits.

Evidence such as an official expressly tying enforcement to criticism, support, affiliation, ideology, or the auditor identity should be preserved. This does not automatically prove liability; it is relevant evidence for later legal analysis.

docs.title: Time/place/manner
docs.text:
Ward supplies the general federal test for content-neutral restrictions in traditional/designated public forums:

  • content neutral;
  • narrowly tailored to a significant governmental interest;
  • ample alternative channels.

The rule need not be the least restrictive conceivable means.

Camenzind applied the same familiar framework to the exterior Cal Expo restrictions and separately analyzed the interior as nonpublic.

docs.title: Text
docs.text: California Constitution article I, section 2(a) is independently phrased and can provide broader protection in some settings.

docs.title: State-law uncertainty preserved
docs.text:
The sweep deliberately avoids claiming a single crisp California government-property test that the California Supreme Court has never announced.

In ISKCON v. City of Los Angeles (2010), the California Supreme Court did not decide whether LAX was a public forum. It held the immediate-funds solicitation prohibition valid even assuming relevant public areas were public forums.

In Camenzind, the Ninth Circuit:

  • expressly treated California forum doctrine as different from the federal doctrine;
  • separated exterior and ticketed/interior areas;
  • held the exterior area public under the California Speech Clause;
  • held the enclosed/ticketed private-event area nonpublic;
  • acknowledged the absence of controlling California Supreme Court authority for the precise issue and therefore predicted state law;
  • included a partial dissent disagreeing with the majority's state-law methodology/result for the interior.

Retained project rule: cite Camenzind accurately and do not rewrite its federal prediction as a California Supreme Court holding.

docs.title: Obsolete-test warning: basic incompatibility
docs.text:
Older California appellate authority, especially U.C. Nuclear Weapons Labs Conversion Project v. Lawrence Livermore Laboratory, proposed a basic incompatibility test for government-property forum classification, and older Ninth Circuit cases such as Carreras and Kuba followed it.

Do not carry that test forward as current California classification law.

In San Leandro Teachers Association v. Governing Board, 46 Cal.4th 822 (2009), the California Supreme Court noted that the formulation had not appeared in California appellate cases since U.C. Weapons Labs and explained that Grayned used incompatibility in time/place/manner analysis after forum status was established. Camenzind later characterized San Leandro as declining to adopt the test and said the older Ninth Circuit applications rest on a hollow foundation.

San Leandro separately classified internal school mailboxes as nonpublic under federal doctrine and rejected a broader California Speech Clause claim on the facts there. This supports the project's rule that California's broader clause does not automatically make every restricted government channel public.

docs.title: Private-property authorities are context, not a universal government-building rule
docs.text: Pruneyard, Ralphs Grocery, and Park Management demonstrate that California can recognize forum rights beyond federal traditional-public-property doctrine and that the inquiry can be area-specific and fact-sensitive. They do not establish that every property open to customers/visitors is a public forum.

docs.title: Recording interaction
docs.text:
Forum doctrine alone does not answer whether filming is protected or regulable in a particular government area. Recording can implicate separate First Amendment newsgathering/recording doctrine, Penal Code § 148(g), privacy, court rules, security rules, open-meeting statutes, and facility-specific policies.

Retained project rule: nonpublic forum is not itself a complete answer to may I record here?

docs.title: Trespass/removal interaction
docs.text:
Forum classification can determine whether a facility restriction is constitutionally permissible. It does not supply the elements of Penal Code § 602 or § 602.1.

The guide therefore rejects both shortcuts:

  • It is a nonpublic forum, therefore refusal to leave is automatically criminal trespass.
  • I am engaged in First Amendment activity, therefore no trespass law can apply.

Analyze constitutional protection, policy authority, removal authority, detention basis, and statutory elements separately.

docs.title: Registry methodology produced by Sweep 005
docs.text:
Every facility registry entry should support area-level records containing:

  • facility;
  • specific area;
  • access status;
  • federal forum classification;
  • California Speech Clause classification;
  • activity analyzed;
  • rule/policy;
  • authority;
  • confidence;
  • last verified.

UNRESOLVED is a valid and preferred classification when authority is inadequate.

docs.title: Explicitly unresolved / queued
docs.text:
Still requires separate research:

  • ordinary administrative-building lobbies;
  • police/sheriff lobbies;
  • DMV/state-service centers;
  • public libraries — Contra Costa system-level Sweep 006 completed; branch-specific classifications and broader statewide library systems remain;
  • courthouse rooms/corridors/clerk areas and exterior plazas;
  • public colleges/universities;
  • K-12 campuses;
  • transit property;
  • public hospitals/clinics;
  • digital/social-media forums;
  • long-term exclusion orders and due process;
  • forum-specific right-to-record doctrine;
  • local ordinances and agency regulations;
  • government-speech edge cases.

docs.title: Sweep 006 — Contra Costa County Public Libraries
Scope
docs.text:
This sweep uses the Contra Costa County Library (CCCL) system as the first real facility-category test of the Registry methodology.

The sweep is intentionally system-level. It does not assign a Registry status to the County Library system or any individual branch. It asks which rules apply across the system, which spaces require branch-specific research, and what controlling or persuasive law governs peaceful First Amendment activity in those spaces.

The standing factual baseline is maintained in docs/california/standing-scenario.md. The facility workflow is maintained in docs/california/facility-investigation-methodology.md.

docs.title: Core research question
docs.text: For an ordinary member of the public peacefully recording, observing, receiving information, or engaging in expression at a Contra Costa County public library, how do the governing rules change with the exact area, activity, access condition, and policy invoked?

docs.title: Source hierarchy used
docs.text:
Priority was given to:

  1. U.S. Supreme Court and published Ninth Circuit authority;
  2. current Contra Costa County Library policies and Board of Supervisors records;
  3. California statutes and official California library-law compilations;
  4. persuasive published federal appellate decisions involving public libraries;
  5. California federal district-court decisions as persuasive/contextual authority.

No incident video, viral clip, or unofficial characterization is treated as legal authority.

docs.title: I. System governance and policy provenance
County-library structure
docs.text:
California Education Code section 19100 is part of the County Free Library Law and authorizes county boards of supervisors to establish and maintain county free libraries.

Official California State Library compilation:

https://www.library.ca.gov/uploads/2025/01/California-Library-Laws-2025.pdf

The Contra Costa County Library policy portal identifies current system policies for patron conduct, children/teen areas, suspension, electronic resources, meeting rooms, exhibits/displays, and related subjects:

https://ccclib.org/policies/

For this project, the policy portal is the starting point, not the end of the authority chain. A policy can establish the rule the County asserts without by itself establishing constitutional validity, removal authority, or criminal-enforcement authority.

docs.title: 2026 Patron Conduct and Suspension policies
docs.text:
The Contra Costa County Board of Supervisors approved amended Patron Conduct and Suspension policies on February 10, 2026, agenda item 26-563 / C.54.

Board record:

https://contra-costa.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?GUID=FE18DC5D-D8D2-4476-A6C2-C7215C123DC5&ID=7870598&Options=&Search=

Current Patron Conduct Policy:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/Patron-Conduct-Policy_ADA.pdf

Current Suspension Policy:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/Suspension-Policy_ADA.pdf

The adoption provenance matters because these are Board-approved system policies rather than merely informal staff practices.

docs.title: II. The library is not one constitutional forum
Controlling Ninth Circuit anchor — Faith Center Church Evangelistic Ministries v. Glover
docs.text:
Authority: Faith Center Church Evangelistic Ministries v. Glover, 480 F.3d 891 (9th Cir. 2007), amended published opinion.

Official Ninth Circuit opinion:

https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2007/03/09/0516132.pdf

docs.title: Narrow retained proposition
docs.text:
The Ninth Circuit classified the Antioch Library meeting room, under the policy and practices then before it, as a limited public forum.

The court examined the specific access sought, the meeting-room policy, permitted speakers and subjects, application/approval requirements, fee conditions, excluded uses, and governmental practice. It expressly rejected reliance on other County meeting rooms because the relevant forum was defined by the access sought and, in that case, was the Antioch Library meeting room.

This is controlling support for the project's area-by-area method.

docs.title: What Faith Center does not establish
docs.text:
It does not hold that:

  • every Contra Costa library interior is a limited public forum;
  • every room in every branch has the same classification;
  • a public library as a whole has one forum classification;
  • photography or videography receives the same analysis as meeting-room speech;
  • a policy violation automatically authorizes removal, detention, citation, or arrest.

The forum must still be defined by the particular access and activity at issue.

docs.title: Meeting-room litigation history
docs.text:
The 2007 Ninth Circuit decision addressed the County's then-current exclusion of religious worship services from the Antioch meeting room at the preliminary-injunction stage.

On remand, the district court later held the religious-service restriction unconstitutional under then-prevailing Establishment Clause doctrine in Faith Center Church Evangelistic Ministries v. Glover, No. C 04-3111 JSW, 2009 WL 1765974 (N.D. Cal. June 19, 2009).

The current CCCL meeting-room policy PDF itself records the policy change: the RELIGIOUS USE heading and the sentence barring religious services are struck through and marked effective July 6, 2009.

Current policy/rules PDF:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/LP-RMS-MeetingRoomRules_2025E_ADA.pdf

Important current-law caveat: the 2009 district court used the then-prevailing Lemon/entanglement framework. The Supreme Court later stated in Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507 (2022), that it had abandoned Lemon and its endorsement-test offshoot.

Official Supreme Court opinion:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/21-418diff_k4l8.pdf

Accordingly:

  • the 2007 Ninth Circuit forum classification remains useful controlling authority for the historical Antioch meeting-room forum and for forum methodology;
  • the 2009 district-court Establishment Clause reasoning is historical and is not carried forward as a current general Establishment Clause test;
  • current County policy, not the superseded religious-use language, controls present facility research.

docs.title: III. California library-exterior anchor — Prigmore v. City of Redding
docs.text:
Authority: Prigmore v. City of Redding, 211 Cal.App.4th 1322, 150 Cal.Rptr.3d 647 (2012), published Third District Court of Appeal.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2012/c068866.html

The case involved leafleting on outdoor grounds of the Redding Municipal Library.

docs.title: Narrow retained propositions
docs.text:
• The forum was defined according to the access sought rather than the entire library campus.
  • On the record before the court, the relevant forum consisted of the public open space on the entry side, the entry/exit-door area, and the adjacent parking lot.
  • Those outdoor areas were treated as a traditional public forum based on their use, unrestricted public access, physical characteristics, congregation features, relationship to nearby public spaces, and the library's function.
  • The court distinguished outdoor areas from the interior.
  • The court declined to adopt the older California "basic incompatibility" formulation as the classification rule.
  • Most challenged restrictions in Redding's outdoor policy were likely invalid at the preliminary-injunction stage, while the vehicle-leafleting ban in the parking lot was upheld on the safety rationale before the court.

docs.title: Scope caution
docs.text:
Prigmore does not establish that every California library exterior or parking lot is automatically a traditional public forum. Property ownership/control, actual use, access, boundaries, physical characteristics, history, and the expressive activity still matter.

Footnote 11 stated broadly that federal courts had treated library interiors as limited public forums, citing Faith Center and Kreimer. This project does not use that footnote as a categorical interior holding because Faith Center itself defined the forum as the Antioch meeting room. The ordinary interior remains separately analyzed.

docs.title: Sweep consequence
docs.text:
Contra Costa branch research should separately classify:

  • ordinary municipal/public sidewalks;
  • library-controlled entry plazas or forecourts;
  • doorway/approach areas;
  • parking lots;
  • interior public-service/reading spaces; and
  • intentionally opened rooms/channels.

Status: DOCTRINE-REVIEWED for the narrow Redding exterior proposition.

docs.title: IV. Main library floors and ordinary patron access
docs.text:
No published Ninth Circuit decision located in this sweep categorically classifies the ordinary reading, stacks, service, or circulation areas of a California public library for every expressive activity.

That gap matters.

docs.title: Persuasive authority — Kreimer
docs.text:
Authority: Kreimer v. Bureau of Police for Town of Morristown, 958 F.2d 1242 (3d Cir. 1992).

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/958/1242/371694/

The Third Circuit treated the public library before it as a limited public forum for First Amendment activity compatible with its purpose, emphasizing acquisition of knowledge through reading, writing, and quiet contemplation.

Of special relevance, the patron rule upheld in Kreimer required patrons to be engaged in activities associated with public-library use while in the building.

docs.title: Contra Costa's current activity requirement
docs.text:
CCCL's 2026 Patron Conduct Policy states that patrons must be engaged in activities associated with the use of a public library. Its examples include reading, studying, quiet conversation, working, using library materials/equipment, and participating in a library program/activity. The policy states that patrons not engaged in such activities may be required to leave.

That language closely resembles the rule examined in Kreimer, but Kreimer is Third Circuit authority and therefore persuasive, not controlling, in California.

docs.title: Recording/observation question
docs.text:
The current Patron Conduct Policy does not expressly say whether peaceful observation, photography, videography, documentation of public officials performing public duties, or gathering information for later speech qualifies as an activity associated with the use of a public library.

The public-source sweep did not locate a dedicated current public-facing CCCL photography/videography policy on the policy portal or in the current Patron Conduct Policy.

Research status: AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED.

This is not a conclusion that recording is permitted or forbidden. It means the public-facing policy materials reviewed in this sweep do not answer the question directly.

docs.title: Persuasive circuit disagreement cautions against a blanket label
docs.text:
Other circuits have used differing forum terminology for public libraries.

  • Kreimer, Third Circuit, described the library before it as a limited public forum for compatible activity.
  • Doe v. City of Albuquerque, 667 F.3d 1111 (10th Cir. 2012), in a challenge to a citywide ban on registered sex offenders entering public libraries, treated the libraries there as designated public forums and recognized the First Amendment interest in receiving information.

Source for Doe:

https://www.leagle.com/decision/infco20120120059

These decisions are persuasive only here. Their differing terminology reinforces the project rule: do not import another court's building-wide label without analyzing the California facility, specific area, governmental intent, policy, practice, and activity.

docs.title: V. Patron-conduct rules relevant to peaceful audits
docs.text: The current Patron Conduct Policy contains several provisions likely to appear in a peaceful recording or observation encounter.

docs.title: Interference and disruption
docs.text:
The policy states that conduct interfering with another person's ability or right to use and benefit from library facilities, disrupting another person's use, or disrupting staff duties can lead to removal or suspension.

It separately addresses fighting or seriously disruptive behavior, threats/intimidation, harassment/stalking, blocking aisles/exits/entrances, loud talking/yelling/profanity, disturbing other patrons or staff, and misuse of designated spaces.

For standing-scenario analysis, those predicates are not silently assumed merely because someone objects to a camera or becomes uncomfortable.

A facility entry should document the actual conduct and actual effect.

docs.title: Distress, alarm, and harassment language
docs.text:
The policy contains reasonable-person language concerning actions or words that cause fear, distress, alarm, or harassment, and it also addresses conduct such as persistent staring or gestures.

That language must be applied to actual facts. It does not independently answer whether peaceful filming from a lawful position is prohibited.

The project's disorderly-conduct, trespass, and standing-scenario chapters remain controlling for California statutory analysis.

docs.title: Policy-compliance clause
docs.text:
The policy also addresses failure to comply with a staff request to stop disruptive behavior, the Patron Conduct Policy, or another library policy.

A staff request and a criminal-law command are not interchangeable.

If a later enforcement event occurs, the facility file must separately identify:

  1. the policy rule;
  2. who has authority to issue an exclusion or removal order;
  3. what property or area the order covers;
  4. the California statute, if any, relied on for detention, citation, or arrest; and
  5. the conduct alleged to satisfy that statute.

docs.title: Project field limitation
docs.text:
Independent of the legal analysis below, the project will not intentionally enter or remain in a specifically designated children's area for an audit and will not intentionally position or aim a camera to record into such an area. Children and their activities are not audit targets.

This is a methodological choice, not a statement that public presence or recording in every such area would be unlawful. Branch research may still document the location, signage, boundaries, and governing policy from ordinary public circulation areas.

Current CCCL policy:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/LP-Children-Teen-Area-Policy_ADA.pdf

The Board-approved policy reserves children's areas primarily for children age 11 and under, parents/guardians, and patrons using the children's collection at staff discretion. Teen areas are reserved primarily for patrons age 12-18, persons accompanying them, and patrons using the teen collection at staff discretion.

Unaccompanied adults may be directed to adult areas.

docs.title: Field significance
docs.text:
This is a concrete area-specific access condition.

An ordinary public library can therefore contain general public reading/service areas, age/purpose-designated areas, reservable study rooms, reservable meeting rooms, staff/restricted areas, and exterior areas under the same roof or at the same address.

The presence of minors may support legitimate privacy and safety interests, but this policy does not itself create a general photography/videography prohibition.

docs.title: VII. Meeting and study rooms
docs.text:
CCCL's current rooms directory:

https://ccclib.org/rooms/

Current meeting-room policy/rules:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/LP-RMS-MeetingRoomRules_2025E_ADA.pdf

docs.title: System-level rule, branch-level implementation
docs.text:
The system encourages meeting-room use for educational, cultural, and community-related meetings, programs, and activities.

The current rooms directory also shows important branch-specific differences:

  • some rooms are reserved directly through CCCL;
  • some community rooms are booked or controlled by a city or town;
  • room capacities, eligibility, fees, hours, and reservation rules vary;
  • some rooms have specialized local rules.

Examples include rooms whose booking is handled by the City of Brentwood, City of Clayton, Town of Danville, City of San Pablo, and other local entities.

docs.title: Registry consequence
docs.text:
A branch entry must not assume that the County controls every room merely because the room is inside or associated with a County Library branch.

For each room, determine:

  • owner/controller;
  • booking authority;
  • governing policy;
  • permitted purposes/speakers;
  • whether the room is open during or outside ordinary branch hours;
  • whether County patron rules remain applicable; and
  • exact forum classification.

Faith Center provides controlling precedent for the historical Antioch meeting room on its record, not automatic classification of every room currently listed in the system.

docs.title: VIII. Exhibits, displays, and non-library materials
docs.text:
Current policy portal:

https://ccclib.org/policies/

Current rules for display/distribution of non-library materials:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2024/10/LP-rulesforexhibitsdisplay-October2024E.pdf

The rules permit non-library informational materials subject to authorization, available space, and subject/use restrictions. They prohibit material used for religious services and instructions on how to vote for a candidate or political party, while allowing announcements of political meetings. The rules also permit branch-specific rules tied to local needs and conditions.

docs.title: Research posture
docs.text:
These display/distribution channels appear intentionally opened for specified speakers and subjects and therefore require a channel-specific forum analysis.

This sweep does not decide whether the political or religious restrictions are constitutional.

Reasons for further review include:

  • the Library affirmatively opens a distribution/display channel to non-library materials;
  • the restrictions are expressly subject-matter based;
  • the religious language must be reconciled with current limited-forum doctrine and with the separate meeting-room litigation history;
  • political-party/candidate restrictions require their own limited-forum reasonableness and viewpoint-neutrality analysis.

Research status: AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED.

Because these restrictions involve political expression, later legal analysis should evaluate the rule neutrally rather than favoring or opposing any party, candidate, or viewpoint.

docs.title: IX. Patron-record privacy is not a camera statute
docs.text:
CCCL privacy page:

https://ccclib.org/privacy/

The Library identifies California Government Code section 7927.105 as protecting registration and patron-use records, including personally identifiable borrowing or resource-use information.

The California State Library's library-law compilation is also a source for library-specific public-record provisions:

https://www.library.ca.gov/uploads/2025/01/California-Library-Laws-2025.pdf

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
Library-record confidentiality and visitor recording are different legal questions.

Government Code section 7927.105 concerns disclosure and confidentiality of qualifying library-maintained patron-use records. It should not be cited as though its text creates a categorical prohibition on a member of the public incidentally photographing or recording another person in a library.

Separate doctrines may still matter, including California constitutional privacy, confidential-communications law, harassment/stalking law, facility-specific policy, restrictions tailored to children or sensitive areas, disruption/interference, and tort/privacy law.

Those issues require their own elements.

docs.title: X. Suspension, exclusion, and due process
docs.text:
Current Suspension Policy:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/Suspension-Policy_ADA.pdf

The policy creates escalating suspension categories ranging from one day through suspensions longer than one year.

For severe or repeat misconduct, the policy provides for written notice identifying the reason and duration and can suspend access to all Contra Costa County Library facilities.

docs.title: Appeals
docs.text:
The current policy provides:

  • written appeal to the County Librarian for suspensions longer than one week and up to one year, with a written response within seven days;
  • a review-panel process for suspensions longer than one year;
  • no stated formal appeal process in the published policy for suspensions of one week or less.

docs.title: Neinast v. Board of Trustees of Columbus Metropolitan Library
docs.text:
Authority: 346 F.3d 585 (6th Cir. 2003), persuasive only.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/346/585/510700/

The Sixth Circuit upheld the process used for a one-day library eviction on its facts where the patron received notice of the charge and an opportunity to present his side. The court did not prescribe one universal procedure for all library exclusions.

docs.title: Van Den Heuvel v. Dorothy
docs.text:
An Eastern District of California screening decision stated that a weeks-to-month countywide library suspension could plausibly implicate a liberty interest while leaving the ultimate issue for later proceedings.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/california/caedce/2%3A2021cv02176/403475/24/

This is nonbinding district-court authority.

docs.title: Current conclusion
docs.text:
The exact constitutional process required for immediate ejection, one-day suspension, one-week suspension, multiweek or multimonth suspension, and systemwide long-term exclusion has not been resolved by a published controlling Ninth Circuit or California appellate library case located in this sweep.

Research status: AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED.

A later chapter should apply ordinary procedural-due-process doctrine and any additional California law to the duration, scope, factual basis, notice, urgency, opportunity to respond, and appeal mechanism.

docs.title: XI. Suspension policy and California trespass
docs.text:
The Suspension Policy states that a suspended person who returns before the listed return date will be asked to leave; if the person refuses, law enforcement will be contacted. It further states that the person is subject to arrest for trespass under California Penal Code section 602.

That policy statement does not identify a subsection of section 602 or walk through statutory elements.

Sweep 002 already established that California trespass provisions are element-specific and area/access-specific.

docs.title: Research consequence
docs.text:
For an actual enforcement event:

  • identify the exact Penal Code subsection;
  • determine whether its property/access predicates apply;
  • distinguish a valid administrative suspension or removal order from an independent criminal offense;
  • do not treat the policy's generic citation to section 602 as completing the criminal-law analysis.

Research flag: POLICY-TO-CRIMINAL-AUTHORITY-GAP.

The flag does not mean arrest would necessarily be unlawful. It means the public-facing policy does not itself supply the complete statutory bridge.

docs.title: XII. Photography and videography — current system finding
docs.text:
As of September 21, 2026, this sweep reviewed:

  • CCCL's public policy index;
  • the current Patron Conduct Policy;
  • the current Suspension Policy;
  • children/teen-area policy;
  • meeting-room policy/rules;
  • exhibits/display rules; and
  • targeted searches of the CCCL public website.

No dedicated current public-facing CCCL policy specifically governing ordinary patron photography or videography inside library facilities was located.

docs.title: What follows
docs.text:
Nothing categorical yet.

A future branch investigation should ask:

  1. Is there an unpublished/internal or branch-specific photography policy?
  2. Are there posted camera/recording signs?
  3. What exact area is involved?
  4. What activity is being recorded?
  5. Is the claimed restriction based on privacy, disruption, program licensing, minors, staff safety, facility control, or another rationale?
  6. Who adopted the rule?
  7. What is the exclusion/removal authority?
  8. If police enforcement follows, what independent offense is claimed?

The constitutional analysis must then combine the project's recording, forum, trespass/removal, privacy, and police-encounter chapters.

Do not use: "There is no photography policy."

Use: "No dedicated public-facing photography/videography policy was located in the sources reviewed as of September 21, 2026."

docs.title: XIII. Special-access conditions
docs.text:
CCCL also operates access models that should not be collapsed into ordinary staffed public hours.

As of the verification pass, Self-Service Sundays is currently available at Concord and San Pablo, with Pittsburg listed as coming soon. It uses advance registration, orientation, a signed user agreement, library-card/PIN access, and operates without library staff onsite.

Current program page:

https://ccclib.org/self-service-sundays/

A Registry entry should distinguish:

  • normal staffed open hours;
  • special enrolled/card-controlled access periods;
  • room-only after-hours access, if applicable;
  • closed hours;
  • emergency or temporary closures.

docs.title: Field rule — define the library area
docs.text:
Do not say: "A public library is a public forum."

Use: Identify the exact area and activity. A meeting room intentionally opened for community meetings can have a different forum analysis from stacks, a children's area, a study room, a staff office, or an exterior sidewalk.

docs.title: Field rule — library purpose matters, but does not answer every activity
docs.text: Libraries may adopt reasonable rules preserving reading, study, information access, safety, and other intended uses. Whether a particular recording or expressive restriction is valid still requires the actual rule, area, activity, purpose, and governing doctrine.

docs.title: Field rule — "library activity" is a real policy predicate
docs.text: CCCL can point to an adopted rule requiring patrons to engage in activities associated with public-library use. Whether a peaceful auditor's particular information-gathering activity satisfies, or can constitutionally be excluded under, that rule remains a separate question.

docs.title: Field rule — protect the policy/removal/crime distinction
docs.text: A patron-conduct violation, staff instruction, suspension notice, removal authority, and California criminal trespass are separate steps. Identify the authority for each.

docs.title: Field rule — patron-record privacy is not camera law
docs.text: Patron-record confidentiality protects qualifying library-maintained records. Do not transform it into a categorical visitor-recording prohibition without separate authority.

docs.title: XV. Branch-research schema produced by this sweep
docs.text:
A Contra Costa branch file should collect at least:

  • branch and building owner;
  • County versus city/town control of specific spaces;
  • exterior sidewalk/plaza ownership;
  • ordinary staffed public hours;
  • special/self-service access periods;
  • entrance/security/check-in conditions;
  • main reading/stacks/service areas;
  • children's and teen areas;
  • study rooms;
  • meeting/community rooms and booking authority;
  • exhibit/display/distribution areas;
  • restrooms;
  • staff/restricted areas;
  • posted photography/recording rules;
  • any branch-specific patron rules;
  • prior suspensions/removals relevant to the issue;
  • exact exclusion/removal authority;
  • exact criminal statute previously invoked, if any;
  • current research flags.

This is the practical output of Sweep 006: system rules first; branch and area facts second.

docs.title: XVII. Open research queue after Sweep 006
docs.text:
The sweep intentionally leaves these issues open:

  • controlling Ninth Circuit/California treatment of ordinary library-floor access for expressive activity beyond Faith Center's meeting-room holding;
  • recording/photography inside public-library interiors;
  • whether and when peaceful governmental observation/recording qualifies under CCCL's "activities associated with use of a public library" requirement;
  • First Amendment retaliation for recording or criticism in a library;
  • exact due process required for different suspension lengths and systemwide exclusions;
  • exact California trespass subsection/authority applicable to return during an administrative library suspension;
  • constitutional review of CCCL exhibit/display political and religious restrictions;
  • current California Speech Clause overlay for library interiors and intentionally opened library channels;
  • branch-specific ownership/control of exterior areas and community rooms;
  • program-specific restrictions involving performers, copyrighted content, or minors;
  • physical seizure/search of recording devices if a library encounter escalates to police.

These are research tasks, not assumptions against or in favor of the Library.

docs.title: XVIII. Sweep conclusion
docs.text:
Contra Costa is a strong first library system because it demonstrates why the Registry must be system → branch → area/activity rather than one facility label.

The current record establishes:

  • Board-approved systemwide patron and suspension rules;
  • age/purpose-designated spaces;
  • intentionally opened meeting and display channels;
  • branch-specific room-control differences;
  • a controlling Ninth Circuit case involving one CCCL meeting room;
  • a current "library activity" requirement with a close persuasive analogue in Kreimer;
  • no dedicated public-facing recording policy located in the sources reviewed;
  • an administrative suspension scheme with duration-dependent appeals; and
  • a generic Penal Code section 602 enforcement statement that still requires a subsection/element bridge before criminal analysis.

The next phase should apply this legal/system spine to one branch at a time without assuming that the answer for one room or branch determines another.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This is the first branch-level implementation of the public-library method produced by Sweep 006.

Facility: Concord Library System: Contra Costa County Library (CCCL) Address: 2900 Salvio Street, Concord, California 94519 Research mode: documentary / pre-field Field observation: none yet

The branch is not assigned one forum classification. This file separately tracks the ordinary exterior, parking areas, entrance/approach, ordinary interior, meeting room, and Self-Service Sunday access regime.

Controlling project baseline:

  • docs/california/standing-scenario.md
  • docs/california/facility-investigation-methodology.md
  • docs/california/public-libraries.md
  • docs/research/FACILITY-PREP-SOP.md

No personal operating preference is treated as law or as a rule for other people.

docs.title: I. Core research question
docs.text:
For an ordinary member of the public peacefully observing, recording, receiving information, or engaging in expression at Concord Library, what rules and constitutional analysis apply to each specific area and access condition?

Key questions:

  1. Who owns and controls the library parcel, front lot, rear lot, and immediate approaches?
  2. Which exterior areas are ordinary public rights-of-way, City/Civic Center parking, or facility-specific property?
  3. What forum classification best fits each exterior area under Prigmore and ordinary public-sidewalk doctrine?
  4. Does the branch have any posted or branch-specific photography/recording rule not located in the system-level online sweep?
  5. How does ordinary staffed access differ from Self-Service Sunday access?
  6. What forum is created by the Concord meeting-room policy?
  7. What authority would support removal or criminal enforcement if a recording/access dispute occurred?

docs.title: II. Verified branch facts
docs.text:
Current CCCL branch page:

https://ccclib.org/locations/7/

As verified September 21, 2026, the page identifies Concord Library at 2900 Salvio Street. Ordinary staffed hours are Monday 10–8, Tuesday 10–8, Wednesday 10–6, Thursday 10–6, Friday 9–5, Saturday 9–5, and Sunday closed during ordinary staffed operations.

The branch page also identifies a meeting room and Self-Service Sundays.

docs.title: Public parking
docs.text:
CCCL expressly describes two free public parking areas:

  • Front / Salvio lot: 3 accessible, 3 short-term/30-minute, and 15 regular spaces.
  • Rear / Parkside lot: a larger public lot behind the library adjacent to the Concord Civic Center, with 3 accessible and approximately 70+ regular spaces.

That is a verified public-use fact. It is not, standing alone, a forum classification.

docs.title: III. Civic Center and physical-context evidence
docs.text:
City library page:

https://www.cityofconcord.org/510/Schools-Library

City Civic Center map:

https://www.cityofconcord.org/446/Building-Map-PDF

The City's Civic Center map identifies:

  • Concord Library;
  • Salvio Street and Parkside Drive;
  • public parking areas;
  • the Library's Public Entrance on the east side;
  • a bike rack adjacent to the Library/Civic Center pedestrian circulation area;
  • pedestrian routes linking parking, the Library, and Civic Center buildings;
  • City Hall/Civic Center functions immediately adjacent to the Library.

This is strong physical/use context. It is not a cadastral or survey map.

City transportation materials also describe the Salvio corridor as part of a high walking/bicycle-demand connection from downtown to the Civic Center and Concord Library.

docs.title: IV. Property, boundary, and record chain
docs.text:
Canonical evidence manifest:

docs/research/evidence/concord-library/README.md

docs.title: A. Current parcels
docs.text:

docs.title: E. Boundary conclusion
docs.text:
The exact surveyed modern ROW edge remains unresolved, but the record is now sufficient to distinguish the legal questions that actually matter:

  • the genuine municipal sidewalk/ROW component can be analyzed under ordinary public-sidewalk doctrine even though its precise edge must still be located;
  • City-owned library/Civic Center exterior areas can be compared directly to Prigmore without waiting for every historical deed where the exact line between two City-owned parcels would not change the forum analysis;
  • exact boundary evidence remains outcome-relevant when a removal/trespass question turns on a few feet between public ROW and facility-specific property.

Prepared City Engineering target:

docs/research/evidence/concord-library/city-engineering-row-request-target-2026-09-22.md

Research flag: PROPERTY/ROW-PARTIALLY-VERIFIED / EXACT-EDGE-UNRESOLVED / FORUM-APPLICATION-NOW-POSSIBLE.

docs.title: V. Exterior forum analysis — Prigmore applied
docs.text:
Canonical analysis:

docs/research/evidence/concord-library/prigmore-exterior-analysis-2026-09-22.md

Earlier working worksheet:

docs/research/evidence/concord-library/prigmore-exterior-worksheet-2026-09-22.md

docs.title: Governing comparator
docs.text:
Prigmore v. City of Redding, 211 Cal.App.4th 1322 (2012), defined the forum by the access sought and treated, on the Redding record, three outdoor areas together:

  1. public open space on the library's entry side;
  2. the entry/exit-door area; and
  3. the adjacent parking lot.

The court emphasized actual use and purpose, public-thoroughfare function and free public access, physical characteristics and boundaries, traditional/historic use, the library's information-dissemination function, adjacency to public buildings/parks, and congregation/rest features.

The holding is property-specific. It does not make every library exterior a traditional public forum.

docs.title: 1. Salvio Street municipal sidewalk / public-ROW component
docs.text:
Classification: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — HIGH CONFIDENCE, SUBJECT TO EXACT-EDGE IDENTIFICATION.

The actual municipal sidewalk component is classic traditional-public-forum property. City GIS identifies the relevant Salvio segment as Concord-owned/jurisdictional with sidewalks on both sides, and City planning treats the corridor as part of the pedestrian/bicycle connection serving the Civic Center and Library.

The unresolved issue is the surveyed edge where public ROW transitions into facility-specific property, not the forum doctrine applicable to an identified municipal sidewalk.

docs.title: 2. Parkside Drive municipal sidewalk / public-ROW component
docs.text:
Classification: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — HIGH CONFIDENCE, SUBJECT TO EXACT-EDGE IDENTIFICATION.

The same reasoning applies to the actual Parkside public-sidewalk/ROW component. The closest City segment is Concord-owned/jurisdictional and reports sidewalks on both sides.

docs.title: 3. Library public entrance / immediate east-side approach
docs.text:
Classification: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — STRONGLY SUPPORTED UNDER PRIGMORE; FIELD/PHYSICAL VERIFICATION PENDING.

The City map marks this as the Library's Public Entrance and shows it integrated with public parking, a bike rack, pedestrian circulation, and adjacent Civic Center buildings. Ordinary staffed access is open to the public.

This is a close functional analogue to the entry/exit area in Prigmore. The present documentary record is weaker than Redding's on congregation features: no current official source reviewed yet establishes benches, newspaper racks, tables, or comparable seating immediately outside the Concord entrance. That missing fact reduces confidence but does not erase the strong entry/civic-circulation analogy.

docs.title: 4. Library/Civic Center connective pedestrian walkway
docs.text:
Classification: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — STRONGLY SUPPORTED; EXACT SUBAREA/FIELD CONDITIONS PENDING.

The City map depicts ordinary pedestrian circulation linking the Library public entrance, bike rack, public parking, and multiple Civic Center buildings. It appears functionally broader than a restricted employee/service path.

Free public access, City ownership, public-building circulation, and similarity to civic walkways strongly support traditional-public-forum treatment under Prigmore's comparative approach.

docs.title: 5. Front Salvio public parking lot
docs.text:
Classification: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — STRONGLY SUPPORTED UNDER PRIGMORE FOR LAWFUL PEDESTRIAN EXPRESSIVE USE; SAFETY RESTRICTIONS REMAIN MATERIAL.

CCCL expressly describes the front lot as public parking serving the branch. It sits immediately at the Library/Civic Center frontage and is materially similar to the adjacent library parking lot included in the forum defined in Prigmore.

This does not eliminate traffic, obstruction, or vehicle-safety rules. Prigmore itself upheld Redding's restriction on placing leaflets on vehicles in the parking lot based on the safety/property rationale before the court.

Under the project's standing scenario — no blocking, interference, unsafe positioning, or occupation of vehicle travel lanes — the forum analogy is substantially stronger than for activity directed at parked vehicles or occurring in traffic lanes.

docs.title: 6. Rear Parkside / Civic Center public parking lot
docs.text:
Classification: PRIGMORE ANALOGY SUBSTANTIAL; FINAL TRADITIONAL-PUBLIC-FORUM CLASSIFICATION PENDING PHYSICAL/USE VERIFICATION.

Supporting facts include public parking designation, City ownership context, adjacency to the Library/Civic Center, ordinary public access, and integration into Civic Center circulation.

The status remains narrower than the front lot because the rear area is a large shared Civic Center parking facility rather than the small lot immediately associated with the Library entrance. Current documentary sources do not yet establish congregation/rest features, historic expressive use, reserved/employee-only subareas, or exact pedestrian circulation through the lot.

docs.title: 7. Vehicle drive aisles / driveway throats
docs.text:
Classification: NO SEPARATE BROAD SPEECH-ZONE CONCLUSION; STRONG SAFETY/TRAFFIC INTERESTS APPLY.

The surrounding forum does not create a right to obstruct or occupy vehicle travel lanes in a manner incompatible with traffic safety. The standing scenario already excludes that conduct.

docs.title: Recording-specific limit
docs.text:
Prigmore is a forum case involving leafleting, not a stand-alone right-to-record case.

Do not write:

Prigmore says you may film in this parking lot.

Use:

Prigmore strongly supports traditional-public-forum treatment for specified Concord exterior areas; any restriction on peaceful recording there must then be analyzed under the applicable First Amendment, California speech, and recording doctrines rather than assumed valid merely because the activity occurs on library grounds.

Exterior status: DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART / AREA-SPECIFIC-CLASSIFICATIONS-ASSIGNED / FIELD-VERIFICATION-PENDING.

docs.title: VI. Ordinary staffed interior
docs.text:
The system-level Sweep 006 applies.

CCCL's 2026 Patron Conduct Policy requires patrons in the building to be engaged in activities associated with use of a public library. The system-level sweep did not locate a dedicated current public-facing ordinary-patron photography/videography policy.

No current online Concord branch source reviewed here states a general photography/videography rule. That narrow finding does not prove the absence of posted signage, internal staff/security guidance, or a newer rule.

The current record does not establish a categorical controlling forum classification for peaceful recording in Concord's ordinary stacks, reading, service, and circulation areas.

Status: AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED.

docs.title: VII. Concord meeting room
docs.text:
Current room directory:

https://ccclib.org/rooms/

Current Concord-specific policy:

https://ccclib.org/concord-meeting-room-use-policy/

The room is expressly opened as meeting space for organizations, businesses, or groups. Published conditions include reservation/approval procedures, one use per month, fee distinctions, use during open library hours, priority for library/Friends programming, compatibility with normal library operations, and branch-specific conduct/use restrictions.

Faith Center Church Evangelistic Ministries v. Glover, 480 F.3d 891 (9th Cir. 2007), held that the historical Antioch Library meeting room was a limited public forum. The current Concord/system written rules retain the core features relevant in Faith Center: defined eligible users/purposes, application and screening, fee/no-fee distinctions, and limits tied to library operations.

Policy-based classification: STRONGLY SUPPORTED — LIMITED PUBLIC FORUM.

This is an application of Faith Center methodology to current written rules, not a claim that Faith Center adjudicated today's Concord room. Actual practice remains a verification item.

Status: DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART / LIMITED-PUBLIC-FORUM-STRONGLY-SUPPORTED / PRACTICE-VERIFICATION-PENDING.

docs.title: VIII. Self-Service Sundays — distinct access regime
docs.text:
Current program page:

https://ccclib.org/self-service-sundays/

Current agreement:

https://cdn-web-main.bibliocms.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/SSS-Agreement-13-and-older-FINAL2_ADA.pdf

Concord Self-Service Sunday runs 12–5 p.m. for approved users. Published conditions include advance enrollment, age 13+, parental consent under 18, library card in good standing, orientation, signed agreement, branch registration, and card/PIN entry. The meeting room is unavailable.

The June 2026 agreement states, among other things, that access is outside normal staffed hours; staff/community/study areas are unavailable; some interior/exterior areas may be security-camera monitored; users must follow library policies and directions; unapproved adults may not be admitted; and violations/refusal to leave may result in suspension of privileges.

The agreement does not state a general prohibition on patron photography/videorecording. That absence is narrow because incorporated policies, lawful instructions, signs, or other rules may still matter.

Status: ACCESS-CONDITION-VERIFIED / RECORDING-FORUM-EFFECT-UNRESOLVED.

docs.title: X. Photography / recording — branch-specific finding
docs.text:
As of September 21, 2026, no dedicated current public-facing Concord-specific ordinary-patron photography/videography rule was located in the branch/system sources reviewed.

Use the narrow formulation:

No dedicated public-facing Concord-specific ordinary-patron photography/videography rule was located in the online sources reviewed as of September 21, 2026.

Do not write:

Concord Library has no photography policy.

Physical signage, internal guidance, security instructions, or newer rules remain unverified.

Status: AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED.

docs.title: XI. Remaining documentary / field queue
docs.text:
The property research has reached the point of diminishing returns for anonymous online acquisition. The known old-record identifiers are resolved; their images require manual acquisition. Exact City ROW edges can be pursued through the prepared engineering request:

docs/research/evidence/concord-library/city-engineering-row-request-target-2026-09-22.md

The highest-value remaining work is now:

  1. current physical verification of the entrance/forecourt, benches/seating, newspaper racks, tables, plaza characteristics, and pedestrian congregation space;
  2. current signs governing parking, library grounds, loitering, solicitation, photography, reserved areas, or exterior access;
  3. identification of reserved/employee-only portions, if any, of the rear Civic Center lot;
  4. exact ROW edge where a few feet would alter the legal classification or enforcement analysis;
  5. current City/County operating, maintenance, parking, security, or access-control agreement if one materially changes exterior control;
  6. Concord-specific staff/security recording guidance or post orders;
  7. removal/exclusion authority and the system-level policy-to-criminal-authority gap as applied to any concrete exterior enforcement scenario.

Observed facts must be recorded separately from legal conclusions.

docs.title: XII. Research flags
docs.text:
• [x] AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED — ordinary interior recording/forum status is not resolved by current controlling authority or published branch policy.
  • [x] PROPERTY/ROW-PARTIALLY-VERIFIED — APNs, City owner fields, assessor map, street attributes, and historic survey chain are developed; exact modern legal edges remain unresolved.
  • [x] EXTERIOR-FORUM-APPLICATION-COMPLETED-IN-PART — area-specific Prigmore classifications are now assigned with confidence qualifiers.
  • [ ] POTENTIAL-FACIAL-CONFLICT — no branch-specific rule has yet been identified that warrants this flag.
  • [ ] POTENTIAL-AS-APPLIED-CONFLICT — no branch-specific enforcement incident has yet been documented.
  • [ ] POTENTIAL-VIEWPOINT-COMPARATOR — no comparator record yet.
  • [ ] POLICY-TO-CRIMINAL-AUTHORITY-GAP — system-level § 602 issue remains in Sweep 006, but no Concord-specific enforcement event has yet been identified.
  • [ ] SUPERSEDED-OR-REVISED — older Self-Service pilot materials are historical; current materials are used here.

docs.title: XIII. Current conclusion
docs.text:
Concord now demonstrates why a facility Registry must be area-specific rather than building-specific.

Current documentary research supports:

  • traditional-public-forum treatment of the actual Salvio and Parkside municipal sidewalk/ROW components, subject to exact-edge identification where visually ambiguous;
  • strongly supported traditional-public-forum treatment under Prigmore for the Library public entrance/immediate approach, the connective Civic Center pedestrian walkway, and the front Salvio public lot;
  • a substantial but not yet final Prigmore case for the large rear Parkside/Civic Center public lot;
  • strongly supported limited-public-forum treatment of the Concord meeting room under Faith Center;
  • unresolved ordinary-interior recording/forum status;
  • a separately conditioned Self-Service Sunday access regime.

The branch remains Gray / unresolved overall because several areas and the recording/removal questions remain open. But the exterior is no longer simply FORUM-APPLICATION-PENDING: the Prigmore analysis has now been performed and produces useful area-level conclusions with explicit confidence limits.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Sweep 008 is the second branch-level Contra Costa County Library investigation and the first deliberate same-category validation of the Facility Prep prototype after Concord.

Facility: Walnut Creek Library System: Contra Costa County Library (CCCL) Address: 1644 N. Broadway, Walnut Creek, California 94596 Research mode: documentary / pre-field Field observation: none yet

Walnut Creek changes the physical problem while holding much of the library-system policy layer constant. The branch occupies a dense downtown civic setting with a civic plaza, Civic Park connection, surface parking, an underground garage, multiple public entrances, public-facing outdoor space, and differently managed room channels.

No branch-wide forum conclusion is assigned. The analysis follows system → branch → area/activity.

Canonical project sources:

  • docs/california/standing-scenario.md
  • docs/california/facility-investigation-methodology.md
  • docs/california/public-libraries.md
  • docs/research/FACILITY-PREP-SOP.md
  • docs/research/evidence/walnut-creek-library/README.md

docs.title: 1. Research questions
docs.text:
Sweep 008 asks:

  1. whether Facility Prep can resolve a non-Concord Contra Costa branch without relying on Concord-only AddressPoint data;
  2. what parcel contains the Library and which adjoining parcels are materially relevant to public access;
  3. how the Broadway/Lincoln civic plaza, formal entrance, Civic Park connection, surface lot and municipal sidewalks compare with Prigmore and ordinary sidewalk/park doctrine;
  4. whether the underground public garage presents a materially different forum problem from the outdoor lot;
  5. how Oak View, Las Trampas and group study rooms differ as opened/purpose-limited channels;
  6. whether a current Walnut Creek-specific ordinary-patron photography/videography rule is publicly posted online;
  7. which unresolved boundary/control facts could actually change removal, trespass or forum analysis.

docs.title: 2. Current branch facts
docs.text:
Official CCCL branch page:

https://ccclib.org/locations/26/

As reviewed September 22, 2026:

  • Monday–Thursday: 10 a.m.–8 p.m.;
  • Friday–Saturday: 9 a.m.–5 p.m.;
  • Sunday: closed;
  • listed facilities include a cafe, computer lab, meeting room and study room.

CCCL identifies:

  • Library underground garage: 120 spaces, four-hour limit;
  • Library surface lot: 20 four-hour spaces and 10 thirty-minute spaces;
  • Broadway Garage: separate nearby downtown garage at 1390 N. Broadway.

The Broadway Garage is not treated as part of the Library parcel merely because it is listed as nearby parking.

CCCL branch history/design page:

https://ccclib.org/about-walnut-creek-library/

It describes the 2010 Library near Civic Park and identifies, among other features, a children's wing and patio, Teen Zone, cafe, conference room, study rooms, Community Art Gallery and Oak View meeting room.

docs.title: Self-Service Sunday
docs.text:
Current CCCL FAQ identifies Self-Service Sundays at Concord and San Pablo, with Pittsburg coming soon. Walnut Creek is not listed as a participating branch and its current branch page lists Sunday closed.

Source:

NO-CURRENT-SELF-SERVICE-SUNDAY-ACCESS-LOCATED / ORDINARY-SUNDAY-CLOSED

docs.title: 5. Facility Prep second-site validation
docs.text: Walnut Creek materially validated the pipeline while exposing hidden first-site assumptions.

docs.title: Countywide core + local enrichment
docs.text:
The parcel layer was reusable outside Concord; the Concord AddressPoint and Road Centerlines layers were not assumed to be countywide.

Working architecture:

countywide parcel core + municipality-specific address / street / ROW / owned-property / facility-control enrichment

docs.title: Recorded-map alias defect found and fixed
docs.text:
The Concord-era map resolver had been tested against LSM/record-of-survey and corner-record references. Walnut Creek's assessor sheet introduced MB shorthand.

The initial Book/Page search did not constrain WebLink's Record Type selector. The adapter was corrected so:

  • LSM / RS → Record of Survey Map;
  • CR → Corner Record;
  • MB / subdivision → Subdivision Map;
  • PM / parcel → Parcel Map.

A live post-fix run confirmed that the actual WebLink search syntax contained Record Type = "Subdivision Map" and returned exactly one relevant result for each tested historical reference.

Validation run:

  • run ID 35779391449;
  • job ID 106920689651;
  • conclusion success;
  • artifact ID 10716842873;
  • artifact ZIP SHA-256 91f683b20188b3f70bb0480df8ef4cf014c399ee410f40fb4f70e3dc6d3432d4.

Detailed checkpoint:

The Facility Prep SOP now preserves the second-site lessons as reusable methodology rather than Walnut Creek-only lore.

docs.title: 6. Civic design and public-access evidence
docs.text:
A City design-period publication states that the Library was designed to be accessible from:

  1. a new civic plaza at Broadway and Lincoln;
  2. a formal entrance on Broadway;
  3. the surface parking lot; and
  4. a Civic Park entrance.

It also states that the underground garage was intended to serve Library patrons, community-center users and other downtown visitors.

Source:

https://www.walnutcreekca.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/84/635672432775130000

The City's Public Art Master Plan independently identifies Library Outdoor Plazas, Civic Park walkways/entries, sidewalks and street furniture as potential public-art locations:

https://www.walnutcreekca.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/11536/636136819628970000

These are strong intended-use/circulation sources, not cadastral surveys.

docs.title: 7. Civic Park

docs.title: Underground garage
docs.text:
The garage is deliberately open to the public, but it is also an enclosed special-purpose vehicle-storage/circulation structure. Public access alone does not make it a public forum.

Current evidence includes:

  • CCCL: 120 Library underground spaces, four-hour limit;
  • City Oak View page: metered underground parking remains accessible during after-hours events;
  • City design source: garage intended for Library patrons, community-center users and other downtown visitors;
  • City sustainability materials: public EV chargers at the Library.

These facts make an employee-only/private-garage characterization implausible, but they do not answer forum classification.

Cornelius, Kokinda and Sammartano are useful cautionary/general comparators for purpose-built access space. Prigmore remains much closer to the open plaza/entrance/surface-lot areas. None directly decides this garage.

Status:

PUBLIC-ACCESS-VERIFIED / FORUM-UNRESOLVED

https://www.walnutcreekca.gov/government/community-development-department/permits/building-permits/site-plans-and-diagrams

https://www.walnutcreekca.gov/government/community-development-department/permits/building-permits/request-building-records

No publicly indexed current Library site/engineering plan was located during this sweep that fixes the exact Broadway/Lincoln/plaza/garage edges.

Under the outcome-determinative boundary gate, a targeted current-plan request is warranted only if the exact line would change the legal result—for example, a location-specific exclusion/trespass dispute at a visually ambiguous plaza/sidewalk transition.

docs.title: 15. Facility Prep validation result
docs.text:
Walnut Creek demonstrates that Facility Prep is becoming a reusable pipeline rather than a Concord-specific script.

  • parcel geometry;

Remained modular:

  • AddressPoint enrichment;

  • municipal owned-property layers;
  • current site/engineering records;

The same-category prototype gate has therefore served its purpose. The next architecture test should be a materially different facility category rather than another library merely to repeat the same parcel pattern.

docs.title: 16. Documentary sweep posture
docs.text:
The Walnut Creek documentary branch sweep is now substantially developed.

What still matters before a final branch entry is not more indiscriminate historical-record searching. The remaining high-value items are:

  1. current physical/signage verification of the civic plaza, entrances, surface lot and garage;
  2. exact modern ROW/site-plan acquisition only where the line becomes outcome-determinative;
  3. current garage conduct/access signs and pedestrian-node layout;
  4. any current cafe lease/control evidence if that subarea is actually analyzed;
  5. ordinary-interior recording/forum doctrine as the broader statewide/library issue develops;
  6. any future concrete removal/trespass incident, analyzed under its actual area/controller/facts.

The branch remains Gray / unresolved overall. That overall status coexists with several area-level conclusions that are already well supported.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Sweep 009 is the first deliberate cross-category Facility Prep validation after the Concord and Walnut Creek public-library tests.

Facility: California Department of Motor Vehicles — Concord Field Office Agency: California Department of Motor Vehicles Address: 2070 Diamond Boulevard, Concord, California 94520 Research mode: documentary / pre-field Field observation: none yet

Official DMV field-office page:

https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/field-office/concord/

As reviewed September 22, 2026, DMV identifies the Concord Field Office at 2070 Diamond Boulevard and lists ordinary office hours Monday–Tuesday and Thursday–Friday 8 a.m.–5 p.m., Wednesday 9 a.m.–5 p.m., Saturday–Sunday closed. The office also has a self-service kiosk.

No facility-wide forum classification is assigned. Sweep 009 follows the project's facility → specific area/activity rule and separately analyzes municipal sidewalk/ROW, facility approaches, customer parking, exterior queueing, entrance threshold, lobby/waiting space, transaction counters, knowledge-test areas, kiosk space, and employee/restricted areas.

Canonical evidence manifest:

docs/research/evidence/concord-dmv/README.md

docs.title: 1. Why DMV is the cross-category test
docs.text:
Concord DMV changes the governmental purpose while preserving enough geography to test which parts of Facility Prep genuinely generalized.

Useful constants:

  • Contra Costa County parcel/assessor sources remain available;
  • Concord municipal GIS/ROW sources can be reused where their actual geographic coverage fits;
  • the same recorded-map custodian and adapters remain available.

Material changes:

  • the operating agency is a California state administrative agency rather than a county library;
  • the facility exists to conduct transactions, examinations, records work, licensing and related administrative services;
  • the interior contains more purpose-limited customer zones;
  • privacy and examination-integrity interests are materially different;
  • the closest legal comparators are no longer the library cases.

The test therefore asks whether the project generalized evidence methods rather than library assumptions.

docs.title: 9. Privacy and purpose-limited DMV rules
docs.text:
DMV's current privacy materials identify substantial protections for personal information, including driver-license/ID numbers, Social Security numbers, photographs, medical/disability information, fingerprints/thumbprints and examination information.

Those interests are materially relevant when analyzing a specific restriction around counters, records or examinations.

They do not themselves create a general camera prohibition.

The proper chain is:

DMV privacy duty → actual information exposed in the physical area → identified restriction → forum classification → constitutional/statutory analysis

docs.title: Knowledge test
docs.text:
DMV's current California Driver's Handbook states that testing aids, including a cell phone, may not be used during a knowledge test.

Status:

CURRENT-PUBLIC-RULE-VERIFIED / EXAMINATION-ACTIVITY-SPECIFIC

This must not be generalized into a branch-wide no-phone or no-camera rule.

docs.title: 10. Federal interior forum analysis
docs.text: No controlling Ninth Circuit or published California appellate decision specifically adjudicating ordinary-patron filming inside a California DMV field office was located.

docs.title: Cornelius / Perry
docs.text: The forum must be defined by the access sought, governmental intent and purpose. Public access to conduct government business does not itself establish a traditional/designated public forum.

docs.title: Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court
docs.text:
Published Ninth Circuit authority strongly supports the administrative-interior analogy.

The judicial/municipal complex there was treated as a nonpublic forum even though members of the public entered to conduct public business. Restrictions in such a forum still must be reasonable in light of the forum's purpose and viewpoint neutral.

docs.title: Close nonprecedential administrative-lobby comparator
docs.text:
Freedom Foundation v. Washington Department of Ecology, No. 20-35007 (9th Cir. Dec. 21, 2020), is an unpublished memorandum and is not binding precedent. Its facts are nevertheless useful: a state-agency lobby organized around reception/security, workspaces, seating and passage to secured areas was treated as nonpublic based on purpose, physical configuration and policy/practice.

It is retained only as a close factual comparator.

docs.title: DMV-specific persuasive cases
docs.text:
Recent out-of-circuit DMV cases, including Martin v. North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles, provide additional persuasive context but do not control California.

The Martin court resolved the individual-capacity claim through qualified-immunity / clearly-established-law analysis and expressly did not need to decide the constitutionality of the particular restriction. It is therefore not represented as a merits holding validating every DMV camera ban.

docs.title: Working federal lobby classification
docs.text:
FEDERAL NONPUBLIC-FORUM TREATMENT STRONGLY SUPPORTED

This applies to the defined ordinary lobby/waiting channel, not every interior subarea by inheritance.

Detailed review:

docs/research/evidence/concord-dmv/interior-forum-authority-review-2026-09-22.md

docs.title: 11. California Speech Clause — interior
docs.text:
Federal classification is not automatically copied into California Constitution article I, § 2(a).

Camenzind v. California Exposition & State Fair, 84 F.4th 1102 (9th Cir. 2023), reinforces that federal and California forum analyses are separate and that current California classification can diverge for some exterior spaces.

No sufficiently close California appellate authority classifying an ordinary state administrative-service lobby like DMV was located in this review.

Current posture:

CALIFORNIA SPEECH-CLAUSE CLASSIFICATION UNRESOLVED / NO CLOSE DMV OR ADMINISTRATIVE-LOBBY STATE AUTHORITY LOCATED

That is an intentionally narrower result than simply labeling the lobby nonpublic under both systems.

docs.title: 12. Recording doctrine — Askins
docs.text:
Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018), is the principal controlling recording authority added to this facility analysis.

It recognizes First Amendment protection for photography/recording of matters of public interest while making clear that the nature of the location and actual governmental restriction matter.

It does not establish an unfettered right to film every government interior.

Sweep 009 therefore preserves the sequence:

forum/area classification → exact recording restriction → actual government justification → recording/privacy/security doctrine

A nonpublic-forum label does not itself equal recording prohibited.

docs.title: 13. Exterior forum analysis
docs.text:
Canonical analysis:

docs/research/evidence/concord-dmv/exterior-forum-analysis-2026-09-22.md

Area Federal posture California posture Actual ordinary Diamond municipal sidewalk / ROW TPF — HIGH CONFIDENCE once location established Public-forum treatment — HIGH CONFIDENCE Actual ordinary Meridian Park municipal sidewalk / ROW TPF — HIGH CONFIDENCE once location established Public-forum treatment — HIGH CONFIDENCE Facility-specific Diamond access drive/walk Nonpublic treatment strongly supported if purpose-built facility segment; footprint unresolved UNRESOLVED DMV customer parking Nonpublic treatment strongly supported; current physical/use verification pending UNRESOLVED; exterior state-law cases materially strengthen public-forum argument Exterior customer queue / immediate approach Nonpublic/purpose-limited treatment strongly supported; exact physical area pending UNRESOLVED Entrance threshold SUBAREA-SPECIFIC / UNRESOLVED UNRESOLVED Drive aisles / vehicle test routes / driveway throats No broad speech-zone conclusion; safety/compatibility interests dominate Same practical caution

docs.title: Ordinary municipal sidewalks
docs.text:
United States v. Grace supplies the paradigmatic ordinary-sidewalk baseline.

The unresolved exact ROW edge remains important in a location-specific exclusion/trespass dispute, but does not prevent classification of a location independently established to be the ordinary municipal sidewalk.

docs.title: Purpose-built access route
docs.text:
United States v. Kokinda and Ninth Circuit Jacobsen v. USPS are substantially closer federal comparators than Prigmore for a special-purpose walkway/approach created to move customers between parking/access facilities and a government service building.

The Diamond approach cannot yet be given a final property-based classification because its current legal geometry is unresolved.

docs.title: Customer parking
docs.text:
The federal record strongly supports special-purpose/nonpublic treatment. Public customer access alone does not show intent to open the parking lot for public discourse.

The project does not import Prigmore merely because both a library and a DMV have public parking.

California is more difficult. Camenzind and earlier exterior-venue cases show broader state Speech Clause protection for some freely accessible parking/walkway areas. DMV's administrative purpose is materially different from fairgrounds/stadium-type venues, and no sufficiently close state authority was located. The California lot classification therefore remains unresolved.

docs.title: 14. Interior subarea matrix
docs.text:
Area Current documentary posture Ordinary lobby / waiting Federal nonpublic-forum treatment strongly supported / California unresolved Customer service counters / transaction zones Purpose-limited; federal nonpublic analogy strong; privacy/rule application pending Knowledge-test stations Purpose-limited examination channel; cell-phone-as-testing-aid restriction verified Self-service kiosk area Public customer access verified; final area classification depends on physical placement Restroom access, if public Physical/access conditions not yet established Employee / records / equipment / secure areas Restricted / not ordinary public-access space

An ordinary patron's ability to enter a lobby or approach a counter does not establish a right to enter employee workspaces, records areas or marked restricted zones.

docs.title: 15. Removal / trespass posture
docs.text:
No Concord DMV enforcement incident is being analyzed.

Keep separate:

  • public access;
  • forum classification;
  • exact facility rule;
  • operational control;
  • direction to leave;
  • administrative exclusion;
  • police detention/arrest;
  • Penal Code trespass elements.

State ownership and DMV operation do not make any employee instruction automatically equivalent to a criminal trespass predicate.

The actual California Penal Code subsection, location, authority and elements would have to be identified for a concrete encounter.

The Diamond access-path mismatch makes this especially important: the controller may differ depending on whether the person's exact location is municipal ROW, a private parcel, an easement, a shared drive or State property.

docs.title: 16. Facility Prep cross-category validation
docs.text:
Sweep 009 validates the reusable property/evidence pipeline across a materially different facility category while exposing two durable additions.
