docs.title: 4. Agency-specific recording policy — CPD Policy 423
docs.text:
Concord Police Department Policy Manual Policy 423 — Public Recording of Law Enforcement Activity is directly relevant and materially more specific than the generic facility-policy record available in earlier sweeps.

Official policy source:

https://www.cityofconcord.org/1196/Department-Policy-Manual

Current Policy 423 states, in substance, that:

  • CPD recognizes the right of persons to lawfully record department members performing official duties;
  • department members will not prohibit or intentionally interfere with lawful recordings;
  • recording may occur from a public place or private property where the individual has the legal right to be present;
  • the act of recording alone is distinct from actual interference;
  • examples of interference include witness/suspect tampering, incitement, a clear safety hazard from proximity, and proximity that interferes with effective officer communication;
  • officers should exercise restraint and should not use highly discretionary arrests merely as a means of preventing exercise of the right to record;
  • when practicable, officers/supervisors should give clear warnings and specific directions identifying what conduct or location change is required before enforcement;
  • device/media seizure is separately limited by law and policy.

Status:

CURRENT-AGENCY-RECORDING-POLICY-VERIFIED / SCOPE-AND-LOBBY-APPLICATION-REQUIRES-AREA-SPECIFIC-ANALYSIS

Policy 423 should not be rewritten as a blanket right to record every person, document, screen, security feature, confidential interaction, or restricted area visible inside Police Headquarters. But it is equally improper to ignore the policy and infer a camera ban merely from the facility's police/security purpose.

docs.title: 5. California Penal Code § 148(g)
docs.text:
Penal Code § 148(g) supplies an important California statutory bridge.

Within the statute's terms, taking a photograph or making an audio/video recording of a public or peace officer, while the officer is in a public place or the recorder is in a place where the recorder has the right to be, does not by itself constitute resisting/delaying/obstructing under § 148(a), and does not by itself create reasonable suspicion to detain or probable cause to arrest.

The alternative location formulation matters here because it is not written solely around traditional public forums.

But § 148(g) does not itself:

  • create a right of entry into a police facility;
  • classify a police lobby as a public forum;
  • invalidate every otherwise lawful conduct restriction;
  • establish that a person remains lawfully present after every direction to leave regardless of the underlying authority;
  • eliminate independent privacy, security, interference, or trespass questions.

The correct chain remains:

defined subarea + lawful presence → officer activity being recorded → recording alone versus additional conduct → Policy 423 + §148(g) → actual narrower facility rule, if any → forum/restriction analysis → removal/trespass analysis

docs.title: 6. Narrow CPD confidentiality / information-security policies
docs.text:
The current Department Policy Manual contains narrower rules that materially matter to records, screens, conversations and secure workspaces without becoming a public lobby-wide camera ban.

Relevant examples include:

  • Policy 803 — Records Unit: secure maintenance/access controls for case files and sensitive reports;
  • Policy 806 — Protected Information: access/security obligations for restricted law-enforcement information and criminal-justice systems;
  • Policy 422 — Body-Worn Cameras: officer-side privacy/confidentiality handling for specified private/confidential communications.

Current distinction:

RECORDS/PROTECTED-INFORMATION/CONFIDENTIAL-CONVERSATION DUTIES VERIFIED / PUBLIC-LOBBY CAMERA PROHIBITION NOT CREATED BY THOSE POLICIES

This supports an important general rule:

A government confidentiality duty governing government-held information does not automatically become a reciprocal duty forbidding a member of the public from recording everything visible or audible from a place where that person is lawfully present.

If genuinely protected information is exposed at a public counter, the specific information, law, physical configuration and any valid protective restriction must still be identified.

Detailed policy review:

docs/research/evidence/concord-police/policy-recording-review-2026-09-22.md

docs.title: 7. Dedicated lobby-camera-rule search
docs.text:
A targeted review of current public-facing CPD pages, the current Policy Manual, Community Service Desk materials, Records Unit materials, and Police Headquarters/Community Room facility pages located Policy 423 but did not locate a separate published rule stating that ordinary members of the public are categorically prohibited from photography or audio/video recording throughout the Concord Police lobby.

Approved finding:

No dedicated public-facing Concord Police Headquarters lobby-wide ordinary-patron photography/videography prohibition was located in the online sources reviewed as of September 22, 2026.

This does not establish:

  • that no current physical sign exists;
  • that no internal security directive exists;
  • that narrower restrictions cannot apply to victims, witnesses, confidential information, screens, records, interviews, security systems, or restricted areas;
  • that every recording made while physically inside the lobby is constitutionally protected;
  • that the public has access outside the stated lobby hours.

Current field-verification target:

ENTRANCE/LOBBY CAMERA-CONDUCT-SIGNAGE + PRIVACY/SECURITY LAYOUT + CONTROLLED-DOOR TRANSITIONS

docs.title: 8. Federal forum doctrine — ordinary lobby
docs.text:
No published Ninth Circuit decision specifically adjudicating an ordinary patron's right to film inside a California police-station lobby was located in this review.

The current federal authorities nevertheless strongly support applying a purpose-limited/nonpublic-forum-type standard to the ordinary public police-service lobby rather than treating it as a traditional or designated public forum.

docs.title: Controlling framework
docs.text:
Cornelius and Perry require the forum to be defined by the access sought. Public ownership and public entry for official transactions do not themselves establish a public forum.

Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002), remains the strongest published Ninth Circuit government-building comparator located for threshold classification. It treated a judicial/municipal complex as a nonpublic forum even though people entered to conduct public business, while still requiring restrictions to be reasonable in light of forum purpose and viewpoint neutral.

Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018), recognizes First Amendment protection for photography/recording of matters of public interest but ties the applicable restriction analysis to the nature of the location. Its actual dispute concerned public/outdoor areas around border facilities and does not create a general right to record in government interiors.

Serrano v. Sanders, No. 23-35437 (9th Cir. May 16, 2024), reinforces peaceful observation/recording principles in a public setting, but it is an unpublished memorandum disposition and not precedent except as allowed by Ninth Circuit Rule 36-3.

Working federal posture:

ORDINARY POLICE LOBBY — LIMITED/NONPUBLIC-FORUM STANDARD STRONGLY SUPPORTED / EXACT LABEL NOT YET NECESSARY TO EVERY RESTRICTION QUESTION / NO PUBLISHED NINTH-CIRCUIT POLICE-LOBBY FILMING HOLDING LOCATED

For the issue most likely to matter, limited and nonpublic forums use the same core restriction standard: a restriction must be reasonable in light of the forum's purpose and viewpoint neutral.

But that classification answers the standard for an actual restriction. It does not prove that a restriction exists.

docs.title: 9. Closest local activity comparator — Wilson v. County of Contra Costa
docs.text:
A particularly important case surfaced during Sweep 010:

Wilson v. County of Contra Costa, No. 14-cv-03491-SI (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2015).

This is unusually close factually because it involved:

  • the Contra Costa County Sheriff's Office;
  • a public sheriff's-office lobby in the same county;
  • a person who entered for law-enforcement/public-service purposes;
  • an audio recorder allegedly in plain view;
  • officers allegedly performing official duties in the lobby;
  • an arrest allegedly triggered when an officer noticed the active recording;
  • Penal Code §§ 602.1(b) and 632 arguments;
  • Ninth Circuit Fordyce recording doctrine.

At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, Judge Susan Illston held that the plaintiff had sufficiently stated a First Amendment retaliation claim against an officer based on recording police officers performing duties in the public CCCSO lobby. The court relied on Fordyce's recognition of a First Amendment right to film matters of public interest and declined to grant qualified immunity on the pleaded facts.

This is a meaningful local activity comparator, but it is not a categorical police-lobby filming holding.

docs.title: Wilson limitations
docs.text:
• federal district-court decision, not binding Ninth Circuit precedent;
  • motion-to-dismiss posture, requiring well-pleaded allegations to be taken as true;
  • no full public-forum classification of the sheriff's lobby;
  • no neutral preexisting lobby-wide anti-recording policy adjudicated;
  • the case later ended after failure-to-prosecute proceedings rather than a final merits judgment after discovery/trial.

Approved status:

HIGHLY-RELEVANT-LOCAL-DISTRICT-COURT-COMPARATOR / PLEADING-STAGE / NONBINDING / NO-FINAL-MERITS-ADJUDICATION

Detailed note:

docs/research/evidence/concord-police/wilson-contra-costa-sheriff-lobby-2015.md

docs.title: 10. Audio privacy — Penal Code § 632
docs.text:
California's two-party/all-party-consent shorthand is too crude for this setting. Penal Code § 632 applies to intentional eavesdropping/recording of a confidential communication without consent of all parties.

The current statutory definition excludes a public gathering, open governmental proceeding, and any other circumstance in which the parties may reasonably expect the communication may be overheard or recorded.

Under Flanagan v. Flanagan, 27 Cal.4th 766 (2002), a conversation is confidential under § 632 when a party has an objectively reasonable expectation that the conversation is not being overheard or recorded.

Thus neither slogan is adequate:

police lobby = all audio is fair game

nor:

police conversation = all audio is confidential.

The actual circumstances matter: counter separation, acoustic privacy, who else can hear, the subject of the interaction, efforts to create privacy, and whether the setting objectively indicates that the communication is confined to the participants.

docs.title: Wilson's lobby application
docs.text:
In Wilson, defendants argued that the plaintiff's audio recording was unlawful under § 632. The court rejected that basis at the pleading stage because the amended complaint alleged that various members of the public were in the area and could hear the conversations. On those alleged facts, defendants had not established an objectively reasonable expectation that the conversation was not being overheard or recorded.

Use:

PUBLIC-LOBBY §632 FACT COMPARATOR / PLEADING-STAGE / NOT A CATEGORICAL AUDIO RULE

This makes current physical verification of the Concord lobby's counter/privacy configuration materially useful rather than cosmetic.

docs.title: 11. Penal Code § 602.1 — public-agency interference and constitutional activity
docs.text: Section 602.1 is especially important in a police lobby because it is often tempting to compress the analysis into asked to leave + refusal = trespass. The statutory text is more demanding.

docs.title: § 602.1(b) elements
docs.text:
For a public agency open to the public, subdivision (b) requires:

  1. intentional interference with lawful agency business;
  2. accomplished by obstructing or intimidating employees carrying on the business or persons there to transact business; and
  3. refusal to leave after a qualifying request by the office manager/supervisor or a peace officer acting at that person's request.

Refusal alone does not supply the obstruction/intimidation element.

Existing controlling/published project authorities such as Dubner also caution against inferring intentional interference merely from refusal.

docs.title: § 602.1(d)(2) — constitutional-activity carveout
docs.text:
Current § 602.1(d)(2) expressly states that the section shall not apply to:

a person on the premises who is engaging in activities protected by the California Constitution or United States Constitution.

The Ninth Circuit in Center for Bio-Ethical Reform, Inc. v. Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, 533 F.3d 780 (9th Cir. 2008), specifically recognized § 602.1 as one of the California statutes using this shall not apply constitutional-activity language.

For Sweep 010 this means the criminal analysis must not simply assume that § 602.1 applies to the very expressive activity whose constitutional protection is disputed.

The proper chain is:

exact activity → is it constitutionally protected on these facts? → if yes, §602.1(d)(2) excludes that protected activity from §602.1 → identify any additional conduct → test obstruction/intimidation/refusal elements against that conduct → consider other independently applicable law

docs.title: The carveout is not immunity for additional unprotected conduct
docs.text:
A person cannot convert actual obstruction, intimidation, threats, or disruptive conduct into protected activity merely by simultaneously engaging in speech or recording.

A nonbinding federal habeas decision, Sherman v. Yolo County Sheriff, illustrates the distinction in a library setting: the record included evidence of abusive/disruptive conduct, patrons leaving, rule violations and repeated refusal. The court did not treat the § 602.1 constitutional-activity carveout as immunizing that independently disruptive conduct.

Section 602.1(e) also expressly preserves the possible application of other law.

docs.title: Wilson and § 602.1(b)
docs.text:
Wilson did not hold that § 602.1(b) can never apply in a public sheriff's lobby. It held that probable cause was not established at the pleading stage on the alleged facts, which included officers physically blocking the plaintiff from leaving and allegations that he had difficulty standing/walking. The court expressly recognized that later evidence might establish intentional interference/refusal.

Current removal posture:

RECORDING-ALONE ≠ §602.1(b) / CONSTITUTIONALLY-PROTECTED-ACTIVITY EXPRESSLY CARVED OUT / ADDITIONAL OBSTRUCTION-INTIMIDATION CONDUCT MUST BE ANALYZED SEPARATELY / OTHER LAW PRESERVED

docs.title: 12. Other police-lobby-specific persuasive authorities
docs.text: Police-lobby cases outside the Ninth Circuit are useful comparators but are not controlling in California.

docs.title: People v. DeRossett, 237 Ill. App. 3d 315 (1992)
docs.text: An Illinois appellate court treated an Urbana police-station lobby as a nonpublic forum. The actual facts involved a prolonged disruptive complaint/refusal episode, making it a poor analogue for quiet, noninterfering recording standing alone.

docs.title: First Defense Legal Aid v. City of Chicago, 319 F.3d 967 (7th Cir. 2003)
docs.text: The Seventh Circuit stated that the interior of a police station is not a public forum in rejecting a claimed attorney-access right. The dispute concerned access to witnesses/suspects and internal station areas, not filming an officer from an ordinary front lobby.

docs.title: Brandt v. Crone, No. 21-1093 (10th Cir. Mar. 28, 2022)
docs.text: The Tenth Circuit confronted speech curtailed in a sheriff's-department lobby and granted qualified immunity because it found no Tenth Circuit/Supreme Court case or clear weight of authority resolving the unique sheriff-lobby setting and perceived disruption there.

docs.title: Hoffman v. Delgado, No. 23-13213 (11th Cir. Jan. 3, 2025)
docs.text:
The unpublished Eleventh Circuit decision involved recording inside the Punta Gorda Police Department lobby under an actual city anti-recording ordinance. The parties proceeded under a limited-public-forum characterization; the panel noted there were good arguments the lobby was actually nonpublic and upheld the ordinance as reasonable/viewpoint neutral on the pleaded facts.

This is materially different from Concord, where no equivalent lobby-wide published anti-recording rule has been located and Policy 423 affirmatively recognizes lawful recording of officers.

docs.title: Reyes v. City of New York litigation
docs.text:
The New York litigation must be separated by authority.

The federal district court initially found the plaintiff unlikely to succeed on the First Amendment theory at the preliminary-injunction stage but likely to succeed under New York right-to-record statutes. The Second Circuit later certified the state-law question rather than deciding the federal merits.

In June 2026, the New York Court of Appeals held that those New York statutes do not extend into publicly accessible police-station lobbies, emphasizing victim, witness, confidential-informant, undercover-officer, investigative and safety concerns.

After that answer, the Second Circuit vacated the statutory preliminary injunction in August 2026 and expressly did not decide the pending First Amendment claim.

docs.title: Massimino v. Benoit, No. 25-1104 (2d Cir. Aug. 17, 2026)
docs.text:
The Second Circuit held that the First Amendment protects recording publicly visible portions of a police station from a public sidewalk and expressly distinguished that lawful exterior vantage from a claimed right of physical access inside the station.

Use:

STRONG EXTERIOR/INTERIOR-BOUNDARY COMPARATOR / SECOND-CIRCUIT ONLY

Detailed authority review:

docs/research/evidence/concord-police/interior-forum-authority-review-2026-09-22.md

docs.title: 13. Concord-specific synthesis: nonpublic forum does not equal camera ban
docs.text:
This is the central doctrinal lesson of Sweep 010.

Concord is not presently an ordinary:

purpose-limited lobby + published no-recording rule

case.

Instead, the documentary record currently looks like:

purpose-limited public police lobby + no separate lobby-wide published camera ban located + CPD Policy 423 affirmatively recognizes lawful public recording of officers + Penal Code §148(g) protects recording-alone within its location conditions + local Wilson comparator allowed a public-sheriff-lobby recording retaliation claim to proceed + §602.1(d)(2) expressly carves out constitutionally protected activity

Therefore a federal limited/nonpublic classification tells us what standard applies to an actual restriction. It does not manufacture a restriction, erase activity-specific protection, or automatically establish criminal trespass.

A valid analysis requires the actual rule or actual additional conduct asserted to justify the restriction/removal.

docs.title: 14. Privacy/security subjects must be separated
docs.text:
Police Headquarters presents materially stronger privacy/security concerns than the DMV or an ordinary civic administrative lobby.

Potentially distinct subjects include:

  • officers performing public-facing official duties;
  • uninvolved members of the public;
  • victims reporting crimes;
  • witnesses;
  • confidential informants;
  • juveniles;
  • undercover personnel;
  • confidential reports and computer screens;
  • private or sensitive conversations;
  • access-control systems and security features;
  • dispatch/records/evidence/holding/interview/operational spaces.

Do not collapse these into recording in the lobby as if they were legally identical.

The project should preserve the activity distinction:

recording an officer performing a public-facing duty ≠ deliberately capturing a victim's private report ≠ capturing protected records/screens ≠ documenting a secure operational area

Those differences may materially affect § 632 confidentiality, the reasonableness/tailoring of a restriction, and whether a direction to relocate is supportable.

docs.title: 15. California Speech Clause
docs.text:
No sufficiently close published California appellate authority was located that classifies an ordinary police-station public lobby under California Constitution article I, § 2(a).

Current posture:

CALIFORNIA SPEECH-CLAUSE CLASSIFICATION UNRESOLVED / NO CLOSE PUBLISHED CALIFORNIA POLICE-LOBBY CASE LOCATED

The federal limited/nonpublic result must not be copied automatically into the California column.

docs.title: 16. Separate opened channel — Police Department Community Meeting Room
docs.text:
The Department separately advertises a public Community Meeting Room at 1350 Galindo Street.

Official source:

https://www.cityofconcord.org/facilities/facility/details/Police-Department-Community-Rooms-33

The City states that nonprofit community groups may use the room for discussion of community issues that address and improve quality of life in Concord. The page states that the Department reserves the right to make reasonable content-neutral time, place, and manner restrictions in contracting for use.

The current Community Service Desk page states the room is available Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., excluding holidays, with capacity 45.

The public facility page says a Community Room Contract is completed after reservation, but the contract itself was not located in the online sources reviewed.

Current posture:

SEPARATELY-OPENED COMMUNITY-DISCUSSION CHANNEL / CONTRACT-NOT-LOCATED-ONLINE / ACTUAL-PRACTICE REVIEW PENDING

This room should not inherit the lobby's forum classification.

docs.title: 17. Required subarea decomposition
docs.text:
Sweep 010 separately tracks:

  • ordinary municipal sidewalk / Galindo frontage;
  • public parking and pedestrian approach;
  • entrance threshold / vestibule;
  • ordinary public lobby / Community Service Desk;
  • Records counter / transaction area;
  • complaint/report-intake interactions;
  • Community Meeting Room;
  • public restrooms, if any;
  • controlled doors / employee-only corridors;
  • dispatch, records workspaces, evidence/property, secure parking, holding/interview, jail, and other operational areas;
  • publicly visible but nonpublic security-sensitive areas.

No building-wide forum label is assigned by inheritance.

docs.title: 20. Methodological lessons emerging from Sweep 010
docs.text: Sweep 010 adds several cross-category lessons that should be considered for promotion into the Facility Prep / Registry methodology after final review.

docs.title: A. Forum classification does not prove a restriction exists
docs.text:
Forum classification answers the constitutional standard for restrictions; it does not prove that a restriction exists.

A purpose-limited/nonpublic government interior may permit reasonable viewpoint-neutral restrictions, but the project still must identify the actual rule, direction, security condition, or additional conduct justification before analyzing constitutionality, removal or trespass.

docs.title: B. Record both vantage point and subject
docs.text:
The subject of the recording can be legally material even when the physical vantage point is identical.

Police-lobby research should separately record:

where the recorder is + what/who is being recorded + whether audio is captured + what privacy/security conditions exist.

docs.title: C. Use separate forum and activity anchors when necessary
docs.text:
Wilson exposes a useful refinement of the anchor-comparator method.

The closest case for forum status may not be the closest case for the specific activity.

For police/sheriff lobbies, a stronger model is:

  • forum/access anchor: Cornelius, Sammartano, plus facility-purpose/access facts;
  • activity anchor: Fordyce, §148(g), agency recording policy, and factually close authority such as Wilson.

One precedent need not perform both jobs.

docs.title: D. Confidentiality duties are not self-executing public-camera bans
docs.text:
Government duties to secure protected information do not automatically impose a reciprocal blanket recording prohibition on a person lawfully present in a public-facing area.

Identify the protected information, applicable law/rule, actual exposure and the tailored restriction.

docs.title: E. Trespass analysis must include statutory constitutional carveouts
docs.text:
Where a trespass/interference statute expressly excludes constitutionally protected activity, the workflow must test that carveout before treating the statute as an enforcement bridge.

For §602.1:

protected activity? → §602.1(d)(2) → additional conduct? → obstruction/intimidation elements → qualifying request → other law

docs.title: 21. Remaining open facts
docs.text:
The documentary sweep and methodology promotion are complete enough for branch review. The highest-value unresolved items are now physical/current rather than broad doctrinal research:

  1. verify the entrance, vestibule, lobby seating/counter configuration, privacy separation, controlled doors, public restroom availability, and camera/conduct/security signs;
  2. correlate the City-owned candidate parcels and public parking/pedestrian approach to the current ground layout;
  3. obtain the Community Room Contract only if that separate opened channel will be classified for publication;
  4. continue maintenance searching for any closer published Ninth Circuit/California police-lobby authority.

These items remain expressly pending and do not need to be guessed or silently filled from analogy. The documentary Sweep 010 branch is otherwise ready for PR/MkDocs review and merge.

docs.title: Sweep 011 — California Lawful Vantage, Visual Privacy, and Exposed Information
docs.text: Issue: #64 Package: GAP-01 Research date: September 28, 2026 Status: Defined GAP-01 slice reviewed; affected qualification rows must be re-evaluated individually.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This sweep supplies the California overlay for NC-VANTAGE-01.A–F and the overlapping functional rows CA-F2.1 and CA-F2.3.

The research question is not whether a camera is categorically lawful or unlawful. It is:

What California/federal authority lets the Field Guide distinguish ordinary observation or recording from a lawful vantage from physical intrusion, limited-audience privacy, device-assisted constructive intrusion, voyeuristic viewing, confidential-audio recording, or actual access to a computer/device?

This sweep deliberately separates:

  1. the observer's exact location and right to remain;
  2. general-public visibility from visibility to only a limited audience or unusual vantage;
  3. ordinary visual observation/photography/video from physical intrusion;
  4. ordinary visual capture from a device that makes otherwise inaccessible private activity obtainable;
  5. visual recording from audio/confidential communications;
  6. seeing a displayed screen/document from accessing a computer, account, system, or stored data;
  7. acquisition from later publication/use; and
  8. direct civilian/privacy authority from Fourth Amendment police-search cases used only as factual analogy.

docs.title: Primary statutory and constitutional sources reviewed
docs.text:
• California Constitution art. I, §§ 1, 2(a), 3(b): https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&article=I
  • Civil Code § 1708.8: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1708.8
  • Penal Code § 647: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=647
  • Penal Code § 632: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632
  • Penal Code § 632.7: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632.7
  • Penal Code § 502: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=502

docs.title: Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn., 7 Cal.4th 1 (1994)
docs.text:
California's constitutional privacy framework requires a legally protected privacy interest, a reasonable expectation of privacy in the circumstances, and a serious invasion; competing interests can affect the ultimate analysis.

Use here: privacy is contextual rather than an on/off label. The state constitutional privacy right can apply to nongovernmental as well as governmental conduct.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/7/1.html

docs.title: Shulman v. Group W Productions, Inc., 18 Cal.4th 200 (1998)
docs.text:
For the common-law intrusion tort, the California Supreme Court described two essential ideas that matter to lawful-vantage analysis:

  • the defendant must intentionally intrude into a private place, conversation, or matter in a manner highly offensive to a reasonable person; and
  • ordinary observation, photography, or recording of a person in a public place generally does not establish the private-place element merely because the person did not want to be observed.

The court also made clear that newsgathering does not create a general constitutional privilege to violate otherwise applicable privacy law.

Use here: strong direct authority against both extremes. Public-place observation is materially different from penetration of seclusion, but a camera is not a universal immunity from privacy law.

Source: https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/shulman-v-group-w-productions-inc-31911/

docs.title: Sanders v. American Broadcasting Companies, Inc., 20 Cal.4th 907 (1999)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court rejected the proposition that being visible or audible to some coworkers automatically destroys all privacy against covert recording. A workplace not generally open to unfettered public access could support a limited expectation against secret television recording even though coworkers could see or hear the interaction.

Use here: limited visibility is not necessarily general-public exposure. The Field Guide must ask who could ordinarily see/hear the matter, from where, and by what means.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/20/907.html

docs.title: Hernandez v. Hillsides, Inc., 47 Cal.4th 272 (2009)
docs.text:
Employees could possess a reasonable visual-privacy expectation against hidden video monitoring in a shared enclosed office. The court separately analyzed whether the intrusion was sufficiently serious/offensive and concluded the claim failed on that second element on the particular facts.

The opinion also recognizes that a camera's persistent lens can be more penetrating than ordinary human observation and discusses California's statutory visual-privacy protections.

Use here: recording technology can change the privacy analysis even where ordinary human observation by a limited set of people could occur.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2009/s147552/

docs.title: Flanagan v. Flanagan, 27 Cal.4th 766 (2002)
docs.text:
For Penal Code § 632, a communication is confidential when a party has an objectively reasonable expectation that it is not being overheard or recorded. The question is not simply whether the speaker expected the contents never to be repeated later.

Use here: audio is a separate branch from visual observation.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/27/766.html

docs.title: Civil Code § 1708.8 — physical and constructive invasion
docs.text:
Subdivision (a) addresses knowing entry/trespass undertaken to capture a visual image, sound recording, or other physical impression of a plaintiff engaged in private, personal, or familial activity where the invasion is offensive to a reasonable person.

Subdivision (b) separately creates constructive-invasion liability for offensively attempting to capture such activity through a device, without physical trespass, when the image/sound/impression could not have been achieved without trespass unless the device were used.

The statute defines private/personal/familial activity through reasonable-expectation-of-privacy concepts and makes clear that failed capture is not necessarily a defense.

Field consequence:

A physically lawful position is important, but it does not end the California privacy analysis when a device is used to obtain private activity that ordinary lawful observation could not have obtained.

Do not rewrite § 1708.8(b) as a ban on ordinary camera zoom. Apply its actual statutory test.

docs.title: Penal Code § 647(i) — private-property peeking posture
docs.text:
Section 647(i) applies when a person, while loitering/prowling/wandering upon the private property of another, peeks in the door or window of an inhabited building or structure without visible or lawful business with the owner/occupant.

Field consequence:

The private-property location predicate matters. Do not rewrite § 647(i) into a general rule that looking through every window from an ordinary public sidewalk is itself this offense.

That does not resolve other privacy laws.

docs.title: Penal Code § 647(j) — instrumentality and protected private zones
docs.text:
Section 647(j)(1) reaches viewing, by listed instrumentalities including cameras/mobile phones and similar devices, the interior of a bedroom, bathroom, changing/fitting/dressing/tanning room, or another area where the occupant has a reasonable expectation of privacy, with intent to invade privacy.

Other subdivisions address concealed-camera recording beneath clothing or of a person in specified private/undress circumstances.

Field consequence:

A transparent barrier does not create a universal "window exception." Subject area, reasonable privacy expectation, method, and statutory intent matter.

docs.title: Penal Code § 632 — confidential audio
docs.text:
Section 632 separately regulates electronic amplification/recording of confidential communications. Its definition excludes communications made in public gatherings, open public proceedings, and other circumstances where the parties may reasonably expect the communication may be overheard or recorded.

Field consequence:

A video that is visually lawful can still create a separate audio question.

Section 632.7 is a distinct communications statute involving specified cellular/cordless communications and should not be silently merged into ordinary in-person § 632 analysis.

docs.title: Penal Code § 502 — actual computer/system access
docs.text:
Section 502 protects computer data/systems from specified unauthorized access and defines/access-regulates conduct involving computers, systems, networks, services, programs, and data.

Field consequence:

Seeing a display that has been left visible from a lawful position and actually accessing a computer/system/account are different factual events. The latter requires its own § 502 and other access-law analysis.

This sweep does not claim that merely photographing a screen visible from a lawful vantage constitutes § 502 access.

docs.title: Public/private property and right to remain
Robins v. Pruneyard Shopping Center, 23 Cal.3d 899 (1979)
docs.text:
California recognized state-constitutional petition/speech protection on the facts of a large privately owned shopping center open to the public. The decision is a special private-property speech doctrine, not a rule converting every private business into public property.

Source: https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/robins-v-pruneyard-shopping-center-30510/

docs.title: Golden Gateway Center v. Golden Gateway Tenants Assn., 26 Cal.4th 1013 (2001)
docs.text:
The judgment rejected a claimed state-constitutional leafleting right in the private residential portion of a complex not freely/openly accessible to the public. The three-justice lead opinion would have imposed a broad state-action limitation under article I, section 2(a), but Chief Justice George concurred in the judgment on a narrower ground and expressly did not join that broad conclusion.

Field consequence:

"Private business" and "open to customers" do not automatically establish a constitutional right to remain for every expressive purpose. Identify the actual access/property right; preserve Pruneyard as a special California private-shopping-center doctrine rather than a universal rule, and do not overread the fractured Golden Gateway opinions.

Source: https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/golden-gateway-center-v-golden-gateway-tenants-assn-32146/

docs.title: Fourth Amendment window/vantage cases — analogy only
docs.text: The following cases concern government searches. They are retained solely because they illustrate why vantage facts matter. They do not create a civilian right to photograph private property.

docs.title: People v. Berutko, 71 Cal.2d 84 (1969)
docs.text:
Police were lawfully present in a common area and observed through an aperture in window coverings. The court treated the lawful/common vantage and what the resident exposed from that vantage as important to the Fourth Amendment analysis.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2d/71/84.html

docs.title: Lorenzana v. Superior Court, 9 Cal.3d 626 (1973)
docs.text:
Research result retained for the converse proposition: police use of a private side-yard vantage not open/common to the public changes the constitutional analysis.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/9/626.html

docs.title: People v. Camacho, 23 Cal.4th 824 (2000)
docs.text:
Research result retained for the same caution: officers' presence in an area of private property where the public was not invited mattered despite visibility through an uncovered window.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/23/824.html

Project rule: never cite these Fourth Amendment cases as though they hold that a private citizen may photograph anything police could constitutionally observe.

docs.title: Transparent barriers — resulting analytical rule
docs.text:
Glass, an uncovered window, or a windshield is a fact, not a conclusion.

Record:

  1. the observer's exact vantage and right to remain;
  2. whether the view was available to the general public or only from an abnormal/limited/private vantage;
  3. blinds, curtains, tint, privacy film, covers, fencing, orientation, and other shielding;
  4. whether the observer crossed, opened, touched, moved, reached through, or defeated anything;
  5. whether the device materially obtained something ordinary lawful observation could not;
  6. the subject/space and whether specialized privacy law applies;
  7. whether audio was captured; and
  8. whether later acquisition/use/publication raises a different legal issue.

docs.title: Visible documents/screens — resulting analytical rule
docs.text:
Do not collapse three different events:

  1. information is visible because its custodian displayed or left it exposed;
  2. an observer records what can ordinarily be seen from the observer's lawful vantage;
  3. an observer accesses a device/system, manipulates property, defeats shielding, or uses a method that obtains what ordinary observation could not.

The governing confidentiality/privacy law must identify whom it regulates and what conduct it restricts. A confidentiality label alone does not answer the observer's legal duties, and visibility alone does not answer every privacy question.

Existing HIPAA/common-space research remains useful for the same proposition-separation method: the covered entity's safeguard duties and the visitor's independently applicable law are different questions.

docs.title: Qualification disposition
docs.text:
After Sweep 011, the existing California overlay is sufficient to run the ordinary analytical test for all GAP-01 rows without inventing a categorical permission rule.

Recommended row dispositions:

Row Pre-sweep Sweep 011 result Reason CA-F2.1 Gap Supported Ordinary observation/recording can now be separated from privacy/audio/intrusion branches. CA-F2.3 Gap Supported Constitutional privacy, intrusion tort, §1708.8, §647(j), §632, and limitations are mapped. NC-VANTAGE-01.A Gap Supported Public/property methodology plus Pruneyard/Golden Gateway private-property boundary supports the right-to-remain question as an analytical test. NC-VANTAGE-01.B Gap Supported Shulman/Sanders plus existing recording doctrine supports the ordinary public-view branch without a universal camera rule. NC-VANTAGE-01.C Gap Supported Transparent barriers are now tied to vantage, shielding, limited audience, privacy-zone statutes, and separately labeled Fourth Amendment analogy. NC-VANTAGE-01.D Gap Supported Visible-information analysis now separates exposure, privacy/confidentiality duties, and actual system/data access. NC-VANTAGE-01.E Gap Supported Physical/constructive intrusion, trespass/manipulation, and computer access are separate changed-fact branches. NC-VANTAGE-01.F Gap Supported Device-assisted constructive intrusion, voyeurism/privacy, and confidential audio are mapped with current California authorities.

Important: Supported means the overlay can run the branch and preserve specialized/unresolved outcomes. It does not mean every visible subject can lawfully be recorded or every privacy statute has been exhaustively cataloged.

docs.title: Remaining boundaries that do not keep GAP-01 open
docs.text:
These become changed-fact or specialized checks rather than activation-blocking holes in the ordinary scenario:

  • courtrooms/court-specific rules;
  • school/child-specific privacy statutes;
  • medical/mental-health or victim-specific confidentiality regimes;
  • intimate-image distribution/publication statutes;
  • highly specialized surveillance equipment;
  • trade-secret/proprietary-information disputes;
  • biometric/facial-recognition collection;
  • publication/private-facts liability distinct from acquisition;
  • federal premises;
  • special contractual confidentiality duties.

If a facility scenario materially supplies one of those facts, open the specialized branch rather than assuming Sweep 011 resolved it.

docs.title: Source hierarchy note
docs.text: California statutes and California Supreme Court privacy cases are direct state authority for the propositions identified above. Fourth Amendment police-search/window cases are marked ANALOGY ONLY. Federal First Amendment recording cases remain a separate constitutional layer and do not displace California privacy law.

docs.title: Sweep 012 — California Conditional Access, Removal, and Derivative Trespass
docs.text: Issue: #66 Package: GAP-02 Research date: September 28, 2026 Status: Defined GAP-02 slice reviewed; affected qualification rows must be re-evaluated individually.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This sweep addresses the recurring sequence:

lawful presence → protected/arguably protected activity → "stop the activity or leave" → refusal/continued activity → exclusion/removal → trespass enforcement

The affected qualification rows are:

  • CA-F3.4
  • CA-F4.1
  • CA-F4.6
  • NC-COMPLAINT-01.M
  • NC-VANTAGE-01.G

The sweep does not assume that:

  • every public-facing government interior is a public forum;
  • every camera/speech restriction is invalid;
  • government must wait for actual disruption before enforcing every valid restriction;
  • every order to leave public property is lawful;
  • refusal to comply with an invalid order can never implicate another law; or
  • a later arrest is automatically unconstitutional merely because protected activity preceded it.

The purpose is to prevent the later word trespass from erasing the upstream legal questions.

docs.title: Penal Code § 602.1(b) — public agency open to the public
docs.text:
Current official text requires, for the public-agency branch:

  1. intentional interference with lawful agency business;
  2. by obstructing or intimidating people attempting to carry on agency business or people there to transact business;
  3. refusal to leave after a qualifying request by the office manager/supervisor or a peace officer acting at that person's request.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.1.

Subdivision (d)(2) expressly states that § 602.1 does not apply to a person on the premises who is engaging in activities protected by the California Constitution or United States Constitution.

Subdivision (e) separately states that § 602.1 does not supersede other law.

docs.title: Project consequence
docs.text:
Do not rewrite § 602.1(b) as:

government employee asks you to leave + you remain = misdemeanor.

The obstruction/intimidation/interference predicate is independent from refusal.

The constitutional exception also requires the Field Guide to resolve the protected-activity question rather than treating the request to leave as self-validating.

But § 602.1(e) means the exception does not immunize conduct from some other independently applicable statute.

docs.title: Penal Code § 602 — recurring public-facility branches
docs.text: Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.

docs.title: § 602(o)
docs.text:
The current statute applies to refusing/failing to leave property not open to the general public after a qualifying request.

Field consequence:

Do not use § 602(o) as the automatic refusal-to-leave statute for an ordinary public-facing government lobby that is presently open to the general public.

A different area of the same facility can have a different access status.

docs.title: § 602(q)
docs.text:
The current statute applies to a public building of a public agency during hours when the building is regularly closed to the public, after a qualifying request, when surrounding circumstances would indicate no apparent lawful business.

Field consequence:

Regular closing time can independently change the legal posture even when the person's earlier presence was lawful.

docs.title: § 602(m)
docs.text: Existing Sweep 002 authority establishes that entering and occupying requires more than transient/minutes-long presence; In re Catalano and Edgerly remain the controlling project anchors for that narrow proposition.

docs.title: Specialized branches
docs.text: Other § 602 subdivisions apply to secured, posted, screened, private, closed, hospital, transit, airport, or other specialized property facts. They must be tested by their own elements.

docs.title: 2. Published Ninth Circuit: refusal alone does not manufacture § 602.1 interference
Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001)
docs.text:
Dubner involved an arrest near the Moscone Convention Center. The published Ninth Circuit opinion analyzed § 602.1's common intentional-interference/refusal structure.

The court held that even assuming Dubner refused to leave, there was no evidence she intentionally interfered with the business. She was taking photographs and conversing while positioned away from the doors. The court expressly rejected the government's argument that intent to interfere could simply be inferred from refusal to leave.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/266/959/582256/

docs.title: Project rule from Dubner
docs.text:
Refusal is not a substitute for the interference predicate.

Because the public-agency branch uses the same intentional-interference-by-obstruction-or-intimidation structure, this is an important published Ninth Circuit anchor for element separation.

Do not misdescribe Dubner as a published holding about every application of § 602.1(b); its facts involved the Moscone Center/convention setting. Its direct value here is the statutory-element separation.

docs.title: 3. Direct public-agency comparator: Mackey v. Meyer
Mackey v. Meyer, No. 15-55186 (9th Cir. Jan. 11, 2017)
docs.text:
Status: unpublished memorandum; not precedent except as allowed by Ninth Circuit Rule 36-3.

Mackey was reading scripture outside a California DMV. A security guard asked him to leave; he refused; DMV personnel requested removal; dispatch told CHP that a preacher was harassing customers and refusing to leave.

The Ninth Circuit specifically analyzed Penal Code § 602.1(b). It stated the two-part structure as intentional interference plus refusal to leave, with intentional interference requiring obstruction or intimidation.

The officer arrived and saw Mackey reading aloud somewhat apart from the line, with no obstruction or intimidation. The panel held there was no probable cause for § 602.1(b) and that the officer was not entitled to qualified immunity on the Fourth Amendment claim.

Official Ninth Circuit memorandum: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/memoranda/2017/01/11/15-55186.pdf

docs.title: Project use
docs.text:
Mackey is an unusually close factual comparator for a public agency but remains nonprecedential.

It strongly illustrates the operational question:

What did the officer actually know about obstruction/intimidation, beyond the labels harassing, refusing to leave, or they want him removed?

It should not be promoted to binding authority.

docs.title: 4. California constitutional line: an unsupported exclusion cannot bootstrap itself
In re Hoffman, 67 Cal.2d 845 (1967)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court considered peaceful antiwar leafleting at Los Angeles Union Station. An officer told participants to stop distributing leaflets/talking to people or leave; they refused and were arrested.

The court held that the primary uses of property can be protected through rules against actual interference, but First Amendment activity could not be prohibited solely because the property was not maintained primarily as a speech forum on those facts.

The court relied on Brown v. Louisiana for a particularly important proposition: where peaceful protesters in a public library had not disrupted the facility, the librarian/officer lacked a constitutionally sufficient basis to order them out merely for their protected protest, and the refusal to leave could not itself constitutionally support the breach-of-peace conviction there.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2d/67/845.html

docs.title: Brown v. Louisiana, 383 U.S. 131 (1966)
docs.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court reversed convictions arising from a peaceful, orderly library protest. The plurality stressed that regulation of public facilities must be reasonable and nondiscriminatory and may not be used as a pretext to punish constitutional activity.

Official U.S. Reports source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-383/pdf/USREPORTS-383-131.pdf

docs.title: Narrow project rule
docs.text:
An otherwise unsupported exclusion order does not automatically become constitutionally sufficient merely because the person refuses it.

This is not a universal right to remain after every order. It is a rule against treating the downstream refusal as if it answers whether the upstream exclusion was lawful.

docs.title: 5. Government can enforce valid restrictions before actual disruption
docs.text: The opposite overstatement is also wrong.

docs.title: Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002)
docs.text:
The Ninth Circuit treated the Nevada judicial/municipal complex before it as a nonpublic forum.

Speech restrictions there still had to be:

  1. reasonable in light of the forum's purpose; and
  2. viewpoint neutral.

The court emphasized that nonpublic-forum reasonableness requires more than ordinary rational-basis review and that the government must have evidentiary support connecting the restriction to a legitimate need.

Official Ninth Circuit opinion: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2002/08/26/0116685.pdf

docs.title: Project consequence
docs.text:
A person does not acquire immunity from a valid rule merely because no actual disruption has occurred yet.

A reasonable, viewpoint-neutral rule designed to preserve the function of a nonpublic forum can regulate activity prospectively.

But the rule must still survive the applicable constitutional test.

docs.title: Simpson v. Municipal Court, 14 Cal.App.3d 591 (1971)
docs.text:
Simpson involved peaceful, nonobstructive picketing inside the California State Capitol.

The court upheld a specific statutory ban on picketing inside the Capitol because it was a narrow restriction directed at a particular expressive method in a location whose deliberative function supplied a substantial governmental interest. Other channels of communication remained open.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/14/591.html

docs.title: Project consequence
docs.text:
Absence of actual disruption is relevant but not universally dispositive.

The legal question is whether the restriction is valid under the applicable constitutional/forum rule—not simply whether misconduct had already occurred.

docs.title: People v. Fogelson, 21 Cal.3d 158 (1978)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court reiterated that government may reasonably regulate protected activity to prevent fraud, harassment, or interference with operations, but regulation affecting First Amendment activity requires precision and narrowly drawn standards related to permissible interests.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/21/158.html

docs.title: 6. Neutral closure and access changes are separate from expressive exclusion
Parrish v. Municipal Court, 258 Cal.App.2d 497 (1968)
docs.text:
The case involved protesters remaining in a county welfare building after it had regularly closed for the day.

The court treated the predecessor of current § 602(q) as a closing-hours rule. The fact that presence had previously been lawful did not freeze the access status indefinitely after regular public closing.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2d/258/497.html

docs.title: Project rule
docs.text:
When facts change, rerun the access analysis.

Examples:

  • regular public hours end;
  • a public room closes for a scheduled use;
  • a security perimeter is lawfully established;
  • the person enters a restricted subarea;
  • a valid neutral facility rule becomes applicable; or
  • independent obstruction/disruption arises.

Do not treat those situations as equivalent to an exclusion imposed solely because an official dislikes recording or criticism.

docs.title: Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)
docs.text:
The Ninth Circuit recognized First Amendment protection for photographing/recording matters of public interest and emphasized that the result depends on the nature of the location.

The plaintiffs sought to photograph only matters exposed to public view from exterior/outdoor areas they alleged were public streets/sidewalks. The court did not create a right to photograph unrestrictedly throughout government interiors.

Official Ninth Circuit opinion: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2018/08/14/16-55719.pdf

docs.title: Project consequence
docs.text:
When the conditional order is:

stop recording or leave

identify separately:

  • the exact area/forum;
  • the subject/activity being recorded;
  • the actual restriction;
  • the government's justification;
  • the restriction's fit/reasonableness;
  • viewpoint/content neutrality;
  • any independent privacy/security rule; and
  • the separate removal/trespass statute.

docs.title: 8. Close local comparator: Wilson v. County of Contra Costa
Wilson v. County of Contra Costa, No. 14-cv-03491-SI (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2015)
docs.text:
Status: federal district court; persuasive only; pleading-stage ruling.

Wilson alleged that he recorded officers performing duties in the public lobby of the Contra Costa County Sheriff's Office and that an officer arrested him after noticing the recording.

The court held that, taking the allegations as true at the motion-to-dismiss stage, he stated a First Amendment retaliation claim against the arresting officer based on recording police officers in the public lobby.

The same opinion separately analyzed § 602.1(b) allegations.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/california/candce/3%3A2014cv03491/279647/103/

docs.title: Project use
docs.text:
Wilson is a useful local fact-pattern comparator, not controlling merits precedent.

It reinforces why the chronology must be preserved:

recording observed → adverse action → claimed trespass/removal basis

docs.title: 9. Retaliation is a separate question from restriction validity
docs.text:
Existing project authority includes O'Brien v. Welty, 818 F.3d 920 (9th Cir. 2016).

A government action that could be lawful for a proper reason may still present a retaliation question if substantially motivated by protected expression, subject to the applicable retaliation doctrine and causation/defense rules.

Official Ninth Circuit opinion: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2016/04/07/13-16279.pdf

For arrest-specific retaliation, the separate Nieves/Gonzalez probable-cause framework remains in the retaliation chapter.

docs.title: Project consequence
docs.text:
Do not collapse these propositions:

  • government could lawfully restrict this activity under X rule;
  • government actually restricted this person for that lawful reason; and
  • the later arrest/exclusion was retaliatory.

They require separate proof.

docs.title: 10. The California five-step derivative-trespass test
docs.text: When a person begins lawfully present in a government area and later receives an activity-based leave order, run these questions in sequence.

docs.title: Step 1 — What exactly triggered the order?
docs.text:
Preserve chronology:

  • activity before employee contact;
  • first employee demand;
  • whether the demand targeted recording/speech/observation;
  • whether a conditional phrase was used, e.g. stop recording or leave;
  • any independent misconduct identified before the order;
  • later-changing facts.

Do not infer motive beyond the evidence.

docs.title: Step 2 — Was the underlying activity restriction valid?
docs.text:
Apply:

  • exact forum/access classification;
  • activity-specific recording/speech law;
  • content/viewpoint analysis;
  • reasonableness/tailoring standard;
  • privacy/security/operational evidence;
  • California Speech Clause where independently applicable;
  • delegated authority/local rule if material.

A public-facing interior can be nonpublic. That does not make every restriction valid.

docs.title: Step 3 — What legal authority supports exclusion/removal?
docs.text:
Identify the actual authority:

  • § 602.1(b);
  • a specific § 602 subdivision;
  • another statute/regulation/order;
  • a lawful facility access rule;
  • local delegated authority;
  • specialized security/court/school law.

Do not substitute the employee's word trespass for this step.

docs.title: Step 4 — Did the alleged offense's independent elements arise?
docs.text:
For § 602.1(b), ask specifically:

  • intentional interference?
  • obstruction or intimidation?
  • qualifying request to leave?
  • refusal?
  • constitutional-activity exception?

Under Dubner's published common structure and the nonprecedential Mackey public-agency comparator, refusal does not retroactively create obstruction/intimidation.

For other statutes, use their own elements.

docs.title: Step 5 — Did later facts independently change the result?
docs.text:
Examples:

  • building closed;
  • person moved into restricted area;
  • person actually blocked service;
  • unreasonable noise arose;
  • lawful security rule was violated;
  • person reentered after a separately valid exclusion;
  • other offense elements arose.

A later independent offense should not be erased merely because the encounter began with protected activity.

Likewise, a later label should not erase the legality question surrounding the earlier exclusion.

docs.title: 11. Field Guide rule for "stop recording or leave"
docs.text:
For the standing peaceful scenario:

Treat "stop recording or leave" as two government acts: a recording restriction and a conditional exclusion. Test the recording restriction first, then identify the legal authority and elements supporting exclusion. A later refusal to leave does not by itself prove the restriction was lawful or supply missing § 602.1 obstruction/intimidation elements.

The converse is equally important:

If the restriction is independently lawful under the applicable forum/activity law, government need not always wait for actual disruption before conditioning continued access on compliance.

This is the GAP-02 balance.

docs.title: 12. Arrest / probable-cause posture
docs.text:
An officer arriving after a call should preserve:

  • exact alleged conduct;
  • complainant's factual basis;
  • exact location/access status;
  • what restriction was allegedly violated;
  • who issued the leave order and with what authority;
  • whether the relevant offense requires obstruction/intimidation or another element;
  • what the officer personally observes;
  • available contrary/exculpatory evidence; and
  • later-changing facts.

The phrase:

the agency wants him trespassed

is not itself an offense element.

Published Dubner and nonprecedential Mackey show why the actual § 602.1 predicates matter.

docs.title: 13. Qualification disposition
docs.text:
After Sweep 012, the California overlay can run the ordinary conditional-access/derivative-trespass branch without assuming either that every exclusion is valid or that every peaceful person has an unlimited right to remain.

Recommended dispositions:

Row Pre-sweep Sweep 012 result Reason CA-F3.4 Gap Supported Policy/order is now separated from constitutional validity, exclusion authority, and criminal elements; valid prospective restrictions are also accounted for. CA-F4.1 Gap Supported California/federal authority now supplies the ordinary test for when government may restrict/revoke access based on a valid facility/activity rule, with local/facility authority preserved as a dependency. CA-F4.6 Gap Supported Brown/Hoffman, neutral closure doctrine, forum rules, and element-level trespass analysis distinguish invalid derivative exclusion from later independent changed facts. NC-COMPLAINT-01.M Gap Supported The complete upstream-restriction → exclusion → offense-elements → later-facts chain is now runnable in California. NC-VANTAGE-01.G Gap Supported Stop/move/leave demands can now be tested against property/forum/activity authority rather than treated as self-validating.

Supported does not mean every facility exclusion has the same answer. It means the ordinary branch has sufficient authority and a defensible field test. Facility-specific rules, local delegated authority, specialized premises, prospective long-term bans, and identification duties remain separate packages where already mapped.

docs.title: 14. Boundaries preserved for other packages
docs.text:
Sweep 012 does not close:

  • GAP-03 delegated authority/preemption;
  • GAP-04 prospective no-entry notices, long-term bans, public-agency § 602(o)/§ 602.1 edge cases, and identification duties;
  • GAP-05 device seizure/search edges;
  • GAP-06 disorder/noise/fighting-words/obstruction doctrine;
  • GAP-07 emergency/dispersal/perimeter cases;
  • GAP-08 law-enforcement records.

If a removal depends on one of those unresolved propositions, apply that open package rather than pretending Sweep 012 supplied it.

docs.title: Core authority hierarchy
docs.text:
Direct/current: - Cal. Penal Code §§ 602, 602.1 - In re Hoffman, 67 Cal.2d 845 - Simpson v. Municipal Court, 14 Cal.App.3d 591 - People v. Fogelson, 21 Cal.3d 158 - Parrish v. Municipal Court, 258 Cal.App.2d 497 - Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 - Sammartano v. First Judicial Dist. Court, 303 F.3d 959 - Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035

Supreme Court support: - Brown v. Louisiana, 383 U.S. 131

Persuasive/nonbinding comparators: - Mackey v. Meyer, No. 15-55186 (9th Cir. Jan. 11, 2017) — unpublished - Wilson v. County of Contra Costa, No. 14-cv-03491-SI (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2015) — district court, pleading stage

docs.title: Sweep 013 — Delegated Authority and Preemption
docs.text:
Qualification target: CA-F3.5 Question: When a California government entity, facility, department, official, or employee relies on a rule, policy, sign, directive, visitor condition, or order, what legal source authorizes that restriction, who may exercise the power, and does superior law displace or limit it?

This sweep builds a statewide authority-chain test. It does not attempt to catalogue every enabling statute, city charter, county charter, special-district act, local ordinance, delegation resolution, or facility rule in California. Those remain local or subject-specific inputs.

The operational sequence is:

Identify the rule-maker → identify the source of power → verify required adoption procedure → verify delegation to the actor → test state/federal preemption → apply the constitutional rule → identify the enforcement bridge.

A policy can fail at any one of those stages. Conversely, the fact that a facility-specific source must still be located does not make the statewide analytical framework incomplete.

docs.title: 1. Baseline: government rulemaking power has a source
docs.text:
Government ownership, employment status, or possession of a building does not itself answer who may create generally applicable rules, what form those rules must take, or how they may be enforced.

The Field Guide should distinguish:

  1. Entity power — what Constitution, statute, charter, or enabling law gives the governmental entity authority over the subject?
  2. Rulemaking form — must the restriction be an ordinance, regulation, resolution, order, formally adopted policy, or some other instrument?
  3. Internal delegation — did the governing entity assign implementation or enforcement authority to the department, officer, manager, security employee, or other actor who invoked it?
  4. Superior-law limits — does state or federal law preempt, supersede, or otherwise conflict with the local/agency rule?
  5. Constitutional validity — even if authorized and nonpreempted, does the restriction satisfy the applicable constitutional standard?
  6. Enforcement bridge — what law makes noncompliance removable, citable, detainable, arrestable, or criminal?

These are separate propositions.

docs.title: 2. State administrative agencies: statutory delegation first
Government Code §§ 11342.1 and 11342.2
docs.text:
California's Administrative Procedure Act does not itself enlarge a state agency's substantive power.

Government Code § 11342.1 provides that nothing in the APA confers or augments state-agency authority to adopt, administer, or enforce regulations, and that a regulation must remain within authority conferred by other law.

Section 11342.2 provides that when a statute expressly or impliedly authorizes a state agency to regulate, the resulting regulation is valid only if it is consistent with the statute, does not conflict with it, and is reasonably necessary to effectuate the statutory purpose.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?article=1.&chapter=3.5.&division=3.&lawCode=GOV&part=1.&title=2.

docs.title: Association of California Insurance Companies v. Jones, 2 Cal.5th 376 (2017)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court treats the enabling statute as the starting point for state-agency rulemaking authority. A state executive agency has only the rulemaking power invested in it by statute; a regulation that alters, amends, enlarges, or impairs the statutory scheme exceeds that delegated authority. Once delegation exists, the regulation must still satisfy the consistency and reasonable-necessity requirements reflected in § 11342.2.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2017/s226529.html

docs.title: American Federation of Labor v. Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board, 13 Cal.4th 1017 (1996)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court reiterates that an administrative agency may not expand its powers in the absence of express or implied legislative authority. In the statutory scheme before it, the court found no implied authority for the additional remedy the agency was asked to provide.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/13/1017.html

docs.title: Project rule
docs.text: For a state agency, do not stop at “the department adopted a policy.” Ask what statute or other law gives the department power over this subject and whether the particular restriction fits within that grant.

docs.title: 3. State-agency policies can be underground regulations
Government Code § 11340.5
docs.text:
California law prohibits a state agency from issuing, utilizing, enforcing, or attempting to enforce a rule, guideline, criterion, bulletin, manual, instruction, order, standard of general application, or other rule that qualifies as a regulation unless it was adopted as required by the APA or falls within an applicable exemption.

Official APA source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?article=1.&chapter=3.5.&division=3.&lawCode=GOV&part=1.&title=2.

California Office of Administrative Law: https://oal.ca.gov/rulemaking_process/ https://oal.ca.gov/underground_regulations/

OAL's ordinary inquiry asks whether the challenged material is a rule or standard of general application, whether it implements/interprets/makes specific the law administered by the state agency or governs its procedure, and whether an express statutory exemption applies.

docs.title: Tidewater Marine Western, Inc. v. Bradshaw, 14 Cal.4th 557 (1996)
docs.text:
Tidewater identifies two principal characteristics of an APA regulation:

  1. the rule is intended to apply generally rather than only to a specific case; and
  2. it implements, interprets, or makes specific the law enforced or administered by the agency, or governs the agency's procedure.

The California Supreme Court held that DLSE interpretive policies fitting that definition were void as regulations because they had not been adopted through the APA. Invalidating the underground regulation did not erase the underlying statute or independently valid legal rule.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/14/557.html

docs.title: Scope boundary
docs.text: The California APA layer is a state executive-agency rulemaking rule. Do not automatically apply it to cities, counties, charter governments, courts, or every local public entity. Local adoption authority and procedure must be traced through the law governing that entity.

docs.title: 4. Cities and counties: Article XI § 7 local police power
docs.text:
California Constitution article XI, § 7 authorizes counties and cities to make and enforce within their limits local, police, sanitary, and other ordinances and regulations that do not conflict with general laws.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?article=XI&lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+7.

This is an important baseline grant, but it does not answer every downstream question. The Field Guide must still determine:

  • whether the measure was adopted by the proper local lawmaking body or authorized delegate;
  • whether a charter changes the allocation of local power;
  • whether state law preempts the measure;
  • whether the measure is constitutional; and
  • what enforcement consequence the law actually authorizes.

docs.title: 5. Counties: statutory powers and governing-body authority
docs.text:
Government Code § 23003 makes a county a body corporate and politic with the powers specified in Title 3 and those necessarily implied from powers expressed there.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=23003.

Government Code § 23004 includes powers to contract, hold property necessary to exercise county powers, and manage, lease, sell, or otherwise dispose of county property as the interests of inhabitants require.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=23004.

These provisions can matter to facility-management authority, but they do not create an automatic criminal offense for violating a facility policy.

Government Code § 25132 provides enforcement consequences for violation of a county ordinance. The Field Guide should not silently transform that rule into a proposition that every county policy, employee instruction, or posted sign is itself a misdemeanor.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=25132.

docs.title: Project consequence
docs.text: For a county facility, locate the ordinance, resolution, charter/statutory delegation, or other source authorizing the policy; then separately locate any criminal/removal authority.

docs.title: 6. Cities: ordinance power is not employee-policy power
docs.text:
California general-law cities exercise legislative power through their governing bodies subject to the Constitution and general law. Government Code §§ 36900 and 37100 are useful statutory anchors for city ordinances and their enforcement.

Statutory sources: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=36900. https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=37100.

The same distinction used for counties applies: a city ordinance can carry consequences that an informal departmental memo or front-desk instruction does not automatically acquire. A city may lawfully delegate implementation authority, but the project should identify the delegation rather than presume it.

docs.title: Sherwin-Williams Co. v. City of Los Angeles, 4 Cal.4th 893 (1993)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court describes the core Article XI § 7 conflict/preemption framework.

A local rule conflicts with general state law when it:

  1. duplicates state law;
  2. contradicts state law; or
  3. enters a field that state law has fully occupied, expressly or by implication.

The court describes duplication as local legislation coextensive with state law and contradiction as local legislation inimical to state law.

For implied field occupation, the court identifies indicators including a subject fully covered in terms indicating exclusive state concern, partial coverage framed in terms showing a paramount state concern intolerant of further local action, or partial coverage where adverse effects on transient citizens outweigh possible local benefit.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/4/893.html

docs.title: Project rule
docs.text:
Do not use “preempted” as a synonym for “unconstitutional” or “bad policy.” Ask what general state law governs the subject and whether the local measure duplicates, contradicts, or intrudes into a fully occupied field.

Subject-specific statutes can modify this analysis, so a facility restriction touching weapons, elections, labor, records, licensing, schools, courts, transit, or another regulated subject may require a separate preemption check.

docs.title: 8. Charter cities: municipal-affairs home rule is a separate branch
docs.text:
California Constitution article XI, § 5 gives charter-city law special force with respect to municipal affairs, subject to the charter's restrictions and the separate treatment of matters governed by general law.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?article=XI&lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+5.

docs.title: State Building & Construction Trades Council v. City of Vista, 54 Cal.4th 547 (2012)
docs.text:
When state law and a charter-city measure conflict, City of Vista describes the home-rule analysis in substance as asking:

  1. whether the local subject can be characterized as a municipal affair;
  2. whether there is an actual conflict between local and state law;
  3. whether the state law addresses a matter of statewide concern; and
  4. if so, whether the state law is reasonably related to resolution of that statewide concern and appropriately tailored against unnecessary interference with local governance.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2012/s173586.html

docs.title: Project consequence
docs.text: A charter-city facility cannot be analyzed as though it were simply another general-law city. The charter, municipal code, resolutions, and delegation instruments may be essential parts of the authority chain.

docs.title: 9. Charter counties are not charter cities
docs.text:
California Constitution article XI provides separate constitutional rules for county charters and county governance.

Official source for article XI, § 3: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?article=XI&lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+3.

docs.title: Dibb v. County of San Diego, 8 Cal.4th 1200 (1994)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court upheld San Diego County charter provisions creating a citizens law-enforcement review board and subpoena authority under the county-charter provisions of article XI.

Critically for this project, Dibb distinguishes charter counties from charter cities. A charter county does not simply inherit the charter-city municipal-affairs doctrine. Its powers must be traced through the county-charter provisions, statutes, and the particular subject involved.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/8/1200.html

docs.title: Project rule
docs.text: Do not write “charter entity” and stop. Identify whether it is a charter city or charter county and use the correct constitutional branch.

docs.title: 10. Special districts, joint powers authorities, boards, and commissions
docs.text: Legislatively created public entities are generally creatures of their enabling law. Their express powers matter, but California law also recognizes genuinely implied powers where necessary to accomplish the statutory purpose.

docs.title: Robings v. Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy, 188 Cal.App.4th 952 (2010)
docs.text:
The published Court of Appeal decision explains that express grants do not necessarily tell the whole story; in the absence of an express restriction, implied powers can arise from the purposes for which an agency was created. The opinion also illustrates the separate statutory structure governing joint powers authorities and the common-powers limitation.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2010/b216702/

docs.title: Project consequence
docs.text:
For a special district, commission, authority, or joint-powers entity:

  1. locate the enabling statute or agreement;
  2. identify the express or necessarily implied power;
  3. identify any express limits;
  4. identify who the governing instrument authorizes to act; and
  5. do not import city/county police-power rules unless the law actually makes them applicable.

docs.title: 11. Internal delegation: entity authority is not automatically employee authority
docs.text:
A recurring facility error is collapsing “the government entity has power over its premises” into “therefore any employee may create or enforce any visitor condition.”

Those are different propositions.
