For the Field Guide, investigate:

  • governing-body ordinance/resolution;
  • charter provision;
  • enabling statute;
  • agency regulation;
  • board-adopted policy;
  • department delegation;
  • director/manager authority;
  • property-management agreement;
  • security contract and scope;
  • posted rule and its approving authority;
  • staff manual or enforcement directive;
  • who may issue warnings, exclusions, suspensions, or trespass notices.

The statewide framework cannot supply a single answer for every local employee. Instead, it supplies the research obligation:

Name the actor, name the power, and show the delegation chain.

If the delegation cannot be located, classify the authority as unresolved rather than assuming it exists or does not exist.

docs.title: 12. Federal preemption is a separate superior-law screen
Arizona v. United States, 567 U.S. 387 (2012)
docs.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court summarizes three familiar federal preemption pathways:

  1. express preemption — Congress expressly displaces state/local law;
  2. field preemption — federal regulation occupies a field so completely that supplemental state/local regulation is excluded; and
  3. conflict preemption — state/local law conflicts with federal law, including when it stands as an obstacle to federal purposes.

Official U.S. Reports source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/567bv.pdf

docs.title: Project rule
docs.text:
Federal preemption is ordinarily subject specific. Identify the federal statute/regulation, any express clause, the field allegedly occupied, the actual operational conflict or obstacle, and any savings clause or preserved state/local authority.

Federal-premises rules are also their own branch: a federal building is not governed merely by California local-government authority.

docs.title: 13. Constitutional validity remains separate
docs.text:
A rule may have a valid enabling statute, proper adoption, proper delegation, no state-law preemption, and no federal preemption and still violate the First Amendment, California Speech Clause, due process, equal protection, or another constitutional rule.

Conversely, a constitutional argument should not obscure a simpler ultra vires or preemption defect.

For expressive restrictions, continue into restriction-audit.md and the applicable forum/activity chapter.

docs.title: 14. Policy validity is not criminal enforceability
docs.text:
Do not collapse:

  • the entity could adopt this restriction;
  • this particular policy was validly adopted;
  • this employee had authority to enforce it;
  • noncompliance authorized removal; and
  • noncompliance satisfied a criminal offense.

For local ordinances, statutes such as Government Code §§ 25132 and 36900 may supply consequences for ordinance violations. They do not make every internal policy or employee command a crime.

For California public-agency trespass/interference, return to Penal Code §§ 602 and 602.1 and the Sweep 012 derivative-trespass analysis.

docs.title: 15. California seven-step authority-chain test
docs.text: When a facility rule materially affects access, recording, speech, observation, identification, or removal, run these questions in sequence.

docs.title: Step 1 — Who made the rule?
docs.text: Classify the rule-maker: Legislature, state executive agency, general-law city, charter city, general-law county, charter county, special district, board/commission, joint-powers authority, court/judicial entity, department, individual official/employee, or contractor/security provider.

docs.title: Step 2 — What legal source gives that entity power?
docs.text: Locate the highest useful source: Constitution, statute/enabling act, charter, ordinance, regulation, resolution/order, joint-powers agreement, property-management instrument, or other valid delegation. Ask whether the claimed power is express or necessarily implied.

docs.title: Step 3 — Was the rule adopted in the legally required form?
docs.text: For a state executive agency, test the APA/underground-regulation issue when a generally applicable rule implements, interprets, or makes specific administered law. For local government, identify the local/statutory adoption procedure rather than importing the state APA automatically.

docs.title: Step 4 — Was power delegated to this actor?
docs.text: Identify who may create, interpret, post, grant exceptions to, or enforce the rule, and who may order departure, issue a suspension/exclusion, or request police enforcement.

docs.title: Step 5 — Does superior law displace it?
docs.text: Check California state/local preemption under Sherwin-Williams, charter-city home rule under article XI § 5 and City of Vista where applicable, charter-county rules separately, and federal express/field/conflict preemption under the subject-specific federal scheme.

docs.title: Step 6 — Does the restriction survive the constitutional/activity test?
docs.text: Apply existing forum, recording, privacy, meeting, petition, speech, due-process, and other constitutional rules.

docs.title: Step 7 — What enforcement consequence actually follows?
docs.text: Identify the separate bridge to administrative consequence, loss of a voluntarily offered service, removal, prospective exclusion, citation, detention, arrest, or prosecution. Do not manufacture that consequence from the word “policy.”

docs.title: 16. Facility-research output
docs.text:
For every material rule, the facility file should record when available:

Field Required content Rule text Exact current restriction Rule-maker Entity/body/person that adopted it Entity type State agency / general-law city / charter city / county / special entity / etc. Enabling authority Constitution/statute/charter/enabling act Adoption instrument Regulation/ordinance/resolution/order/policy Adoption date/version Current effective source Required procedure APA/local charter/statutory process where material Delegation chain Governing entity → department → official/employee/security State preemption None identified / issue identified / unresolved Federal preemption None identified / issue identified / unresolved Constitutional status Apply Restriction Audit separately Enforcement bridge Actual removal/offense/penalty authority Confidence Verified / partially verified / unresolved

docs.title: 17. Qualification disposition
docs.text:
Sweep 013 supplies a California-wide method for answering the ordinary delegated-authority/preemption question in CA-F3.5.

Row Pre-sweep Sweep 013 result Reason CA-F3.5 Gap Supported The statewide framework now distinguishes entity type, enabling authority, required rulemaking form, internal delegation, California state/local preemption, charter-city/charter-county differences, federal preemption, constitutional review, and the separate enforcement bridge.

Supported does not mean every California facility's delegation chain has already been located. It means the Field Guide can identify the correct authority branch and the evidence that must be gathered. The actual charter, ordinance, regulation, enabling act, resolution, delegation, or local rule remains a facility-specific dependency where material.

docs.title: 18. Boundaries preserved for other packages
docs.text:
Sweep 013 does not close:

  • GAP-04 public-agency trespass, prospective exclusions, longer bans, and identification duties;
  • GAP-05 device seizure/retention and search edges;
  • GAP-06 disorder/noise/fighting-words/obstruction doctrine;
  • GAP-07 emergency/dispersal/perimeter doctrine;
  • GAP-08 law-enforcement records.

It also does not attempt a subject-by-subject preemption sweep of every California regulatory field. When a facility restriction depends on a specialized statute or federal scheme, research that scheme before applying a preemption conclusion.

docs.title: Core authority hierarchy
docs.text:
Direct/current: - Cal. Const., art. XI, §§ 3, 5, 7 - Cal. Gov. Code §§ 11340.5, 11342.1, 11342.2 - Cal. Gov. Code §§ 23003, 23004, 25132 - Cal. Gov. Code §§ 36900, 37100 - Sherwin-Williams Co. v. City of Los Angeles, 4 Cal.4th 893 - Dibb v. County of San Diego, 8 Cal.4th 1200 - American Federation of Labor v. UIAB, 13 Cal.4th 1017 - Tidewater Marine Western, Inc. v. Bradshaw, 14 Cal.4th 557 - State Building & Construction Trades Council v. City of Vista, 54 Cal.4th 547 - Association of California Insurance Companies v. Jones, 2 Cal.5th 376 - Arizona v. United States, 567 U.S. 387

Published supporting authority: - Robings v. Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy, 188 Cal.App.4th 952

Official administrative guidance: - California Office of Administrative Law rulemaking and underground-regulation materials

docs.title: Sweep 014 — Public-Agency Exclusion, Prospective Trespass, and Identification
docs.text:
Qualification targets:

  • CA-F4.3 — public-property/public-agency distinctions;
  • CA-F4.5 — never-entered / entered-and-left / currently-remains / prospective-no-entry notice;
  • CA-F4.7 — suspension/exclusion process where material;
  • CA-F5.8 — identification request versus legal duty;
  • NC-COMPLAINT-01.D — prospective trespass notice and identification.

This sweep addresses a recurring public-facility sequence:

lawful public access → allegation such as "disruptive" or "harassing" → immediate leave demand → prospective exclusion/no-return notice → later reentry → claimed trespass → demand for name or physical identification

The sweep does not assume the allegation is true merely because an employee, caller, security worker, or officer uses a legal-sounding label. It also does not assume that public ownership creates an unlimited right to remain.

The operational sequence is:

exact area/access status → actual conduct and rule → immediate-removal authority → prospective-exclusion authority → scope/duration/process → later-reentry statute → officer knowledge/reliance → identification stage and source of duty

Three important outcomes are preserved rather than forced into categorical rules:

  1. California's ordinary public-agency/current-access trespass branches can now be separated and analyzed.
  2. The First Amendment supplies binding limits on some broad prospective exclusions, but the effect of an individualized prior ban on Penal Code § 602(o) remains materially unsettled in the California authorities reviewed.
  3. California does not have a current general pedestrian carry-ID statute equivalent to Nevada's Hiibel statute, but the effect of refusing to identify during an otherwise lawful detention remains an unresolved California § 148 boundary after Vanegas and the older California cases.

docs.title: 1. Current California trespass statutes do not create one generic "trespassed" status
docs.text:
Primary source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.

The current Penal Code uses different factual predicates for different kinds of trespass.

For the ordinary public-facility problem, the most important distinctions are:

  • § 602(o): refusal/failure to leave property not open to the general public after the specified request;
  • § 602(q): refusal/failure to leave a public building of a public agency during hours when the building is regularly closed to the public, after the specified request and under the objective lawful-business condition;
  • § 602.1(b): intentional interference with public-agency business by obstruction or intimidation plus refusal after a qualifying request;
  • § 602(t): a specialized prospective reentry/refusal provision for private property after a qualifying prior conviction and notice;
  • specialized secured/posted/screened-area provisions that must be tested on their own facts.

The phrase "you are trespassed" does not identify which of these statutes applies.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
A leave order, an administrative exclusion, and a criminal-trespass offense are separate legal objects. Identify each one.

Sweep 012 already established the derivative-trespass sequence for an immediate "stop the activity or leave" demand. Sweep 014 adds the later prospective-exclusion and reentry branches.

docs.title: 2. Public ownership and "open to the general public" are different questions
docs.text: Section 602(o) turns on whether the exact land, real property, or structure is not open to the general public. Ownership by a public entity does not answer that question.

docs.title: James v. City of Long Beach, 18 F. Supp. 2d 1078 (C.D. Cal. 1998)
docs.text:
Status: federal district court; persuasive only.

James involved a city-owned baseball facility during a game. Access required a ticket. The district court concluded that the facility was not open to the general public for the relevant § 602(o)-predecessor analysis because entry was restricted to ticket-holders.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/FSupp2/18/1078/2449844/

Project consequence:

Public property can be access-restricted. Ask whether anyone may presently enter the exact area under ordinary conditions or whether entry requires permission, a ticket, authorization, screening, appointment, or another condition.

The converse matters too. A public-facing lobby or ordinary public service floor that anyone may enter during business hours is not converted into § 602(o) property merely because the government owns it.

Section 602(q) separately covers regularly closed public buildings. Section 602.1(b) separately addresses a public agency open to the public.

This supplies the ordinary public-property/public-agency distinction required by CA-F4.3 without pretending every area of a public building has the same access status.

docs.title: 3. "Disruptive," "harassing," and similar labels are allegations, not elements
docs.text:
For the standing peaceful scenario, preserve the conduct underneath the characterization.

Examples of factual questions:

  • What precisely was said or done before the first leave order?
  • Was service actually obstructed?
  • Was an employee or member of the public intimidated?
  • Was a doorway, queue, counter, aisle, or workstation blocked?
  • Was there unreasonable noise?
  • Was another person followed, threatened, crowded, or repeatedly targeted?
  • Was a valid facility rule actually violated?
  • Did the official identify conduct, or only apply a conclusion such as "harassing customers"?
  • Did the alleged disruption precede the exclusion, or did conflict arise only after the person was told to stop recording or leave?

Penal Code § 602.1(b) requires intentional interference with public-agency business by obstruction or intimidation plus refusal after a qualifying request. Sweep 012's published Dubner anchor and nonprecedential Mackey DMV comparator remain controlling project guardrails against treating refusal or generalized labels as substitutes for missing interference facts.

Current statutory source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.1

Project rule:

Translate the allegation into observable facts and the actual offense or policy elements before relying on it to support removal, exclusion, detention, or arrest.

If the allegation is knowingly false, retaliatory, or contradicted by objective evidence, those issues remain separate retaliation, false-report, and police-investigation branches. Sweep 014 does not infer motive from the label alone.

docs.title: 4. Immediate removal and prospective exclusion are not the same government act
docs.text:
A same-day order to leave can be limited to ending a present violation or restoring facility operations. A prospective exclusion changes future access even after the immediate facts have ended.

For every prospective exclusion, record:

  • issuing authority;
  • legal source and delegation;
  • exact property/areas covered;
  • start and end dates;
  • whether it is one branch, one room, one building, a campus, or systemwide;
  • conduct relied on;
  • evidence supporting that conduct;
  • whether future risk is independently supported;
  • permitted access for unrelated government business;
  • exceptions or appointment procedures;
  • written notice;
  • opportunity to respond;
  • appeal/review procedure;
  • effect of an appeal;
  • reentry consequences;
  • actual criminal statute claimed to apply later.

Sweep 013 supplies the authority/delegation chain. Sweep 014 adds the constitutional breadth/duration and later-reentry analysis.

docs.title: 5. Binding Ninth Circuit: Reza limits broad prospective exclusions from a government forum
Reza v. Pearce, 806 F.3d 497 (9th Cir. 2015)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published/binding federal authority in California.

Reza arose from an Arizona Senate building, which the Ninth Circuit treated as a limited public forum for the relevant activity. Officials attributed disruption during a legislative hearing to Reza. Two days later, the Senate President barred him from the building. Reza later attempted to enter for a scheduled meeting with another senator and was arrested for trespass.

The amended published opinion found material factual disputes about whether Reza actually disrupted the proceeding and whether there was a legitimate future-disruption basis. On the plaintiff-favorable summary-judgment facts, a complete building-wide and initially indefinite ban was unreasonable. The court emphasized the breadth of the exclusion, its impact on unrelated future hearings and access to elected representatives, the absence of sufficient evidence that the asserted safety risk was real, and the availability of narrower restrictions.

Official Ninth Circuit source: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2015/11/19/13-15154.pdf

docs.title: Narrow project rule from Reza
docs.text:
A prior incident does not automatically justify a broad future exclusion from a government forum. Preserve whether the alleged misconduct actually occurred, what future risk the record supports, how broadly the ban reaches, how long it lasts, and what otherwise lawful government access it forecloses.

This is not a categorical rule that government can never suspend someone after disruption. The constitutional test remains forum- and activity-specific, and valid safety/operational restrictions can be enforced.

docs.title: Officer-reliance distinction
docs.text:
Reza separately granted qualified immunity to officers who later enforced the facially valid exclusion order under Arizona's criminal-trespass law.

That result must not be imported as though Arizona's trespass statute were California law. Its project value is the analytical separation:

  • underlying exclusion validity;
  • facial order and issuing authority;
  • later officer knowledge;
  • the actual jurisdiction's reentry/trespass statute; and
  • qualified-immunity / reasonable-reliance questions.

A potentially unconstitutional exclusion and an officer's later civil liability are not necessarily the same question.

docs.title: Walsh v. Enge, 154 F. Supp. 3d 1113 (D. Or. 2015)
docs.text:
Status: District of Oregon; persuasive only.

Walsh applied Ninth Circuit First Amendment doctrine to a Portland City Hall exclusion following disruption of a city council meeting. It treated lengthy prospective exclusion from future meetings and City Hall access as constitutionally problematic rather than assuming that one disruption creates indefinite future exclusion power.

Project use: comparator for breadth, duration, future forum access, and alternatives. Do not treat it as binding California authority.

docs.title: Catron v. City of St. Petersburg, 658 F.3d 1260 (11th Cir. 2011)
docs.text:
Status: Eleventh Circuit; persuasive only.

Catron involved trespass warnings from public parks. The Eleventh Circuit recognized that the plaintiffs had sufficiently alleged a procedural-due-process problem where the warning scheme provided no way to contest the warning or its scope. The opinion did not create an unlimited right to occupy public property and arose outside the Ninth Circuit.

Project use: due-process comparator for meaningful review of a government-imposed future access restriction.

docs.title: 7. Procedural due process: identify the protected interest before prescribing procedure
Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976)
docs.text:
Status: U.S. Supreme Court.

Procedural due process first requires a protected liberty or property interest. If government is depriving such an interest, the required procedure is context-sensitive and ordinarily considers:

  1. the private interest affected;
  2. the risk of erroneous deprivation and probable value of additional safeguards; and
  3. the government's interest and burdens of additional procedure.

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/424/319

docs.title: Field Guide consequence
docs.text:
Do not write:

Every exclusion from every public building requires a formal hearing before it takes effect.

Instead ask:

  • What liberty, property, speech, petition, service-access, or other protected interest is actually burdened?
  • Is the restriction immediate/emergency, one day, weeks, months, indefinite, or permanent?
  • Is it one room or every facility in a system?
  • How serious is the risk from allowing continued access during review?
  • What facts are disputed?
  • Was there notice of the conduct and rule?
  • Could the person give their side?
  • Is there prompt review or appeal?
  • Does the ban remain in force during appeal?
  • Can necessary government business still be conducted by appointment or another channel?

Reza supplies binding First Amendment limits in the government-forum setting. Mathews supplies the general procedural framework. Catron and library cases remain persuasive comparators for the amount of process in particular public-access settings.

This authority is sufficient to run CA-F4.7's ordinary process branch while preserving facility-specific interests and procedures.

docs.title: 8. A prior no-return notice does not have one settled California § 602(o) effect
docs.text:
This is the most important unresolved trespass boundary in Sweep 014.

Current § 602(o) expressly applies to property not open to the general public. It also contains owner-to-police request provisions, including limited-duration standing requests in specified circumstances. Those request provisions concern authorization for police assistance; they do not expressly create a universal individualized no-return offense for an otherwise public-facing government building.

By contrast, current § 602(t) expressly creates a prospective reentry/refusal offense for specified private property after a qualifying prior conviction and notice, with defined time limits tied to the conviction.

Current source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.

That textual contrast is important but does not itself resolve how § 602(o) applies after an individualized ban.

docs.title: 9. Blankenhorn: important but not a clean prospective-public-property holding
Blankenhorn v. City of Orange, 485 F.3d 463 (9th Cir. 2007)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

Blankenhorn involved a privately owned shopping center that was generally open to the public. The plaintiff had received a prior "Notice Forbidding Trespass."

In the probable-cause analysis, the majority said the notice arguably rendered the shopping center not open to the public with respect to Blankenhorn. The opinion emphasized that the question was not whether Blankenhorn ultimately was guilty of trespass but whether officers reasonably could think probable cause existed.

The case therefore matters, but it should not be rewritten as:

A prior trespass notice conclusively converts every otherwise public-facing property into property "not open to the general public" under § 602(o).

It involved private commercial property, a probable-cause/qualified-immunity posture, and conditional language.

Judge Berzon's partial dissent read the predecessor of § 602(o) differently, reasoning that the statutory request requirement called for a contemporaneous request and that a prior individualized notice did not itself satisfy it.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/485/463/577982/

The majority/dissent disagreement is one reason this project preserves the later-notice branch as unresolved rather than converting Blankenhorn into a categorical rule.

docs.title: 10. California federal district courts expose the unresolved § 602(o) boundary
docs.text:
No published California appellate decision located in this sweep squarely resolves whether an individualized prospective ban, by itself, makes a public-facing government area that is otherwise open to the general public "not open to the general public" for purposes of current § 602(o).

Federal district decisions applying California law point in different directions.

docs.title: Han v. City of Los Angeles
docs.text:
Status: C.D. Cal.; persuasive only.

In pretrial treatment of an otherwise public-facing private marketplace, the court examined Blankenhorn's conditional "arguably" language and rejected using a prior ban notice to transform the statutory phrase "not open to the general public" into individualized status for that trial. The court emphasized that Blankenhorn focused on what reasonable officers could have believed rather than conclusively deciding the statutory elements.

Source: https://docs.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/california/cacdce/2%3A2014cv08582/603656/95

docs.title: Garcia v. City of Santa Clara
docs.text:
Status: N.D. Cal.; persuasive only; later Ninth Circuit disposition did not create a published California statutory construction resolving the general issue.

The district-court litigation treated Blankenhorn as supporting the proposition that a specific person can, at least arguably, be excluded from property otherwise open to the public. Other federal district decisions have used similar reasoning.

Source: https://docs.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/california/candce/3%3A2010cv02424/228199/163

docs.title: Qualification consequence
docs.text:
The split is not resolved by choosing the interpretation the project prefers.

Field rule:

If later criminal enforcement depends on a prior individualized ban converting otherwise generally open property into § 602(o) property, flag the statutory effect as RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED unless a more specific statute, ordinance, valid restricted-area rule, closing condition, or other controlling authority independently resolves the facts.

The prior notice still matters as evidence of notice, access instructions, intent, and officer knowledge. It simply does not eliminate the need to identify the criminal statute that actually governs later reentry.

docs.title: 11. Reentry posture: rerun the law at the time of return
docs.text:
When a person comes back after an earlier exclusion, do not analyze only the earlier encounter.

Record:

  • current date/time;
  • whether the exclusion has expired;
  • exact property/area covered;
  • whether public hours are open;
  • whether the person has legitimate government business;
  • whether an appeal/review changed the order;
  • whether there is an appointment or express authorization;
  • whether a specific restricted-area or specialized statute applies;
  • what current statute is claimed to prohibit entry/remain;
  • whether a fresh request to leave occurred;
  • whether the person leaves when currently requested;
  • what officers know about the order's source, scope, and validity.

A valid prior administrative exclusion can have legal consequences. But the phrase "you were trespassed before" is not a substitute for the elements of the California offense being asserted now.

docs.title: 12. Identification: request, name, physical ID, search, citation, and booking are separate
docs.text:
The Field Guide must keep at least six different propositions separate:

  1. officer may ask for identification;
  2. person must verbally state a name;
  3. person must carry a physical ID document;
  4. person must produce a document they possess;
  5. officer may search the person or belongings for ID;
  6. arrest/citation/booking rules create specific identification consequences.

The answer to one does not decide the others.

docs.title: 13. No current general pedestrian carry-ID statute located
docs.text:
The current California corpus and this targeted sweep have not identified a general statute requiring an ordinary pedestrian merely present in public to carry a government identification card.

Hiibel v. Sixth Judicial District Court, 542 U.S. 177 (2004), upheld Nevada's own stop-and-identify statute during a lawful Terry stop. Hiibel did not enact such a statute for California.

Kolender v. Lawson, 461 U.S. 352 (1983), invalidated California's former vague identification scheme. That historical decision does not invalidate every current specialized identification statute.

Project rule:

Do not cite Hiibel as though it creates a California stop-and-identify statute. Find the California source applicable to the actual encounter.

docs.title: 14. Landeros: refusal cannot create its own reasonable suspicion
United States v. Landeros, 913 F.3d 862 (9th Cir. 2019)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

Landeros held that where officers lacked reasonable suspicion that a passenger had committed an offense, the passenger's refusal to identify himself did not itself create reasonable suspicion and did not justify prolonging the traffic stop to investigate him.

Official source: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2019/01/11/17-10217.pdf

Field rule:

An officer may ask for identification during a consensual encounter. Refusal does not manufacture the reasonable suspicion needed to detain a person who was not otherwise lawfully detainable.

Landeros does not resolve every California-law consequence of refusal during an otherwise valid, particularized Terry detention.

docs.title: 15. Vanegas confirms that the lawful-detention identification boundary remains open
Vanegas v. City of Pasadena, 46 F.4th 1159 (9th Cir. 2022)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

Vanegas involved an investigation of reported conduct outside a courthouse. The officers had an independent probable-cause basis under Penal Code § 415(2), so the panel did not need to decide whether refusal to identify during the investigation itself supplied probable cause under § 148(a)(1).

On the § 148 theory, the panel held that no controlling authority or robust consensus made the officers' asserted mistake clearly unconstitutional and granted qualified immunity. The majority expressly left open whether the failure to identify actually supplied § 148 probable cause.

Official source: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/08/31/21-55478.pdf

Judge Bumatay's separate concurrence emphasized that he could find no California decision categorically holding that failure to identify during a police investigation, without more, supplies § 148 probable cause. Other separate reasoning in Vanegas read the law more broadly.

Project consequence:

The California-law duty to affirmatively identify oneself during every otherwise lawful Terry detention is not treated as settled by Vanegas.

This is a genuine RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED boundary, not merely missing research.

docs.title: 16. California § 148 cases narrow the slogans but do not erase the unresolved detention issue
People v. Quiroga, 16 Cal.App.4th 961 (1993)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Quiroga held, among other things:

  • verbal argument and slow compliance are not automatically § 148 obstruction;
  • refusing to provide a name after arrest while being transported did not itself violate § 148 where booking had not begun and no police duty was shown to have been delayed;
  • in the narrow felony-booking context, withholding identity can obstruct the booking process;
  • misdemeanor/infraction identification contexts are governed by their own statutory procedures.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/16/961.html

docs.title: In re Chase C., 243 Cal.App.4th 107 (2015)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Chase C. applied the actual-obstruction requirement in a police-investigation setting and held on its facts that refusal to identify before booking did not constitute § 148 obstruction. It reinforces that noncooperation cannot simply be relabeled obstruction without an obstructed lawful duty.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2015/d067787.html

These cases strongly reject a generic "silence equals § 148" rule. They do not squarely overrule the older identification-production cases discussed below.

docs.title: 17. Older production cases must be read with their facts and later Garcia limitation
People v. Loudermilk, 195 Cal.App.3d 996 (1987)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Loudermilk contains broad language that, as part of a lawful Terry investigation, police may require a suspect to produce proof of identification if the suspect has it.

But the case involved materially specific facts: officers were investigating a reported shooting, the detained person matched the description, a weapon was implicated, a lawful weapons frisk occurred, and the suspect said he had no identification after a wallet was discovered.

The opinion itself cautioned that it was not holding that a suspect may be detained and searched merely because the suspect refused to identify or produce proof.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/195/996.html

docs.title: People v. Long, 189 Cal.App.3d 77 (1987)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Long likewise upheld a direction to produce written identification on particular facts involving a lawful detention, suspected drug intoxication, apparent inconsistency between the person's denial of identification and a visible wallet, and later safety/evidence concerns when the wallet was produced.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/189/77.html

Do not convert Long into a rule authorizing officers to reach into any Terry detainee's pocket for identification.

docs.title: People v. Garcia, B187453 (Cal. Ct. App. Dec. 14, 2006)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Garcia directly rejected a generalized "patdown search for identification." The officer had lawfully detained a bicyclist who said he had no identification and searched him solely to locate identification. The court held that Terry's protective-frisk doctrine cannot be turned into an evidence search for ID.

Garcia expressly distinguished Long and Loudermilk as fact-specific.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2006/b187453.html

Project rule:

A lawful detention is not, by itself, a license to conduct a Terry patdown for identification. Search authority requires its own justification.

The separate question whether a lawfully detained person can be ordered to state or produce identity in every investigative detention remains unresolved after Vanegas and the older cases.

docs.title: 18. False identity is independently regulated
docs.text:
Current Penal Code § 148.9 makes specified false/fictitious identification conduct a misdemeanor upon lawful detention or arrest when the statutory purpose/elements are satisfied.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148.9

The statute tells a detainee what not to do. Its text is not itself a universal affirmative carry-ID statute.

Field rule:

Silence/refusal and false identity are different legal acts. Do not infer permission to lie from uncertainty about an affirmative identification duty.

docs.title: 19. Citation, traffic, arrest, and booking stages can create specific identification consequences
Penal Code § 853.5 — infraction citation procedure
docs.text:
Current § 853.5 supplies identification, signature, and fingerprint procedures after an infraction arrest in the citation/release process.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=853.5

The statute is not a general pre-offense pedestrian stop-and-identify law.

docs.title: Vehicle Code § 40302 / People v. McKay, 27 Cal.4th 601 (2002)
docs.text:
McKay concerned a bicyclist already stopped for a Vehicle Code violation. The California Supreme Court emphasized that he was not arrested merely because he failed to carry identification; the predicate was the underlying Vehicle Code offense, after which the citation/custody statute required satisfactory evidence of identity for release.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/27/601.html

docs.title: Felony booking
docs.text:
Quiroga recognizes a narrow booking-stage § 148 consequence where withholding identity actually impedes felony booking.

Project sequence:

underlying offense/detention authority → citation/arrest/booking stage → stage-specific identification statute or duty → consequence of noncompliance

Do not reverse that sequence into:

no ID → therefore detention/arrest is justified.

docs.title: 20. An exclusion notice does not itself create a new identification statute
docs.text:
A public employee or officer may want a person's name to document an exclusion. That administrative convenience does not by itself answer whether California law compels the person to provide it.

For an exclusion encounter, ask separately:

  • Is the contact consensual or a lawful detention?
  • What suspected offense or other legal basis supports detention?
  • Is the person being arrested or cited for an independently supported offense?
  • Does a citation/release or booking statute apply?
  • Does the facility's valid rule condition future voluntary access on an identification process?
  • If so, is the question administrative access or criminal compulsion?
  • Is the person merely silent/refusing, or affirmatively giving false information?
  • Is any physical search for identification separately lawful?

Field Guide rule:

"We need your ID so we can trespass you" is not itself the source of an identification duty. Identify the detention/arrest/citation/access authority that supplies the duty or consequence.

A person may still face a practical administrative consequence if a valid facility rule conditions a future service or appeal process on enough information to identify the affected person. That is analytically distinct from arresting someone merely for refusing an unsupported ID demand.

docs.title: 21. Public-agency exclusion / reentry decision tree
docs.text: When government says a person is "trespassed" from public property, run this sequence.

docs.title: Step 1 — Current access status
docs.text:
Is the exact area:

  • presently open to the general public;
  • closed for the day;
  • ticketed/appointment-only;
  • restricted to authorized people;
  • subject to valid screening;
  • temporarily closed for a lawful use; or
  • governed by a specialized statute/regulation?

docs.title: Step 2 — Conduct before the restriction
docs.text:
Record actual facts before labels.

For "disruptive" or "harassing":

  • identify the conduct;
  • identify the rule/offense;
  • test its elements;
  • preserve contrary objective evidence.

docs.title: Step 3 — Immediate order
docs.text:
Who ordered departure, under what authority, and was the underlying rule valid?

Use Sweeps 012 and 013.

docs.title: Step 4 — Prospective exclusion
docs.text:
If the order extends beyond the current encounter:

  • identify issuing authority/delegation;
  • exact scope;
  • duration;
  • evidence/future-risk rationale;
  • viewpoint neutrality;
  • impact on unrelated government access;
  • notice and review procedure.

Use Reza and, where procedural due process is implicated, Mathews.

docs.title: Step 5 — Later return
docs.text:
Do not assume the old order itself equals a current criminal offense.

Identify:

  • current access facts;
  • order still in force?;
  • exact California offense claimed;
  • whether a fresh request occurred;
  • whether a specialized no-entry law applies;
  • whether § 602(o)'s "not open to the general public" predicate is actually satisfied.

If the criminal theory depends only on an individualized prior ban changing otherwise generally open property into § 602(o) property, preserve the unresolved Blankenhorn/Han/Garcia boundary.

docs.title: Step 6 — Police reliance
docs.text:
Separate:

  • legality of the underlying exclusion;
  • what the officer reasonably knew;
  • facial validity/source/scope of the order;
  • independent offense elements;
  • qualified-immunity issues.

Reza illustrates why these can produce different answers.

docs.title: Step 7 — Identification
docs.text:
Separate:

  • request;
  • lawful detention;
  • verbal name;
  • physical document;
  • search for ID;
  • false identity;
  • citation/release;
  • booking.

Do not invent a general ID duty from the exclusion notice itself.

docs.title: 22. Field rule for recurring "you're being trespassed" encounters
docs.text:
For the standing peaceful scenario:

A public employee or officer saying "you're trespassed" does not identify a California crime. Determine whether the present area is open to the general public, what conduct preceded the order, what authority supports immediate removal, whether a separate prospective exclusion was validly issued, and what statute applies if the person later returns.

For allegation-driven exclusions:

"Disruptive," "harassing," and "interfering" are factual conclusions to test, not magic words that satisfy statutory or constitutional predicates.

For prospective bans:

A prior incident can support a future restriction when the actual facts and governing law justify it, but breadth, duration, unrelated future access, viewpoint neutrality, and evidence of future risk matter. Reza does not permit a broad ban to bootstrap itself from an unsupported disruption allegation.

For identification:

California has specialized identification duties and consequences, but this sweep does not identify a general pedestrian carry-ID statute. The legal effect of refusing to identify during every otherwise lawful Terry detention remains unresolved; detention alone also does not authorize a patdown search for ID.

docs.title: 23. Qualification dispositions
docs.text:
Sweep 014 closes the research package without falsely converting unsettled law into a categorical answer.

Row Pre-sweep Sweep 014 disposition Reason CA-F4.3 Gap Supported Current § 602(o), § 602(q), § 602.1(b), area-specific access doctrine, and public-property examples now permit the ordinary public-agency/public-property branch to distinguish ownership, general-public access, closing, and interference. CA-F4.5 Gap Researched-Unresolved Immediate/remain/left postures are runnable, but the effect of an individualized prospective ban on otherwise generally open property under § 602(o) remains genuinely unsettled after Blankenhorn and conflicting district-court treatments. CA-F4.7 Gap Supported Reza supplies binding prospective-exclusion First Amendment limits; Mathews supplies the general procedural framework; exact protected interest and procedure remain facility/fact dependent rather than unresearched. CA-F5.8 Gap Researched-Unresolved The no-general-carry-ID/request-versus-duty/search/citation/booking boundaries are researched, but Vanegas expressly leaves the otherwise-lawful-detention § 148 identification issue unresolved against mixed older California authority. NC-COMPLAINT-01.D Gap Researched-Unresolved The branch can distinguish prospective notice, later reentry, officer reliance, and identification stages, but two outcome-determinative California edges remain genuinely unresolved: individualized § 602(o) effect and the general lawful-detention affirmative-ID duty.

Resulting provisional totals if the package review accepts these dispositions:

  • 60 Supported
  • 4 Researched-Unresolved
  • 9 Gap
  • 0 Not Applicable
  • 4 open research packages: GAP-05 through GAP-08

A Researched-Unresolved result is not an activation-blocking Gap under the project's status model, but it must remain visible to the field user and may not be rewritten as a favorable categorical answer.

docs.title: 24. Boundaries preserved for remaining packages
docs.text:
Sweep 014 does not close:

  • GAP-05 device physical seizure/retention, container/plain-feel, consent, and compelled-access edges;
  • GAP-06 unreasonable noise, fighting words/threats/offensive speech, and broader obstruction doctrine;
  • GAP-07 assembly/dispersal/emergency-perimeter and observer/newsgathering doctrine;
  • GAP-08 law-enforcement records and specialized evidence disclosure.

A "disruptive" allegation may therefore trigger GAP-06 if the claimed offense is Penal Code § 415 or another disorder/noise/threat provision. Sweep 014 supplies the rule that the label must be converted into facts and elements; GAP-06 will supply the remaining offense-specific case law.

Emergency closures/perimeters remain GAP-07.

docs.title: Sweep 015 — Recording-Device Seizure, Retention, Search, and Compelled Access
docs.text:
Qualification target: CA-F5.9

This sweep addresses a recurring field sequence:

phone/camera records encounter → officer asks to see it → person offers or refuses → officer takes physical custody → device is retained → government seeks or conducts digital search → government seeks an unlock method

The essential rule is that these are different Fourth/Fifth Amendment events.

Operational sequence:

encounter stage → government act → initial seizure authority → duration/diligence → digital-search authority → frisk/plain-view/plain-feel/consent limits → news-material overlay → compelled-access method

Do not collapse:

  • a request to view one recording;
  • consent to view that recording;
  • physical possession of the device;
  • temporary securing of the device;
  • evidentiary seizure;
  • prolonged retention while a warrant is sought;
  • digital browsing/search;
  • forensic extraction; and
  • compelled biometric/passcode access.

docs.title: 1. Physical seizure and digital search are separate Fourth Amendment questions
docs.text:
A property seizure occurs when government meaningfully interferes with a person's possessory interests. The Fourth Amendment therefore protects more than privacy in digital contents; it also protects the possessory interest in the physical device.

Supreme Court anchors include:

  • United States v. Jacobsen, 466 U.S. 109 (1984);
  • United States v. Karo, 468 U.S. 705 (1984); and
  • Soldal v. Cook County, 506 U.S. 56 (1992).

Karo source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/468/705

For a recording device, ask separately:

  1. Could police lawfully take physical custody?
  2. Could they lawfully keep it for the time they did?
  3. Could they lawfully inspect digital contents?
  4. Could they lawfully compel a method of access?

A yes to one does not automatically answer the others.

docs.title: 2. Riley does not prohibit every physical seizure of a phone
Riley v. California, 573 U.S. 373 (2014)
docs.text:
Status: U.S. Supreme Court; controlling.

Riley holds that a lawful arrest does not ordinarily authorize a warrantless search of the digital contents of a cell phone under the search-incident-to-arrest doctrine.

Official U.S. Reports: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/573BV.pdf

But Riley expressly distinguishes securing the physical phone from searching its digital contents. The defendants conceded that officers could seize and secure their phones to prevent destruction of evidence while seeking a warrant. Riley also explains that, once the phone is secured, the arrestee ordinarily cannot personally delete its data.

Field Guide rule:

Riley is a digital-search rule, not a no-physical-seizure rule.

A valid arrest may permit officers to take custody of a phone found on the arrestee even though Riley generally requires a warrant or another recognized exception before police search the stored digital contents.

That physical custody is still subject to ordinary Fourth Amendment limits, including the basis for seizure and the reasonableness of continued retention.

docs.title: 3. Temporary seizure on less than probable cause is narrow, not a generic phone-hold rule
United States v. Place, 462 U.S. 696 (1983)
docs.text:
Status: U.S. Supreme Court.

Place permits a limited temporary detention of luggage on reasonable suspicion for the specific investigative purpose presented there, but held the approximately 90-minute seizure unreasonable on the facts. Duration, diligence, and the intrusion on possessory interests matter.

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/462/696

Do not rewrite Place as:

Police may take any phone for as long as needed whenever they reasonably suspect it contains evidence.

The permissible scope of a limited property detention depends on the actual investigative basis and purpose. A more substantial evidentiary seizure ordinarily requires stronger authority.

docs.title: 4. Evidentiary seizure ordinarily requires probable cause plus lawful seizure authority
Arizona v. Hicks, 480 U.S. 321 (1987)
docs.text:
Status: U.S. Supreme Court.

Hicks holds that the plain-view doctrine does not permit evidentiary seizure based merely on reasonable suspicion. The object's incriminating character must be supported by probable cause, along with lawful access to the object.

Source: https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/480/321/

For an ordinary phone or camera:

The fact that the object is visibly a phone or camera does not itself make its incriminating character immediately apparent.

If police claim the device itself is evidence, identify:

  • probable cause connecting this particular device to an offense;
  • the warrant or recognized exception permitting the physical seizure;
  • whether officers are merely securing it temporarily or taking it into evidence; and
  • whether the same authority permits any digital search.

docs.title: 5. Preservation exigency must be genuine, not speculative
docs.text: A recognized exigency can sometimes permit immediate warrantless action where officers have probable cause and reasonably face imminent evidence destruction or another urgent circumstance.

docs.title: Riley / Camou
docs.text:
In Riley, the Supreme Court rejected a categorical remote-wiping justification for warrantless phone searches after arrest. Once officers secure the device, the arrestee cannot personally delete the data; the Court also identified practical methods to address remote wiping and preserved true case-specific exigency.

In United States v. Camou, 773 F.3d 932 (9th Cir. 2014), the published Ninth Circuit applied Riley and rejected a warrantless phone-content search performed approximately an hour and twenty minutes after arrest. The government failed to show an imminent "now or never" evidence-destruction problem, and even a genuine exigency would have to be limited in scope to the need that justified it.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/12-50598/12-50598-2014-12-11.html

Field rule:

"There might be evidence on the phone" and "someone could theoretically delete it" are not interchangeable with a demonstrated exigency.

A real imminent destruction threat can change the analysis. The claimed exigency and the action taken must match.

docs.title: 6. Retention can become unreasonable even if initial seizure was valid
docs.text: The Fourth Amendment continues to apply after the moment police first take the property.

docs.title: United States v. Song Ja Cha, 597 F.3d 995 (9th Cir. 2010)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

Song Ja Cha states the important general rule that a seizure reasonable at inception can become unreasonable because of its duration or other circumstances. The case involved a residence rather than a phone, but its duration/diligence principle is binding in the circuit.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/09-10147/09-10147-2011-02-25.html

docs.title: United States v. Dass, 849 F.2d 414 (9th Cir. 1988)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

Dass held lengthy detention of mailed packages unreasonable where officers had probable cause but waited days before diligently obtaining warrants. Probable cause did not permit police to retain property indefinitely while obtaining warrants at their leisure.

Source: https://openjurist.org/849/f2d/414

docs.title: United States v. Sullivan, 797 F.3d 623 (9th Cir. 2015)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

Sullivan is an important counterweight against creating a bright-line deadline. The Ninth Circuit held a 21-day laptop retention reasonable under the specific totality of circumstances, emphasizing the defendant's incarceration, parole status/search conditions, failure to seek return, later consent, and the government's evidentiary interests.

Official opinion: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2015/07/29/12-10196.pdf

Sullivan distinguishes Dass rather than overruling its diligence rule.

docs.title: Duration factors
docs.text:
For a retained phone/camera, preserve:

  • strength of the initial seizure basis;
  • whether the owner is free or incarcerated;
  • real-world need for the device;
  • whether the owner expressly requested its return;
  • whether police promptly began a warrant application;
  • investigative complexity;
  • whether an appropriate magistrate was reasonably available;
  • whether police actually needed the device after initial investigation;
  • whether a less intrusive preservation method was available; and
  • the total duration before warrant/search/return.

There is no safe project slogan such as "24 hours is lawful" or "three days is automatically unconstitutional."

docs.title: 7. Very recent Ninth Circuit phone cases are useful comparators but nonprecedential
Carlson v. Chavez, No. 25-3038 (9th Cir. Sept. 9, 2026)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit memorandum; NOT FOR PUBLICATION / nonprecedential under Rule 36-3.

The majority rejected speculative evidence-destruction exigency and separately concluded that continued retention of a phone became unreasonable after the investigating detective indicated it was not needed. The memorandum relies on established warrant/exigency and duration principles but is not itself precedential authority.

Official memorandum: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/memoranda/2026/09/09/25-3038.pdf

Project use: current factual comparator for a citizen's phone taken as supposed evidence; do not cite it as binding doctrine.

docs.title: Langham v. Noyd, No. 24-7292 (9th Cir. Dec. 23, 2025)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit memorandum; NOT FOR PUBLICATION / nonprecedential.

The majority treated a 36-day phone retention before pursuit of a search warrant as unreasonably prolonged on the facts. The dissent disputed the clearly-established-law analysis. The memorandum is a useful duration/diligence comparator, not a precedential deadline.

Official memorandum: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/memoranda/2025/12/23/24-7292.pdf

docs.title: United States v. Sessions, No. 21-50125 (9th Cir. Jan. 18, 2024)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit memorandum; NOT FOR PUBLICATION / nonprecedential.

Sessions illustrates the opposite factual direction: retention of a lawfully seized phone was upheld where the owner was incarcerated, did not seek return, and a later independent investigation obtained a warrant. It reinforces Sullivan's totality approach.

Official memorandum: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/memoranda/2024/01/18/21-50125.pdf

docs.title: 8. Terry frisk does not become a search for evidence merely because a phone is present
Minnesota v. Dickerson, 508 U.S. 366 (1993)
docs.text:
Status: U.S. Supreme Court.

A Terry frisk is a protective weapons search. Dickerson permits seizure of nonthreatening contraband detected through lawful touch only when its incriminating character is immediately apparent and the officer does not exceed the protective frisk by additional manipulation.

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/508/366

California's published People v. Garcia, B187453 (Cal. Ct. App. Dec. 14, 2006), reviewed in Sweep 014, similarly rejects converting a Terry patdown into a generalized search for identification.

For recording devices:

Feeling a rectangular phone during a lawful patdown ordinarily establishes that an object feels like a common lawful device. It does not by itself make the phone contraband, establish probable cause that it contains evidence, or authorize digital browsing.

Different facts can matter—for example, an independently supported evidentiary nexus, a warrant, a lawful arrest, or a genuine safety concern involving a different object.

docs.title: 9. Containers and devices: physical access does not equal digital-content access
docs.text:
Traditional container doctrine can authorize physical inspection of some physical containers under recognized exceptions. Modern digital devices are different for stored data.

Camou, applying Riley, rejected treating a cell phone as an ordinary container for purposes of the vehicle exception to justify a warrantless digital-content search.

Project rule:

A phone can be physically located inside a pocket, bag, case, or vehicle without its digital contents becoming just another physical container compartment.

Analyze the authority to:

  1. open the physical bag/case;
  2. seize the physical device; and
  3. search the device's digital contents

separately.

docs.title: 10. Consent is limited to what was actually authorized
Florida v. Jimeno, 500 U.S. 248 (1991)
docs.text:
Status: U.S. Supreme Court.

The scope of consent is measured by objective reasonableness—what the typical reasonable person would have understood from the exchange. A person can delimit the scope of consent.

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/500/248

For the project scenario, offering to show one identified recording should not be silently converted into consent to browse unrelated photographs, messages, accounts, contacts, location history, cloud files, or applications.

Useful evidence-preserving language:

I am offering only this identified recording. I do not consent to any broader search of my device.

A clear limitation is useful evidence of scope, not a magic incantation. The actual exchange and conduct still matter.

If an officer orders physical surrender despite the refusal of consent:

I do not consent to seizure or search. If you are ordering me to hand it over, I am complying under protest and not consenting.

Physical compliance with an asserted police command is not necessarily voluntary consent. The validity of the order must be analyzed independently.

docs.title: 11. Search incident to arrest: physical custody versus stored data
docs.text:
A lawful custodial arrest can support seizure of physical property associated with the arrestee under ordinary arrest/property doctrines.

But Riley rejects the proposition:

arrest → automatic authority to inspect everything stored on the phone.

For ordinary digital contents, identify:

  • a search warrant;
  • valid consent;
  • genuine case-specific exigency;
  • parole/probation or another recognized special search condition; or
  • another actual exception.

Do not assume a special-condition case applies to an ordinary member of the public.

docs.title: 12. Compelled biometric unlocking: Payne now supplies a binding Ninth Circuit rule, but narrowly
United States v. Payne, 99 F.4th 495 (9th Cir. 2024)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published/binding.

Payne involved a California parolee subject to broad parole search conditions. The Fourth Amendment digital search was sustained on that special parole basis. That portion of the case must not be generalized to an ordinary person without such a search condition.

The Fifth Amendment holding is separately important. Officers physically selected and used Payne's thumb to unlock the phone. The Ninth Circuit held that compelled use non-testimonial on those facts because it required no cognitive exertion and did not force Payne to reveal the contents of his mind.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/22-50262/22-50262-2024-04-17.html

The court expressly cautioned that the opinion should not be read to all biometric-unlock situations. The testimonial result might differ if police required the person to independently select which finger would unlock the device.

Field rule:

Do not say "biometrics are always unprotected by the Fifth Amendment." Payne is narrower.

And do not use Payne's parole-search holding to bypass Riley for an ordinary person.

docs.title: 13. California published biometric case: People v. Ramirez
People v. Ramirez, H049957 (Cal. Ct. App. 2023)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Ramirez held, on its warrant-based facts, that compelling a fingerprint to unlock a phone was non-testimonial. The warrants and incorporated probable-cause materials were central to the Fourth Amendment analysis; the court also found good faith as an alternative suppression ground.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2023/h049957.html

Ramirez is consistent with Payne's narrow physical-characteristic reasoning. It is not authority for warrantless digital searching of an ordinary person's phone.

docs.title: 14. Alphanumeric passcodes remain a distinct Fifth Amendment problem
docs.text: Payne repeatedly contrasts a biometric physical characteristic with forcing a person to reveal information held in the mind, such as a phone passcode. But the case did not itself decide every compelled-passcode/foregone-conclusion scenario.

docs.title: In re Grand Jury Subpoena Dated April 18, 2003, 383 F.3d 905 (9th Cir. 2004)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

In the document-production context, the Ninth Circuit held that compelled production can be testimonial and explained that the foregone-conclusion doctrine depends on the government's prior knowledge of existence, possession, and authenticity rather than using the compelled act to discover those facts.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/383/905/495139/

That doctrine informs passcode litigation but is not a published Ninth Circuit holding that resolves every compelled phone-passcode scenario.

Project status: ordinary device seizure/search analysis is supported, but the precise compelled alphanumeric passcode / foregone-conclusion application remains a specialized RESEARCHED-UNRESOLVED edge. Do not turn that edge into either:

Police can always force the passcode if they have a warrant.

or:

A passcode can never be compelled.

The exact order, warrant, requested act, government's prior knowledge, and testimonial implications matter.

docs.title: 15. Federal Privacy Protection Act can independently restrict seizure of newsgathering materials
42 U.S.C. § 2000aa
docs.text:
The federal Privacy Protection Act generally restricts government officers/employees, in connection with criminal investigation or prosecution, from searching for or seizing defined work product or documentary materials possessed by persons connected to public dissemination, subject to enumerated statutory exceptions.

Current text: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000aa

Definitions: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000aa-7

Remedies: https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000aa-6

The definitions expressly include photographs, motion-picture films, video/audio recordings, and other electronically recorded media.

Important limits/exceptions include, depending on the subsection:

  • probable cause that the possessor committed or is committing the offense to which the materials relate;
  • specified limitations on that suspect exception;
  • immediate need to prevent death or serious bodily injury;
  • subpoena/compliance and destruction/concealment conditions for documentary materials; and
  • exclusions in the definitions for contraband, fruits of crime, and instrumentalities.

docs.title: Credential-neutral project point
docs.text:
The PPA's text asks about the defined materials and a purpose to disseminate public communication. It does not make possession of a government-issued "press credential" the statutory trigger.

That does not mean every phone carried by every person automatically receives PPA protection. The dissemination purpose, material category, criminal-investigation context, and exceptions must actually fit.

Persuasive outside-circuit cases can be used only as comparators: - Garcia v. Montgomery County, Maryland (D. Md. 2015) — video-card seizure from person filming police; factual PPA questions survived; - Sennett v. United States, 667 F.3d 531 (4th Cir. 2012) — independent photographer/newsgatherer and suspect-exception analysis.

The statute itself is the primary authority.

docs.title: 16. California has a separate newsperson warrant-protection layer
Penal Code § 1524(g)
docs.text:
Current California law states that no search warrant shall issue for items described in Evidence Code § 1070.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=1524.

Section 1524(f) broadly defines documentary evidence to include photographs, audio/video recordings, films, computer printouts, and similar material.

docs.title: Evidence Code § 1070 / California Constitution art. I, § 2(b)
docs.text:
Evidence Code § 1070 protects qualifying newspersons against contempt for refusing to disclose sources or unpublished information. "Unpublished information" includes notes, outtakes, photographs, tapes, and other undisclosed data.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1070.

California Constitution: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.+2.&article=I

docs.title: Miller v. Superior Court, 21 Cal.4th 883 (1999)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court describes the state shield law as affording very strong contempt immunity for protected unpublished information, subject to constitutional conflicts such as a criminal defendant's fair-trial rights. Unpublished information need not be confidential.

Source: https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/miller-v-superior-court-people-32069/

docs.title: Scope caution
docs.text:
The California shield-law text uses defined newsperson/media-connection categories. This project does not assume that every ordinary citizen with a phone automatically satisfies § 1070 merely because they plan to post a recording.

That is materially different from the PPA's statutory dissemination-purpose language.

Field Guide sequence:

federal PPA applicability → California §1524(g)/§1070 applicability → ordinary Fourth Amendment warrant/seizure rules

Do not merge the three into one generic "journalist privilege."

docs.title: 17. First Amendment sensitivity does not erase ordinary evidence law
docs.text:
Recording police/public officials can be protected expressive/newsgathering activity. Seizing expressive material for the purpose of suppressing publication can raise additional First Amendment concerns.

But the project should not claim:

Because the recording is First Amendment material, police can never lawfully seize it as evidence.

A properly supported evidentiary seizure can still be lawful, subject to the Fourth Amendment and any additional PPA/shield-law restrictions that actually apply.

Conversely:

"It's evidence" is not a blank check to suppress, browse, retain, or destroy expressive material.

Purpose, authority, duration, dissemination protections, and search scope remain separate.

docs.title: Step 1 — Identify the encounter stage
docs.text:
Is this:

  • consensual contact;
  • Terry detention;
  • lawful arrest;
  • warrant execution;
  • parole/probation/special-condition search; or
  • another specialized setting?

Do not import a parole rule into an ordinary street/public-facility encounter.

docs.title: Step 2 — Identify the government act
docs.text:
Is the officer:

  • asking to see a recording;
  • asking you to hand over the device;
  • briefly holding it;
  • seizing it into evidence;
  • retaining it while seeking a warrant;
  • browsing digital content;
  • imaging/extracting data;
  • demanding a passcode; or
  • compelling biometric unlocking?

Name the act before naming the authority.

docs.title: Step 3 — Test initial physical seizure authority
docs.text:
Ask whether there is:

  • a warrant;
  • lawful arrest/property authority;
  • probable cause plus a recognized warrant exception;
  • genuine preservation exigency;
  • a narrowly justified Place-type temporary detention;
  • valid consent;
  • a special search condition; or
  • another specific rule.

The statement "your video is evidence" is a conclusion, not the authority.

docs.title: Step 4 — Test duration and diligence
docs.text:
If police keep the device:

  • when was it taken?
  • when did they begin seeking a warrant?
  • when was the warrant submitted/issued?
  • did the owner request return?
  • is the owner free and dependent on the device?
  • is continued retention still necessary?
  • what changed after the initial investigation?

Use Song Ja Cha / Dass / Sullivan rather than a fixed hour/day rule.

docs.title: Step 5 — Test digital search authority separately
docs.text:
Riley ordinarily requires a warrant for stored contents even after lawful arrest.

Check:

  • warrant;
  • consent and exact scope;
  • genuine case-specific exigency;
  • valid parole/probation/special search condition;
  • another recognized exception.

docs.title: Step 6 — Test frisk / physical container doctrines separately
docs.text:
A Terry frisk is for weapons. Plain feel requires immediately apparent incriminating character without exploratory manipulation.

A lawful physical search of a bag/case does not itself authorize browsing the phone discovered inside it.

docs.title: Step 7 — Check dissemination/news-material statutes
docs.text:
If the device contains material prepared/held for public dissemination:

  • check the Privacy Protection Act;
  • check §1524(g)/Evidence Code §1070 only if the California newsperson definitions actually fit;
  • preserve exceptions.

docs.title: Step 8 — Analyze compelled access method
docs.text:
• physical thumb/fingerprint selected by police: Payne supplies a narrow non-testimonial rule;
  • biometric requiring user choice/cognitive act: Payne expressly leaves room for a different result;
  • alphanumeric passcode: separate testimonial/foregone-conclusion analysis; do not state a categorical rule.

docs.title: 19. Practical field language
docs.text:
These phrases preserve distinctions; they are not magic words.

If asked to show one recording:

I am offering only this identified recording. I do not consent to any broader search of my device.

If ordered to surrender the device:

I do not consent to seizure or search. If you are ordering me to hand it over, I am complying under protest and not consenting.

If police say they are keeping it:

Are you seizing this device as evidence? What legal basis are you relying on, and are you seeking a warrant?

If the encounter continues:

I am requesting return of my device if you are not obtaining a warrant or no longer need to retain it.

Do not physically resist an attempted seizure.

Preserve:

  • exact time of seizure;
  • officer identities;
  • asserted offense/evidence nexus;
  • whether a warrant was mentioned;
  • whether return was requested;
  • property/evidence receipt;
  • case/report number;
  • later warrant and inventory;
  • date/time of return; and
  • whether data was searched/copied/altered/deleted.

docs.title: 20. Common bad field rules
docs.text: Bad slogan Better rule "Riley means cops can't take my phone." Riley generally protects digital contents; physical seizure is separately analyzed. "They can take it because it has evidence." Identify probable cause and the warrant/exception authorizing physical seizure, then separately analyze retention and digital search. "Once seized, they can hold it until the case ends." Continued retention must remain reasonable; duration and diligence matter. "If they arrest me, they can search the phone." Riley generally rejects digital search incident to arrest. "A frisk lets them take anything they feel." Terry is weapons-protective; plain-feel seizure requires immediately apparent incriminating character without extra manipulation. "I showed them one video, so they can inspect the phone." Consent scope is what was reasonably authorized; expressly limiting the offered recording helps preserve the boundary. "Remote wiping always creates exigency." Riley/Camou require a genuine case-specific imminent need, not a categorical possibility. "Biometrics are always Fifth-Amendment-free." Payne is narrow and expressly warns against extending its result to every biometric scenario. "Passcodes can never be compelled." The Ninth Circuit act-of-production/foregone-conclusion framework is fact sensitive; no categorical project rule is stated. "My video is journalism, so it can never be seized." Check PPA/shield-law applicability and exceptions plus ordinary Fourth Amendment authority.

The specialized alphanumeric-passcode/foregone-conclusion application remains a Researched-Unresolved edge, but it does not prevent the ordinary CA-F5.9 decision tree from operating. The guide expressly identifies the boundary rather than inventing a rule.

docs.title: 22. Boundaries preserved for later work
docs.text:
Sweep 015 does not attempt to complete:

  • every digital-warrant particularity issue;
  • cloud-provider/ECPA/CalECPA procedure;
  • every forensic extraction technique;
  • every probation/parole search condition;
  • every Fifth Amendment passcode/foregone-conclusion permutation;

  • evidence-return procedure after criminal cases;
  • law-enforcement records disclosure regarding seized-device evidence, which remains GAP-08.

The operational device branch is complete enough for qualification; those specialized changed-fact branches remain separately labeled.
