docs.title: Sweep 016 — Disorder, Unreasonable Noise, Fighting Words, Threats, and Obstruction
docs.text:
Qualification targets:

  • CA-F6.1 — disturbance / noise;
  • CA-F6.2 — obstruction / interference;
  • CA-F6.3 — fighting words / threats / analogous speech offenses.

This sweep addresses a recurring public-facility pattern:

peaceful recording or questioning → employee/patron objects → activity is relabeled "disruptive," "harassing," "hostile," "aggressive," or "interfering" → police are asked to remove/arrest → Penal Code § 415, § 148, § 602.1, or a threat theory is invoked

The central project rule is:

Translate the characterization into observable conduct and the elements of an identified law.

"Disruptive," "harassing," "aggressive," "hostile," and "causing a disturbance" are not self-executing California crimes.

Operational sequence:

actual conduct → exact offense/subsection → speech/conduct distinction → constitutional narrowing rule → actual interference/danger/effect → changed facts

This sweep does not treat the standing peaceful scenario as a defense to conduct that actually changes. If a person later threatens violence, blocks operations, uses sound as a guise to disrupt, physically interferes, or substantially delays a lawful police duty, rerun the branch on those facts.

docs.title: 1. Penal Code § 415 has three separate offenses
docs.text:
Current primary source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=415

Section 415 separately covers:

  1. unlawful fighting in public or challenging another person in public to fight;
  2. maliciously and willfully disturbing another person by loud and unreasonable noise; and
  3. using offensive words in public that are inherently likely to provoke an immediate violent reaction.

A report that someone is "disturbing the peace" is therefore incomplete. Identify the subsection and the conduct.

The 2026 Judicial Council instructions remain consistent with the controlling narrowing cases:

  • CALCRIM 2688 — fighting/challenge to fight;
  • CALCRIM 2689 — loud and unreasonable noise;
  • CALCRIM 2690 — offensive words.

Current Judicial Council instruction index: https://www.justia.com/criminal/docs/calcrim/2600/

docs.title: In re Brown, 9 Cal.3d 612 (1973)
docs.text:
Status: California Supreme Court; controlling state authority.

In re Brown rejected a construction of § 415 that would criminalize all loud public speech merely because someone is disturbed by it.

The court distinguished communicative shouting from volume used as disruptive conduct. For loud shouting/cheering used as communication, § 415's noise branch is constitutionally narrowed to two circumstances:

  1. a clear and present danger of imminent violence; or
  2. purported communication used as a guise to disrupt lawful endeavors rather than a genuine effort to communicate.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/9/612.html

The current CALCRIM 2689 instruction states the same two alternatives.

Source: https://www.justia.com/criminal/docs/calcrim/2600/2689/

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
A raised voice, chanting, criticism, or loud advocacy is not automatically § 415(2). Ask whether the sound created the constitutionally narrowed danger/disruption condition.

This is not a universal right to yell anywhere. Brown expressly recognizes that precisely drafted, content-neutral time/place/manner rules can regulate volume in appropriate places. A hospital quiet-zone rule, meeting rule, school rule, ordinary workplace operational limit, or valid facility restriction must be analyzed under its own source and constitutional test.

The point is narrower: the generic statewide § 415(2) offense cannot be used as a catch-all "you were loud and somebody complained" statute.

docs.title: 3. A changed-fact noise comparator: People v. Superior Court (Commons)
People v. Superior Court (Commons), 135 Cal.App.3d 812 (1982)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Commons applied In re Brown in a materially different setting. The person was laughing and shouting very loudly in a hotel hallway around 1 a.m.; residents came out into the hall, and the court concluded the facts supported probable cause under the "guise to disrupt" branch.

Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-court-of-appeal/1839130.html

Project use:

Brown protects loud communication from being criminalized merely because it annoys or disturbs. Commons shows that context, communicative purpose, place, hour, and actual disruptive use of volume can change the result.

Do not turn either case into a categorical volume rule.

docs.title: Jefferson v. Superior Court, 51 Cal.App.3d 721 (1975)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Jefferson rejected probable cause under § 415(3) where an officer heard a person use a vulgar epithet but did not know to whom the words were directed.

The court emphasized:

  • profanity or a vulgar epithet alone is insufficient;
  • context matters;
  • the words must be uttered in a provocative manner; and
  • there must be a clear and present danger that violence will immediately erupt.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/51/721.html

docs.title: In re John V., 167 Cal.App.3d 761 (1985)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

John V. confirms that § 415(3) is the fighting-words branch and that the inquiry is fact/context specific. The history of antagonism, proximity, manner of delivery, and actual circumstances can matter.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/167/761.html

docs.title: CALCRIM 2690
docs.text:
The current Judicial Council instruction requires:

  • offensive words inherently likely to provoke an immediate violent reaction; and
  • a clear and present danger that the other person will immediately erupt into violence.

It directs the factfinder to consider all circumstances and the person to whom the statement was addressed.

Source: https://www.justia.com/criminal/docs/calcrim/2600/2690/

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text: "He swore at me" and "he insulted me" do not establish § 415(3). Identify the words, addressee, manner, distance, surrounding conduct, and immediate violence risk.

docs.title: 5. Speech directed at police receives special contextual protection
City of Houston v. Hill, 482 U.S. 451 (1987)
docs.text:
Status: U.S. Supreme Court.

Hill invalidated an ordinance that broadly criminalized verbal interruption/challenge to police. The Court held that the First Amendment protects a significant amount of verbal criticism and challenge directed at officers.

Source: https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/482/451/

docs.title: Duran v. City of Douglas, 904 F.2d 1372 (9th Cir. 1990)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published/binding in California.

A person directed obscene gestures and expletives at an officer. The Ninth Circuit held the speech did not supply lawful grounds for the detention/arrest theory asserted there. Criticism of police, including crass criticism, is protected unless independent unlawful conduct supplies authority.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/904/1372/388209/

docs.title: United States v. Poocha, 259 F.3d 1077 (9th Cir. 2001)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published/binding.

Poocha applied the same rule to profanity directed at a National Park Service officer. Yelling an obscenity, even accompanied by aggressive posture such as clenched fists and puffed chest on those facts, did not turn the expression into fighting words.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/259/1077/575656/

docs.title: In re Alejandro G., 37 Cal.App.4th 44 (1995)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

California does not adopt a categorical rule that words addressed to a police officer can never be fighting words. Instead, officer status is part of the totality.

A trained officer is expected to exercise greater restraint than an average citizen. But in Alejandro G., the speaker went beyond vulgar criticism and expressly challenged the officer to fight, accompanied by threats of actual violence. The court held those facts could satisfy § 415(3).

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/37/44.html

docs.title: Project synthesis
docs.text:
Police criticism/profanity is ordinarily protected; officer status makes immediate violent reaction less readily inferred, not legally impossible. An actual challenge to fight or genuine threat of violence can change the branch.

Do not use "fighting words" as a synonym for words an officer strongly dislikes.

docs.title: 6. Audience anger does not automatically authorize suppression
Center for Bio-Ethical Reform, Inc. v. Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, 533 F.3d 780 (9th Cir. 2008)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published/binding.

The Ninth Circuit held in the school-perimeter protest context that a speech restriction based on the audience's reaction to the content is content based. Listener hostility does not become a content-neutral justification merely because officials characterize the reaction as disruption.

Source: https://openjurist.org/533/f3d/780/center-for-bio-ethical-reform-inc-v-los-angeles-county-sheriff-department

The underlying case also involved school-specific safety/access law. Do not generalize its exact result to every government interior.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
A patron saying "I don't want to be recorded," becoming angry, complaining to staff, or demanding removal is evidence of the encounter. It does not itself transform otherwise protected speech into disorderly conduct.

Government may address actual threats, obstruction, unlawful noise, or other independent misconduct. The project should identify that misconduct rather than making listener hostility the missing element.

docs.title: 7. Penal Code § 148: verbal challenge is not the same as obstruction
docs.text:
Current § 148(a)(1) punishes willful resistance, delay, or obstruction of a public/peace officer or EMT in the discharge or attempted discharge of a duty when no other punishment is prescribed.

Current primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148

A § 148 conviction also requires the officer to be acting lawfully in the relevant duty.

docs.title: People v. Quiroga, 16 Cal.App.4th 961 (1993)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Quiroga holds that § 148 does not criminalize mere failure to respond to police orders "with alacrity." The person had a First Amendment right to dispute the officer's actions verbally.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/16/961.html

docs.title: Mackinney v. Nielsen, 69 F.3d 1002 (9th Cir. 1995)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published/binding.

Mackinney applied California § 148 and federal First Amendment doctrine. A few seconds of delayed compliance and subsequent verbal protest did not create probable cause for § 148. The Ninth Circuit treated verbal challenge to police as clearly protected.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/69/1002/609814/

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Questioning an officer, disputing legal authority, criticizing police conduct, or failing to comply instantaneously is not by itself § 148.

This is not a license to physically resist, flee a lawful detention, or substantially impede an officer's lawful task.

docs.title: 8. Conduct can cross the § 148 line without an assault
In re Muhammed C., 95 Cal.App.4th 1325 (2002)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

The minor repeatedly remained next to a patrol car and continued interacting with an arrestee despite five orders to step away. Officers had to interrupt their processing activity to address him. The court upheld the finding that the conduct caused actual delay.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/95/1325.html

docs.title: In re N.S., G065591 (Cal. Ct. App. Sept. 8, 2026)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal; current authority.

N.S. is school-specific as to the lawfulness of the underlying search, but its § 148 comparison is useful and current. The juvenile:

  • physically left the location where the lawful search was to occur;
  • required the officer to pursue him;
  • repeatedly refused five commands; and
  • delayed the weapon investigation about ten minutes.

The Court of Appeal distinguished Quiroga: this was more than slow compliance or verbal criticism because the conduct substantially interfered with and delayed a lawful investigation.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2026/g065591.html

docs.title: Project rule
docs.text:
The ordinary line is not:

speech = protected; physical contact = obstruction.

The better rule is:

protected verbal challenge does not become § 148 merely because it is annoying or inconvenient, but conduct—including conduct accompanied by words—can violate § 148 when it actually resists, delays, or obstructs an officer's lawful performance.

Always preserve the lawfulness-of-officer-duty element.

docs.title: 9. Public-agency interference: § 602.1(b) requires actual statutory predicates
docs.text:
Current primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.1

For a public agency open to the public, § 602.1(b) requires:

  1. intentional interference with lawful public-agency business;
  2. by obstructing or intimidating employees carrying on business or people there to transact business;
  3. a qualifying request to leave from the manager/supervisor or a peace officer acting at that person's request; and
  4. refusal.

Section 602.1(d)(2) says the section does not apply to constitutionally protected activity.

docs.title: Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

Dubner concerned the related business-establishment form of § 602.1 then in force. It held that refusal to leave did not itself establish the missing intentional interference. Photographing/observing from away from the entrance did not supply obstruction/intimidation.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/266/959/582256/

docs.title: People v. Turner, A147603 (Cal. Ct. App. 2017)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal; § 602.1(a) private-business application.

Turner expressly relied on Dubner and again treated refusal alone as insufficient. On Turner's different facts, however, multiple requests over hours, repeated interruption of employees' duties, police calls/paperwork, and related conduct were sufficient for probable cause of interference.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2017/a147603.html

docs.title: Mackey v. Meyer, 675 F. App'x 705 (9th Cir. 2017)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit memorandum; unpublished/nonprecedential.

Mackey is the direct California DMV comparator. Dispatch characterized a preacher as "harassing" customers, but video/audio did not show obstruction or intimidation. The panel held the officer lacked probable cause under § 602.1(b).

Source: https://openjurist.org/675/fappx/705/mark-mackey-v-darren-meyer-4337855

Project use: direct factual cross-check only; do not elevate it over published authority.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
"Harassing customers" is not itself a § 602.1(b) element. Ask what the person did that allegedly obstructed or intimidated agency employees or members of the public transacting business. Refusal to leave does not manufacture that missing predicate.

Sweep 012 remains the primary derivative-trespass chapter. Sweep 016 adds this obstruction/interference layer.

docs.title: 10. "Harassment" is not one generic California public-facility crime
docs.text:
A person can commit specifically defined offenses that use concepts such as harassment, stalking, threats, repeated following, intimidation, or interference.

But a facility employee's statement:

"He's harassing people"

does not identify which law has been violated.

For example, Penal Code § 646.9 stalking has defined course-of-conduct / following / credible-threat elements and statutory exclusions for constitutionally protected activity. A one-time complaint that a lawful recorder made someone uncomfortable does not silently become those elements.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=646.9

Field rule:

Ask for the conduct and the statute/rule. Do not analyze the adjective as though it were an offense.

docs.title: 11. Fighting words and true threats are different doctrines
docs.text:
Section 415(3) focuses on words inherently likely, in context, to provoke an immediate violent reaction by the listener.

A true threat doctrine asks a different constitutional question: whether the communication expresses threatened unlawful violence and whether the constitutionally required speaker mental state exists.

Do not merge them.

docs.title: Counterman v. Colorado, 600 U.S. 66 (2023)
docs.text:
Status: U.S. Supreme Court.

Counterman holds that true-threat prosecutions require a subjective mental-state floor. The First Amendment requires proof at least that the speaker consciously disregarded a substantial risk that the communication would be viewed as threatening violence—recklessness.

Source: https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/600/22-138/

This does not mean every rude, angry, hyperbolic, or offensive remark is a true threat.

docs.title: 12. California Penal Code § 422 has its own demanding elements
docs.text:
Current primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=422

Section 422 criminal-threat analysis is separate from § 415. California requires, among other things:

  1. a willful threat to commit a crime resulting in death or great bodily injury;
  2. specific intent that the statement be taken as a threat, even without intent actually to carry it out;
  3. a statement that, on its face and under the circumstances, is sufficiently unequivocal, unconditional, immediate, and specific to convey gravity of purpose and an immediate prospect of execution;
  4. actual sustained fear; and
  5. reasonableness of that fear.

docs.title: In re George T., 33 Cal.4th 620 (2004)
docs.text:
Status: California Supreme Court.

The California Supreme Court independently reviewed a student's "dark poetry" and concluded the ambiguous poem and surrounding circumstances did not establish a § 422 criminal threat.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2004/s111780.html

Because § 422 requires specific intent that the statement be taken as a threat, its statutory mens rea is more demanding than Counterman's constitutional minimum of recklessness regarding threatening character.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
"He threatened me" is an allegation. Record the exact words, surrounding conduct, addressee, immediacy, specificity, speaker mental-state evidence, actual fear, duration of fear, and whether the claimed offense is § 422, § 415, stalking, or something else.

The standing scenario assumes no threats. If genuine threats appear, that is a changed fact and the branch must be rerun.

docs.title: 13. Public-official criticism and threat analysis
docs.text:
The project should not erase the distinction between:

  • "You're violating the Constitution";
  • profanity or insults;
  • "I'm going to sue you";
  • "I'm filing a complaint";
  • "I'm requesting your records";
  • "I'm publishing this";
  • aggressive but nonthreatening criticism;
  • a challenge to fight; and
  • a serious expression of threatened unlawful violence.

The first group can be protected petition/criticism activity even when unwelcome.

An actual challenge to fight can implicate § 415(1) or, depending on the words/context, § 415(3). A true threat can implicate § 422 or another specialized law.

Never transform legal/political consequences—lawsuit, complaint, records request, publication—into a threat of unlawful violence merely because the official experiences them as hostile.

docs.title: 14. Disorder / obstruction decision tree
docs.text: When an employee, caller, guard, or officer says "disruptive," "harassing," "disturbing," "hostile," or "interfering":

docs.title: Step 1 — Preserve chronology
docs.text:
Record what happened before the label or leave demand.

Do not infer disruption from the later argument over whether the person must leave.

docs.title: Step 2 — Name the actual offense/rule
docs.text:
Possible branches include:

  • § 415(1) fighting/challenge to fight;
  • § 415(2) loud/unreasonable noise;
  • § 415(3) fighting words;
  • § 148(a)(1) officer obstruction;
  • § 602.1(b) public-agency interference;
  • § 422 criminal threats;
  • § 646.9 stalking;
  • meeting-specific § 403 / Brown Act rules;
  • a valid local/facility operational rule;
  • another identified statute.

If nobody can identify the rule, preserve that fact. Do not invent one.

docs.title: Step 3 — Convert the adjective to conduct
docs.text:
Examples:

  • "loud" → decibel/voice level, duration, place, activity interrupted;
  • "harassing" → exact words, following, proximity, repeated conduct, targeted person;
  • "obstructing" → what doorway, line, task, officer duty, or transaction was actually impeded;
  • "intimidating" → conduct creating fear/coercion and who experienced it;
  • "threatening" → exact words/conduct and threatened unlawful harm;
  • "aggressive" → volume, posture, distance, movement, contact, actual threats.

docs.title: Step 4 — Apply the constitutional narrowing rule
docs.text:
• communicative noise → In re Brown;
  • offensive words → Jefferson / Alejandro G.;
  • criticism of police → Hill / Duran / Poocha / Mackinney;
  • listener hostility → Center for Bio-Ethical Reform;
  • true threats → Counterman plus the actual California statute.

docs.title: Step 5 — Check actual effect
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Did lawful business stop?
  • Did a public transaction become impossible?
  • Was anyone blocked?
  • Did an officer have to abandon/delay a lawful duty?
  • Was the delay substantial rather than momentary?
  • Was there an immediate violence risk?
  • Was the volume communication or a guise to disrupt?
  • Was fear of threatened unlawful violence actually sustained where the statute requires it?

docs.title: Step 6 — Rerun changed facts
docs.text:
If conduct escalates after protected activity begins, do not freeze the legal analysis at the original lawful moment.

A person can begin with protected recording/criticism and later commit an independent offense. Conversely, an official cannot retroactively manufacture an earlier offense merely because a later argument occurs.

docs.title: 15. Field rules for common video claims
"You're causing a disturbance."
docs.text: Which § 415 subsection or other law are you relying on, and what specific conduct satisfies it?

docs.title: "You're being too loud."
docs.text: Volume alone is not the complete § 415(2) test for communicative speech. Preserve whether there was imminent violence or whether the voice was being used as a guise to disrupt lawful activity. Separate valid facility volume rules from the generic criminal statute.

docs.title: "You're harassing customers."
docs.text: Identify the conduct. For § 602.1(b), the question is intentional interference by obstruction or intimidation plus the qualifying refusal—not the label "harassment."

docs.title: "You can't talk to the officer like that."
docs.text: Criticism, profanity, and verbal challenge to police receive substantial First Amendment protection. Actual threats, fighting words in context, or conduct that substantially obstructs a lawful duty are different.

docs.title: "You're interfering with my investigation."
docs.text: What lawful duty was actually delayed or obstructed, and by what conduct? Mere verbal disagreement or momentary slow compliance does not automatically satisfy § 148.

docs.title: 16. Qualification dispositions
docs.text:
Row Pre-sweep Sweep 016 result Reason CA-F6.1 Gap Supported In re Brown, current CALCRIM 2689, and Commons now supply the California communicative-noise narrowing rule and a changed-fact disruptive-noise comparator. CA-F6.2 Gap Supported Current §§148/602.1 plus Quiroga, Mackinney, Muhammed C., current published In re N.S., Dubner, published Turner, and the limited unpublished Mackey comparator now separate protected challenge/refusal labels from actual delay, obstruction, intimidation, and interference. CA-F6.3 Gap Supported Jefferson, John V., Alejandro G., Hill, Duran, Poocha, Counterman, §422, and George T. now supply the fighting-words/police-criticism/true-threat branches with context and limitations preserved.

If package review accepts these dispositions, provisional totals become:

  • 64 Supported
  • 4 Researched-Unresolved
  • 5 Gap
  • 0 Not Applicable

Open activation-blocking research packages become GAP-07 and GAP-08.

docs.title: 17. Boundaries preserved for GAP-07 and facility-specific work
docs.text:
Sweep 016 does not close:

  • § 403 meeting-disruption doctrine beyond the already reviewed meeting branch;
  • § 407–409 unlawful-assembly/dispersal warning doctrine;
  • emergency police-line/perimeter authority;
  • post-warning observer-versus-participant questions;
  • statutory news-representative emergency protections;
  • emergency/protest-scene recording/newsgathering doctrine.

Those remain GAP-07.

Local noise ordinances, facility conduct policies, court decorum rules, library conduct codes, school rules, and specialized restrictions remain local/facility dependencies. Sweep 013 authority/delegation and the restriction-audit framework apply before treating them as enforceable.

  • In re Alejandro G., 37 Cal.App.4th 44 (1995)
  • In re Muhammed C., 95 Cal.App.4th 1325 (2002)

  • People v. Turner, A147603 (Cal. Ct. App. 2017)

docs.title: Current Judicial Council instructions
docs.text:
• CALCRIM 2688
  • CALCRIM 2689
  • CALCRIM 2690

docs.title: Nonprecedential comparator
docs.text: • Mackey v. Meyer, 675 F. App'x 705 (9th Cir. 2017) — memorandum / not precedent under Ninth Circuit Rule 36-3

docs.title: Sweep 017 — Assembly, Dispersal, Emergency Perimeters, and Observer Recording
docs.text:
Qualification targets:

  • CA-F7.3 — assembly/dispersal warning, scope, and opportunity to comply;
  • CA-F8.1 — emergency/perimeter authority;
  • CA-F8.2 — observer versus participant/interference;
  • CA-F8.3 — emergency/protest recording and statutory-press versus constitutional newsgathering.

This sweep addresses the recurring sequence:

protest/emergency scene → police declare a closure or unlawful assembly → warning/order to move or disperse → observer/recorder remains or tries to comply → arrest/force/§148 theory → official later characterizes everyone present as participants

The operational sequence is:

exact event/area → actual statutory predicate → participant/observer status → lawful warning and audibility → route/opportunity to comply → remaining/reentry conduct → independent interference/unlawful conduct → recording/newsgathering overlay → force/arrest authority

The project does not assume that peaceful presence near unlawful conduct makes a person part of it, and does not assume that "press" statutes define the entire First Amendment right to observe government.

docs.title: 1. California unlawful-assembly law is constitutionally narrowed
docs.text:
Current statutes:

  • Penal Code § 407 — unlawful assembly;
  • Penal Code § 408 — participation in rout/unlawful assembly;
  • Penal Code § 409 — remaining after lawful warning to disperse;
  • Penal Code § 416 — assembly with purpose to disturb peace/commit unlawful act and refusal to disperse.

Official code source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?division=&chapter=1.&part=1.&lawCode=PEN&title=11.

docs.title: In re Brown, 9 Cal.3d 612 (1973)
docs.text:
Status: California Supreme Court; controlling.

Although § 407's text includes "violent, boisterous, or tumultuous," In re Brown constitutionally narrows §§407–408 when the group assembled to do a lawful act. The assembly must actually be violent or pose a clear and present danger of imminent violence.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/9/612.html

The 2026 Judicial Council instructions reflect that narrowing and omit "boisterous or tumultuous" as independently sufficient.

CALCRIM 2685: https://www.justia.com/criminal/docs/calcrim/2600/2685/

CALCRIM 2686: https://www.justia.com/criminal/docs/calcrim/2600/2686/

docs.title: Collins v. Jordan, 110 F.3d 1363 (9th Cir. 1997)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published/binding in California.

Collins arose from San Francisco's response to demonstrations following the Rodney King verdict. The Ninth Circuit held that limited violence on one day did not justify a blanket ban on all peaceful demonstrations the next day. Protected demonstrations may be stopped when they themselves become violent or pose a clear and present danger of imminent violence; prior similar violence does not automatically make all later demonstrations unlawful.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/110/1363/527029/

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
A contentious, angry, loud, unpopular, or "boisterous" gathering is not automatically an unlawful assembly. For a lawful-purpose gathering, identify actual violence or the clear and present danger of imminent violence.

A group assembled to commit an independently unlawful act remains a separate §407 branch.

docs.title: 2. §408 participation and §409 remaining are different offenses
CALCRIM 2685 / In re Wagner
docs.text:
Section 408 requires willful participation in an unlawful assembly and knowledge that the assembly is unlawful.

In In re Wagner, 119 Cal.App.3d 90 (1981), the Court of Appeal explained that a person participates by knowingly taking part; a person who was part of a lawful assembly that becomes unlawful must disassociate after learning of the unlawful conduct.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/119/90.html

Current CALCRIM 2685 similarly requires:

  1. willful participation; and
  2. knowledge that the assembly was unlawful.

docs.title: §409 is broader once its predicates exist
docs.text:
Section 409 can reach a person who remains at the place of a riot, rout, or unlawful assembly after lawful warning, even if that person did not participate in the underlying violence.

That does not make every nearby observer criminal. The predicate riot/rout/unlawful assembly and lawful warning still must exist, and constitutional narrowing matters.

docs.title: Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published/binding.

Dubner is unusually important for the citizen-observer scenario. Dubner was photographing a demonstration and was not carrying signs, chanting, distributing literature, or blocking the entrance. The Ninth Circuit held that the protest lacked sufficient violence/imminent-danger circumstances to justify treating nonparticipants as §409 violators. It stated that absent those compelling circumstances, police are at least required to differentiate participants from innocent bystanders.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/266/959/582256/

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Do not use "everyone was at the protest" as a substitute for the actual §408 or §409 branch.

For §408, ask whether the person knowingly participated.

For §409, ask whether a qualifying riot/rout/unlawful assembly existed, whether the person was at its place, whether a lawful warning was given/heard, and whether the person willfully remained.

docs.title: 3. A §409 warning is not just any command to leave
Penal Code § 726
docs.text:
Section 726 supplies the traditional dispersal-command authority. It directs qualifying officials, when persons are unlawfully or riotously assembled, to go among them or as near as possible and command them, in the name of the People of the State, immediately to disperse.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=726.

docs.title: CALCRIM 2686
docs.text:
The current official jury instruction states:

  • no particular words are required;
  • the words must be sufficient to tell a reasonable person that the speaker is acting officially and ordering people to leave; and
  • the order must be communicated in a reasonable way that ensures the order is heard.

Source: https://www.justia.com/criminal/docs/calcrim/2600/2686/

The instruction derives the warning rule from §726 and California cases including In re Bacon, People v. Cipriani, and In re Wagner.

docs.title: In re Wagner / People v. Cipriani
docs.text:
Amplified/public-address warnings can satisfy §726. The nineteenth-century wording does not require an unamplified officer literally to stand inside a dangerous crowd. The method and location are facts bearing on whether the order was effectively communicated.

Wagner: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/119/90.html

Cipriani: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/18/299.html

docs.title: No invented fixed countdown
docs.text:
The reviewed authorities do not establish a universal California rule such as "police must wait exactly five minutes."

The field question is instead:

Was a lawful order reasonably communicated so it could be heard, and did the person then willfully remain?

For force, route and practical ability to comply become independently important.

docs.title: 4. Opportunity and route to comply matter when force is used
Nelson v. City of Davis, 685 F.3d 867 (9th Cir. 2012)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published/binding.

Officers attempted to clear a large party and fired pepperball projectiles toward a group of unarmed, compliant people. The Ninth Circuit emphasized that the officers:

  • lacked amplification adequate to make the dispersal warning audible over the crowd;
  • did not tell the group how to leave;
  • blocked the group's primary egress;
  • used force against people who were attempting to comply and awaiting instructions; and
  • had minimal governmental interest in applying that force to those individuals.

The court held the force unconstitutional on the plaintiff-favorable summary-judgment facts.

Official Ninth Circuit source: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2012/07/11/10-16256.pdf

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
A dispersal order does not create a practical ability to comply when police block the exit, make the order inaudible, or use force against people attempting to leave.

Do not convert Nelson into a fixed waiting-period rule. Its role is to preserve audibility, egress, compliance behavior, warning before force, threat level, and individualized governmental interest.

docs.title: 5. Prior violence does not create a prospective all-demonstration ban
docs.text:
Collins is the principal binding rule:

The government may not ban all later demonstrations simply because earlier similar activity involved limited violence.

The constitutional inquiry follows the actual present conditions. If the current assembly itself becomes violent or creates imminent danger, changed facts can justify dispersal and enforcement.

Current Ninth Circuit Boudjerada v. Medary, No. 24-2419 (9th Cir. Feb. 14, 2025) is unpublished and therefore only a comparator. It distinguished a temporary seven-hour nighttime curfew responding to ongoing unrest from the broad prospective demonstration ban in Collins. Do not use Collins as a categorical anti-curfew rule.

docs.title: 6. §409.5 emergency closure requires the statute's actual predicates
docs.text:
Current Penal Code §409.5: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.5.

Two principal closure branches matter.

docs.title: Subdivision (a) — calamity menace
docs.text:
Specified officials may close the area where a calamity creates a menace to public health or safety, for the duration of the menace.

The statutory examples include flood, storm, fire, earthquake, explosion, accident, or other disaster.

docs.title: Subdivision (b) — command post
docs.text: Specified officers may close the immediate area surrounding an emergency field command post or other command post activated to abate a covered calamity, riot, or civil disturbance.

docs.title: Subdivision (c) — criminal consequence
docs.text:
Current §409.5(c) is textually narrower than a generic "crossed police tape" offense. It applies to an unauthorized person who:

  1. willfully and knowingly enters an area closed under (a) or (b); and
  2. willfully remains after receiving notice to evacuate or leave.

This conjunction matters.

The statute therefore should not be paraphrased as:

Anyone already inside any area behind police tape is automatically committing §409.5.

Other lawful orders/statutes may still apply.

docs.title: Police tape is evidence, not the legal source
docs.text:
A rope, marker, guard, barricade, or police line may manifest a valid closure. It does not eliminate the need to identify:

  • the statutory authority;
  • the predicate calamity/command post;
  • authorized closing official;
  • geographic scope;
  • current duration;
  • notice; and
  • the criminal elements actually asserted.

docs.title: 7. §409.6 proves closure statutes are not interchangeable
docs.text:
Avalanche-area §409.6 uses different misdemeanor wording and expressly reaches an unauthorized person who willfully remains after notice even if the person did not newly enter after the closure.

That textual difference reinforces the project rule:

Do not rewrite specialized closure statutes into one generic perimeter offense.

Official source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.6.

docs.title: Leiserson v. City of San Diego, 184 Cal.App.3d 41 (1986)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Leiserson involved a television cameraman at the PSA crash disaster scene.

The court held that §409.5(d)'s statutory news-media access provision cannot be defeated merely because the disaster area is dangerous—the statute already presupposes a health/safety menace.

But the access is not unlimited. Police may impose restrictions when they reasonably determine unrestricted press access will interfere with emergency operations. Restrictions may last only so long and extend only so far as necessary to prevent actual interference; the media must receive the maximum access that can be afforded without interference.

The judgment nevertheless favored the City because substantial evidence supported a finding that officers reasonably believed the crash site might also be a crime scene, a separate basis not governed by §409.5(d)'s disaster-access guarantee.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/184/41.html

docs.title: Narrow rule
docs.text:
For a qualifying §409.5 disaster closure, qualifying news representatives receive statutory access subject to necessary emergency-operation interference limits. That statutory access does not create unrestricted access to an independently valid crime-scene exclusion.

Do not convert Leiserson into a general constitutional entitlement for every camera holder.

docs.title: 9. §409.7 creates a separate protest/demo statutory protection
docs.text:
Current Penal Code §409.7 applies when peace officers:

  • close the immediate area around an emergency/other command post; or
  • establish a police line or rolling closure

at a demonstration, march, protest, or rally involving constitutionally protected activity.

Current text: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.7.

For a duly authorized representative of a news service, online news service, newspaper, or radio/television station/network, §409.7 provides:

  • entry into covered closed areas;
  • protection from intentional assault/interference/obstruction while gathering/processing information for public communication;
  • protection from citation for failure to disperse, curfew, or §148(a)(1) when gathering/receiving/processing information; and
  • a specified opportunity to contact a supervisory officer after detention unless circumstances make that impossible.

Subdivision (b) preserves enforcement of other applicable laws for unlawful activity.

Subdivision (c) says the section itself does not impose criminal liability.

docs.title: Scope caution
docs.text:
The statute does not define "duly authorized representative" or "online news service."

This sweep did not locate controlling published California appellate authority supplying a universal credential test for those terms.

Accordingly:

The special statutory qualification of an independent self-publisher/auditor under §409.7 can be a Researched-Unresolved changed-fact issue. Do not promise the special exemption merely because someone calls themselves press, and do not make a government press credential a prerequisite unless an applicable authority actually requires it.

For the project's ordinary member-of-public baseline, do not rely on §409.7 unless the facts support its statutory category.

docs.title: 10. Special press statutes are not the whole First Amendment
docs.text: The user's standing project rule does not depend on professional press credentials. That remains correct for the ordinary constitutional analysis.

docs.title: Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

Fordyce recognizes a First Amendment interest in filming matters of public interest, including police/protest activity.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/55/436/578292/

docs.title: Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

Askins confirms that photographing and recording matters of public interest are First Amendment-protected activities, while requiring location/restriction/justification analysis rather than a universal "camera everywhere" rule.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/16-55719/16-55719-2018-08-14.html

docs.title: Leigh v. Salazar, 677 F.3d 892 (9th Cir. 2012)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published.

Leigh explains that the Supreme Court recognizes a qualified First Amendment right of access for the press and public to observe government activities. A court analyzing a claimed right of access applies the Press-Enterprise experience/logic framework; if the right attaches, government closure must be justified by an overriding interest and narrow tailoring.

The Ninth Circuit remanded rather than declaring unrestricted access to every government operation.

Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/11-16088/11-16088-2012-04-16.html

docs.title: Project rule
docs.text:
§§409.5 and 409.7 can create special statutory access for qualifying news representatives. They do not define who has ordinary First Amendment protection to stand at a lawful vantage and observe/record government.

Conversely, ordinary constitutional recording rights do not automatically create the same statutory privilege to cross a valid emergency perimeter or disregard a valid dispersal order.

docs.title: 11. Index Newspapers is important but must be characterized accurately
Index Newspapers LLC v. U.S. Marshals Service, 977 F.3d 817 (9th Cir. 2020)
docs.text:
Status: published Ninth Circuit order resolving an emergency motion to stay a preliminary injunction.

The Portland litigation involved federal officers' treatment of journalists and legal observers documenting protests. The published order recognized powerful First Amendment retaliation/newsgathering interests and denied a stay of a preliminary injunction that, under the unusual federal/local posture, allowed journalists and legal observers to remain despite certain general dispersal orders.

But the posture matters:

  • the order reviewed preliminary injunctive relief;
  • local Portland officials had separately stipulated that journalists/legal observers would not be required to disperse;
  • the federal defendants' claimed statutory authority did not itself provide general street-clearing authority;
  • the injunction preserved arrests for independent crimes and prohibited interference with lawful federal activity.

Source: https://openjurist.org/977/f3d/817/index-newspapers-llc-v-united-states-marshals-service-4795058

docs.title: What not to write
docs.text:
Do not turn Index Newspapers into:

"The First Amendment universally exempts anyone who identifies as press or legal observer from every lawful dispersal order."

That is broader than the decision.

docs.title: 12. Current Ninth Circuit: Los Angeles Press Club v. Noem (2026)
Los Angeles Press Club v. Noem, No. 25-5975 (9th Cir. Apr. 1, 2026)
docs.text:
Status: Ninth Circuit, published/current.

This current case arose from 2025 Southern California immigration-enforcement protests. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's determination that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on First Amendment retaliation claims based on evidence of officers targeting journalists, legal observers, and peaceful protesters, including people standing away from unlawful actors and people attempting to comply with dispersal orders.

The panel stressed that peaceful protest and newsgathering are protected but do not license unlawful/violent activity.

Crucially, the Ninth Circuit did not reach the alternative right-of-access merits theory because the retaliation theory was sufficient. It also held that portions of the injunction were overbroad and vacated/remanded for narrower relief.

Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-9th-circuit/118261014.html

docs.title: Project consequence
docs.text:
Los Angeles Press Club is strong current authority against retaliatory force targeted at peaceful First Amendment activity. It is not a new universal right-of-access/dispersal exemption holding.

Together with Index Newspapers, it supports careful separation of:

  • protected observation/reporting;
  • targeted retaliation;
  • general dispersal authority;
  • statutory press exceptions;
  • actual interference/unlawful conduct; and
  • scope of equitable relief.

docs.title: 13. Observer, journalist, legal observer, protester, and passerby are factual roles—not magic labels
docs.text:
At a dynamic scene, record actual behavior:

  • standing off to the side;
  • photographing/recording;
  • interviewing;
  • wearing press/legal-observer identification;
  • chanting/carrying signs;
  • moving with demonstrators;
  • blocking traffic/access;
  • throwing objects;
  • damaging property;
  • physically interfering with police;
  • assisting another person in unlawful conduct;
  • attempting to leave;
  • unable to hear the order;
  • unable to identify an exit;
  • intentionally remaining after hearing a lawful order.

docs.title: Dubner's critical rule
docs.text:
Where the assembly does not meet the violence/imminence threshold, police may not simply collapse an innocent observer into participants for §409.

Where a qualifying riot/rout/unlawful assembly does exist and §409's lawful-warning elements are met, §409 can reach nonparticipants who willfully remain.

That is why observer status matters but is not an absolute immunity label.

docs.title: 14. Recording at emergency/protest scenes
docs.text: Use this sequence.

docs.title: A. Is the recorder at a lawful vantage?
docs.text: If outside a valid closure/perimeter and not obstructing, the ordinary Fordyce/Askins and Penal Code §148(g) recording protections apply.

docs.title: B. Has a valid closure changed the lawful vantage?
docs.text:
Identify:

  • §409 unlawful-assembly dispersal;
  • §409.5 calamity/command-post closure;
  • §409.7 special protest/media rule;
  • crime-scene authority;
  • another local/state/federal source.

Do not assume the tape itself is the statute.

docs.title: C. Is the recorder merely observing or participating/interfering?
docs.text: Use Dubner, §408 knowledge/participation rules, §148, and Sweep 016.

docs.title: D. Does a special media statute apply?
docs.text:
If yes, apply its exact category and exceptions.

If not or uncertain, ordinary constitutional rights remain but do not automatically authorize crossing a valid perimeter.

docs.title: E. Is enforcement targeted because of recording/reporting?
docs.text:
Use retaliation doctrine, Fordyce, Index Newspapers, and current Los Angeles Press Club.

A restriction genuinely justified by safety/interference is different from force/arrest motivated by hostility to documentation.

docs.title: 15. Force during crowd dispersal
docs.text:
Sweep 017 does not attempt an exhaustive less-lethal force manual. But the ordinary field branch now has a controlling warning/compliance anchor.

Under Nelson:

  • warning audibility matters;
  • actual threat posed by the individual matters;
  • attempts to comply matter;
  • blocked egress matters;
  • instructions about how to leave matter; and
  • force must be proportionate to the individualized governmental interest.

Current Los Angeles Press Club adds a First Amendment retaliation overlay where evidence shows peaceful reporters/observers/protesters were targeted because of protected activity.

The presence of some violent people in a larger crowd does not create an unlimited constitutional license to use indiscriminate force against peaceful persons.

docs.title: 16. Field questions
docs.text:
When police declare an unlawful assembly:

What conduct makes this assembly violent or creates a clear and present danger of imminent violence?

When a dispersal order is given:

What area must I leave, and which route should I use?

If the warning cannot be heard:

Preserve that fact. California's current instruction requires reasonable communication that ensures the order is heard.

If an observer is treated as a participant:

What conduct are you attributing to me apart from my presence or recording?

At a perimeter:

What authority is this closure under—§409.5, a crime-scene order, another statute, or something else?

For a qualifying news representative:

Is this a §409.5 disaster closure or a §409.7 demonstration/police-line closure?

These questions preserve the issue; they do not create an entitlement to disobey a valid order on scene.

docs.title: 17. Qualification dispositions
docs.text:
Row Pre-sweep Sweep 017 result Reason CA-F7.3 Gap Supported In re Brown, Collins, Wagner, Dubner, §§407–409/726, and current CALCRIM 2685–2686 now supply violence/imminence, participation, warning/audibility, willful-remain, and observer/bystander distinctions. CA-F8.1 Gap Supported Current §§409.5–409.7 plus Leiserson now supply calamity/command-post/police-line predicates, criminal-entry/remain distinctions, duration/scope, and special media-access limits. CA-F8.2 Gap Supported Dubner supplies the ordinary observer-versus-participant rule; Wagner supplies §408 knowing participation; Nelson supplies compliance/egress/force distinctions; independent obstruction remains under Sweep 016. CA-F8.3 Gap Supported Fordyce/Askins/Leigh, published Index Newspapers, current published Los Angeles Press Club, §148(g), and §§409.5/409.7 now separate ordinary constitutional recording/newsgathering from special statutory media access and retaliation.

A specialized Researched-Unresolved edge remains: no controlling published California appellate authority located in this sweep supplies a universal test for who qualifies as a "duly authorized representative" or "online news service" under §409.7. The ordinary member-of-public field branch does not depend on claiming that special status.

If package review accepts these dispositions, provisional totals become:

  • 68 Supported
  • 4 Researched-Unresolved
  • 1 Gap
  • 0 Not Applicable

Only GAP-08 remains activation-blocking.

docs.title: 18. Boundaries preserved
docs.text:
Sweep 017 does not complete:

  • every municipal emergency/curfew ordinance;
  • every specialized wildfire evacuation statute;
  • military/federal closure law;
  • every use-of-force/crowd-control weapon issue;
  • court-specific press access;
  • credential-program equal-protection litigation;
  • the full meaning of §409.7's undefined media terms;
  • law-enforcement record disclosure after an incident.

The final item is GAP-08.

• In re Brown, 9 Cal.3d 612 (1973)

docs.title: Ninth Circuit published/binding
docs.text:
