docs.title: Limited comparators
docs.text: • Boudjerada v. Medary, No. 24-2419 (9th Cir. Feb. 14, 2025) — unpublished; curfew/Collins distinction only

docs.title: Sweep 018 — Law-Enforcement Records and Specialized Evidence Disclosure
docs.text:
Qualification target:

  • CA-F9.4 — access to policy, incident, dispatch/body-camera/CCTV, peace-officer, and analogous evidence subject to applicable exemptions.

This sweep completes the ordinary California post-incident records branch needed after a public-facility or police encounter.

The operational sequence is:

record/custodian → investigatory-record status → mandatory information carveout → critical-incident audio/video override → peace-officer-record override → privacy/safety/redaction → electronic format/cost → retention/preservation separately

The central distinction is:

A record may be a public record without being fully disclosable, and an investigatory-record exemption does not erase later statutes that affirmatively require disclosure of specified information, recordings, or officer records.

This sweep uses the current recodified CPRA numbering. Older cases refer to former Government Code § 6254(f). Current Government Code § 7923.630 expressly preserves the pre-recodification construction of that law; the 2021 recodification was not intended to change its substance.

docs.title: 1. Start with the custodian and the actual record
docs.text:
After an encounter, potentially useful records can be held by different agencies:

  • incident/offense reports;
  • arrest/citation records;
  • 911 recordings;
  • CAD/dispatch event records;
  • radio traffic;
  • body-worn-camera video/audio;
  • dash-camera or other agency video;
  • police photographs;
  • government-facility CCTV;
  • use-of-force records;
  • officer complaint/investigation records;
  • exclusion/trespass notices;
  • facility emails or communications;
  • personal-device public-business recordings;
  • retention/deletion logs.

A police department may possess a copy of a facility's CCTV because it was collected for an investigation while the original facility also retains its own copy for routine security/operations. Those copies can present different custody, purpose, retention, and exemption facts.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Request the record from the agency reasonably likely to hold it, and identify duplicate custodians when appropriate. Do not assume that a police department, host agency, county, city, or facility necessarily holds every item.

The ordinary CPRA public-record definition, personal-device doctrine, request procedure, and preservation framework remain in public-records-evidence-preservation.md / Sweep 003.

docs.title: 2. Current law-enforcement investigatory-record exemption — Government Code § 7923.600
docs.text:
Current primary source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7923.600.

Section 7923.600 preserves a broad CPRA exemption for specified:

  • complaint/investigation records;
  • intelligence and security-procedure records;
  • investigatory or security files compiled by state/local police; and
  • investigatory/security files compiled by another state/local agency for correctional, law-enforcement, or licensing purposes.

This is the recodified successor to former § 6254(f).

docs.title: Government Code § 7923.630 — recodification continuity
docs.text:
Section 7923.630 expressly records that this article was derived from former § 6254(f) and that dividing it into multiple sections was not intended to alter its construction or relationships.

Current source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7923.630.

Project consequence:

Pre-recodification California Supreme Court cases such as Williams and Haynie remain material to current §§ 7923.600–7923.630. Cite the current statute and identify the former number only when explaining the older opinion.

docs.title: 3. Williams: the investigatory-file exemption is broad and does not expire merely because the case ends
Williams v. Superior Court (Freedom Newspapers, Inc.), 5 Cal.4th 337 (1993)
docs.text:
Status: California Supreme Court; controlling.

Williams construed former § 6254(f), now the § 7923.600 article.

The court rejected a case-by-case FOIA-style balancing test for ordinary law-enforcement investigatory files. The Legislature instead chose a broad record/file exemption while affirmatively requiring disclosure of specified information derived from those records.

Important propositions:

  • qualifying law-enforcement investigatory files are broadly exempt absent a later specific disclosure statute;
  • the exemption does not automatically terminate when the investigation concludes;
  • otherwise nonexempt material can acquire investigatory-file status when compiled as part of a concrete and definite law-enforcement investigation; and
  • the mandatory-information provisions must still be honored.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/5/337.html

docs.title: Do not overread Williams
docs.text:
Later legislation now affirmatively requires disclosure of some materials that would once have fallen within the broad investigatory exemption, especially:

  • critical-incident audio/video under Government Code § 7923.625; and
  • specified peace-officer records under Penal Code § 832.7(b).

Those later statutes must be applied before declaring a record categorically unavailable.

docs.title: 4. Haynie: actual investigations are exempt, but not everything police do is an investigation
Haynie v. Superior Court, 26 Cal.4th 1061 (2001)
docs.text:
Status: California Supreme Court; controlling.

Haynie involved a police stop prompted by a report of possible armed suspects. The requester sought recordings/statements surrounding the stop.

The Supreme Court held that records of an actual investigation undertaken to determine whether a violation of law may occur or has occurred fall within the law-enforcement investigatory exemption.

But the court expressly cautioned that the exemption does not shield everything law enforcement officers do. Inquiries made for crime prevention/public safety that are unrelated to determining whether a civil or criminal violation may occur/has occurred are not automatically "records of investigations."

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/26/1061.html

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text: Ask why the record was created. A targeted inquiry into suspected law violation can be an exempt investigation even if no arrest or charge results. Routine/public-safety data collection is not automatically investigatory merely because police created it.

docs.title: 5. ACLU / Castañares: mass/routine collection and assistance footage are not automatically investigatory
American Civil Liberties Union Foundation of Southern California v. Superior Court, 3 Cal.5th 1032 (2017)
docs.text:
Status: California Supreme Court.

The court rejected the proposition that bulk automated-license-plate-reader data was automatically a record of investigation merely because law enforcement collected it. The investigatory exemption requires a sufficiently targeted relationship to suspected law violations; the catchall exemption remained a separate question.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2017/s227106.html

docs.title: Castañares v. Superior Court, 98 Cal.App.5th 295 (2023)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Castañares applied the same distinction to police drone footage and described three useful categories:

  1. footage placed in an investigatory file — exempt under § 7923.600;
  2. footage created while investigating whether a law violation occurred, even without a formal file — ordinarily exempt under Haynie; and
  3. footage created to determine what kind of noncriminal public assistance is needed — not automatically investigatory.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2023/d082048.html

docs.title: CCTV / routine video consequence
docs.text:
Routine facility CCTV is not automatically a law-enforcement investigatory record merely because police later become interested in it.

If police obtain a copy for an actual investigation, the police-held copy can acquire investigatory-file status. The original facility-held copy must be analyzed based on that custodian's own purpose, exemptions, privacy/security interests, and retention rules.

Do not promise that requesting the same file from another custodian necessarily defeats a valid exemption; analyze each agency and source separately.

docs.title: 6. Mandatory arrest information — Government Code § 7923.610
docs.text:
Current source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7923.610.

Section 7923.610 requires state/local law-enforcement agencies to make specified arrestee information public, subject to item-specific safety/investigation limitations.

The required information includes categories such as:

  • name/occupation;
  • physical description and identifying data specified by statute;
  • time/date of arrest and booking;
  • location;
  • factual circumstances;
  • bail;
  • release/holding information; and
  • charges/warrants/parole/probation holds.

docs.title: Critical distinction
docs.text:
The statute mandates specified information. It does not necessarily compel production of the entire underlying arrest report.

An agency cannot answer "investigatory file" and ignore the mandatory-information provision. Conversely, the existence of mandatory arrest information does not erase all exemptions applicable to the report itself.

docs.title: 7. Mandatory complaint/request/response information — § 7923.615
docs.text:
Current source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7923.615.

Subject to statutory safety/investigation and victim protections, law enforcement must make public specified information regarding complaints or requests for assistance, including:

  • time, substance, and location of complaints/requests;
  • time and nature of the response;
  • recorded time/date/location of occurrence and report;
  • specified victim information;
  • factual circumstances; and
  • general descriptions of injury, property, or weapons.

docs.title: 911 / CAD / dispatch consequence
docs.text:
Section 7923.615 is extremely useful after a complaint-driven encounter because it requires specified information about the call/request and response.

It does not automatically mean:

"The agency must give me the complete unredacted 911 audio, CAD event, or radio recording."

If the actual audio/CAD/radio record is part of an exempt investigation, Williams/Haynie can still govern the record while § 7923.615 requires disclosure of the enumerated information.

Request both:

  1. the actual record; and
  2. in the alternative, all information required by § 7923.615 if the agency invokes § 7923.600.

That prevents an agency from treating an investigatory-record exemption as though it eliminates the mandatory public-information floor.

docs.title: 8. Victim/authorized-requester information — § 7923.605
docs.text:
Current source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7923.605.

Section 7923.605 creates a separate disclosure branch for specified victims, authorized representatives, insurers, and persons suffering bodily injury/property damage/loss from listed incidents.

The branch can include:

  • names/addresses;
  • property descriptions;
  • date/time/location;
  • diagrams;
  • party/witness statements;

subject to statutory safety/investigation limitations.

It does not require release of officer analysis/conclusions merely because a requester falls within the branch.

Classification: specialized requester-status branch. Use when the requester actually qualifies.

docs.title: 9. Critical-incident audio/video — Government Code § 7923.625
docs.text:
Current official source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7923.625.

This is the main specialized CPRA disclosure statute for law-enforcement audio/video recordings that depict a defined critical incident.

A critical incident is a recording that depicts:

  1. an incident involving discharge of a firearm at a person by a peace/custodial officer; or
  2. an incident in which officer force against a person resulted in death or great bodily injury.

The statute applies to qualifying recordings regardless of whether the medium is a body-worn camera, dash camera, or another audio/video source within the provision.

docs.title: Active-investigation delay
docs.text:
The statute does not allow indefinite use of the generic investigatory-file exemption.

In simplified operational terms:

  • during the initial statutory period, disclosure can be delayed if release would substantially interfere with an active criminal/administrative investigation;
  • continued delay after that period requires the agency to continue demonstrating substantial interference;
  • after one year, continued delay requires the heightened clear-and-convincing-evidence showing;
  • the agency must periodically reassess/notify as the statute requires; and
  • once the basis for delay resolves, disclosure must occur promptly.

The current text controls the exact notice/reassessment deadlines; do not rely on memory when drafting a demand or litigating a delay.

docs.title: Privacy redaction
docs.text:
The statute permits privacy-protective blurring/distortion when the privacy interest outweighs disclosure, but the redaction cannot interfere with full, complete, and accurate comprehension and the agency may not otherwise edit the recording.

If privacy cannot adequately be protected by redaction, the statute contains a narrower public-withholding branch plus access provisions for specified subjects/authorized representatives/heirs, subject to active-investigation delay.

docs.title: Not every BWC recording is a § 7923.625 recording
docs.text:
Subdivision (f) expressly leaves other audio/video records to other applicable law.

Therefore:

BWC footage of an ordinary detention, trespass complaint, or non-GBI force encounter is not automatically subject to § 7923.625 merely because a body camera captured it.

It may still be disclosable under another statute or CPRA rule; it can also fall within § 7923.600's investigatory exemption.

docs.title: 10. Sacramento Television Stations — current interpretation of critical-incident recordings
Sacramento Television Stations Inc. v. Superior Court, 112 Cal.App.5th 306 (2025)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

The court addressed how much audio/video must be released when recordings relate to a critical incident.

Important propositions:

  • § 7923.625 was enacted as a specific limitation on the older broad investigatory-record exemption for defined critical-incident recordings;
  • the statutory command can require disclosure sufficient to depict the relevant incident/context rather than permitting an agency to release only an artificially narrow fragment;
  • a claimed active-investigation delay still requires the evidentiary showing the statute specifies.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2025/c102316.html

Project use:

For critical-incident recordings, begin with § 7923.625 itself rather than assuming Williams/Haynie categorically controls the video.

docs.title: 11. BWC retention — Penal Code § 832.18 is not the disclosure statute
docs.text:
Current source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=832.18.

Penal Code § 832.18 is primarily a body-worn-camera policy/best-practices and retention provision.

Its retention framework includes:

  • nonevidentiary BWC data should ordinarily be retained for a minimum period identified by the statute before routine deletion/recycling;
  • evidentiary categories specified by the statute should be retained for a longer minimum period; and
  • criminal-prosecution or other legal circumstances can require additional retention.

The current statute should be checked for the exact period/category before relying on a retention deadline.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Do not cite § 832.18 as though it automatically makes BWC footage public. Disclosure comes from the CPRA and specific disclosure statutes; § 832.18 principally informs policy/retention.

This is consistent with the California Supreme Court's current 2026 retention discussion in City of Gilroy v. Superior Court.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2026/s282937.html

docs.title: 12. Peace-officer personnel/misconduct records — Penal Code § 832.7
docs.text:
Current official source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=832.7.

The current statute, including amendments effective January 1, 2026, begins from confidentiality for peace/custodial officer personnel records but creates explicit public-disclosure categories in subdivision (b).

Critically, § 832.7(b)(1) applies notwithstanding the ordinary personnel confidentiality rule, Government Code § 7923.600, or other law for the enumerated categories.

Current public categories include records relating to:

docs.title: Force/firearm
docs.text:
• officer discharge of a firearm at a person;
  • officer force resulting in death or great bodily injury;
  • a sustained complaint finding of unreasonable/excessive force; and
  • a sustained finding that an officer failed to intervene against clearly unreasonable/excessive force.

docs.title: Sexual assault
docs.text: • sustained findings of statutorily defined sexual assault involving a member of the public.

docs.title: Dishonesty
docs.text: • sustained findings of dishonesty directly related to crime reporting/investigation/prosecution or officer-misconduct reporting/investigation, including false statements/reports, evidence destruction/falsification/concealment, and perjury.

docs.title: Prejudice/discrimination
docs.text: • sustained findings of specified prejudicial/discriminatory conduct based on protected characteristics.

docs.title: Unlawful arrest/search
docs.text: • sustained findings that an officer made an unlawful arrest or conducted an unlawful search.

docs.title: Prohibited agreements
docs.text: • the current statute also includes the specified prohibited agreement category tied to Penal Code § 13510.9.

docs.title: Broad incident record package
docs.text:
For records within the public categories, the statute reaches far more than a one-page disciplinary outcome. Depending on the category, the disclosure package can include:

  • investigative reports;
  • photographs;
  • audio/video;
  • interview transcripts/recordings;
  • autopsy reports;
  • materials presented to prosecutors or disciplinary/charging bodies;
  • findings/recommended findings; and
  • records reflecting discipline/corrective action.

The exact current statutory list controls.

docs.title: Sustained means sustained
docs.text:
Penal Code § 832.8 defines "sustained" as a final determination after investigation and opportunity for applicable administrative appeal that the conduct violated law or policy.

Current source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=832.8.

Where § 832.7 requires a sustained finding, a mere complaint/allegation is not enough.

The firearm-discharge and force-causing-death/GBI categories are different: their public status does not depend on a sustained misconduct finding.

docs.title: 13. § 832.7 redaction and delay are structured, not a free-form secrecy license
docs.text:
Current § 832.7 authorizes specified redactions/delays, including protection of:

  • personal data;
  • anonymity of whistleblowers, complainants, victims, and specified witnesses;
  • legally protected medical/financial/private information; and
  • specified safety interests.

It also contains investigation-delay rules and current production timing rules for the public categories.

The statute does not authorize an agency to black out everything merely because personnel information appears somewhere in the file.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Ask the agency to identify the statutory paragraph supporting each withholding/redaction and release reasonably segregable material.

For a live request, check the current 2026 text for the precise delay/timing branch because the Legislature has amended § 832.7 repeatedly.

The current statute also provides that ordinary copy charges do not include agency search/edit/redaction labor for these records.

docs.title: 14. Copley Press is historical context, not the final current rule
Copley Press, Inc. v. Superior Court, 39 Cal.4th 1272 (2006)
docs.text:
Status: California Supreme Court; controlling as to the then-existing confidentiality statute but materially altered by later legislation for enumerated categories.

Copley broadly applied the former peace-officer personnel confidentiality scheme to disciplinary appeal records.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/39/1272.html

The Legislature later enacted SB 1421/SB 16 and subsequent amendments creating current § 832.7(b)'s affirmative public categories.

Do not write:

"Copley says peace-officer discipline is confidential, so none of it is public."

The correct current sequence is:

Does § 832.7(b) place this record/incident in an affirmative public category? → If yes, apply the current disclosure/redaction/delay provisions → If no, analyze the remaining confidentiality/CPRA rules.

docs.title: 15. Becerra / First Amendment Coalition — later § 832.7 is a genuine override
Becerra v. Superior Court, 44 Cal.App.5th 897 (2020)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

Becerra held that qualifying § 832.7(b) records do not become unavailable merely because the custodian agency holds records concerning officers employed by another agency. The public-record mandate focuses on responsive qualifying records in the state/local agency's possession.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2023/a165888.html

(The 2023 published follow-on opinion summarizes and applies the 2020 Becerra holding; citation: 44 Cal.App.5th 897.)

docs.title: First Amendment Coalition v. Superior Court, 98 Cal.App.5th 884 (2023)
docs.text:
Status: published California Court of Appeal.

The court described § 832.7(b) as changing the former confidentiality rule. Its "notwithstanding" clause can override conflicting state-law confidentiality provisions; the opinion specifically addressed Government Code § 11183.

It does not mean that every nonconflicting exemption or constitutional privacy interest disappears.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2023/a165888.html

docs.title: Project rule
docs.text: Treat § 832.7(b) as an affirmative statutory disclosure command with its own redaction/delay scheme—not as a suggestion layered beneath the older blanket confidentiality rule.

docs.title: Long Beach Police Officers Association v. City of Long Beach, 59 Cal.4th 59 (2014)
docs.text:
Status: California Supreme Court.

The court held that names of officers involved in on-duty shootings were generally disclosable on the record before it because the agencies failed to make a particularized showing sufficient to overcome the substantial public interest in officer identity.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2014/s200872.html

Current Penal Code § 832.7(i) expressly states that the chapter does not limit public access provided by Long Beach.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text: Do not assume officer names are automatically secret merely because the record concerns police activity. Safety/privacy can matter, but the agency must apply the actual governing rule rather than a categorical officer-name exemption.

docs.title: 17. Redaction costs — National Lawyers Guild v. City of Hayward
National Lawyers Guild v. City of Hayward, 9 Cal.5th 488 (2020)
docs.text:
Status: California Supreme Court.

The City attempted to charge a requester for staff time spent editing/redacting exempt material from police body-camera video.

The Supreme Court held ordinary redaction work was not chargeable to the requester as "data extraction" under the electronic-record cost provision.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2020/s252445.html

Current electronic-record/copy provisions:

  • § 7922.530 — copies/direct duplication;
  • § 7922.570 — electronic-form availability;
  • § 7922.575 — specified compilation/extraction/programming cost branch.

Official sources:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.530

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.570

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.575

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text: Redaction is not automatically a requester-billable "extraction" cost merely because the record is electronic video.

docs.title: 18. Practical classification by common evidence type
docs.text: Requested material Ordinary starting point Important override / limitation Incident/offense report § 7923.600 / Williams-Haynie investigatory analysis §§ 7923.610/.615 mandatory information; §832.7 if qualifying officer incident/misconduct Arrest report Often investigatory record §7923.610 mandatory arrestee information 911 audio May be investigatory depending on actual incident/inquiry §7923.615 requires specified complaint/request/response information even if audio itself exempt CAD/dispatch event Same purpose-specific analysis §7923.615 mandatory information; record itself not automatically compelled Radio traffic Can be investigatory; retention separate Mandatory information branch may still apply; local/state retention schedules matter BWC/dash video — ordinary stop May be investigatory Not automatically §7923.625; other CPRA/§832.7 branches can apply BWC/dash/video — officer shooting or force causing death/GBI Specific critical-incident branch §7923.625 disclosure/delay/privacy rules; §832.7 may independently apply Routine facility CCTV Public-record/exemption analysis at host agency Not automatically investigatory; police-acquired investigative copy can be treated differently Drone/automated video Purpose-specific Castañares / ACLU: targeted suspected-law-violation inquiry differs from routine/assistance collection Officer shooting/use-of-force records §832.7(b) affirmative public category statutory redaction/delay rules; critical-incident video separately §7923.625 Complaint alleging ordinary misconduct Personnel/confidentiality starting point Public only if current §832.7 category/predicate satisfied or another disclosure rule applies Sustained dishonesty/discrimination/unlawful arrest-search/excessive-force finding §832.7(b) public category apply current incident-record package/redaction/delay rules Exclusion/trespass notice / facility emails ordinary CPRA / facility custodian may become investigatory if police compile for investigation; original host-agency records separately analyzed

docs.title: Step 1 — send parallel requests to likely custodians
docs.text:
For a public-facility police response, consider separate requests to:

  • responding law-enforcement agency;
  • facility/department;
  • city/county/state host agency;
  • contracted security entity if legally subject to the request or records are held by the public agency.

docs.title: Step 2 — request the actual evidence
docs.text:
Request categories narrowly enough to identify the incident:

  • incident/report number if known;
  • date/time/location;
  • involved officer/employee names if known;
  • 911;
  • CAD/event chronology;
  • dispatch/radio;
  • BWC/dash/video;
  • photographs;
  • CCTV;
  • exclusion notices;
  • complaints;
  • employee recordings;
  • relevant communications.

docs.title: Step 3 — invoke mandatory information separately
docs.text:
If police claim § 7923.600:

Please also provide all information required to be made public under Government Code §§ 7923.610 and 7923.615, as applicable.

That avoids treating the record exemption as an information blackout.

docs.title: Step 4 — identify critical-incident video if applicable
docs.text:
If the event depicts an officer firearm discharge at a person or force resulting in death/GBI:

Please process responsive audio/video under Government Code § 7923.625 and identify any statutory basis and timeline for delayed disclosure/redaction.

docs.title: Step 5 — identify § 832.7 categories if applicable
docs.text:
If records concern a qualifying officer incident or sustained finding, cite the specific current § 832.7(b)(1) category.

Do not demand all officer personnel files.

docs.title: Step 6 — request segregable material and legal bases
docs.text:
For every withholding/redaction:

  • ask for the current statutory basis;
  • request reasonably segregable nonexempt material;
  • request the required written denial;
  • preserve dates/timing.

docs.title: Step 7 — request retention schedules separately
docs.text:
Disclosure and retention remain different.

Request:

  • BWC policy;
  • CCTV retention schedule;
  • CAD/audio retention schedule;
  • deletion/destruction logs if the evidence is missing;
  • any preservation notice or litigation hold actually issued.

docs.title: 20. Sample focused request language
docs.text:
Pursuant to the California Public Records Act, I request records concerning the incident at [location] on [date] at approximately [time], including the incident/event report, 911 audio, CAD/dispatch event record, radio traffic, body-worn and dash-camera recordings, photographs, facility CCTV obtained or retained by your agency, and any exclusion/trespass notice relating to the incident.

If you withhold an investigatory record under Government Code § 7923.600, please nevertheless disclose all information required by §§ 7923.610 and 7923.615 and identify the legal basis for each withholding or redaction.

For any audio/video depicting a critical incident within Government Code § 7923.625(e), please process the recording under § 7923.625 and identify any claimed statutory delay, redaction, or withholding provision.

For records subject to Penal Code § 832.7(b), please process them under the current public-disclosure, redaction, and delay provisions of that section.

Please provide reasonably segregable nonexempt portions and responsive electronic records in the electronic form in which they are held when required by the CPRA.

Adapt the request. Do not cite a specialized branch that plainly does not fit the incident.

docs.title: 21. Common bad field rules
docs.text: Bad slogan Better rule "Police reports are exempt." Investigatory records can be broadly exempt, but §§7923.610/.615 mandate specified arrest/complaint/response information and later statutes can require records. "The investigation is closed, so the whole file becomes public." Williams says the ordinary investigatory-file exemption does not automatically expire when the investigation ends. "Everything police collect is an investigatory record." Haynie/ACLU/Castañares distinguish targeted law-violation investigations from routine/public-safety/assistance collection. "911 calls are automatically public." Request the audio, but preserve that §7923.615 mandates specified information and does not necessarily compel the underlying recording. "All bodycam is public after 45 days." §7923.625's special timeline applies only to defined critical-incident recordings. Other BWC footage follows other law. "BWC is exempt because it is evidence." Critical-incident §7923.625 and qualifying §832.7 records can override ordinary investigatory withholding. "§832.18 makes bodycam public." §832.18 is principally a BWC policy/retention statute; disclosure is a separate CPRA question. "Officer personnel records are confidential." Start with confidentiality, then apply current §832.7(b)'s affirmative public categories and procedures. "Every complaint about an officer is public." Many §832.7 categories require a sustained finding; firearm discharge and death/GBI force categories operate differently. "Copley means disciplinary records are always secret." Later SB1421/SB16/current §832.7 create explicit public categories notwithstanding older confidentiality rules. "Police can charge me for hours of BWC redaction." National Lawyers Guild rejects ordinary redaction labor as chargeable electronic data-extraction cost. "The same CCTV copy has the same result everywhere." Custodian, purpose, compilation into an investigation, privacy/security, and specific overrides can change the analysis. "I requested it, so it must be preserved forever." Disclosure and retention remain separate under City of Gilroy and the applicable retention law/policy.

docs.title: 22. Qualification disposition
docs.text:
Row Pre-sweep Sweep 018 result Reason CA-F9.4 Gap Supported Current §§7923.600–.630, Williams/Haynie/ACLU/Castañares, §§7923.610/.615 mandatory information, §7923.625 critical-incident recordings, current Penal Code §§832.7–832.8 officer-record mandates, Long Beach, National Lawyers Guild, and retention cross-checks now make the ordinary incident/dispatch/BWC/CCTV/officer-record evidence branch runnable while preserving record-specific exemptions, redactions, custodian facts, and specialized laws.

If accepted, provisional matrix totals become:

  • 69 Supported

This satisfies the substantive CA-GATE-03 no-activation-blocking-Gap research condition.

It does not activate California. The separate non-row controls remain, including final/independent qualification review, national standing-baseline work, human/bootstrap review requirements, and the authorized activation decision.

docs.title: 23. Boundaries preserved
docs.text:
Sweep 018 does not claim exhaustive treatment of:

  • every CPRA exemption in Parts 5–6;
  • every victim-specific statute;
  • juvenile records;
  • medical records;
  • coroner records beyond ordinary law-enforcement treatment;
  • criminal discovery / Pitchess motion procedure;
  • subpoenas/civil discovery;
  • federal FOIA;
  • federal-agency records;
  • every local retention schedule;
  • every proprietary surveillance/vendor system;
  • every ALPR/facial-recognition/database statute;
  • every litigation privilege.

Those become specialized or changed-fact branches, not reasons to leave the ordinary CA-F9.4 field decision tree as an unresearched Gap.

docs.title: Healdsburg facility baseline
docs.text: Verified: October 7, 2026 Scope: Four documentary pre-field facility records in Sonoma County, under the Active California framework. Evidence boundary: Official facility, access, and policy sources. This sweep asserts no incident, misconduct, field observation, or comprehensive enforcement-history finding.

docs.text:

docs.title: Narrow documentary forum conclusions
docs.text:
• Ordinary municipal sidewalks receive the traditional-forum baseline once the actual street-side strip is distinguished from a facility approach. No unmapped paved area is assigned that result.
  • Police and City Hall public-service lobbies are federal NPF project inferences at medium confidence from their documented service purpose. A broader intentional opening could change the classification. Separate California labels remain open; NPF does not itself justify a recording restriction.
  • The library-purpose interior fits the existing federal LPF analysis. Its meeting-room terms and California interior classification remain open.
  • A council meeting opened to public participation is a federal LPF for that defined channel. Brown Act attendance, recording, comment, and removal rules are addressed in the existing public-meetings chapter. The chamber outside a covered open meeting is not classified by analogy alone.
  • The City’s description of the Plaza as a public park with walking, picnics, and community gatherings supports the ordinary-park TPF baseline. A performance permit is an activity restriction to test, not automatic reclassification of the park.

These are project applications of the qualified framework, not site-specific judicial holdings. Missing signs alone do not make every documentary classification unresolved; missing facts are retained where they could change the answer.

The existing California public-forum, public-library, indoor-common-space, and public-meeting chapters own the controlling framework and its limits. Primary references for the added park and meeting citations are Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators’ Association, 460 U.S. 37, 45–46 (1983), decided February 23, 1983 (binding federal Supreme Court forum framework; does not adjudicate this Plaza), and Norse v. City of Santa Cruz, 629 F.3d 966 (9th Cir. 2010) (en banc), decided December 15, 2010 (binding Ninth Circuit meeting-channel analysis; does not designate this room for all-hours expression). Official opinions reviewed October 7:

  • https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep460/usrep460037/usrep460037.pdf
  • https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2010/12/15/07-15814.pdf

Government Code §54953.5 is the binding California covered-open-meeting recording provision already reviewed in the qualified meeting chapter; this facility addition does not revise that chapter’s legal conclusion.

docs.title: What field verification can answer
docs.text:
A peaceful documentary visit can verify posted hours, public entrances, signs, counters, room access, visible control transitions, ordinary public circulation, and current complaint/meeting information. Record observations with date and defined location. A visit cannot by itself establish title, deeded right-of-way, policy history, or constitutional validity.

Each facility record separates those field items from legal and records gaps. Complete property/ROW work where a few feet could change the vantage or rule. Use targeted records requests for unpublished directives, control documents, incorporated terms, and implementation; avoid requesting a duplicate of the publicly available manual or policy.

No event history or rights-risk clearance is asserted in this baseline. Absence of an enforcement-history field means it has not been established for publication, not that adverse events are known not to exist.

docs.title: Concord DMV — Exterior Forum Analysis
docs.text:
Facility: California DMV — Concord Field Office Address: 2070 Diamond Boulevard, Concord, CA 94520 Analysis date: 2026-09-22 Federal anchors: Grace, Kokinda, Cornelius, Jacobsen California overlay: Camenzind, Park Management, Prigmore, current Field Guide California Speech Clause methodology

This is an area-specific documentary analysis. It does not assign one forum label to the DMV parcel, parking, entrance, sidewalks, or interior as a whole.

docs.title: 1. Why DMV differs from the library sites
docs.text:
The Concord and Walnut Creek library sweeps supplied close library-exterior evidence under Prigmore. A DMV field office has a materially different governmental purpose.

The current record supports:

  • a State-owned parcel used by DMV for administrative transactions and testing;
  • an ordinary municipal street system around the tract;
  • a State parcel that directly fronts Meridian Park Boulevard;
  • a public address on Diamond Boulevard even though the State parcel is separated from Diamond by a separately owned parcel on both the assessor sheet and the 1978 subdivision map;
  • no current online DMV source located that intentionally opens exterior property for expressive activity.

The correct question is therefore not is DMV public property? but:

what exact exterior area is being used, what is its physical/legal function, and what forum doctrine fits that area?

docs.title: 2. Property / access predicates
docs.text:
Current official parcel evidence resolves APN 126-490-004 to CALIFORNIA STATE OF, with DEPT MOTOR VEHICLES in the second-name field.

Assessor Book 126 Page 49 and recorded Subdivision Map 212M47 independently show the land corresponding to current parcel 04 / historical Lot 4 directly adjoining Meridian Park Boulevard while Lots 1 and 2 lie between it and Diamond Boulevard.

The 1978 subdivision map contains no apparent labeled access easement carrying Lot 4 across Lot 1 to Diamond. That negative observation is not conclusive and does not exclude a later easement or shared-access arrangement.

Accordingly:

STATE PARCEL VERIFIED / DIRECT MERIDIAN FRONTAGE STRONGLY SUPPORTED / DIAMOND ACCESS LEGAL GEOMETRY UNRESOLVED

docs.title: A. Actual ordinary Diamond Boulevard municipal sidewalk / ROW
docs.text:
Federal: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — HIGH CONFIDENCE once the person's actual position is established as ordinary municipal sidewalk/ROW.

California: PUBLIC-FORUM TREATMENT — HIGH CONFIDENCE for an ordinary municipal sidewalk.

United States v. Grace supplies the ordinary-sidewalk baseline. Concord Road Centerlines independently identifies the relevant Diamond segment as Concord-owned/jurisdictional and reports a sidewalk on the relevant side.

The unusual parcel geometry does not change the doctrine applicable to a person who is actually on the ordinary municipal sidewalk. It does mean the project must not extend that label automatically into the DMV approach merely because the facility uses a Diamond Boulevard address.

docs.title: B. Actual ordinary Meridian Park Boulevard municipal sidewalk / ROW
docs.text:
Federal: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — HIGH CONFIDENCE once exact municipal-sidewalk location is established.

California: PUBLIC-FORUM TREATMENT — HIGH CONFIDENCE for an ordinary municipal sidewalk.

This location has an especially strong property chain:

  • current State parcel directly fronts Meridian Park Boulevard;
  • 1978 subdivision owner certificate dedicated the mapped Meridian Park Boulevard portion to public use;
  • current Concord Road Centerlines identifies the closest Meridian Park segment as Concord-owned/jurisdictional and reports sidewalk presence.

The exact surveyed ROW edge remains unresolved, but that does not prevent classification of an area independently established to be the ordinary municipal sidewalk.

docs.title: C. Facility-specific access drive / walkway from Diamond Boulevard
docs.text:
Federal: NONPUBLIC-FORUM TREATMENT STRONGLY SUPPORTED IF THE AREA IS A PURPOSE-BUILT FACILITY ACCESS ROUTE RATHER THAN ORDINARY MUNICIPAL ROW; LEGAL/PHYSICAL FOOTPRINT STILL UNRESOLVED.

Kokinda and Ninth Circuit Jacobsen v. USPS, 993 F.2d 649 (9th Cir. 1993), are the closer federal comparators for a walkway or access route constructed to move patrons between parking/access facilities and a government service building. A visually continuous path does not automatically inherit the forum status of an adjoining municipal sidewalk when the government-controlled segment is physically/functionally a special-purpose access route.

That conclusion is conditional because the current Diamond approach has not yet been legally mapped. The approach could include municipal ROW, an easement across private parcel 01, State-controlled driveway/walkway, or a combination.

California: UNRESOLVED.

California's Speech Clause can treat freely accessible exterior spaces more broadly than federal forum doctrine. Camenzind v. California Exposition & State Fair, 84 F.4th 1102 (9th Cir. 2023), held exterior unticketed state fairgrounds—including parking lots and sidewalks leading to gates—to be a public forum under the California Speech Clause, relying on current California-law analysis including Park Management.

But the DMV approach is materially different from a large event/exhibition venue designed for mass public pedestrian circulation. No close California case resolving a purpose-built DMV or administrative-office access drive/walk was located. Do not force the Camenzind result onto this different property without current physical/use facts.

docs.title: D. DMV customer parking area
docs.text:
Federal: NONPUBLIC-FORUM TREATMENT STRONGLY SUPPORTED, SUBJECT TO CURRENT PHYSICAL/USE VERIFICATION.

The governmental purpose appears to be vehicle storage and circulation incidental to DMV transactions, not public discourse. No evidence located in this sweep shows an intent to open the DMV parking area as a forum for public expression. Under Cornelius and the special-purpose-access reasoning of Kokinda, public customer use alone does not create a traditional or designated public forum.

This is deliberately different from the library analysis. Prigmore was a property-specific California library-exterior case whose record tied the entrance side, parking lot, public open space and congregation characteristics together. It is not a categorical rule that all government customer parking lots are traditional public forums.

California: UNRESOLVED / PUBLIC-FORUM ARGUMENT MATERIALLY STRONGER THAN UNDER FEDERAL LAW.

Camenzind and earlier exterior-venue cases show that California Speech Clause analysis can treat publicly accessible parking/walkway areas as public forums. But current California doctrine remains fact-sensitive and the DMV's special-purpose administrative character differs substantially from fairgrounds, stadiums, entertainment venues and the Redding library grounds.

Until the current DMV parking footprint, access practice, pedestrian circulation, signs and any expressive-use policy/practice are verified, the guide should not assign a final California classification.

docs.title: E. Exterior customer queue / immediate entrance approach
docs.text:
Federal: NONPUBLIC / PURPOSE-LIMITED TREATMENT STRONGLY SUPPORTED; CURRENT CONFIGURATION PENDING.

If a defined area exists principally to stage customers awaiting entry or transactions, its governmental purpose is orderly access to an administrative service. Cornelius, Kokinda and administrative-building cases support reserving such a space for compatible access use, subject to reasonableness and viewpoint neutrality.

California: UNRESOLVED.

The result may depend on whether the queue is located on ordinary municipal sidewalk, an open exterior plaza-like space, a purpose-built facility walkway, or a controlled entrance apron. The physical area must be defined before state classification.

docs.title: F. Drive aisles, vehicle test lanes, driveway throats and similar moving-vehicle areas
docs.text:
Posture: NO BROAD SPEECH-ZONE CONCLUSION; SAFETY/COMPATIBILITY INTERESTS DOMINATE.

Whatever forum classification applies to neighboring pedestrian areas, active vehicle routes present materially stronger safety and operational interests. The project's standing scenario excludes blocking traffic or interfering with vehicle operations.

docs.title: G. Entrance threshold
docs.text:
Posture: SUBAREA-SPECIFIC / UNRESOLVED.

The transition between an exterior walkway/queue and the interior administrative lobby may be physically narrow and operationally important. Do not infer its classification from either the municipal sidewalk or the interior without current layout and policy evidence.

docs.title: 4. Comparator matrix
docs.text: Area Federal anchor Federal posture California posture Actual Diamond municipal sidewalk Grace TPF — HIGH CONFIDENCE Public forum — high confidence Actual Meridian Park municipal sidewalk Grace + current City road evidence TPF — HIGH CONFIDENCE Public forum — high confidence Facility-specific Diamond access route Kokinda / Jacobsen Nonpublic treatment strongly supported if special-purpose facility segment UNRESOLVED DMV customer parking Cornelius / Kokinda Nonpublic treatment strongly supported UNRESOLVED; Camenzind exterior cases material Exterior customer queue Cornelius / Kokinda Nonpublic/purpose-limited treatment strongly supported UNRESOLVED Moving-vehicle areas compatibility/safety No broad speech-zone conclusion No broad speech-zone conclusion Entrance threshold area-specific UNRESOLVED UNRESOLVED

docs.title: 5. Recording consequence
docs.text:
Forum classification is only the framework for testing a particular recording restriction.

Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018), recognizes First Amendment protection for photographing/recording matters of public interest while making the permissibility of restrictions dependent on the nature of the location and the actual governmental justification.

Therefore:

  • high-confidence municipal-sidewalk status materially strengthens protection for peaceful recording from that location;
  • a nonpublic DMV access/parking classification would permit greater regulation but still requires reasonableness and viewpoint neutrality under federal forum doctrine;
  • DMV privacy/security interests must be connected to the actual restriction rather than invoked as an abstract reason that all recording is prohibited;
  • the currently located knowledge-test cell-phone restriction applies to examination activity and is not silently expanded into a branch-wide camera ban;
  • no dedicated public-facing California DMV ordinary-patron photography/videography rule was located in the online sources reviewed.

docs.title: 6. Outcome-determinative access gate
docs.text:
The Diamond Boulevard access mismatch is one of the situations where deeper boundary research can be outcome-determinative.

If an actual encounter occurs on or immediately beside the Diamond approach, determine whether the person is on:

  1. municipal sidewalk/ROW;
  2. private parcel 01;
  3. an access easement;
  4. State-owned DMV property; or
  5. another separately controlled segment.

That distinction could change forum classification, the identity of the lawful controller, and removal/trespass analysis.

By contrast, perfect title reconstruction is unnecessary for a person whose location is independently established on the ordinary municipal sidewalk or well inside the State-owned customer facility.

docs.title: 7. Remaining physical verification
docs.text:
Highest-value field/current-plan checks are:

  • actual Diamond access-drive/walk alignment and signs;
  • actual public entrance location(s);
  • whether the public customer lot is entirely on the State parcel;
  • pedestrian route from Meridian Park Boulevard, if any;
  • exterior queuing configuration;
  • current parking/vehicle-test lanes and restricted markings;
  • posted camera/cell-phone/conduct/security signs;
  • exact transitions where municipal sidewalk becomes facility-specific access space.

docs.title: Facility Prep — Cross-Category Validation Checkpoint
docs.text: Facility: California DMV — Concord Field Office Date: 2026-09-22 Branch: field-guide/sweep-09-concord-dmv

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Test whether the Facility Prep architecture developed against two public-library sites survives a materially different government-facility category without importing library-specific property assumptions, policy assumptions, or forum conclusions.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
CROSS-CATEGORY VALIDATION SUCCESSFUL, WITH A NEW ACCESS-PATH STAGE AND A DOCTRINAL RESET.

The reusable evidence pipeline transferred to the DMV site, but the first administrative-facility test exposed a new class of problem that the library sites had not forced into the foreground:

public facility address ≠ parcel frontage ≠ legal public access path.

It also confirmed that the legal comparator must reset when the governmental purpose changes.

docs.title: What generalized successfully
docs.text:
The Concord DMV completed the reusable chain:

official facility address → countywide parcel/APN → owner/address fields → candidate adjoining parcels → assessor-map acquisition/hash → human map review → exact recorded-map follow-up → municipal road/sidewalk leads → policy/control research → area-specific forum analysis

Key current results:

  • APN 126-490-004;
  • owner field CALIFORNIA STATE OF;
  • second owner/name field DEPT MOTOR VEHICLES;
  • Assessor Book 126 Page 49;
  • exact historical subdivision reference WILLOWICK 4, Map Book 212 Page 47;
  • official Recorded Maps entry 212M47, entry 148419, three public imaged pages;
  • Concord Road Centerlines results for Diamond Boulevard, Meridian Park Boulevard and Galaxy Way.

The same Contra Costa parcel core therefore transferred from municipal-library property to a State-owned administrative facility without code changes.

docs.title: New issue exposed — address/frontage mismatch
docs.text:
DMV and the current parcel feed identify the public facility address as 2070 Diamond Boulevard.

But both the current assessor sheet and the exact 1978 subdivision map place the land corresponding to the DMV parcel / historical Lot 4 directly on Meridian Park Boulevard while separate Lots/Parcels 1 and 2 lie between it and Diamond Boulevard.

No labeled westward access easement across Lot 1 to Diamond is apparent on the reviewed 1978 subdivision drawing.

That does not establish that no access right exists today. It establishes that the public address is not a sufficient legal substitute for researching the actual access route.

Architecture consequence:

When a facility address and parcel frontage do not align, Facility Prep should create an ADDRESS/FRONTAGE-MISMATCH flag and separately resolve the actual public ingress/egress path before assigning ownership/control or forum consequences to the approach.

Current access evidence may require a later easement, deed, site plan, acquisition file, shared-access agreement, or current engineering record rather than more historical-map searching.

docs.title: Municipal enrichment remained modular
docs.text:
Because this DMV is also in Concord, the existing Concord Road Centerlines adapter could legitimately be reused as a jurisdiction-specific enrichment.

That is not evidence that a road adapter generalized across facility categories or cities. It means its geographic coverage actually includes this address.

This distinction remains important:

countywide parcel core + municipality-specific ROW enrichment + facility/agency-specific policy/control research

docs.title: Recorded-map handling transferred successfully
docs.text:
The assessor sheet exposed TRACT 5292 (WILLOWICK 4) MB 212-47.

The existing Contra Costa Recorded Maps adapter correctly translated MB to source value Subdivision Map, resolved the exact index record, and the existing public-page renderer retrieved all three imaged pages.

The resulting evidence clarified the historical street/lot geometry and dedication chain without being treated as a current title opinion.

This confirms that the recorded-map components are reusable evidence-acquisition modules independent of the library category.

docs.title: Doctrinal reset
docs.text:
The property pipeline generalized; the legal anchor did not.

The library sites had close library-specific exterior authority in Prigmore and room-channel authority in Faith Center.

For DMV, the closer structure is:

  • ordinary municipal sidewalk → Grace / ordinary sidewalk doctrine;
  • purpose-built government access walk → Kokinda / Ninth Circuit Jacobsen comparison;
  • administrative public lobby → Cornelius + published Ninth Circuit Sammartano;
  • state administrative-lobby factual comparison → unpublished/nonprecedential Freedom Foundation only as a close factual comparator;
  • recording activity → Askins, separately from forum classification;
  • California Speech Clause → independently analyzed under current authorities including Camenzind, not copied from the federal forum label.

Architecture consequence:

A cross-category Facility Prep run must reset the area/activity anchor authority from the governmental purpose and physical area. Reuse the comparator method, not the previous facility's cases or classifications.

docs.title: Agency-purpose rules did not become site-wide restrictions
docs.text:
The DMV test also exposed a useful policy-scope distinction.

DMV publicly identifies significant privacy interests in personal records and publishes a rule that a cell phone may not be used as a testing aid during a knowledge examination.

Neither fact is silently transformed into a general field-office camera ban.

Architecture consequence:

Preserve the scope of an agency rule at the activity/channel where it applies. A privacy duty or examination-integrity rule is evidence relevant to a specific restriction; it is not itself proof of a facility-wide prohibition.

The current search did not locate a dedicated public-facing California DMV field-office ordinary-patron photography/videography rule.

docs.text:

docs.title: Cross-category architecture consequence
docs.text:
After Concord Library, Walnut Creek Library and Concord DMV, the project has now validated a reusable core consisting of:

  • official facility/address identification;
  • countywide parcel/APN normalization where a genuine countywide source exists;
  • assessor-map acquisition and hashing;
  • candidate-neighbor discovery plus human relevance screening;
  • exact recorded-map/reference follow-up;
  • public scanned-record rendering where the ordinary public viewer exposes it;
  • source-specific municipal ROW enrichment;
  • outcome-determinative boundary stop rules;
  • raw → normalized → reviewed evidence separation;
  • area-specific anchor-authority analysis.

The DMV test adds two durable stages:

  1. frontage/access-path validation when the public address does not correspond to direct parcel frontage; and
  2. facility-purpose doctrinal reset before carrying forum conclusions into a new category.

The prototype can now proceed to another materially different facility type without treating its current modules as universally statewide. Source coverage and legal anchors remain explicit, modular and independently validated.

docs.title: Concord DMV — Interior Forum Authority Review
docs.text: Reviewed: 2026-09-22 Question: What forum framework best fits the ordinary public-facing interior of a California DMV field office, and what does that classification establish about recording?

docs.title: Controlling framework
docs.text:
No controlling Ninth Circuit or published California appellate decision specifically adjudicating ordinary-patron filming inside a California DMV field office was located in this review.

The principal controlling federal framework therefore comes from the general public-forum cases already carried in the Field Guide, particularly Perry Education Association, Cornelius, and Minnesota Voters Alliance, together with Ninth Circuit government-building authority.

docs.title: Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court
docs.text:
Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002), is especially useful for the threshold classification problem.

The Ninth Circuit treated the judicial/municipal complex before it as a nonpublic forum even though members of the public entered the building to conduct public business. The decision reinforces several Field Guide rules:

  • government ownership does not create a traditional public forum;
  • public entry to transact government business does not itself create a public forum;
  • the purpose and actual use of the defined area matter;
  • even in a nonpublic forum, restrictions must remain reasonable in light of the forum's purpose and viewpoint neutral;
  • the government's asserted safety/order rationale is not automatically self-proving merely because the forum is nonpublic.

This makes Sammartano a substantially closer controlling comparator for an administrative-service lobby than the library-exterior analysis in Prigmore.

docs.title: Freedom Foundation v. Washington Department of Ecology
docs.text:
Freedom Foundation v. Washington Department of Ecology, No. 20-35007 (9th Cir. Dec. 21, 2020), is an unusually close administrative-lobby factual comparator, but it is an unpublished memorandum and is not precedent except as permitted by Ninth Circuit Rule 36-3.

The panel treated a state agency headquarters lobby as nonpublic where the physical space was organized around reception/security, workspaces, visitor seating and passage between secured areas, and agency policy/practice reserved the lobby for agency-related business rather than general public communication. The panel emphasized government intent, physical configuration, and actual policy/practice under Cornelius.

Opinion:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/20-35007/20-35007-2020-12-21.html

Use it as a close factual comparator, not as binding authority. It reinforces rather than replaces the published Sammartano / Cornelius framework.

docs.title: Martin v. North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles
docs.text:
Martin v. North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles, No. 1:25-CV-344-DAB-JGM (M.D.N.C. May 12, 2026), is a recent out-of-circuit federal district-court case involving a person who entered a DMV branch with a camera, encountered a No Cell Phones sign, entered an area marked for employees/authorized personnel, and later received a branch-specific trespass warning.

Published opinion:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/north-carolina/ncmdce/1%3A2025cv00344/101683/31/

The court described the inside of a DMV branch as a nonpublic forum, citing Avedisian v. Holcomb, 853 F. Supp. 185 (E.D. Va. 1994), and also cited Rodriguez v. Roberson for the proposition that filming in a DMV was not a clearly established right in that litigation.

Important limit: Martin resolved the individual-capacity claim through qualified-immunity / clearly-established-law analysis and expressly stated that it did not need to determine the constitutionality of the particular speech restriction. It therefore should not be summarized as a merits holding that every DMV filming prohibition is constitutional.

It is also not controlling in California or the Ninth Circuit.

docs.title: Avedisian / Rodriguez
docs.text: Avedisian and Rodriguez provide additional DMV-specific persuasive context, but they are out-of-circuit district-court authorities. Their proper role in this project is to corroborate that treating a transactional DMV interior as a special-purpose/nonpublic forum is not a novel analogy—not to displace controlling Ninth Circuit law or independently settle California's Speech Clause.

docs.title: Working federal classification
docs.text:
For the ordinary Concord DMV public lobby/waiting area, current authority strongly supports:

FEDERAL NONPUBLIC-FORUM TREATMENT STRONGLY SUPPORTED / PUBLISHED GENERAL NINTH-CIRCUIT FRAMEWORK + CLOSE NONPRECEDENTIAL ADMINISTRATIVE-LOBBY COMPARATOR / DMV-SPECIFIC CASES PERSUASIVE ONLY

That is a confidence-qualified project conclusion, not a holding that every square foot inside the building has identical status.

Separate subareas remain necessary:

  • ordinary lobby / waiting;
  • customer transaction counters;
  • knowledge/examination stations;
  • kiosk area;
  • restrooms, if publicly available;
  • employee/restricted zones;
  • entrance threshold or any exterior queue.

docs.title: California Speech Clause
docs.text:
Federal classification does not automatically answer California Constitution article I, § 2(a).

Camenzind v. California Exposition & State Fair, 84 F.4th 1102 (9th Cir. 2023), confirms that the federal and California forum analyses must be kept separate and also acknowledges uncertainty in the California classification doctrine for some nontraditional spaces.

No sufficiently close California appellate authority classifying an ordinary state administrative-service lobby like DMV was located in this review.

Current state-law posture:

CALIFORNIA SPEECH-CLAUSE CLASSIFICATION UNRESOLVED / NO CLOSE DMV OR ADMINISTRATIVE-LOBBY STATE AUTHORITY LOCATED

Do not automatically copy the federal nonpublic label into the California column.

docs.title: Recording consequence — Askins
docs.text:
The recording question is separate from forum classification.

In Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018), the Ninth Circuit stated that the First Amendment protects photography and recording of matters of public interest and emphasized that whether a location is public depends on the nature of the location. The court rejected resolving a challenged government photography restriction through broad conclusory assertions and remanded for factual development concerning the particular outdoor locations and restrictions.

Opinion:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/16-55719/16-55719-2018-08-14.html

Askins therefore does not create an unfettered right to film every government interior. It does reinforce two rules directly relevant here:

  1. recording matters of public interest can itself be protected First Amendment activity; and
  2. the permissible restriction depends materially on the specific place and rule being challenged.

Accordingly, a nonpublic-forum classification does not itself mean recording prohibited.

An identified restriction still must be tested under the standard applicable to the forum and activity. Relevant doctrines may include:

  • First Amendment recording/newsgathering law;
  • California Constitution article I, § 2(a);
  • reasonableness in light of the forum's purpose;
  • viewpoint neutrality;
  • privacy/confidentiality law;
  • examination integrity;
  • actual obstruction/interference;
  • security and restricted-area rules;
  • retaliation;
  • removal/trespass authority.

The current online policy search has not located a dedicated California DMV ordinary-patron camera rule. Therefore the project should not analyze an imaginary ban. If a branch sign or staff directive is encountered, preserve the exact wording, scope, location, asserted authority, and application before testing constitutionality.

docs.title: Exterior comparator warning
docs.text:
Do not extend the interior nonpublic classification outward by property line.

An ordinary municipal sidewalk remains governed by ordinary sidewalk doctrine. A purpose-built DMV access walk, queue, parking area, or driveway requires its own access/purpose/history analysis. Grace and Kokinda provide the relevant ordinary-sidewalk versus special-purpose-access contrast; Prigmore should not be imported merely because the DMV also has a public parking lot.

docs.title: Concord DMV — Policy / Privacy Search Review
Current official sources
docs.text:
Primary current sources reviewed include:

  • Concord field-office page: https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/field-office/concord/
  • DMV Privacy and Security: https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/privacy-and-security/
  • How Information is Protected or Disclosed: https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/privacy-and-security/how-your-information-is-shared/
  • DMV Records Requests: https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/customer-service/records-request/
  • DMV Conditions of Use / data-use policy: https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/conditions-of-use/
  • California Driver's Handbook — Testing Process: https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/the-testing-process/

Targeted searches were also run against current DMV public-facing material for combinations of photography, videography, filming, camera, recording, cell-phone, field-office, testing, examination, and patron/customer rules.

docs.title: Photography / videography finding
docs.text:
Approved wording:

No dedicated public-facing California DMV field-office ordinary-patron photography/videography rule was located in the online sources reviewed as of September 22, 2026.

Do not shorten this to DMV has no photography policy.

This finding does not establish:

  • absence of branch signs;
  • absence of internal staff/security directives;
  • absence of testing/examination-specific device restrictions;
  • absence of privacy rules applicable to particular information or conduct;
  • absence of a later policy;
  • a constitutional right to record every public-facing DMV subarea.

Physical/signage verification remains important.

docs.title: Testing-area device restriction
docs.text:
DMV does publish a narrower current rule for knowledge testing. The California Driver's Handbook states that applicants may not use testing aids during a knowledge test and expressly gives a cell phone as an example.

That rule belongs to the examination activity/channel. It is strong evidence that a knowledge-testing station is a purpose-limited environment with an examination-integrity interest.

It must not be generalized into a branch-wide no phones or no cameras rule. The project should distinguish:

ordinary lobby use ≠ transaction counter ≠ knowledge test in progress ≠ restricted employee area

A patron merely carrying or using a phone elsewhere in the branch is not shown to violate the knowledge-test rule simply because a test-taker could not use the phone as an aid during an examination.

docs.title: DMV privacy interests
docs.text:
DMV's current privacy policy states that it collects and protects sensitive personal information under the California Constitution, Information Practices Act, Public Records Act, Driver's Privacy Protection Act, Vehicle Code, and related regulations.

Examples identified by DMV include:

  • names and addresses;
  • dates of birth;
  • Social Security numbers;
  • driver-license/identification numbers;
  • photographs;
  • medical and disability information;
  • fingerprints/thumbprints;
  • examination/test information.

DMV states that access to personal/confidential information is limited to personnel whose work requires it and that physical information is protected through security measures. DMV also states that records relating to a person's physical or mental condition are confidential under Vehicle Code § 1808.5.

The separate DMV disclosure page identifies additional protections and disclosure rules for residence addresses, driver-license numbers, photographs, fingerprints, medical information, and other record categories.

docs.title: Legal consequence
docs.text:
These privacy duties are material to the government interests that could support a reasonable restriction in a transaction, records, examination, or other purpose-limited area.

They are not themselves a general camera prohibition. A rule governing public recording must still be identified and analyzed under the applicable forum, speech/recording, privacy, and reasonableness doctrines.

Keep separate:

DMV duty to protect information → actual information exposed by the physical layout → identified rule/restriction → forum classification → constitutional/statutory analysis

Do not reason backward from DMV holds confidential information to everything visible to an ordinary patron is legally unrecordable.

docs.title: Current branch fact
docs.text: DMV's official page confirms the Concord Field Office at 2070 Diamond Boulevard and identifies a self-service kiosk. Kiosk/public-service availability supports ordinary public access to defined customer areas but does not establish public-forum status.

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text:
Highest-value remaining checks are:

  • current physical signs at the entrance, lobby, counters, testing areas, and kiosk;
  • any additional current examination/device-use instructions at the branch;
  • any internal/public facility-conduct rule that is actually invoked against recording;
  • whether counter orientation or public screens expose protected data in a way material to a narrowly tailored operational restriction.

docs.title: Evidentiary limit

Road Centerlines is not a cadastral/ROW-boundary layer.

Accordingly:

  • centerline geometry ≠ ROW edge;

docs.title: Access-path issue
docs.text:
The unusual fact pattern is now narrow and concrete:

  1. DMV and GIS use 2070 Diamond Boulevard as the facility address;
  2. APN 126-490-004 is State-owned/DMV;
  3. Assessor Book 126 Page 49 depicts parcel 04 directly on Meridian Park Boulevard but separated from Diamond Boulevard by parcel 01;
  4. parcel 01 is currently a separately owned private parcel in the GIS.

Therefore the current legal/physical public entrance drive from Diamond is not resolved merely by the address.

Status:

PUBLIC-FACILITY-ADDRESS-VERIFIED / DIAMOND-INGRESS-PATH-AND-LEGAL-GEOMETRY-UNRESOLVED

The project should identify the actual driveway/walkway and determine whether its relevant portions are State property, public ROW, easement, shared access, or another control arrangement before relying on that location in a removal/trespass analysis.

docs.title: Outcome-determinative gate
docs.text:
This issue is worth deeper research because a plausible answer could change the legal framework for a person standing on the approach from Diamond Boulevard.

By contrast, perfect reconstruction of every tract boundary is not necessary to conclude that a person actually standing on an identified ordinary Concord municipal sidewalk is in a traditional public forum.

The exact recorded subdivision map WILLOWICK #4, Book 212 Page 47, has now been retrieved and reviewed. It confirms the historical frontage mismatch but does not establish the present Diamond access arrangement. If that access becomes outcome-determinative, the next high-value sources are current DMV/DGS acquisition or site records, later easement/deed instruments, and/or current City site/engineering records rather than broader historical-map searching.

docs.title: Page 1 — ownership / dedication certificates
docs.text:
The owner's certificate identifies Eastman Concord Venture as the record-title party for the subdivision lands and states that the owners dedicate to public use the portions designated on the map as Meridian Park Blvd. The certificate also states that the map shows easements on the premises or of record.

docs.title: Page 2 — City approval / acceptance posture

Current Concord Road Centerlines independently identifies Meridian Park Boulevard as Concord-owned/jurisdictional today. The present road status therefore has later/current support independent of the 1978 certificate language.

docs.title: Page 3 — lot and street geometry

docs.title: Lot 4 / current DMV parcel

The map depicts Diamond Boulevard along the west side, Galaxy Way along the north, and Meridian Park Boulevard along the east.

docs.title: Access from Diamond Boulevard
docs.text:
No labeled access easement connecting Lot 4 westward across Lot 1 to Diamond Boulevard is apparent on the reviewed subdivision drawing.

This is a negative visual observation, not a title conclusion. It does not establish that no such right exists today because:

  • an easement could have been created after the 1978 map;
  • a later deed/site plan/parcel adjustment could alter access rights;
  • a shared-access instrument may exist outside the subdivision-map notation;
  • an access route could arise through another current legal arrangement.

The 1978 map therefore does not resolve the current Diamond Boulevard access path. Instead, it strengthens the need for a targeted current deed/easement/site-plan inquiry if the legal status of that approach becomes outcome-determinative.

docs.title: Street / ROW geometry observations
docs.text:
The drawing depicts the subdivision's street relationships and dimensional linework, including the Meridian Park Boulevard dedication/widening area and the Diamond Boulevard frontage of Lots 1 and 2.

For current forum work, the safest present conclusions remain:

  • an identified ordinary municipal sidewalk/ROW component is analyzed under ordinary sidewalk doctrine;
  • the exact current ROW edge is not established merely by this historical map;
  • the DMV's facility-specific driveway/walkway from Diamond must not be assumed to be municipal ROW;
  • the State parcel's direct Meridian Park frontage is substantially better supported than any direct Diamond frontage.

docs.text:
Current status:

  • map identity: OFFICIAL-INDEX-RESOLVED;

  • current State parcel direct Diamond frontage: NOT SUPPORTED; INTERVENING PARCEL SHOWN;
  • present Diamond access easement/shared-drive right: UNRESOLVED;
  • current exact municipal ROW edges: UNRESOLVED.

docs.title: Research consequence
docs.text:
Broad historical map searching is no longer the best next move. The exact assessor-referenced subdivision map has been resolved and reviewed, and it confirms rather than eliminates the current access question.

If exact access control matters, the next high-value source family is current evidence: State/DMV/DGS acquisition or site records, later easement/deed instruments, and/or City site/engineering records showing the legal driveway/walkway connection from Diamond Boulevard.

This is an application of the Facility Prep outcome-determinative boundary gate: continue only far enough to answer a concrete access/removal question, not to reconstruct title history for its own sake.
