docs.text:
This is a human visual review of the official Contra Costa County assessor-map sheet preserved by Facility Prep v0.2. The PDF contains no usable extractable text through the current parser, so the map was reviewed visually.

This sheet is evidence of assessor parcel geometry and record-reference notation. It is not treated as a survey, deed, final right-of-way determination, or complete easement report.

docs.title: Reviewed observations
docs.text:
1. Parcel 06 on Assessor Book 111 Page 24 is labeled LIBRARY, approximately 0.84 acres. The sheet prints 3356 OR 502 beneath the LIBRARY label.
  2. Parcel 14 is immediately east of parcel 06 and is labeled CITY OF CONCORD, approximately 3.68 acres. The sheet prints 636 OR 390 beneath that label.
  3. Parcel 06 directly fronts Salvio Street on the north and lies immediately east of Parkside Drive.
  4. Parcel 14 also fronts Salvio Street on the north and continues substantially farther south/east than the library parcel.
  5. The Salvio Street corridor is drawn with 40 dimension callouts on each side of the depicted centerline. This is a useful right-of-way research lead but is not treated as a final legal ROW determination without engineering/recorded-source confirmation.
  6. Near the north end of Parkside Drive, the sheet shows a 50' dimension and an additional narrow-line/dimension treatment adjacent to parcel 06. The exact legal meaning of those lines must be resolved from recorded or engineering sources rather than inferred from the assessor sheet alone.
  7. The sheet revision table includes a 10/10/96 entry stating CREATE 013 & 014.
  8. The sheet contains additional historic easement/right-of-way notation along Willow Pass Road, including a permanent-easement notation, but those southern references are not presently treated as establishing rights affecting the Concord Library parcel.

docs.title: Official-record notation convention
docs.text:
The OR abbreviation can now be interpreted with substantially greater confidence because other official Contra Costa County-hosted records expressly pair a full citation with the same shorthand convention.

For example, a County-hosted legal description states that a deed was recorded in Book 1396 of Official Records, Page 312, then later refers to the same parcel as (1396 OR 312):

https://www.contracosta.ca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/73288/Appendix-F---Hazards-Hazardous-Materials-and-Wildfire-Supporting-Info-PDF

Another County-hosted title/legal-description record uses the same pattern, including shorthand such as (535 OR 213) after describing records by Book and Page of Official Records:

https://www.contracosta.ca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/52264/Appendix-M---Phase-I-Environmental-Site-Assessment-PDF

Accordingly, the assessor-sheet notations are now reasonably read as:

  • 3356 OR 502 → Book 3356 of Official Records, Page 502;
  • 636 OR 390 → Book 636 of Official Records, Page 390.

This resolves the citation format, not the content or legal effect of either instrument. The underlying records still need to be retrieved before the project states what they conveyed, reserved, dedicated, or otherwise established.

docs.title: Concord Library — Exterior Prigmore Analysis
docs.text:
Facility: Concord Library Address: 2900 Salvio Street, Concord, California 94519 Analysis date: 2026-09-22 Authority: Prigmore v. City of Redding, 211 Cal.App.4th 1322, 150 Cal.Rptr.3d 647 (2012)

Published opinion:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2012/c068866.html

This is an area-specific documentary analysis. It does not assign one forum label to the entire Concord Library/Civic Center site.

docs.title: 1. Prigmore framework
docs.text:
Prigmore defined the forum by the access sought, rather than by the entire library property. On the Redding record, the relevant forum consisted of:

  1. public open space on the entry side of the library;
  2. the entry/exit-door area; and
  3. the adjacent parking lot.

The court then examined whether those outdoor areas were traditional public forums. It emphasized:

  • actual use and purpose of the property, particularly public-thoroughfare function and free public access;
  • physical characteristics, location, and boundaries;
  • traditional/historic use of the property and similar properties;
  • the library's public information-dissemination function;
  • adjacency to parks and other public buildings;
  • congregation/rest features at the Redding entrance, including benches and a newspaper rack.

The holding was property-specific. It does not make every library parking lot or entrance a traditional public forum.

docs.title: 2. Concord facts relevant to the comparison
Government ownership and civic setting
docs.text:
Current City GIS identifies:

  • APN 111-240-006 — 2900 Salvio Street — owner field CONCORD CITY OF — 0.84 acres;
  • adjoining APN 111-240-014 — 1950 Parkside Drive — owner field CONCORD CITY OF — 3.68 acres.

The City-owned-parcels layer returns the library parcel as City-owned. A 2020 Contra Costa County Library Commission packet separately states that the Concord Library building is owned by the City of Concord.

The library sits immediately within/alongside the Concord Civic Center rather than as a stand-alone commercial-style site.

docs.title: Public access and parking
docs.text:
The current Contra Costa County Library branch page expressly describes two public parking areas:

  • a smaller front lot off Salvio Street;
  • a larger rear lot off Parkside Drive adjacent to the Concord Civic Center.

No reservation, admission fee, gate, membership requirement, or similar exterior access condition has been located for ordinary staffed operations.

docs.title: Public entrance and pedestrian circulation
docs.text:
The City's Civic Center accessibility map identifies:

  • a Public Entrance on the east side of the Concord Library;
  • a bike rack immediately along the library/Civic Center pedestrian circulation area;
  • the front Salvio parking row;
  • the large Parkside-side parking area;
  • pedestrian routes connecting parking, the library, and City Hall/Civic Center buildings.

Official map:

https://www.cityofconcord.org/446/Building-Map-PDF

The map was created by the City's GIS Division on February 19, 2020.

docs.title: Street/sidewalk context
docs.text:
The City's Road Centerlines layer identifies the closest relevant Salvio Street and Parkside Drive segments as:

  • owner: Concord;
  • jurisdiction: Concord;
  • sidewalks: Yes / Yes.

City transportation materials describe the Salvio bikeway/pedestrian connection as serving a high walking/bicycle-demand corridor from downtown to the Civic Center and Concord Library.

City engineering materials also treat sidewalk/driveway work as public-right-of-way subject matter, while expressly cautioning that exact property lines require boundary work.

docs.title: Historical/survey context
docs.text:
Contra Costa Public Works' Recorded Maps index ties APN book/page 111 24 to recorded survey 7LSM51, dated September 24, 1940. The survey uses the course of Salvio Street, as extended, as its basis for bearings and identifies an older deed chain at 454 OR 154.

The historical survey is context only; it is not treated as a current ROW plat.

docs.title: A. Salvio Street municipal sidewalk / public ROW component
docs.text:
Classification: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — HIGH CONFIDENCE, SUBJECT TO EXACT-EDGE IDENTIFICATION.

Reasoning:

  • ordinary public sidewalks are the classic traditional-public-forum category;
  • the closest Salvio segment is characterized by the City's own GIS as Concord-owned/jurisdictional with sidewalks on both sides;
  • the corridor is part of the City's pedestrian/bicycle access network serving the Civic Center and Library.

The unresolved issue is not the forum doctrine applicable to a genuine municipal sidewalk. The unresolved issue is the surveyed edge separating public ROW from facility-specific property where pavement or landscaping makes the transition visually ambiguous.

docs.title: B. Parkside Drive municipal sidewalk / public ROW component
docs.text:
Classification: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — HIGH CONFIDENCE, SUBJECT TO EXACT-EDGE IDENTIFICATION.

The same reasoning applies to the actual public-sidewalk/ROW component along Parkside. City GIS characterizes the relevant street segment as Concord-owned/jurisdictional with sidewalks on both sides.

Again, the precise edge remains a boundary question, not a reason to classify an identified municipal sidewalk as nonpublic.

docs.title: C. Library public entrance and immediate east-side pedestrian approach
docs.text:
Classification: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — STRONGLY SUPPORTED UNDER PRIGMORE; FIELD/PHYSICAL VERIFICATION PENDING.

This area is the closest Concord analogue to the Redding entry/exit area:

  • it is the City's mapped Public Entrance to the library;
  • it is connected to publicly designated parking and Civic Center pedestrian circulation;
  • it is government-owned property serving a public library;
  • it is integrated with adjacent government buildings rather than isolated from public civic space;
  • current sources show ordinary open public access during staffed hours.

The Concord documentary record is somewhat less complete than the Redding record concerning congregation features. No current official source reviewed yet establishes benches, newspaper racks, tables, plaza seating, or a comparable invitation to linger immediately outside the Concord entrance.

That missing fact weakens the comparison somewhat but does not erase the strong similarity in public-access, library-entry, and civic-campus function.

docs.title: D. Pedestrian walkway connecting the library entrance with the Civic Center / front parking circulation
docs.text:
Classification: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — STRONGLY SUPPORTED; EXACT SUBAREA BOUNDARIES AND FIELD CONDITIONS PENDING.

The City map depicts this as ordinary pedestrian circulation linking a public entrance, bike rack, public parking, and multiple Civic Center buildings. Its use is therefore broader than a restricted employee/service walkway.

Under Prigmore, the relevant considerations strongly favor public-forum treatment: free public access, government ownership, public-building circulation, and functional similarity to civic walkways/sidewalks.

Field verification should still confirm that no gate, access-control sign, security boundary, or materially different physical condition exists today.

docs.title: E. Front public parking lot off Salvio Street
docs.text:
Classification: TRADITIONAL PUBLIC FORUM — STRONGLY SUPPORTED UNDER PRIGMORE FOR LAWFUL PEDESTRIAN EXPRESSIVE USE; SAFETY RESTRICTIONS REMAIN MATERIAL.

The front lot is expressly described by the Library as public parking and sits immediately at the library/Civic Center frontage. This is materially similar to the adjacent library parking lot included in the forum defined in Prigmore.

The important limitation is activity-specific. Prigmore itself upheld Redding's prohibition on placing leaflets on vehicles in the parking lot based on the safety/property rationale before the court. Thus, traditional-public-forum status does not eliminate content-neutral vehicle, traffic, obstruction, or pedestrian-safety rules.

For the project's standing scenario — peaceful recording/observation without blocking traffic, interfering with vehicles, or approaching people — the forum comparison is substantially stronger than for an activity occurring in travel lanes or involving parked vehicles themselves.

docs.title: F. Rear public parking lot off Parkside Drive / Civic Center lot
docs.text:
Classification: PRIGMORE ANALOGY SUBSTANTIAL; FINAL TRADITIONAL-PUBLIC-FORUM CLASSIFICATION REMAINS PENDING PHYSICAL/USE VERIFICATION.

Supporting factors:

  • the Library expressly describes the lot as public parking for the branch;
  • it is adjacent to the library and Civic Center;
  • the adjoining parcel is City-owned in current GIS;
  • the City map depicts the lot as part of public Civic Center circulation;
  • access appears ordinary and unrestricted in the documentary record.

Reasons for retaining a narrower status than the front lot/entrance:

  • the rear lot is a large shared Civic Center parking facility, not simply the small lot immediately associated with the library entrance;
  • current documentary sources do not establish congregation/rest features there;
  • current evidence does not establish a historic expressive-use pattern;
  • exact pedestrian circulation, signage, and any reserved/restricted portions should be field-verified.

Prigmore prevents treating the lot as nonpublic merely because it is used for parking, but it also does not compel a categorical result for every government parking facility.

docs.title: G. Vehicle drive aisles / driveway throats
docs.text:
Classification: NO SEPARATE BROAD SPEECH-ZONE CONCLUSION; STRONG SAFETY/TRAFFIC INTERESTS APPLY.

These areas are primarily for moving vehicles. Any expressive right associated with the surrounding forum does not create a right to obstruct or occupy travel lanes in a manner incompatible with traffic safety.

Under the project's standing scenario, the relevant conduct occurs from lawful pedestrian positions and does not block entrances, traffic, or vehicle circulation.

docs.title: 4. Prigmore factor matrix
docs.text: Factor Concord documentary record Effect Government ownership Library and adjoining Civic Center parcels returned with City owner fields; library building ownership independently documented Strongly favors forum comparison Free public access Branch public parking; mapped public entrance; no exterior reservation/admission condition located Strongly favors Public thoroughfare / circulation City sidewalks; mapped pedestrian routes; bike rack; downtown-to-Civic-Center walking/bikeway planning Strongly favors sidewalks/approaches Public-library function Active public library Favors under Prigmore Adjacent public buildings Integrated Concord Civic Center Favors Entry-side congregation features Public entrance/circulation verified; benches/newspaper rack/plaza seating not yet verified Mixed / field verification needed Clear physical boundaries Parcel and assessor geometry developed; exact ROW edge still unresolved Limits boundary precision, not all forum analysis Traditional/historic expressive use Not established Neutral / unresolved Parking function Two public lots; front lot closely associated with library; rear lot shared Civic Center use Front lot stronger; rear lot requires more verification Safety/traffic interest Parking and drive aisles necessarily involve vehicles Supports reasonable content-neutral safety restrictions

docs.title: 5. Recording-specific consequence
docs.text:
This note classifies forums; it does not rely on Prigmore as a stand-alone right-to-record case. Prigmore concerned leafleting.

Where an exterior area is a traditional public forum, a restriction on protected expressive activity is subject to traditional-public-forum standards, including the applicable content-based or content-neutral/time-place-manner analysis. Whether a particular recording restriction is valid still requires the separate recording/photography doctrine and the actual restriction asserted.

Accordingly, the project should not write:

Prigmore says you may film in this parking lot.

The supported formulation is:

Prigmore strongly supports traditional-public-forum treatment for specified Concord exterior areas; any restriction on peaceful recording there must then be analyzed under the applicable First Amendment/California speech and recording doctrines rather than assumed valid merely because the activity occurs on library grounds.

docs.text: Concord exterior area Current status Salvio municipal sidewalk / ROW TPF — HIGH CONFIDENCE; exact edge pending Parkside municipal sidewalk / ROW TPF — HIGH CONFIDENCE; exact edge pending Public entrance / immediate east approach TPF — STRONGLY SUPPORTED; field verification pending Civic Center/library connective pedestrian walkway TPF — STRONGLY SUPPORTED; exact subarea/field verification pending Front Salvio public lot TPF — STRONGLY SUPPORTED under Prigmore; safety rules remain applicable Rear Parkside/Civic Center public lot PRIGMORE-ANALOGY-SUBSTANTIAL; final classification pending Vehicle travel lanes / driveway throats No independent broad speech-zone conclusion; safety controls substantial

docs.title: 7. Remaining verification before finalizing the branch exterior
docs.text:
The exterior analysis no longer requires waiting for every old deed before useful forum conclusions can be drawn. The highest-value remaining work is now factual:

  • field or equally reliable current imagery verification of the entrance, benches/seating, newspaper racks, tables, plaza/forecourt characteristics, and pedestrian congregation space;
  • current signs governing parking, library grounds, loitering, solicitation, photography, or reserved areas;
  • identification of any reserved/employee-only portions of the rear lot;
  • exact ROW edge only where a few feet of location would change the legal classification or enforcement analysis;
  • any current City/County agreement that materially changes exterior operational control.

Until those checks are complete, retain the confidence qualifiers above rather than assigning the whole exterior one categorical label.

docs.title: Concord Library — Exterior / Prigmore Working Worksheet
docs.text:
Facility: Concord Library, 2900 Salvio Street, Concord, CA 94519 Prepared: 2026-09-22 Status: DOCTRINAL-WORKSHEET / FINAL-AREA-CLASSIFICATION-PENDING

This worksheet applies the property-specific method reflected in Prigmore v. City of Redding, 211 Cal.App.4th 1322 (2012), to the currently known Concord facts. It is intentionally preliminary. It does not assign one forum status to the entire Library/Civic Center exterior.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
For each exterior area, keep separate:

  1. ownership / parcel;
  2. operational control;
  3. public ROW or easement status;
  4. ordinary public access and use;
  5. physical design and relationship to the facility;
  6. congregation / passage features;
  7. posted restrictions and actual practice;
  8. the exact expressive activity at issue;
  9. forum classification and applicable restriction standard.

A fact established for one area does not automatically carry into another.

docs.title: Area 1 — Salvio Street public sidewalk / street frontage
Established or strongly supported facts
docs.text:
• City Road Centerlines OBJECTID 199013 identifies the relevant Salvio segment with street owner and jurisdiction Concord.
  • The returned segment reports sidewalks Yes / Yes.
  • The facility address 2900 falls in the segment's right-side address range.
  • Assessor Book 111 Page 24 depicts Salvio along the Library frontage and shows dimension callouts around the street centerline.
  • City engineering materials treat sidewalks/driveways as ordinary public-ROW work items.

docs.title: Unresolved
docs.text:
• exact surveyed ROW edge;
  • exact point where the public sidewalk/ROW ends and APN 111-240-006 begins;
  • any unusual dedication/easement affecting the frontage;
  • current signs or site-specific restrictions.

docs.title: Working doctrine posture
docs.text:
If a particular segment is confirmed to be an ordinary municipal sidewalk within the public street ROW, ordinary traditional-public-forum sidewalk doctrine becomes the principal rule. Prigmore then supplies useful library-site context but is not necessary to transform an ordinary public sidewalk into a forum.

Current status: STRONGLY-SUPPORTED-PUBLIC-STREET-CONTEXT / EXACT-STRIP-MAPPING-PENDING.

docs.title: Established or strongly supported facts
docs.text:
• CCCL expressly describes a free public front parking lot serving the branch.
  • Published inventory: 3 accessible, 3 short-term/30-minute, 15 regular spaces.
  • The lot is part of the public-facing approach to the Library.
  • Current GIS/assessor evidence resolves the Library parcel and adjacent Civic Center parcel, but the exact parking-lot overlay has not yet been completed with current survey/ROW evidence.

docs.title: Prigmore-relevant similarities
docs.text:
• government/library setting;
  • public parking use;
  • physical relationship to library access;
  • likely pedestrian movement between parking and entrance.

docs.title: Material unknowns
docs.text:
• exact parcel/control of each portion of the lot/driveway;
  • whether the lot functions as a pedestrian/congregation area or primarily vehicle storage/circulation;
  • benches, newspaper racks, plazas, shade/seating, or other congregation features;
  • customary nonparking public use;
  • signs or restrictions;
  • exact relationship between the lot and public sidewalk/entry path.

docs.title: Working doctrine posture
docs.text:
Prigmore is a strong comparator but does not create a categorical rule that all public-library parking lots are traditional public forums.

Current status: PRIGMORE-COMPARATOR-STRONG / CLASSIFICATION-UNRESOLVED.

docs.title: Area 3 — Main entrance / forecourt / pedestrian approach
Established or strongly supported facts
docs.text:
• ordinary patrons use this area to enter and leave the Library during staffed hours;
  • City/Civic Center mapping confirms the Library's physical relationship to Salvio, Parkside, parking, and Civic Center circulation;
  • the Library parcel is City-owned in current GIS and labeled LIBRARY on the assessor sheet.

docs.title: Prigmore-relevant similarities
docs.text: The entry/exit area in Prigmore received separate area-specific analysis. For Concord, the entrance/forecourt is therefore a distinct candidate forum area rather than merely an extension of the ordinary interior.

docs.title: Material unknowns
docs.text:
• exact physical dimensions/layout;
  • whether the approach lies wholly within APN 111-240-006 or partly within ROW/shared Civic Center space;
  • benches/seating or congregation features;
  • customary waiting, meeting, information-distribution, or community use;
  • signs and circulation/security rules;
  • whether the area functions principally as passage or also as an intentionally/publicly used gathering space.

docs.title: Working doctrine posture
docs.text:
No classification yet. The combination of boundary evidence and physical/site-use facts is outcome-relevant.

Current status: DISTINCT-AREA-IDENTIFIED / PRIGMORE-ANALYSIS-PENDING.

docs.title: Area 4 — Rear Parkside / Civic Center parking area
Established or strongly supported facts
docs.text:
• CCCL describes a larger free public rear lot behind the Library, adjacent to the Civic Center, with 3 accessible and approximately 70+ regular spaces.
  • the City Civic Center map labels nearby parking as public.
  • adjoining APN 111-240-014 is returned by current City GIS with owner field CONCORD CITY OF and approximately 3.68 acres.
  • Parkside OBJECTID 199079 is returned as Concord-owned/jurisdictional with sidewalks Yes/Yes and an address range including 1950 Parkside.

docs.title: Material unknowns
docs.text:
• which portions of the rear parking/circulation area fall within APN 111-240-014, the Library parcel, ROW, or another interest;
  • current operational controller of the shared lot;
  • ordinary nonparking use and congregation features;
  • signs/restrictions;
  • exact pedestrian route between rear parking, Civic Center buildings, Library entrance, and public sidewalks.

docs.title: Working doctrine posture
docs.text:
The rear lot must be analyzed separately from the smaller front Library lot. Its Civic Center/shared-campus function may produce a materially different factual record even though both are publicly described parking.

Current status: PUBLIC-PARKING-USE-VERIFIED / CONTROL-AND-FORUM-UNRESOLVED.

docs.title: Area 5 — Parkside sidewalk / shared Civic Center pedestrian circulation
Established or strongly supported facts
docs.text:
• current City Road Centerline attributes identify the relevant Parkside segment as Concord-owned/jurisdictional and report sidewalks on both sides;
  • APN 111-240-014 is the current GIS candidate immediately adjoining the Library parcel and is City-owned in the returned data;
  • City materials identify 1950 Parkside as a Civic Center/Permit Center address.

docs.title: Unresolved
docs.text:
• exact legal ROW edge;
  • whether a particular path is ordinary street sidewalk, internal Civic Center walkway, or another access interest;
  • public-access easements/dedications;
  • physical continuity and signage;
  • customary use.

docs.title: Working doctrine posture
docs.text:
Do not classify all visible pavement as one sidewalk. A confirmed municipal ROW sidewalk and an internal Civic Center walkway may require different forum analysis despite appearing continuous on the ground.

Current status: MIXED-AREA-RISK-IDENTIFIED / EXACT-AREA-MAPPING-PENDING.

docs.title: Evidence gaps that actually matter to classification
docs.text:
The remaining boundary work is no longer an abstract title exercise. The highest-value missing facts are the ones that distinguish:

  • ordinary municipal sidewalk from parcel-internal walkway;
  • Library parcel from shared Civic Center parcel;
  • public street ROW from parking/driveway/forecourt;
  • Library-controlled parking from Civic Center-controlled/shared parking;
  • passage-only space from an area designed or customarily used for congregation/expression.

Current City Engineering/ROW records can resolve much of the first three categories. A later field/site-layout verification can resolve physical design, signs, seating, and customary-use observations.

docs.title: Provisional doctrinal order after boundary acquisition
docs.text:
Once current ROW/control evidence is obtained, analyze in this order:

  1. confirmed Salvio/Parkside municipal sidewalks — ordinary public-sidewalk / traditional-public-forum doctrine;
  2. entrance/forecourt — area-specific Prigmore comparison;
  3. front parking lot — property-specific Prigmore comparison;
  4. rear Civic Center parking/circulation — separate Prigmore / government-campus analysis based on its own control/use record;
  5. internal pedestrian paths — classify individually based on ownership/control, access, purpose, design, and practice.

No current evidence supports collapsing these into one exterior forum classification.

docs.title: Concord Library — Recorded-Map / Instrument Checkpoint
docs.text:
Facility: Concord Library, 2900 Salvio Street, Concord, CA 94519 Prepared: 2026-09-22 Status: AUTOMATED-PUBLIC-RECORD-DISCOVERY-SUBSTANTIALLY-EXHAUSTED / MANUAL-ROW-RECORD-STAGE

This checkpoint consolidates the deeper recorded-map and recorded-instrument work performed after Facility Prep resolved current APN 111-240-006, adjoining City parcel 111-240-014, assessor Book 111 Page 24, and City Road Centerline evidence.

docs.title: 1. Assessor annotation → historical survey
docs.text:
The assessor-map annotation 7 LSM 51 was resolved through Contra Costa County Public Works' public Laserfiche Recorded Maps search to:

docs/research/evidence/concord-library/record-of-survey-7LSM51-review-2026-09-22.md

The survey is historical geometry/provenance evidence. It predates the present Library and current parcel configuration and is not treated as the modern legal boundary.

docs.title: 2. APN-wide Public Works recorded-map search
docs.text:
Facility Prep separately searched the Public Works Recorded Maps index using APN metadata 111 24 rather than relying only on the single annotation printed on the assessor sheet.

Result:

This means the current public Recorded Maps index exposed no additional map carrying the exact APN metadata 111 24. It does not prove that no other recorded map, dedication, survey, engineering plan, deed, or easement affects the property.

docs.title: 4. Official Records identifiers
docs.text:
The assessor sheet and 7LSM51 supplied three Official Records references. Contra Costa RecorderWorks recognizes all three through its public Old Book workflow:

Reference Public RecorderWorks document ID Current state 3356 OR 502 16109166 identifier resolved; image not viewable online; manual copy required 636 OR 390 12566187 identifier resolved; image not viewable online; manual copy required 454 OR 154 12286714 identifier resolved; image not viewable online; manual copy required

Canonical acquisition-target note:

docs/research/evidence/concord-library/manual-record-acquisition-targets-2026-09-22.md

The automated acquisition stop rule applies. No paid copy transaction, authentication bypass, CAPTCHA bypass, or alternate image route was attempted.

docs.title: 5. Current conclusion
docs.text:
The useful anonymous/publicly machine-readable County record path has now been pushed substantially beyond the original APN lookup:

address → current APN/geometry → assessor sheet → assessor annotation → historical record of survey → public Recorded Maps APN search → road-vicinity cross-check → exact Official Records identifiers

No clearly relevant later/current Public Works recorded map surfaced through the tested APN or road-vicinity searches. The remaining exact modern boundary questions should therefore move to targeted acquisition, not increasingly broad blind automation.

The decisive remaining targets are:

  1. ordinary copies of 3356 OR 502 and 636 OR 390 if their contents are needed to interpret the present parcel chain;
  2. City of Concord Engineering records fixing the current Salvio Street and Parkside Drive public-right-of-way edges adjacent to APNs 111-240-006 and 111-240-014;
  3. any current dedication/easement/ROW plan referenced by those engineering records;
  4. any City/County agreement that allocates operational control of the Library exterior, Civic Center parking, entrance walks, or shared circulation differently from fee ownership.

Until those records are obtained, current parcel ownership/control context is strongly developed, but the exact legal ROW edge remains unresolved.

docs.title: 6. Facility Prep lesson
docs.text:
For future facilities, an APN-wide or road-vicinity recorded-map search should be used as a discovery cross-check, not as an invitation to follow every same-street result. A returned map with mismatched parcel/APN metadata remains an unpromoted lead unless geometry or another official source ties it to the facility.

When exact known instrument identifiers have been resolved and no clearly relevant later map appears in the public index, Facility Prep should stop broad automated searching and generate a targeted custodian/engineering acquisition request.

docs.title: Acquisition
docs.text:
Facility Prep resolved the assessor-map annotation 7 LSM 51 through the County Public Works Recorded Maps search. The public search returned entry 126622, name 7LSM51, record type Record of Survey Map, one imaged page, APN metadata 111 24, and a recording date of September 24, 1940.

The entry is an imaged Laserfiche document rather than an electronic PDF. The ordinary anonymous ElectronicFile.aspx route therefore reports an empty electronic file, but the public document viewer exposes the scanned page. Facility Prep reproduced that ordinary public rendering route and preserved a rendered page in the review artifact.

No authentication, CAPTCHA bypass, access-control bypass, paid transaction, or nonpublic endpoint was used.

docs.title: Human-reviewed map observations
docs.text:
The rendered survey sheet states that it depicts:

A portion of the property of the Concord Home Acres Company.

It identifies that company's deed as Book 454 of Official Records, Page 154, and states that the property is located in Rancho Monte del Diablo.

The survey further states that the course of Salvio Street, as extended, was taken as the basis for bearings. The drawing depicts a 10.60-acre tract and shows:

  • the Sacramento Northern Railway along the west side;
  • Willow Pass Road along the south side, with directional notes toward Concord and Pittsburg;
  • a line labeled as the centerline/course of Salvio Street as extended;
  • iron-bar and iron-pipe monument references;
  • survey bearings and distances around the depicted tract.

The sheet is dated June 1940 and shows County approval/filing in September 1940.

docs.title: What this record supports
docs.text:
7LSM51 is verified historical survey evidence tied by County metadata to assessor Book 111 Page 24. It provides a contemporaneous surveyed relationship among the larger historical tract, Salvio Street, Willow Pass Road, and the former Sacramento Northern Railway corridor.

It also supplies a new underlying-record lead: 454 OR 154.

docs.title: What this record does not yet establish
docs.text:
The survey predates the present Concord Library building, the current parcel configuration, and the assessor-sheet revision that created parcels 013 and 014 in 1996. It therefore is not treated as the current legal boundary of APN 111-240-006 or 111-240-014.

The sheet does not by itself establish:

  • the current Salvio Street right-of-way edge at the library;
  • the current Parkside Drive right-of-way edge;
  • title to a particular modern sidewalk strip;
  • the boundaries of the current front or rear parking areas;
  • current easements, dedications, or access rights;
  • current City/County operational-control allocation;
  • constitutional forum status.

Those questions remain dependent on later/current recorded maps, engineering/dedication material, title/control records, and physical-area overlay.

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text:
1. Resolve Book 454 OR Page 154 through the County Recorder index and determine whether the underlying instrument is publicly viewable or requires manual copy acquisition.
  2. Search the County Public Works Recorded Maps collection by APN/assessor-book reference 111 24, not merely by the single assessor annotation, to identify later subdivision, parcel-map, survey, or corner-record material affecting the current parcels.
  3. Prioritize later/current records over this 1940 survey when determining modern parcel and right-of-way edges.
  4. Preserve 7LSM51 as historical geometry/provenance evidence even if later records supersede its practical boundary value.

docs.text:
Concord Police Department Policy Manual:

https://www.cityofconcord.org/1196/Department-Policy-Manual

Policy 423, Public Recording of Law Enforcement Activity, is a material facility-specific source.

Current verified policy propositions include:

docs.title: Audio privacy — Penal Code § 632
docs.text:
Penal Code § 632 applies to intentional recording/eavesdropping of a confidential communication without consent of all parties. The statutory definition excludes circumstances in which parties may reasonably expect the communication to be overheard or recorded.

Under Flanagan v. Flanagan, 27 Cal.4th 766 (2002), the confidentiality test is whether a party has an objectively reasonable expectation that the conversation is not being overheard or recorded.

This means neither of the following is safe as a categorical field rule:

  • public police lobby = all audio may always be recorded; or
  • police conversation = automatically confidential.

The actual acoustic/physical setting, privacy measures, participants and circumstances matter.

The local Wilson case supplies a concrete lobby application: at the pleading stage, the court rejected a § 632 theory where the plaintiff alleged that various members of the public were present and could hear the conversations.

Current audio posture:

§632-FACT-SPECIFIC / FLANAGAN-OBJECTIVE-CONFIDENTIALITY-TEST / WILSON-PUBLIC-LOBBY-APPLICATION-PERSUASIVE-ONLY

docs.title: Closest local officer-recording comparator — Wilson
docs.text:
Wilson v. County of Contra Costa, No. 14-cv-03491-SI (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2015), involved recording officers in the public lobby of the Contra Costa County Sheriff's Office.

At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, the Northern District of California held that the plaintiff had sufficiently pleaded a First Amendment retaliation claim based on recording officers performing their duties in that public lobby and declined to grant qualified immunity on the facts alleged. The court relied on Fordyce's First Amendment right to film matters of public interest.

Limits are substantial:

  • federal district court, not binding Ninth Circuit precedent;
  • pleading-stage allegations assumed true;
  • no formal lobby public-forum classification;
  • no neutral preexisting lobby-wide anti-recording rule adjudicated;
  • no final merits adjudication after discovery/trial; the case later ended after failure-to-prosecute proceedings.

Status:

HIGHLY-RELEVANT-LOCAL-DISTRICT-COURT-COMPARATOR / PLEADING-STAGE / NONBINDING / NO-FINAL-MERITS-ADJUDICATION

docs.title: Penal Code § 602.1 — important constitutional-activity carveout
docs.text:
Section 602.1(b) does not reduce a public-agency trespass/interference case to asked to leave + refused.

Its public-agency offense requires intentional interference with lawful agency business by obstructing or intimidating employees/persons carrying on or transacting business, followed by refusal after a qualifying request.

Current § 602.1(d)(2) adds a critical limitation:

This section shall not apply to a person on the premises engaging in activities protected by the California Constitution or United States Constitution.

That means the analysis must first identify whether the activity at issue is constitutionally protected rather than assuming § 602.1 applies merely because an employee objects to recording.

But the carveout is not immunity for additional unprotected conduct. Actual obstruction, intimidation, threats, interference or other independent unlawful behavior must be analyzed separately. Section 602.1(e) also preserves the possible application of other law.

For Sweep 010 the removal chain is therefore:

exact subarea + lawful presence → actual activity → is that activity constitutionally protected? → §602.1(d)(2) if yes → any additional obstruction/intimidation conduct? → qualifying request/authority → any other applicable trespass or criminal provision

docs.title: Important Concord-specific distinction
docs.text:
This is not presently an ordinary police lobby + published no-recording rule case.

CPD Policy 423 affirmatively recognizes lawful recording of officers performing official duties. Wilson supplies a highly relevant local officer-recording comparator, and § 148(g) says recording alone does not itself establish § 148(a), reasonable suspicion or probable cause within its location conditions.

Therefore a purpose-limited/nonpublic federal forum classification does not itself answer whether a specific recording is allowed or prohibited.

The working chain is:

defined lobby subarea → lawful presence → subject/activity being recorded → forum/access anchor + activity-specific anchor → Policy 423 + §148(g) + Wilson → actual narrower rule → privacy/§632/security facts → restriction standard → §602.1 constitutional carveout/elements → removal/trespass analysis

docs.title: Methodological consequence
docs.text:
Sweep 010 is now strongly supporting a two-anchor method for facilities in which forum status and a specific expressive activity have different best authorities:

  • forum/access anchor: cases such as Cornelius / Sammartano plus facility-purpose and access facts;
  • activity anchor: cases/statutes/policies addressing the actual activity, such as Fordyce, § 148(g), CPD Policy 423 and Wilson for recording officers.

Forum classification determines the constitutional standard applicable to a restriction. It does not prove that a restriction exists, and it does not by itself resolve whether the specific activity is protected.

docs.title: Concord Police Headquarters — Interior Forum / Recording Authority Review
docs.text: Reviewed: 2026-09-22 Question: What forum framework best fits the ordinary public-facing Concord Police lobby, and what does that classification establish about recording?

docs.title: Current bottom line
docs.text:
No published Ninth Circuit or California appellate decision specifically adjudicating an ordinary patron's right to film inside a California police-station lobby was located in this review.

The current federal record nevertheless strongly supports treating the ordinary police service lobby / front-counter channel as a purpose-limited governmental interior rather than a traditional or designated public forum.

Working federal posture:

FEDERAL LIMITED/NONPUBLIC-FORUM STANDARD STRONGLY SUPPORTED / NO PUBLISHED NINTH-CIRCUIT POLICE-LOBBY FILMING HOLDING LOCATED

For the practical restriction standard relevant here, both a limited public forum and a nonpublic forum generally permit restrictions that are reasonable in light of the forum's purpose and viewpoint neutral. The project should not overstate the exact label where the controlling authority does not require that distinction to answer the specific restriction question.

But forum classification is only one layer. A newly located Northern District of California case involving recording officers in the public lobby of the Contra Costa County Sheriff's Office materially strengthens the activity-specific recording side of the analysis. Wilson v. County of Contra Costa, No. 14-cv-03491-SI (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2015), allowed a First Amendment retaliation claim based on recording officers in that public sheriff's lobby to proceed at the pleading stage and declined to grant qualified immunity on the facts alleged.

California Constitution article I, § 2(a) remains separately unresolved for this particular interior.

docs.title: Cornelius / Perry
docs.text: The forum must be defined by the access sought. Government ownership and public entry for official business do not by themselves create a traditional or designated public forum. Government may reserve property for its intended use, subject to the constitutional rules applicable to the forum it has actually created.

docs.title: Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002)
docs.text:
Sammartano remains the strongest published Ninth Circuit government-building comparator located for the threshold classification issue.

The Ninth Circuit treated the judicial/municipal complex there as a nonpublic forum even though members of the public entered to conduct public business. The decision reinforces that:

  • public access for governmental transactions is not itself forum creation;
  • purpose, location, governmental intent, and actual use matter;
  • restrictions in a nonpublic forum must remain reasonable in light of the forum purpose and viewpoint neutral;
  • asserted safety/order interests still require a real relationship to the restriction rather than functioning as a categorical constitutional exemption.

A police headquarters has materially stronger privacy, witness/victim, and operational-security concerns than the ordinary administrative parts of the Sammartano complex, while also having a clearly opened front-counter service function. Those differences belong in the reasonableness/application analysis rather than being used to skip forum analysis.

docs.title: Askins v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)
docs.text:
Askins recognizes First Amendment protection for photography/recording of matters of public interest and emphasizes that the legality of a restriction depends on the nature of the location and the actual governmental rule/justification.

Its actual dispute concerned public/outdoor areas around ports of entry. It does not establish a right to record in every government interior.

docs.title: Serrano v. Sanders, No. 23-35437 (9th Cir. May 16, 2024)
docs.text:
The Ninth Circuit stated that the clearly established right to record law-enforcement officers performing official duties in public places necessarily includes peaceful observation from a non-obstructive position.

Important limit: Serrano is an unpublished memorandum disposition and is not precedent except as allowed by Ninth Circuit Rule 36-3. It involved a public scene rather than a police lobby.

docs.title: Closest local activity comparator — Wilson v. County of Contra Costa
Wilson v. County of Contra Costa, No. 14-cv-03491-SI (N.D. Cal. May 6, 2015)
docs.text:
Wilson is unusually important because it arose in the same county and involved the public lobby of the Contra Costa County Sheriff's Office.

The amended complaint alleged that the plaintiff entered the 24-hour sheriff's-office lobby for police/public-service purposes, used an audio recorder that was in plain view, recorded officers performing their duties in the public lobby, and was seized/arrested when an officer noticed the recording.

At the Rule 12(b)(6) stage, Judge Susan Illston held that the plaintiff had stated a First Amendment retaliation claim against the officer. The court relied on Fordyce's First Amendment right to film matters of public interest and treated the allegation that officers were being recorded while performing duties in the public lobby as sufficient protected-activity pleading for the retaliation claim.

The court also declined to grant qualified immunity on the pleaded facts.

docs.title: Penal Code § 632 in Wilson
docs.text:
Defendants argued that the audio recording was unlawful because it captured a confidential communication without consent. The court rejected that theory at the pleading stage because the amended complaint alleged that various members of the public were present in the area and could hear the conversations. On those allegations, defendants had not established an objectively reasonable expectation that the conversation was not being overheard or recorded.

This provides a highly useful California-specific caution:

police lobby + audio recording ≠ automatically confidential communication under §632

but it does not establish the opposite categorical rule. A separated interview, victim report, acoustically isolated counter, or conversation surrounded by privacy measures may present materially different facts.

docs.title: Penal Code § 602.1(b) in Wilson
docs.text: The court also examined § 602.1(b). It did not hold that a public sheriff's lobby can never support a trespass/interference arrest. Instead, on the pleaded facts, the plaintiff alleged that officers physically prevented him from leaving and that he had difficulty standing/walking, so the court found the asserted probable-cause theory insufficient at that stage. The court expressly recognized that later evidence could potentially establish intentional interference and refusal.

docs.title: Procedural limitation
docs.text:
Wilson is not a binding or final merits precedent:

  • it is a federal district-court ruling;
  • the key decision was at the motion-to-dismiss stage;
  • it did not conduct a formal public-forum classification of the sheriff's lobby;
  • it did not adjudicate a neutral, preexisting lobby-wide anti-recording rule;
  • the case later ended after an order to show cause concerning failure to prosecute, rather than a final trial/summary-judgment merits decision on the surviving recording claim.

Approved use:

HIGHLY-RELEVANT-LOCAL-DISTRICT-COURT-COMPARATOR / PLEADING-STAGE / NONBINDING / NO-FINAL-MERITS-ADJUDICATION

Detailed note:

wilson-contra-costa-sheriff-lobby-2015.md

docs.title: Methodological consequence of Wilson
docs.text:
Wilson demonstrates why the project should not demand that one case answer both:

  1. what forum is this? and
  2. is this particular recording activity protected/restrictable?

For police/sheriff lobbies, a two-anchor method is stronger:

  • forum/access anchor — Cornelius, Sammartano, and facility-purpose/access evidence;
  • activity anchor — Fordyce, Penal Code § 148(g), agency recording policy, and close local cases such as Wilson.

docs.title: California statutory bridge — Penal Code § 148(g)
docs.text:
Penal Code § 148(g) provides that photographing or audio/video recording a public or peace officer, while the officer is in a public place or the recorder is in a place the recorder has the right to be, does not by itself constitute resisting/delaying/obstructing under § 148(a), and by itself does not create reasonable suspicion or probable cause.

For Sweep 010 this is significant because the statute is not written solely around traditional public forums. The alternative recorder is in a place ... [they have] the right to be makes lawful presence a central factual/legal question even in an interior.

But § 148(g) does not itself create a right of access, convert a lobby into a public forum, or invalidate every otherwise lawful recording restriction.

docs.title: Other police-station-specific persuasive authorities
docs.text: These authorities are useful because they confront police facilities more directly, but they do not control the Ninth Circuit/California result.

docs.title: People v. DeRossett, 237 Ill. App. 3d 315 (1992)
docs.text:
An Illinois appellate court treated an Urbana police-station lobby as a nonpublic forum. The defendant's conduct, however, involved an extended disruptive complaint and refusal to leave after being given a complaint form and other options. The case supports purpose-limited treatment of a police lobby but is a poor analogue for quiet, noninterfering recording standing alone.

Use:

POLICE-LOBBY FORUM/PURPOSE COMPARATOR / OUT-OF-STATE / DISRUPTIVE-CONDUCT FACTS

docs.title: First Defense Legal Aid v. City of Chicago, 319 F.3d 967 (7th Cir. 2003)
docs.text:
The Seventh Circuit stated that the interior of a police station is not a public forum while rejecting a claimed First Amendment access right for attorneys seeking witnesses/suspects inside police facilities.

Limit: the actual dispute involved access to witnesses/suspects and interrogation/internal station areas, not an ordinary visitor filming officers from a front public lobby.

Use:

GENERAL POLICE-INTERIOR PURPOSE/ACCESS CONTEXT — PERSUASIVE / NOT A LOBBY-FILMING HOLDING

docs.title: Hoffman v. Delgado, No. 23-13213 (11th Cir. Jan. 3, 2025)
docs.text:
In an unpublished Eleventh Circuit decision involving a police-department lobby and a city anti-recording ordinance, the court analyzed the lobby under the limited-public-forum standard because the parties proceeded on that characterization. The panel expressly observed that there were good arguments the lobby was actually a nonpublic forum.

The court upheld the challenged recording restriction as reasonable and viewpoint neutral on the pleaded facts, describing police lobbies as places generally used by people with legitimate public business to address public-safety needs rather than as places opened for discussion of all topics.

Limits:

  • unpublished/nonprecedential in the Eleventh Circuit;
  • not controlling here;
  • involved an actual anti-recording ordinance that Concord has not been shown to have;
  • therefore useful for police-lobby purpose/reasonableness comparison, not a direct answer to Concord Policy 423.

docs.title: Brandt v. Crone, No. 21-1093 (10th Cir. Mar. 28, 2022)
docs.text:
The Tenth Circuit confronted speech curtailed in a sheriff's-department lobby and held that the sheriff was entitled to qualified immunity because no Tenth Circuit/Supreme Court case or clear weight of authority had resolved the unique character of a sheriff's lobby and the First Amendment limits on responding to perceived disruption there.

Use:

SHERIFF-LOBBY UNCERTAINTY/QUALIFIED-IMMUNITY COMPARATOR / TENTH-CIRCUIT ONLY

It does not answer the California/Ninth Circuit question and predates the current Concord-specific combination of § 148(g) and Policy 423.

docs.title: Reyes v. City of New York litigation
docs.text:
The NYPD litigation is useful but must be separated into its components.

The federal district court initially found the plaintiff unlikely to succeed on his First Amendment theory at the preliminary-injunction stage but likely to succeed under New York state/city right-to-record statutes.

In 2025, the Second Circuit reserved decision and certified the New York statutory question rather than deciding the federal First Amendment merits.

In June 2026, the New York Court of Appeals held that New York's state and city right-to-record statutes do not extend into publicly accessible police-station lobbies. Its reasoning emphasized victim, witness, confidential-informant, undercover-officer, investigative, and safety concerns.

In August 2026, after receiving that answer, the Second Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction that had rested on the statutory theory and remanded. It expressly stated that it was expressing no view on the still-pending constitutional claim.

Limits:

  • the New York Court of Appeals holding construes New York statutes, not the First Amendment and not California law;
  • the Second Circuit's August 2026 disposition does not resolve the First Amendment merits;
  • the privacy/security considerations are useful factual reasoning, not controlling California doctrine;
  • Concord's Policy 423 and California Penal Code § 148(g) have materially different text and must be analyzed independently.

docs.title: Massimino v. Benoit, No. 25-1104 (2d Cir. Aug. 17, 2026)
docs.text:
The Second Circuit held that the First Amendment protects recording the publicly visible exterior of a police station from a public sidewalk. The court expressly distinguished that lawful exterior vantage from a claimed right of physical access inside the station.

The opinion is therefore especially useful for the exterior/interior boundary:

public sidewalk + publicly visible police-station exterior ≠ right to enter and record inside police station

It also cautions that even exterior recording can remain subject to properly tailored restrictions tied to concrete privacy or safety interests.

docs.title: The Concord-specific wrinkle — Policy 423
docs.text:
Concord is not presently an ordinary anti-recording-policy case.

CPD Policy 423 affirmatively states that the Department recognizes lawful public recording of officers performing official duties and directs members not to prohibit or intentionally interfere with such lawful recording. It permits recording from a public place or private property where the individual has the legal right to be present, subject to interference/safety limits.

Therefore the analysis cannot jump from:

police lobby is limited/nonpublic

to:

recording is prohibited.

Instead use:

defined lobby subarea + lawful presence + officer/public activity being recorded + Policy 423 + Penal Code § 148(g) + Wilson + any actual narrower lobby rule + privacy/security facts + forum restriction standard

A nonpublic-forum classification expands the government's regulatory authority; it does not manufacture a restriction that the agency has not adopted.

docs.title: Visitor/victim/witness privacy
docs.text:
Police-station-specific cases identify legitimate concerns that are substantially more acute than at many administrative buildings. Those interests include protecting:

  • victims reporting sensitive crimes;
  • witnesses and confidential informants;
  • undercover personnel;
  • juveniles;
  • confidential records and computer displays;
  • investigative/tactical information;
  • confidential or sensitive conversations.

Those interests can matter to whether a particular restriction is reasonable. They do not establish that every image or recording made while lawfully present in the lobby is categorically prohibited.

The project should preserve the subject/activity distinction:

recording an officer performing a public-facing official interaction ≠ deliberately capturing a victim's private report ≠ filming protected records/screens ≠ filming a secure operational area

Wilson adds a useful local audio-privacy comparator: where conversations in a sheriff's lobby were alleged to be audible to various members of the public, the court did not accept § 632 confidentiality as a basis for dismissing the recording claim. That result remains fact- and posture-specific.

docs.title: California Speech Clause
docs.text:
No sufficiently close published California appellate authority was located that classifies an ordinary police-station public lobby under California Constitution article I, § 2(a).

Current state-law posture:

CALIFORNIA SPEECH-CLAUSE CLASSIFICATION UNRESOLVED / NO CLOSE PUBLISHED CALIFORNIA POLICE-LOBBY CASE LOCATED

Do not copy the federal limited/nonpublic result automatically into the California column.

Current official sources
docs.text:
Primary current sources reviewed:

docs.title: CPD Policy 423 — Public Recording of Law Enforcement Activity
docs.text: Policy 423 is a highly material facility-specific source.

docs.title: Verified propositions
docs.text:
The current policy states that the Concord Police Department recognizes the right of persons to lawfully record department members performing official duties and directs members not to prohibit or intentionally interfere with lawful recordings.

It further provides that:

  • recording may occur from a public place or private property where the individual has the legal right to be present;
  • recording alone is distinct from actual interference;
  • interference may include tampering with a witness/suspect, inciting unlawful conduct, creating a clear officer-safety hazard through proximity, or being so close as to interfere with effective officer communication;
  • the individual may not present an undue safety risk;
  • when practicable, officers/supervisors should give clear warnings and directions explaining what conduct or location change is required before enforcement;
  • officers should exercise restraint and should not use highly discretionary arrests merely as a means of preventing the exercise of the right to record;
  • seizure or collection of cameras/media is separately constrained by law and policy.

Current status:

CURRENT-AGENCY-RECORDING-POLICY-VERIFIED

docs.title: Penal Code § 148(g)
docs.text:
California Penal Code § 148(g) states that taking a photograph or making an audio/video recording of a public or peace officer, while the officer is in a public place or the recorder is in a place the recorder has the right to be, does not by itself constitute resisting/delaying/obstructing under § 148(a), nor by itself create reasonable suspicion to detain or probable cause to arrest.

This is a highly important bridge for the lobby analysis, but it is not a lobby-access statute and does not itself decide forum classification.

The correct chain remains:

lawful presence / defined subarea → officer activity being recorded → actual conduct beyond recording → exact facility restriction, if any → forum/recording analysis → removal/trespass analysis

docs.title: Lawful-presence hinge
docs.text:
Policy 423 and § 148(g) both make the recorder's lawful location important.

For Police Headquarters, lawful presence may depend on facts including:

  • stated lobby hours;
  • whether the individual remains in the ordinary public lobby or crosses a controlled/restricted threshold;
  • whether the individual is using or seeking access to an opened public service/channel;
  • whether a valid, applicable rule limits conduct in that subarea;
  • whether actual conduct interferes with police services, witnesses, victims, or officer communication;
  • whether a direction to relocate or leave rests on a lawful rule and proper authority.

Do not collapse lawful presence into either government-owned property or door was unlocked.

docs.title: Narrow confidentiality / information-security policies
docs.text: The same current Department Policy Manual contains narrower rules that are relevant to the reasonableness and tailoring of restrictions around records, screens, conversations and secure workspaces.

docs.title: Policy 803 — Records Unit
docs.text:
Policy 803 requires case reports/files to be maintained securely, limits Records Unit access to authorized personnel, and calls for additional access controls for sensitive reports.

This is strong evidence that police records and records workspaces can present legitimate confidentiality/security interests. It is not a rule addressed to ordinary lobby patrons and does not itself prohibit a patron from operating a camera in the public lobby.

docs.title: Policy 806 — Protected Information
docs.text:
Policy 806 governs protected information and the Department's handling/access/security obligations for restricted law-enforcement data, including systems and information subject to legal or criminal-justice access controls.

Again, this can support protection of actual protected information, screens or systems. It should not be transformed into a building-wide public-camera rule.

docs.title: Policy 422 — Body-Worn Cameras
docs.text:
Policy 422 includes officer-side provisions for muting/stopping audio in specified private or confidential circumstances, including certain attorney, religious-advisor and physician communications in custody.

This is useful privacy-context evidence, not a patron-camera rule. It shows that the Department itself distinguishes between ordinary official activity and conversations for which confidentiality can become materially stronger.

Current distinction:

RECORDS/PROTECTED-INFORMATION/CONFIDENTIAL-CONVERSATION DUTIES VERIFIED / PUBLIC-LOBBY CAMERA PROHIBITION NOT CREATED BY THOSE POLICIES

docs.title: Current dedicated lobby-camera-rule search
docs.text:
Targeted review of current public-facing CPD pages, the Department Policy Manual, the Community Service Desk materials, the Records Unit materials, and City police-facility pages located Policy 423 but did not locate a separate published rule stating that ordinary members of the public are categorically prohibited from photography or audio/video recording throughout the Concord Police lobby.

Approved wording:

No dedicated public-facing Concord Police Headquarters lobby-wide ordinary-patron photography/videography prohibition was located in the online sources reviewed as of September 22, 2026.

Do not shorten this to Concord PD allows filming in the lobby or Concord PD has no camera rule.

The search finding does not establish:

  • absence of a current sign at the physical entrance/lobby;
  • absence of an internal security directive;
  • absence of narrower restrictions around records, victims, witnesses, interviews, computer screens, confidential conversations, evidence/property, or secure areas;
  • a right to record every person or item visible from the lobby;
  • a right to remain after a lawful exclusion based on independent grounds.

docs.title: Privacy and security are separate from the existence of a blanket ban
docs.text:
A police lobby can contain people and information with substantially different privacy/security interests than an ordinary administrative lobby. Potentially material subjects include:

  • victims reporting crimes;
  • witnesses and confidential sources;
  • juveniles;
  • undercover officers;
  • protected police records or screens;
  • tactical/security information;
  • conversations that may carry separate audio-privacy implications;
  • doors, access-control systems, and restricted operational areas.

Those interests may support reasonable, appropriately scoped restrictions depending on the forum, location, information exposed, and actual rule. They should not be treated as self-executing proof that every recording is forbidden.

The policy-manual review reinforces a useful narrower rule:

A confidentiality duty governing government-held information does not automatically become a reciprocal duty forbidding a member of the public from recording everything visible or audible from a place where that person is lawfully present.

If the government exposes genuinely protected information at a public counter, the specific information, applicable law, physical configuration and any valid protective restriction must still be identified.

docs.title: Public-service purpose
docs.text:
The City's Community Service Desk page expressly calls the desk the department's primary public-facing point of contact and locates it in the police lobby. Current services include assistance/information, non-emergency report intake, referrals, and administrative/front-counter services. The Records Unit also serves the public at the lobby counter.

The current Community Service Desk page expressly states that Concord Police no longer offers LiveScan or fingerprinting services. Stale City material referring to fingerprinting should not be used as a current lobby function.

This strongly establishes ordinary public access for defined police-service purposes during stated business hours. It does not establish that the lobby was intentionally opened for unrestricted expressive activity.

docs.title: Separate community-room channel
docs.text:
The Police Department advertises a public Community Meeting Room for nonprofit community groups discussing issues affecting quality of life in Concord, subject to contract/restrictions.

That channel should be analyzed separately from the lobby. A room intentionally opened for community discussion may have a different forum classification and restriction framework from the transactional public-service lobby immediately outside it.

docs.title: Local Comparator — Wilson v. County of Contra Costa (N.D. Cal. 2015)
docs.text:
Reviewed: 2026-09-22 Case: Wilson v. County of Contra Costa, No. 14-cv-03491-SI (N.D. Cal.) Material order: May 6, 2015, ECF No. 103 Court: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California

Primary accessible order:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/california/candce/3%3A2014cv03491/279647/103/

docs.title: Why this case matters unusually strongly to Sweep 010
docs.text:
This is not a generic out-of-circuit police-lobby analogue. It involved:

  • the Contra Costa County Sheriff's Office;
  • a public sheriff's-office lobby in the same county as Concord;
  • a person who entered for ordinary law-enforcement/public-service purposes;
  • an audio recorder allegedly in plain view;
  • officers allegedly performing official duties in the lobby;
  • an arrest allegedly triggered when an officer noticed the active recording;
  • California Penal Code §§ 602.1(b) and 632 arguments;
  • Ninth Circuit Fordyce recording doctrine.

It is therefore the closest California/local factual comparator located so far for the question of recording officers while lawfully present in a public law-enforcement lobby.

docs.title: What the May 6, 2015 order actually held
docs.text:
At the Rule 12(b)(6) pleading stage, Judge Susan Illston held that the plaintiff had stated a First Amendment retaliation claim against defendant Challand.

The amended complaint alleged that the plaintiff was recording police officers performing their duties in the public lobby of the CCCSO and that Challand seized/arrested him after noticing the recording.

The court relied on the Ninth Circuit's recognition in Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995), of a First Amendment right to film matters of public interest. Taking the pleaded facts as true, the court concluded that the retaliation claim could proceed.

The court also declined to grant qualified immunity at that stage. It reasoned that, on the allegations before it, defendants had not established that recording violated Penal Code § 632 and had not met their burden to show Challand was entitled to qualified immunity.

docs.title: California audio-recording issue
docs.text:
Defendants argued that the plaintiff's audio recording was unlawful under Penal Code § 632 because it captured a confidential communication without consent.

The court rejected that argument at the pleading stage because the amended complaint alleged that various members of the public were present in the area and could hear the conversations. On those allegations, defendants had not established an objectively reasonable expectation that the conversation was not being overheard or recorded.

This is highly relevant to a police-lobby field guide because it demonstrates that:

police lobby + audio recording ≠ automatically a confidential communication under §632

But the inverse is equally important:

Wilson ≠ every conversation in every police lobby is nonconfidential

The actual acoustic/physical setting, participants, subject matter, privacy measures, and objectively reasonable expectations remain fact-specific.

docs.title: Trespass / § 602.1(b) issue
docs.text:
The same order addressed Penal Code § 602.1(b), which concerns intentional interference with lawful business conducted by employees of a public agency open to the public, obstruction of persons attempting to carry on business, and refusal to leave after a qualifying request by a supervisor.

The court did not hold that a public sheriff's lobby can never support a § 602.1(b) arrest. Instead, it held that the pleaded facts made probable cause implausible at that stage because the plaintiff alleged that officers physically blocked him from leaving and that he had difficulty standing/walking.

The order expressly recognized that later evidence could potentially show intentional interference and refusal sufficient to support probable cause.

This fits the Field Guide's existing rule:

public access + recording ≠ immunity from independently satisfied trespass/interference elements

and equally:

request to leave + recording ≠ automatic satisfaction of §602.1(b).

docs.title: Procedural limitations
docs.text:
This case must be used carefully.

  1. It is a federal district-court decision, not binding Ninth Circuit precedent.
  2. The key First Amendment ruling occurred on a motion to dismiss, requiring the court to accept well-pleaded factual allegations as true and draw reasonable inferences for the plaintiff.
  3. The order did not perform a full public-forum classification of the sheriff's lobby.
  4. It did not adjudicate a neutral, preexisting lobby-wide anti-recording policy comparable to the ordinances/policies litigated in Hoffman or Reyes.
  5. The action did not proceed to a final merits judgment on the surviving recording claim. The docket shows a September 2015 order to show cause for failure to prosecute followed by judgment; the recording issue therefore was not finally resolved after discovery/trial.

Approved status:

HIGHLY-RELEVANT-LOCAL-DISTRICT-COURT-COMPARATOR / PLEADING-STAGE / NONBINDING / NO-FINAL-MERITS-ADJUDICATION

docs.title: Effect on the Concord Police analysis
docs.text:
Wilson materially strengthens the need to avoid this invalid shortcut:

police lobby is purpose-limited → therefore recording officers there is unprotected

At least one Northern District of California court, applying Ninth Circuit Fordyce doctrine to a Contra Costa public sheriff's lobby, allowed a First Amendment retaliation claim based on recording officers in that lobby to proceed and rejected qualified immunity at the pleading stage on the allegations presented.

That does not prove a categorical right to film everything in Concord Police Headquarters. Instead it supports the more exact analysis already emerging in Sweep 010:

lawful presence + public-facing officer activity + recording conduct + actual privacy/interference facts + actual facility rule + forum standard

For Concord specifically, the relevance is enhanced by CPD Policy 423 and Penal Code § 148(g), neither of which supports treating recording alone as obstruction.

docs.title: Registry / Field Guide consequence
docs.text:
For California police/sheriff lobbies, Wilson should be retained as a local persuasive anchor for officer-recording activity, separate from the forum-classification anchor.

That produces a useful two-anchor method:

  • forum/access anchor: controlling general forum doctrine such as Cornelius / Sammartano plus facility-purpose facts;
  • activity anchor: Fordyce, § 148(g), agency recording policy, and highly relevant local cases such as Wilson.

One precedent need not perform both jobs.

Both references were followed into Contra Costa Public Works' Recorded Maps index. The index independently returns matching Walnut Creek subdivision records; see recorded-map-review-2026-09-22.md.

These historical maps are chain/context evidence. They are not automatically the controlling modern parcel or ROW survey.

docs.title: Official Records notation
docs.text:
The sheet contains:

NE COR. LEASE 1217 OR 76

Its precise location/application is not clear enough from this review to assign the notation to parcel 39 or to infer a lease affecting the Library. It remains a record-reference lead only unless later evidence makes it outcome-determinative.

docs.title: Source disclaimer
docs.text:
The assessor sheet expressly states that it was prepared for assessment purposes only, assumes no liability for the accuracy of the delineated information, and warns that assessor parcels may not comply with local lot-split or building-site ordinances.

Accordingly:

  • the sheet strongly corroborates parcel identity and relative parcel arrangement;
  • it does not establish a survey-grade legal boundary;
  • it does not establish the exact North Broadway or Lincoln Avenue ROW edge;
  • it does not establish every easement or operational-control allocation;
  • it does not itself establish constitutional forum classification.

docs.title: Research consequence
docs.text: Unlike Concord, the Walnut Creek sheet immediately reveals a denser mixed civic geometry: the Library parcel directly adjoins a much larger City civic/park parcel and the City's historical design materials describe multiple entrances, outdoor plazas, surface parking, and an underground garage. The next legal analysis therefore must distinguish those specific exterior circulation areas rather than treat the 2.202-acre assessor parcel as one forum.

docs.title: Walnut Creek Library — Current Access / Control Review
docs.text: Review date: 2026-09-22 Purpose: Preserve current official-source facts that materially affect the area-specific forum/control analysis after the parcel pass.

docs.title: Library and parking
docs.text:
Official CCCL branch page:

https://ccclib.org/locations/26/

Current public facts reviewed:

Source:

https://www.walnutcreekca.gov/Home/Components/News/News/3966/17

The Broadway Garage is not treated as Library-property evidence merely because it is offered as nearby parking.

docs.title: Underground Library garage — current access facts
docs.text:
The current City Oak View rental page states that the Library underground parking is metered and remains accessible when the Library is closed for after-hours Oak View events.

Source:

https://www.walnutcreekartsrec.org/parks-facilities/facility-rentals/walnut-creek-library-oak-view-room

The City's sustainability materials independently identify public EV chargers at the Walnut Creek Library.

These facts strengthen the conclusion that the garage is intentionally open to members of the public rather than an employee-only/security garage. They still do not establish traditional-public-forum status. The garage remains an enclosed special-purpose parking/circulation facility requiring its own forum analysis.

Current City park directory:

docs.title: Oak View Room — current City control
docs.text:
Current City page:

https://www.walnutcreekartsrec.org/parks-facilities/facility-rentals/walnut-creek-library-oak-view-room

The City currently presents Oak View as a rentable second-floor room for meetings, corporate events, trainings, book signings, dinners and social events. Current features include:

  • separate after-hours entrance;

  • City Facility Rentals inquiry/application/contract process;
  • Library programming priority during Library operating hours;
  • social events limited to periods when the Library is closed;
  • underground parking accessible for after-hours events.

The City page also expressly states that smaller rooms such as Las Trampas are reserved directly through the Contra Costa County Library website and are not facilitated by the City rental office.

This is the strongest current public source located for present Oak View/Las Trampas booking control.

docs.title: Las Trampas control discrepancy
docs.text:
Current live CCCL room sources provide direct CCCL/online reservation for Las Trampas:

  • https://ccclib.org/las-trampas-room-policy/
  • https://ccclib.org/rooms/

Working treatment:

CURRENT-LIVE-SOURCES-SUPPORT-CCCL-LAS-TRAMPAS-BOOKING / OLDER-PDF-DISCREPANCY-PRESERVED

This does not necessarily establish every underlying property/control allocation. It does establish that the project's current-use description should follow the newer mutually corroborating live City/CCCL sources while preserving the older conflicting document for history and any later authority question.

docs.title: Current parking-system distinction
docs.text:
City downtown parking page:

https://www.walnutcreekca.gov/community/what-s-happening/parking-downtown

The City separately describes its three downtown City garages — Broadway, Lesher Center and South Locust — as 24-hour public garages. That page also notes public EV chargers for visitors to the Library and City Hall.

docs.title: Current engineering / ROW evidence family
docs.text:
Walnut Creek Encroachment Permits:

https://www.walnutcreekca.gov/government/public-works/engineering-services/encroachment-permits

https://www.walnutcreekca.gov/government/community-development-department/permits/building-permits/request-building-records

This identifies the next high-value current-boundary source family. If the exact Broadway/Lincoln/plaza/garage edge becomes outcome-determinative, current City building/engineering plans are a better next step than indiscriminately retrieving century-old subdivision maps.
